fact: The cortex's front quarter, home to the primary motor cortex that sends the corticospinal tract down to the spinal cord to move the body on command.

name: Parietal Lobe
fact: The cortex region the thalamus routes touch and body-position signals into — where a scattered sense of skin and joints becomes one coherent map of the body.

name: Temporal Lobe
fact: The lobe that houses the amygdala at its medial edge, and on its surface carries the language and emotion processing the amygdala's neighbourhood implies.

name: Occipital Lobe
fact: The cortex's rearmost lobe, reached by the optic radiation — a thick, myelinated white-matter tract that is vision's last stop before it becomes seeing.

name: Meninges
fact: Three membranes — dura, arachnoid, and pia mater — wrapped around the brain so it never has to touch bone directly.

name: Cerebrospinal Fluid
fact: A liter of fluid, mostly water, made inside the brain's own ventricles and replaced three to four times a day, floating the brain so its own weight can't crush it.

name: Blood-Brain Barrier
fact: Tight junctions between capillary cells, policed by astrocyte end-feet, that keep most of what's in the blood from ever reaching brain tissue.

name: Cranial Nerve
fact: One of 12 nerve pairs that connect straight to the brain rather than routing through the spinal cord — 10 of them plug directly into the brain stem.

name: Spinal Nerve
fact: One of 31 nerve pairs, one above each vertebra, each splitting into a sensory branch heading up and a motor branch heading back out to the body.

name: Peripheral Nervous System
fact: Every nerve outside the brain and spinal cord — built from the spinal nerves and cranial nerves that branch out to reach the entire body.

name: Central Nervous System
fact: The brain and spinal cord together — the two organs the rest of the nervous system exists to serve and connect to.

name: Nervous System
fact: Central plus peripheral: an organ system so extensive that all of one body's nerves, laid end to end, could circle the Earth two and a half times.

name: Autonomic Nervous System
fact: The involuntary branch of the peripheral nervous system, run by the hypothalamus, that keeps heart rate, digestion, and breathing going without being asked.

name: Sympathetic Nervous System
fact: The autonomic branch that emerges from the spinal cord's chest and abdominal segments to run the fight-or-flight response.

name: Parasympathetic Nervous System
fact: The autonomic branch carried chiefly by the cranial nerves, running the rest-and-digest state that undoes what sympathetic activation just did.

name: Short-Term Memory
fact: A held pattern of ongoing synaptic activity in the frontal lobe's prefrontal cortex, gone within seconds unless something consolidates it.

name: Long-Term Memory
fact: What a short-term memory becomes once the hippocampus finishes gradually reorganizing it into the cortex's own long-lived networks.

name: Neuroplasticity
fact: Cells that fire together wire together: a synapse used repeatedly recruits more receptors and strengthens, while an unused one fades.

name: Neurogenesis
fact: Neural stem cells dividing into working neurons — in adult mammals this still happens in the hippocampus, though how much it happens in adult humans is genuinely contested.

name: Hippopotamus
fact: Grazes grasslands by night and cools in the river by day; its skin oozes a reddish natural sunscreen.

name: Jackal
fact: Egypt's 'jackal' turned out on closer genetic inspection to be a distinct wolf species.

discovered.note: Genetic testing shows it's a distinct species, more closely related to the grey wolf than to the golden jackal.

name: Ibis
fact: A wading marsh bird, mummified by the millions in antiquity, that had vanished from Egypt by the 1850s.

name: Boat
fact: A hollowed or lashed hull, buoyant long before anyone added a sail or an engine.

name: Egyptian Cobra
fact: North Africa's hooding cobra, delivering venom by direct bite rather than a spray.

name: Heart
fact: Cardiac muscle so packed with mitochondria for oxygen that it almost never fatigues.

name: Ra
fact: Egyptian sun god who crossed the sky by day in one barque and the underworld by night in another.

name: Osiris
fact: Egyptian king of the dead, murdered by his brother Set and made whole again by Isis.

name: Isis
fact: Egypt's most powerful goddess -- a healer and magician who revived Osiris and raised Horus in hiding.

name: Horus
fact: Falcon-headed son of Isis and Osiris; lost his eye to Set in battle, and Thoth restored it.

name: Set
fact: Egyptian god of chaos, storms and the desert who murdered his own brother Osiris.

name: Anubis
fact: Jackal-headed god of embalming who weighed the hearts of the dead against Ma'at's feather.

name: Thoth
fact: Ibis-headed god of writing, wisdom and the moon, also shown as a baboon.

name: Bastet
fact: Cat goddess of Bubastis, daughter of Ra, whose annual festival drew crowds by the hundred thousand.

name: Sobek
fact: Crocodile god of the Nile's waters and marshes, merged with Ra as Sobek-Ra.

name: Hathor
fact: Cow goddess of music and love -- the gentle form the rampaging Sekhmet settled back into.

name: Sekhmet
fact: Lioness goddess of war and plague, daughter of Ra, sent to punish a rebellious humanity.

name: Nephthys
fact: Sister of Isis and wife of Set, who helped gather and mourn Osiris's dismembered body.

name: Nut
fact: Sky goddess arched above her husband Geb, mother of Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys.

name: Geb
fact: Earth god whose laughter was said to cause earthquakes; husband of the sky goddess Nut.

name: Shu
fact: God of air and light who forced Geb and Nut apart; fog and cloud were called his own bones.

name: Khnum
fact: Ram-headed god who fashioned human bodies and their life force from clay on a potter's wheel.

name: Ptah
fact: Creator god of Memphis, patron of craftsmen, said to have conceived the world in his heart.

name: Amun
fact: 'The Hidden One' -- a minor Theban god who rose to King of the Gods, merged with Ra as Amun-Ra.

name: Ma'at
fact: Goddess of truth and cosmic order; her ostrich feather was weighed against the hearts of the dead.

name: Khonsu
fact: Moon god of Thebes, son of Amun -- 'the Traveller,' credited with instant miraculous healings.

name: Taweret
fact: Hippopotamus goddess who protected women in childbirth and sided with Horus against Set.

name: Serket
fact: Scorpion goddess who guards against venom, carved guarding Tutankhamun's canopic shrine.

name: Wadjet
fact: Cobra goddess of Lower Egypt who became the uraeus, the rearing serpent on the pharaoh's crown.

name: Apep
fact: The 'World-Encircler' -- a giant serpent that attacked Ra's sun barque every night in the underworld.

name: Raven
fact: A kleptoparasite of wolves -- it trails packs to steal from their kills, and has led wolves to prey.

name: Spear
fact: The oldest wooden spears are 300,000 years old; stone, bronze and iron tips came later, bound on.

name: Hammer
fact: Perhaps the oldest tool with definite evidence: unhafted stone hammerstones date to 3.3 million years ago.

name: Rune
fact: Germanic letters cut in straight strokes -- a horizontal line would split the wood grain.

name: Odin
fact: Chief of the AEsir. His ravens report the world to him each day; he traded an eye for wisdom.

name: Thor
fact: Odin's son, god of thunder. Wields the hammer Mjolnir, gripped only with his iron gloves.

name: Loki
fact: Shapeshifting trickster. As a mare he bore Sleipnir; he also fathered the wolf Fenrir and a serpent.

name: Freyja
fact: Vanir goddess of love and war. Rides a cat-drawn chariot and owns the necklace Brisingamen.

name: Frigg
fact: Odin's wife. Orion's Belt was known in Scandinavia as 'Frigg's Distaff,' her spinning tool.

name: Baldr
fact: Odin and Frigg's son. Every object swore never to harm him except the mistletoe that killed him.

name: Heimdall
fact: Watchman of the rainbow bridge Bifrost. His horn Gjallarhorn will sound the start of Ragnarok.

name: Tyr
fact: God of law and single combat. Lost his right hand in the wolf Fenrir's jaws binding it.

name: Njord
fact: Vanir sea god, father of Freyr and Freyja. His mountain marriage to Skadi failed within nights.

name: Skadi
fact: Giantess of winter and skiing. Chose her husband by his feet alone, expecting the god Baldr.

name: Sif
fact: Thor's wife, her golden hair cut off by Loki and replaced with real gold by dwarven smiths.

name: Bragi
fact: God of poetry, said to have runes carved on his own tongue. Greets the slain into Valhalla.

name: Idun
fact: Keeper of the apples that keep the gods young. The giant Thjazi once stole her, eagle-shaped.

name: Hel
fact: Loki's daughter, half flesh and half corpse. Rules the dead who die of sickness or old age.

name: Vidar
fact: Odin's silent, near-mightiest son. His huge shoe is made to kill the wolf Fenrir.

name: Freyr
fact: Vanir god of harvest, rides the golden boar Gullinbursti; traded his sword for a giantess.

name: Mane
fact: Hair, and only males grow one — starting at adolescence as testosterone rises, full size by about age four.

name: Ossicone
fact: A bone core under skin, not a horn or antler — forms before birth, fuses to the skull only at maturity.

name: Tooth
fact: Enamel is the hardest tissue a body makes — 96% mineral, laid down over a bony root.

name: Trunk
fact: Nose and upper lip, fused in early fetal development. No bone at all — just up to 150,000 muscles.

name: Shoulder Hump
fact: Pure muscle, not fat — a power source for digging that no other living bear has.

name: Sagittal Crest
fact: A ridge of bone down the skull's midline, grown to anchor the muscle that powers a bite.

name: Claw
fact: Keratin sheath over the last bone in a toe — the same protein as hair, horn, and hoof.

name: Cecum
fact: A fermentation chamber off the gut — in a koala, about 2 metres long, the largest of any animal its size.

name: Pouch
fact: A fold of skin over the mammary glands, so young barely past embryo stage can still nurse.

name: Red Blood Cell
fact: Round in almost every mammal — oval in exactly one, a shape that keeps blood moving when dehydrated.

name: Hoof
fact: Keratin grown into a hard wall around a single toe bone that carries the animal's whole weight.

name: Knuckle
fact: Where finger bones meet — some apes lock this joint rigid and walk on the back of it.

name: Nuclear Envelope
fact: A double membrane around the genome, its outer layer wired straight into the ER, perforated by thousands of pores.

name: Endoplasmic Reticulum
fact: A network of membrane tubules threading through the cytoplasm, physically continuous with the nucleus.

name: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
fact: Ribosomes stud its outer face, giving it a rough look under the microscope and a job making proteins.

name: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
fact: The same tubular network minus the ribosomes — its business is building lipids, not protein.

name: Nucleolus
fact: The largest thing inside the nucleus, and a ribosome factory with no membrane of its own.

name: Golgi Apparatus
fact: Stacked membrane sacs that take in what the rough ER ships out, then modify, sort and repackage it.

name: Lysosome
fact: A membrane bag of over sixty digestive enzymes, budded straight off the Golgi apparatus.

name: Vacuole
fact: Smaller vesicles fuse into one big one; in a mature plant cell it can fill most of the space.

name: Cytoskeleton
fact: Microtubules plus actin filaments plus intermediate filaments: the scaffolding every cell builds itself from.

name: Centriole
fact: Nine microtubule triplets ringed into a cylinder, always kept in a pair near the nucleus.

name: Cilia
fact: Hundreds of short hairs beating in unison, each built on a nine-plus-two ring of microtubules.

name: Flagella
fact: The same nine-plus-two core as a cilium, just one or two per cell instead of hundreds, and far longer.

name: Cell Wall
fact: A rigid cellulose layer laid down just outside the membrane — a plant cell building its own exoskeleton.

name: Plasmid
fact: A loop of DNA a bacterium keeps on the side, copying itself independently of the main chromosome.

name: Diffusion
fact: Molecules drift from where they're crowded to where they're not — no energy required, no pump needed.

name: Osmosis
fact: Diffusion's special case: water alone, crossing a selective membrane toward wherever solutes are thicker.

name: Active Transport
fact: Moving a substance the wrong way down its own gradient — and it always costs a burnt ATP.

name: Endocytosis
fact: The membrane folds around something outside, pinches shut, and the outside becomes an inside.

name: Exocytosis
fact: The Golgi apparatus's shipping side in action: a vesicle docks at the membrane and empties itself outward.

name: Phagocytosis
fact: A cell doesn't just absorb a bacterium — it wraps its whole membrane around it and swallows it whole.

name: Muscle Cell
fact: Actin ordered into thousands of repeating sarcomeres, burning ATP directly to slide past itself.

name: White Blood Cell
fact: Its lysosomes are loaded and waiting for whatever it engulfs by phagocytosis.

name: Guard Cell
fact: One of the only epidermal cells that keeps its chloroplasts — the other reason it can pump salt and swell.

name: Palisade Cell
fact: Long, tightly packed cylinders under a leaf's upper skin, carrying more chloroplasts than any other leaf cell.

name: Goblet Cell
fact: A secretory cell built around an oversized Golgi apparatus, its whole shape swollen with mucin granules.

name: Mucus
fact: Ninety to ninety-five percent water; the rest is mucin, and together they trap whatever the air brings in.

name: Ciliated Cell
fact: Hundreds of beating hairs on one cell, sweeping the trachea's mucus blanket up and out.

name: Blood
fact: Mostly plasma by volume, but the two kinds of cell suspended in it do entirely different jobs.

name: Nitrogen Gas
fact: N2 — two nitrogen atoms locked by a triple bond so strong almost nothing can break it, which is why it makes up 78% of the air and does almost nothing while it is there.

name: Fox
fact: Most widely distributed member of the dog family, found across the entire Northern Hemisphere.

name: Bow
fact: A flexed stave that stores energy in its limbs, released through a string to launch an arrow.

name: Taiko
fact: Japanese drum family with cowhide heads stretched over a wooden shell, beaten with sticks.

name: Izanagi
fact: Primordial Shinto god who churned the sea into Japan's islands, then fled the underworld Yomi in horror.

name: Izanami
fact: Primordial Shinto goddess who died bearing the fire god Kagutsuchi and became ruler of the underworld Yomi.

name: Amaterasu
fact: Shinto sun goddess and mythical ancestor of Japan's imperial line; hid in a cave, darkening the world.

name: Susanoo
fact: Shinto storm god exiled from Heaven for his rampage; slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi.

name: Tsukuyomi
fact: Shinto moon god who killed the food goddess Uke Mochi in disgust, forever separating day from night.

name: Kagutsuchi
fact: Shinto fire god; his birth killed his mother Izanami, so his father beheaded and dismembered him in revenge.

name: Inari
fact: Shinto kami of rice, fertility and industry, whose messengers are white foxes -- kitsune.

name: Ryujin
fact: Shinto dragon king of the sea, ruling a palace of red and white coral beneath the waves.

name: Fujin
fact: Shinto wind god, one of the eldest kami, shown carrying a huge bag of winds on his shoulders.

name: Raijin
fact: Shinto thunder god who beats drums ringed with the tomoe symbol from atop the clouds.

name: Hachiman
fact: Shinto god of war and archery, syncretic spirit of Emperor Ojin; guardian kami of the samurai.

name: Tenjin
fact: Shinto god of scholarship -- the deified spirit of the exiled courtier-poet Sugawara no Michizane.

name: Uke Mochi
fact: Shinto food goddess killed by Tsukuyomi; crops and livestock grew from her corpse afterward.

name: Mikaboshi
fact: Shinto star god, the only deity who refused to submit to the heavenly gods' conquest of the earth.

name: Ame-no-Iwato
fact: The heavenly rock cave where Amaterasu hid after Susanoo's rampage, plunging the world into darkness.

name: Ame-no-Uzume
fact: Shinto goddess of dawn and mirth; her bawdy dance lured Amaterasu out of hiding and founded kagura dance.

name: Sarutahiko
fact: Shinto guardian kami with a seven-span nose and eyes like mirrors; blocked the descent of the heavenly gods.

name: Tectonic Plate
fact: Earth's brittle outer shell broken into semirigid slabs — seven major ones, a dozen or so smaller.

name: Divergent Boundary
fact: Where two plates pull apart and magma rises to freeze into new crust, mostly along mid-ocean ridges.

name: Convergent Boundary
fact: Where two plates are driven together — one dives beneath the other, or both crumple upward instead.

name: Transform Boundary
fact: Where two plates grind sideways past one another along a fault, neither building crust nor destroying it.

name: Earthquake
fact: The ground's sudden release of strain built up along a locked fault, radiating out as seismic waves.

name: Mid-Ocean Ridge
fact: A continuous seam of brand-new seafloor, welling up along a divergent boundary for about 65,000 km.

name: Taxonomy
fact: The nested system — kingdom down to species — that gives every living thing exactly one place and one name.

discovered.note: Linnaeus's Systema Naturae ranks all life into a nested hierarchy, named with two-part Latin binomials.

name: Tree of Life
fact: A branching diagram connecting every classified group of life back through common ancestry.

discovered.note: Darwin sketches the first version, diagramming evolution's branching pattern.

name: Cladistics
fact: Grouping organisms by shared derived traits, not overall looks — the method behind the whale-hippo surprise.

name: Island
fact: Land walled in by water on every side. Isolation is exactly what makes island wildlife so distinctive.

name: Fossil
fact: Ancient remains preserved in rock after minerals slowly replace the original bone or shell.

name: Genetic Drift
fact: Random, chance shifts in a population's allele frequencies — strongest of all in small populations.

name: Gene Flow
fact: Alleles moving between populations as individuals, pollen, or seeds cross from one to another.

name: Adaptation
fact: A trait shaped over generations by natural selection to fit its bearer to its environment.

name: Sexual Selection
fact: Mate choice or rivalry favouring traits that win breeding success, not just plain survival.

name: Artificial Selection
fact: Humans, not nature, choosing which individuals breed — the same mechanism, a different judge.

name: Reproductive Isolation
fact: Populations diverged enough that they can no longer produce fertile offspring together.

name: Speciation
fact: The point at which diverging populations can no longer interbreed and become separate species.

name: Adaptive Radiation
fact: One ancestral population fanning rapidly into many species, each fit to a different niche.

name: Homology
fact: Shared underlying structure — the same bone plan in a wing, a flipper, and a hand — from common descent.

name: Vestigial Structure
fact: A once-useful body part reduced to a nonfunctional leftover once selection stopped favouring it.

name: Fossil Record
fact: The total, ordered archive of fossils across rock strata — evolution's clearest paper trail.

name: Transitional Fossil
fact: A fossil bridging two groups, carrying features of both the ancestral and the descendant form.

name: Living Fossil
fact: A living species so little changed from its fossil relatives it looks like it stepped out of deep time.

discovered.note: A living coelacanth, presumed extinct for 65 million years, is hauled up off South Africa, coining the term.

name: Extinction
fact: The permanent disappearance of a species when the last individual dies without descendants.

name: Mass Extinction
fact: A sudden, global loss of a large share of species all at once, resetting evolution's course.

name: Camouflage
fact: Colouring or pattern that blends its bearer into the background — adaptation you can see at a glance.

name: Peacock
fact: A pheasant relative native to South Asia; males spread an iridescent, eye-marked tail in courtship.

name: Owl
fact: Comb-like serrations on its flight feathers muffle the wingbeat, letting it hunt almost silently.

name: Helmet
fact: Protective head covering; Bronze Age Aegean warriors wore bronze and boar's-tusk designs.

name: Lyre
fact: Ancient stringed instrument; its classic form used a hollowed tortoise shell as a soundbox.

name: Poppy
fact: The scarlet corn poppy grows wild among cereal crops; a different species yields opium.

name: Arrow
fact: A projectile shaft tipped with a point -- among the oldest weapons humans have made.

name: Cicada
fact: Nymphs feed on root sap underground for years before emerging to moult into winged adults.

name: Cerberus
fact: Three-headed dog, offspring of Echidna and Typhon, that guards the gates of the underworld.

name: Zeus
fact: King of the Olympian gods, ruler of sky and thunder. Roman Jupiter. Won his throne from the Titans.

name: Hera
fact: Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage. Roman Juno. Homeric epithet Boopis, 'cow-eyed.'

name: Poseidon
fact: God of the sea and earthquakes, 'the Earth-Shaker.' Roman Neptune. Carries a trident.

name: Hades
fact: God of the dead and ruler of the underworld. Roman Pluto. Also called Plouton, 'the rich one.'

name: Athena
fact: Goddess of wisdom and war strategy. Roman Minerva. Sprang fully armed from Zeus's head.

name: Apollo
fact: God of prophecy, music and archery. Chief epithet Phoebus, 'bright.' Twin brother of Artemis.

name: Artemis
fact: Goddess of the hunt, wilderness and the moon. Roman Diana. Twin sister of Apollo.

name: Ares
fact: God of war and battle-frenzy. Roman Mars. Called by Zeus 'the most hateful of all gods.'

name: Aphrodite
fact: Goddess of love and beauty. Roman Venus. Name means 'foam-arisen,' born of the sea.

name: Hermes
fact: Messenger of the gods and guide of souls to the underworld. Roman Mercury. Patron of travelers and thieves.

name: Dionysus
fact: God of wine, ecstasy and theatre. Roman Bacchus. Called the 'twice-born' god.

name: Demeter
fact: Goddess of grain and the harvest. Roman Ceres. Her grief for Persephone brings winter.

name: Persephone
fact: Queen of the underworld and goddess of spring growth. Roman Proserpina. Daughter of Demeter.

name: Hephaestus
fact: God of fire, the forge and craftsmen. Roman Vulcan. Epithet Amphigyeeis, 'the lame one.'

name: Cronus
fact: Titan king who ruled the Golden Age. Roman Saturn. Overthrew his father Uranus, and was overthrown by Zeus.

name: Gaia
fact: Primordial personification of the Earth. Roman Terra. Mother of Uranus and the Titans.

name: Ouranos
fact: Primordial personification of the sky, first ruler of the cosmos. Castrated by his son Cronus.

name: Rhea
fact: Titaness of motherhood, wife of Cronus. Roman Ops. Saved infant Zeus with a trick of stone and cloth.

name: Eros
fact: God of desire and love. Roman Cupid. Ovid gives him gold arrows that kindle love and lead ones that repel it.

name: Nike
fact: Winged personification of victory. Roman Victoria. Daughter of the Titan Pallas and the river Styx.

name: Helios
fact: God who personifies the sun. Roman Sol. Drives a four-horse chariot across the sky each day.

name: Selene
fact: Goddess who personifies the moon. Roman Luna. Sister of Helios and Eos.

name: Eos
fact: Goddess who personifies the dawn. Roman Aurora. Homer's constant epithet: 'rosy-fingered.'

name: Pan
fact: God of the wild, shepherds and flocks. Roman Faunus. Has the legs and horns of a goat.

name: Hypnos
fact: God who personifies sleep. Roman Somnus. Twin brother of Thanatos, death, and son of Nyx, night.

name: Heracles
fact: Greatest of the Greek heroes. Roman Hercules. Son of Zeus, famed for his Twelve Labors.

name: Odysseus
fact: King of Ithaca, hero of the Odyssey. Roman Ulysses. Known for his cunning, metis.

name: Indian Rhinoceros
fact: Wart-like bumps armor its deeply folded skin — adults face almost no natural predator.

name: Spotted Hyena
fact: A bite 40% stronger than a leopard's lets it crush bone that would defeat most carnivores.

name: Sloth
fact: Leaves can take more than a month to digest — no other mammal's gut works that slowly.

name: Three-Banded Armadillo
fact: The only armadillo that can roll its whole body into a sealed, armored ball.

name: Hedgehog
fact: Its spines are just hair, stiffened with keratin — and two back muscles roll it into a spiky, sealed ball.

name: Meerkat
fact: Eye sockets covering over a fifth of its skull power the binocular vision behind its sentry watch.

name: Large Intestine
fact: Cecum, colon, rectum, anal canal in series — built to reclaim water and salt, not absorb nutrients.

name: Colon
fact: Ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid — one tube bent twice, by the liver then the spleen.

name: Haustra
fact: Segmented pouches once blamed on short muscle bands — now thought to be the enteric nervous system's work.

name: Rectum
fact: Where the colon's muscle bands blend into one sheath and the pouches vanish: a smooth reservoir for feces.

name: Appendix
fact: Reassessed since the early 2000s: not vestigial. Its wall is packed with immune tissue standing watch.

name: Peristalsis
fact: A wave of muscle: relax ahead, contract behind. The colon mostly skips it for a few big daily pushes.

name: Gut Flora
fact: The body's largest bacterial ecosystem — a relationship that's mutualistic, not just commensal.

name: Vitamin K
fact: Gut bacteria — E. coli among them — convert it between forms and can synthesize their own share.

name: Beak
fact: A bony core sheathed in keratin — the rhamphotheca — its shape set entirely by what the bird eats.

name: Talon
fact: A bird of prey's claw — the foot that does the killing; the hooked beak only tears flesh afterward.

name: Air Sac
fact: Thin sacs that push air through the lungs one-way on both breaths — no other vertebrate manages that.

name: Hollow Bone
fact: Marrow swapped for air and internal struts — lighter, and plumbed straight into the lung's air sacs.

name: Keel
fact: The sternum's midline ridge, giving flight muscle leverage — ratites are literally named for lacking one.

name: Flight Muscle
fact: Pectoralis for the downstroke, supracoracoideus for the up — pulling through a shoulder pulley tendon.

name: Flight Feather
fact: The stiff, asymmetric-vaned feathers of wing and tail carry the whole aerodynamic load.

name: Hummingbird
fact: A shoulder joint that rotates the whole wing — the only bird family that can truly hover and fly backward.

name: Penguin
fact: Wings became short, stiff flippers — the same bones as a flying bird's wing, just built for the sea.

name: Flamingo
fact: Comb-like lamellae line the bill, worked upside-down in the mud to filter out its food.

name: Albatross
fact: A sheet of tendon locks the wing open at the shoulder, so it glides on the wind without spending muscle.

name: Ostrich
fact: Only two toes per foot, not four — no other living bird is reduced that far.

name: Brown Kiwi
fact: The only bird with nostrils at its bill-tip, smelling worms in soil it can't see or feel.

name: Toucan
fact: A hollow, oversized bill covering up to half its body surface — used to reach fruit and dump heat.

name: Woodpecker
fact: A hyoid bone wraps around the skull as an internal seatbelt, cushioning the brain from every peck.

name: Pelican
fact: The throat pouch is a fishing net, not a pantry — it drains the water out before the fish goes down.

name: Heron
fact: Twenty-plus neck vertebrae fold into a tight S, cocking the dagger bill to strike.

name: Cormorant
fact: Stands wing-spread after a river dive — a study on the great cormorant found the pose dries its plumage.

name: Parrot
fact: The upper beak hinges free of the skull instead of fusing to it, adding bite force.

name: Swift
fact: Legs too short for much but clinging — it eats, mates and sleeps on the wing.

name: Cartilage
fact: Collagen-rich connective tissue with no blood supply of its own — firm but flexible where bone is rigid.

name: Whisker
fact: A hair whose root carries 100–200 nerve endings — enough to feel a gap's width in the dark.

name: Floating Clavicle
fact: A collarbone with no joint to the rest of the skeleton — anchored only by connective tissue.

name: Retractable Claw
fact: Sheathed in skin and fur at rest, so the point never dulls on the ground.

name: Tapetum Lucidum
fact: A riboflavin-and-zinc mirror behind the retina — nearly 130 times as reflective as a human eye.

name: Righting Reflex
fact: A falling cat rights itself by inner ear, then twists its front half and rear half in turn.

name: Purr
fact: Made possible by a fully bony hyoid — a big cat's stays gristly, so it roars instead.

name: Barbed Tongue
fact: A muscle studded with backward-hooked keratin spines — a built-in hairbrush.

name: Vomeronasal Organ
fact: A mouth-roof organ wired to its own nerve, not the main smell nerve — it reads pheromones.

name: Slit Pupil
fact: Snaps to a vertical slit in bright light — stays round in a cat the size of a tiger.

name: Manx
fact: A dominant mutation shortens the spine to nothing — lethal if inherited from both parents.

name: Siamese
fact: A heat-sensitive enzyme switches pigment on only where the skin runs cool.

name: Sphynx
fact: A recessive keratin-gene mutation stops each hair from growing a proper root.

discovered.note: First bred from Prune, a spontaneously hairless kitten born in Toronto.

name: Devon Rex
fact: Its curl looks like the Cornish Rex's but comes from a mutation at a different gene entirely.

name: Scottish Fold
fact: A dominant cartilage-gene mutation folds the ear — and softens joints all over the body.

name: Tide
fact: Raised mainly by the Moon's pull on the sea, with a smaller pull from the Sun added in.

name: Intertidal Zone
fact: Flooded and drained twice a day; barnacles mark its top, kelp its lowest fringe.

name: Tide Pool
fact: Seawater stranded in a rocky hollow at low tide, a miniature and harshly changeable sea.

name: Barnacle
fact: A crustacean, not a mollusk. It cements its head to rock and kicks food in with feathery legs.

name: Mussel
fact: Anchors itself to rock with byssus, tough protein threads spun by a gland in its foot.

name: Periwinkle
fact: Grazes rock on a mucus-lubricated foot, then seals its shell to the stone with the same mucus.

name: Limpet
fact: Clings to rock with one powerful suction foot and homes back to its own worn scar after grazing.

name: Chiton
fact: Eight overlapping shell plates on a muscular girdle; its teeth are capped with iron-rich magnetite.

name: Hermit Crab
fact: Has no shell of its own. It lives in an empty snail shell and moves to a bigger one as it grows.

name: Sea Star
fact: Moves on hundreds of tube feet run by a water-filled hydraulic system, not muscle alone.

name: Sand Dollar
fact: A sea urchin flattened for burrowing in sand, its spines reduced to short, mobile ones.

name: Dog Whelk
fact: A predatory sea snail that uses a spine on its own shell's lip to pry open a barnacle's plates.

name: Bladder Wrack
fact: A brown seaweed kept afloat near the surface by paired air bladders along its fronds.

name: Sea Lettuce
fact: A green alga only two cells thick, simple enough to grow from seawater into a brackish estuary.

name: Razor Clam
fact: Buried in shore sand, it can dig itself down almost as fast as a person can dig after it.

name: Brittle Star
fact: Whips its thin arms in snake-like curves to move; a lost arm snaps off easily and regrows.

name: Porcelain Crab
fact: A filter feeder closer kin to hermit crabs than true crabs, gripping kelp holdfasts with spiny legs.

name: Frogspawn
fact: A clump of eggs wrapped only in jelly, no shell — most amphibians must lay it in water or it dries out.

name: Tadpole
fact: A fully aquatic larva with a tail and gills, hatched from spawn — nothing like the frog it will become.

name: Gill
fact: A feathery, blood-vessel-rich fringe that pulls dissolved oxygen straight out of water.

name: Lung
fact: An air sac that only finishes growing once a tadpole's gills are on their way out.

name: Metamorphosis
fact: Thyroid hormone remakes a gilled swimmer into an air-breather, tail eaten by its own cells.

name: Amphibian Skin
fact: Little keratin, no scales — a permeable membrane that must stay damp to work at all.

name: Cutaneous Respiration
fact: Breathing through the skin itself — some salamanders rely on it completely and have no lungs at all.

name: Indicator Species
fact: Permeable skin and a water-bound larva make an amphibian population an early warning for pollution.

name: Lateral Line
fact: A row of pressure-sensing "plaques" down the head and flanks, for water, not air.

name: Caecilian
fact: Limbless and burrowing, built so much like an earthworm most people miss that it's a vertebrate.

name: Japanese Giant Salamander
fact: Among the largest living amphibians at 1.5 m — its wrinkled skin exists purely to breathe underwater.

name: Surinam Toad
fact: Eggs sink into the mother's back skin, which closes into pockets until a toadlet climbs out.

name: Batrachotoxin
fact: The frog doesn't make its own poison — it concentrates it from the ants and mites it eats.

name: Olm
fact: Blind and pale from a lifetime in cave rivers, larval for life — its tissues ignore thyroxine.

name: Siren
fact: Keeps functioning lungs and external gills side by side for life, unlike any other salamander.

name: Gallium
fact: Melts at 29.8°C, liquid in your palm — Mendeleev predicted it in 1871, four years before it was found.

name: Dry Ice
fact: Frozen carbon dioxide. Below 5 atmospheres it has no liquid phase — it sublimates straight to gas.

name: Housefly
fact: Musca domestica tastes through chemoreceptors on its feet, and has only one pair of wings, not two.

name: Rat
fact: Rattus norvegicus. Its incisors never stop growing — about 12 cm a year — so it gnaws constantly.

name: Feral Pigeon
fact: Descended from the rock dove, and it still nests on window ledges the way its ancestors nested on sea cliffs.

name: Garden Snail
fact: Cornu aspersum. Hermaphrodite — a mating pair each fire a calcite 'love dart' before mating.

name: Common Toad
fact: Bufo bufo walks on four legs rather than hopping, and returns every spring to the exact pond it hatched in.

name: Green Alga
fact: Chlorophyta — chlorophyll a and b, starch storage, mostly fresh water. Land plants share all three.

name: Potassium Nitrate
fact: KNO3, saltpetre. Bacteria turn manure's ammonia into nitrate; wash it through ash and it crystallises.

name: Glycerol
fact: Named from the Greek for sweet — the backbone left once a fat's three fatty acids are split off it.

name: Toluene
fact: Named for tolu balsam, the resin it was isolated from in 1841 — now mostly made from petroleum instead.

discovered.note: First isolated from tolu balsam, the resin that gives it its name.

name: TNT
fact: 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene, first made in 1863 as a yellow dye — a military explosive only from 1902.

discovered.note: First used as a military explosive, decades after it was made as a yellow dye.

name: Gunpowder
fact: 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal, 10% sulfur — a ratio traced to its 11th-century Chinese origin.

discovered.note: The earliest known written formula for it appears in the Chinese military text Wujing Zongyao.

name: Dynamite
fact: Nobel's 1867 patent: nitroglycerin soaked into kieselguhr, a diatom silica, stable enough to ship.

discovered.note: Nobel patents it, nitroglycerin soaked into diatom silica to make it stable enough to ship.

name: Nitroglycerin
fact: Sobrero made it first, in 1846, and was so alarmed by how easily it detonates he opposed weaponising it.

discovered.note: Ascanio Sobrero first makes it, and is alarmed enough to oppose weaponising it.

name: Wind Shear
fact: Wind changing speed or direction with height. Enough of it over a thunderstorm tilts the updraft into a spin.

name: Tornado
fact: A supercell's rotating mesocyclone, stretched and tightened by wind shear until it touches the ground.

name: Tsunami
fact: Not a wind-driven wave — the whole water column shoved sideways by a subduction-zone earthquake.

name: Liquid Hydrogen
fact: Boils at -252.87°C, just 20 degrees above absolute zero — colder than every other cryogenic liquid but helium.

name: Liquid Nitrogen
fact: Boils at -196°C. Splashed on something warm it floats on its own vapour — the Leidenfrost effect.

name: Antiproton
fact: The proton's antimatter twin — same mass, opposite charge — confirmed to exist in 1955 at Berkeley.

discovered.note: Confirmed to exist at Berkeley.

name: Antihydrogen
fact: A positron bound to an antiproton — a whole antimatter atom, first made at CERN in 1995.

discovered.note: First made at CERN, a positron bound to an antiproton.

name: Pyrope
fact: Magnesium aluminium silicate garnet, carried up from the mantle in basalt and kimberlite pipes.

name: Spessartine
fact: Manganese aluminium silicate garnet — the orange member, grown in granite pegmatite and rhyolite.

name: Grossular
fact: Calcium aluminium silicate garnet, grown where metamorphism cooks impure limestone.

name: Andradite
fact: Calcium iron silicate garnet — swap in chromium and its demantoid variety outshines emerald in fire.

name: Uvarovite
fact: Calcium chromium silicate garnet, always green, grown in chromium-rich serpentinite.

name: Heliodor
fact: Golden beryl, coloured by iron in its Fe3+ state — grown in the same granite pegmatites as beryl itself.

name: Morganite
fact: Pink beryl, coloured by manganese in its Mn2+ state — the same element that turns red beryl scarlet in a hotter state.

name: Red Beryl
fact: Manganese-coloured beryl grown in volcanic gas cavities, not pegmatite — rarer than diamond.

name: Amethyst
fact: Quartz coloured violet by iron impurities plus natural background irradiation.

name: Citrine
fact: Quartz whose iron centres have been driven from purple to gold — most of it is heat-turned amethyst.

name: Rose Quartz
fact: Quartz pink not from a dissolved impurity but from microscopic fibres of a mineral related to dumortierite.

name: Smoky Quartz
fact: Quartz with aluminium standing in for a little silicon, smoked brown by the same irradiation that colours amethyst.

name: Aventurine Quartz
fact: Quartz glittering with included flakes of fuchsite mica — the sparkle is reflection, not the quartz's own colour.

name: Tiger's Eye
fact: Silicified crocidolite — asbestos fibres replaced by quartz, then stained gold-brown by iron oxide.

name: Rutilated Quartz
fact: Quartz grown around needles of rutile, titanium dioxide, that crystallised first and got trapped.

name: Chalcedony
fact: Cryptocrystalline quartz, its crystals too small to see — deposited from silica-laden groundwater in rock cavities.

name: Agate
fact: Chalcedony banded in successive layers as silica-bearing water deposits it again and again in the same cavity.

name: Carnelian
fact: Chalcedony coloured brownish-red by impurities of iron oxide — hematite, specifically.

name: Jasper
fact: Opaque chalcedony, its common red-brown colour is iron inclusions running right through it.

name: Chrysoprase
fact: Chalcedony coloured apple-green by trace nickel — unlike emerald's chromium, in a completely different host.

name: Bloodstone
fact: Green jasper flecked red — the spots are hematite inclusions, not literally blood, whatever the legend says.

name: Moss Agate
fact: Chalcedony with dendrites of manganese or iron oxide branching through it like moss — no plant was ever involved.

name: Petrified Wood
fact: Wood buried and starved of oxygen, its cell walls replaced molecule by molecule with chalcedony carried in by water.

name: Tourmaline
fact: A boron silicate that crystallises in granite pegmatite — boron is what makes it tourmaline at all.

name: Schorl
fact: Iron-rich tourmaline, black and by far the commonest kind — about 95% of all tourmaline found is this.

name: Dravite
fact: Magnesium-rich tourmaline, brown, named for the Drave district where it was first described.

name: Rubellite
fact: Manganese-rich tourmaline, pink to red — the lithium-bearing elbaite branch of the tourmaline family.

name: Indicolite
fact: Blue tourmaline — an iron and titanium pair trading an electron back and forth, the same trick that colours sapphire.

name: Watermelon Tourmaline
fact: A single crystal zoned pink to green as it grew — manganese ran out and iron took over partway through.

name: Padparadscha
fact: Corundum needing both ruby's chromium and sapphire's iron and titanium together to land on pink-orange.

name: Spinel
fact: Magnesium aluminium oxide — grown alongside ruby in metamorphosed limestone, and mistaken for it for centuries.

name: Sodalite
fact: Sodium aluminosilicate with chlorine locked in its cage structure — a feldspar relative too low in silica to be one.

name: Hauyne
fact: A sulfate cousin of sodalite, in the same feldspathoid family, first found in Vesuvius's ejected limestone blocks.

name: Lapis Lazuli
fact: Not one mineral but a rock: sodalite-group lazurite for the blue, pyrite for the gold flecks.

name: Scapolite
fact: A calcium-sodium aluminosilicate that traps chlorine, carbonate or sulfate in its structure — metamorphosed feldspar.

name: Zircon
fact: Zirconium silicate — chemically nothing like the metal zirconium is cut from, though it is zirconium's ore.

name: Vesuvianite
fact: A complex calcium-magnesium-aluminium silicate grown where limestone gets baked by an intruding melt — a skarn mineral.

name: Taaffeite
fact: Beryllium magnesium aluminium oxide, close kin to spinel — it was sold as spinel for years before anyone noticed.

discovered.note: Every known piece had been sold and catalogued as spinel until one buyer's stone tests wrong.

name: Benitoite
fact: Barium titanium silicate, blue and fluorescent — first mistaken for sapphire before its own mineral was recognised.

name: Topaz
fact: An aluminium silicate that locks fluorine into every unit — fluorine is what makes it topaz and not something else.

name: Chrysoberyl
fact: Beryllium aluminium oxide — shares beryllium and aluminium with beryl, but is a completely different mineral.

name: Alexandrite
fact: Chromium-bearing chrysoberyl that reads green in daylight and red under incandescent light — same trick as ruby's chromium, doubled.

name: Cymophane
fact: Cat's-eye chrysoberyl — parallel needle-like inclusions focus light into one moving band across the stone.

name: Andalusite
fact: Aluminium silicate, Al2SiO5 — one of three minerals with that exact formula, sorted out by pressure and heat.

name: Chiastolite
fact: Andalusite grown around carbon and clay swept to its corners, leaving a black cross in cross-section.

name: Sillimanite
fact: Al2SiO5 again, but andalusite's higher-temperature twin — the same formula, rearranged by more heat.

name: Kyanite
fact: Al2SiO5 a third time — andalusite's higher-pressure twin, grown deeper where the rock is squeezed harder.

name: Enstatite
fact: Magnesium silicate pyroxene, MgSiO3 — the iron-free end of a solid-solution series that runs to ferrosilite.

name: Hypersthene
fact: Enstatite with enough iron mixed in to sit halfway to ferrosilite — common in both igneous rock and meteorites.

name: Iolite
fact: Cordierite to a mineralogist: a magnesium iron aluminium silicate grown by baking clay-rich rock.

name: Peridot
fact: Gem-grade olivine, specifically its magnesium-rich forsterite end — one of only two gems that form in the mantle, not the crust.

name: Sinhalite
fact: Magnesium aluminium borate, close enough to spinel's own recipe that it was mistaken for peridot for decades.

name: Kunzite
fact: Spodumene coloured lilac-pink by manganese — the same lithium aluminium silicate, a different trace element.

discovered.note: Named for the mineralogist who first described it.

name: Hiddenite
fact: Spodumene coloured green by chromium — kunzite's twin, with ruby and emerald's own colouring element instead.

name: Zoisite
fact: Calcium aluminium silicate grown in calcium-rich schist — colourless until a trace element gets into it.

name: Tanzanite
fact: Zoisite coloured blue-violet by vanadium, then heat-treated to burn off a brownish veil and leave the blue.

name: Thulite
fact: Zoisite coloured pink by manganese — tanzanite's sibling, with manganese standing in for vanadium.

name: Moonstone
fact: Feldspar that cooled slowly enough to separate into alternating orthoclase and albite layers, scattering light between them.

name: Labradorite
fact: Calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar — thin exsolved layers inside it split light the way a soap film does.

name: Albite
fact: The sodium end of the plagioclase feldspar series — pure NaAlSi3O8, calcium's opposite number.

name: Sunstone
fact: Albite-type feldspar glittering with flat copper platelets grown inside it — Oregon's stone specifically owes its sparkle to copper.

name: Amazonite
fact: A green-blue microcline feldspar, its colour tied to trace lead locked in the same triclinic structure.

name: Jadeite
fact: A sodium aluminium pyroxene — one of two unrelated minerals both called jade, made only where plates subduct.

name: Nephrite
fact: A calcium magnesium iron amphibole — jade's other mineral, chemically nothing like jadeite despite the shared name.

name: Chrysocolla
fact: A hydrous copper silicate that grows where malachite and azurite weather further in silica-bearing water.

name: Dioptase
fact: Hydrous copper silicate, deep emerald-green — grown in the same oxidised copper-deposit zone as malachite, with silica instead of carbonate.

name: Dolomite
fact: Calcium magnesium carbonate — limestone with roughly half its calcium swapped for magnesium by passing groundwater.

name: Aragonite
fact: Calcite's higher-pressure polymorph — identical formula, CaCO3, packed into a different crystal shape.

name: Rhodochrosite
fact: Manganese carbonate, rose-red from Mn2+ — baked further by metamorphism and it turns into the silicate rhodonite.

name: Rhodonite
fact: Manganese silicate — what rhodochrosite becomes when metamorphism drives off its carbon dioxide and leaves silicate behind.

name: Smithsonite
fact: Zinc carbonate, grown the same way malachite is — in the weathered, oxidised cap above a metal-sulfide deposit.

name: Cerussite
fact: Lead carbonate, formed the same way malachite is — weathering in carbon-dioxide-charged water above a lead deposit.

name: Anglesite
fact: Lead sulfate — what galena becomes when it oxidises in air, the lead equivalent of pyrite turning to hematite.

name: Celestine
fact: Strontium sulfate, precipitated out of evaporating water exactly the way gypsum is, with strontium standing in for calcium.

name: Titanite
fact: Calcium titanium silicate, also called sphene — one of the few common minerals built around titanium.

name: Epidote
fact: A calcium aluminium iron silicate that grows where hot fluids alter calcium-rich feldspar — iron is what turns it pistachio-green.

name: Staurolite
fact: An unusually aluminium-rich silicate that grows in schist alongside garnet, twinning into a natural cross.

name: Danburite
fact: Calcium borosilicate, grown where boron-bearing fluids cook limestone during contact metamorphism.

name: Datolite
fact: Calcium borosilicate with a hydroxyl group — a classic mineral of gas cavities in basalt, grown alongside zeolites.

name: Axinite
fact: A calcium aluminium borosilicate that grows where a granite intrusion's boron-rich fluids meet its contact zone.

name: Dumortierite
fact: An aluminium borosilicate that grows fibrous in aluminium-rich rock cooked by regional metamorphism.

name: Prehnite
fact: Calcium aluminium silicate, another classic mineral of gas cavities in basalt — named for the officer who first brought it to Europe.

name: Petalite
fact: Lithium aluminium silicate, grown in the same lithium-bearing granite pegmatites as spodumene.

name: Euclase
fact: A hydroxyl-bearing beryllium aluminium silicate — beryl's chemistry with water folded into the structure.

name: Brazilianite
fact: Sodium aluminium phosphate, grown in phosphate-rich granite pegmatite — named for the country its type locality is in.

name: Beryllonite
fact: Sodium beryllium phosphate — pegmatite chemistry that swaps beryl's silicate framework for a phosphate one.

name: Amblygonite
fact: A lithium aluminium fluorophosphate, grown alongside spodumene as one more lithium mineral in the same pegmatite.

name: Phosphophyllite
fact: A rare zinc iron phosphate, grown in hydrothermal veins — named for its leaf-like, phyllite-style cleavage.

name: Hambergite
fact: Beryllium borate with a hydroxyl group — one of the few gem minerals built directly from beryllium and boron.

name: Scheelite
fact: Calcium tungstate, CaWO4 — named for the chemist who discovered tungsten, and still an ore of it today.

name: Cassiterite
fact: Tin oxide, SnO2 — the ore the Bronze Age's tin was smelted from, and still the main tin ore now.

name: Jet
fact: Driftwood buried in marine mud and compressed for millions of years — lignite dense enough to carve and polish.

name: Amber
fact: Fossilised conifer resin, sometimes with an insect from millions of years ago trapped inside as it set.

name: Tortoiseshell
fact: Keratin scutes from a hawksbill sea turtle's carapace — the trade nearly took the species with it, and is now banned worldwide.

name: Australopithecus afarensis
fact: Walked upright by 3.7 million years ago -- the Laetoli footprints prove it -- with a brain a third our size.

name: Homo habilis
fact: ‘Handy man’ -- the first Homo species, named for knapping the Oldowan stone tools that made it famous.

name: Homo erectus
fact: First hominin with a humanlike stride, and the first to walk out of Africa into Asia and Europe.

name: Homo heidelbergensis
fact: Big-brained, organized big-game hunter, likely ancestor of both Neanderthals and modern humans.

name: Homo neanderthalensis
fact: Stocky and cold-built for Ice Age Europe. Buried its dead, and left DNA in most people alive outside Africa.

name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
fact: A 7-million-year-old skull from Chad -- maybe the earliest hominin, though its bipedalism is disputed.

name: Orrorin tugenensis
fact: A 6-million-year-old Kenyan hominin known mainly from a femur shaped for upright walking.

name: Ardipithecus ramidus
fact: 'Ardi' -- a 4.4-million-year-old Ethiopian hominin that walked upright yet still climbed trees.

name: Australopithecus africanus
fact: South Africa's 'southern ape', known from cave finds like the Taung Child and Mrs. Ples.

name: Paranthropus boisei
fact: 'Nutcracker Man' -- huge molars and jaw muscles for grinding tough plants, an extinct side branch.

name: Homo rudolfensis
fact: A bigger-brained contemporary of Homo habilis, found near Kenya's Lake Turkana.

name: Homo antecessor
fact: Found in Spain's Atapuerca caves, with cut-marked bones showing its people practiced cannibalism.

name: Homo naledi
fact: A small-brained Homo species whose bones were found deep in a South African cave chamber.

name: Homo floresiensis
fact: The 'Hobbit' -- a metre-tall hominin that shrank on the Indonesian island of Flores.

name: Denisovan
fact: Known almost entirely from DNA out of a Siberian cave -- a sister lineage to the Neanderthals.

name: Australopithecus sediba
fact: Found by a 9-year-old boy at Malapa, South Africa -- a mix of ape-like and human-like traits.

name: Oldowan Tool
fact: The oldest recognized stone-tool kit: sharp flakes struck off a stone core with a hammerstone, nothing more.

name: Acheulean Handaxe
fact: A teardrop struck symmetrically from both faces of a stone core -- the same design used for 1.5 million years.

name: Fire Drill
fact: Spin a wooden shaft against a wooden board by hand until the hot dust it grinds off glows into an ember.

name: Bow Drill
fact: A cord wound around the spindle and driven by a bow turns hand-spinning into fast, steady strokes.

name: Ochre
fact: An iron-rich earth pigment, red from hematite, ground fine enough to paint or stain skin.

name: Cave Painting
fact: Animal figures in mineral pigment on cave walls, like those at Lascaux and Altamira.

name: Venus Figurine
fact: Faceless, wide-hipped female carvings found from Spain to Russia, most made 26,000 to 21,000 years ago.

name: Atlatl
fact: A hooked shaft that extends the throwing arm, hurling a dart far harder than any bare hand can.

name: Woolly Mammoth
fact: A tundra grazer built for cold -- shaggy coat, curved tusks -- eating roughly 180 kg of grass and sedge a day.

name: Mammoth-Bone Hut
fact: A dome of mammoth bones and tusks, weighted and covered with hide, on treeless Ice Age steppe.

name: Coke
fact: Coal heated past 1,000°C with no air doesn't burn — it comes apart, leaving this near-pure carbon behind.

name: Pig Iron
fact: Cast in branching sand moulds off one channel — piglets nursed by a sow is where the name comes from.

name: Deadly Nightshade
fact: Atropa belladonna. Renaissance women dropped its juice into their eyes to dilate the pupils -- bella donna, beautiful lady.

name: Atropine
fact: A tropane alkaloid that blocks the nervous system's rest-and-digest signal, which is why it dilates pupils and speeds a stopped heart.

name: Poison Hemlock
fact: Purple-blotched hollow stems along streams and ditches. Socrates was made to drink a decoction of it in 399 BC.

name: Water Hemlock
fact: Its tuberous root is widely cited as North America's most acutely toxic native plant -- seizures can begin within an hour.

name: Castor Bean
fact: The mottled seed yields castor oil, a mild laxative -- and, left behind in the pressed mash, one of the most toxic proteins known.

name: Ricin
fact: A ribosome-inactivating protein: it shuts down protein synthesis inside a cell so completely that a few milligrams can kill an adult.

name: Oleander
fact: Every part of this Mediterranean shrub carries cardiac glycosides -- the same class of chemistry China has used medicinally to treat heart failure.

name: Aconite
fact: Monkshood. Its hooded purple flower conceals aconitine in every tissue, historically smeared on arrow tips and used as wolf bait.

name: Autumn Crocus
fact: Colchicum autumnale flowers leafless in fall. Its colchicine is still prescribed for gout, and used in labs to double a plant's chromosomes.

name: Mayapple
fact: One umbrella-shaped leaf shelters a rhizome so rich in podophyllotoxin it became the starting material for the chemotherapy drug etoposide.

name: Yew
fact: Every part except the sweet red aril carries taxine alkaloids. The bark's taxol was developed into paclitaxel, a chemotherapy drug.

name: Pokeweed
fact: Birds strip its magenta-stemmed berry clusters unharmed and scatter the seed; the same fruit sickens the mammals that eat it.

name: Larkspur
fact: Delphinium, named for the dolphin-shaped spur on its unopened bud. Its methyllycaconitine is the leading cause of cattle deaths on western rangeland.

name: Lily of the Valley
fact: Its convallatoxin is potent enough that even the water a cut stem stands in becomes toxic -- Soviet-era medicine once paired it with alcohol to treat dropsy.

name: Giant Hogweed
fact: Its sap contains furanocoumarins that bind skin's DNA when hit by sunlight, causing burns and blistering that can recur for years.

name: Strychnine Tree
fact: Strychnos nux-vomica. Its bitter seeds concentrate strychnine, an alkaloid so effective a rodent poison it is still sold as one.

name: Rhododendron
fact: Some species load their nectar with grayanotoxin -- Xenophon's soldiers recorded being poisoned by wild honey made from it in 401 BC.

name: Horse Chestnut
fact: The glossy brown seed -- a conker -- is packed with the saponin aescin, toxic raw but processed medicinally to treat vein disorders.

name: Datura
fact: Jimsonweed. Its trumpet flower points upward and opens toward dusk; British troops in 1676 Jamestown ate it and spent a fortnight out of their minds.

name: Angel's Trumpet
fact: Brugmansia. Its pendulous trumpet flowers hang downward, the mirror image of its herbaceous relative datura, which points its blooms up.

name: Cannabis
fact: Resin glands on the female flower buds manufacture cannabinoids, chief among them the psychoactive THC.

name: THC
fact: Tetrahydrocannabinol, the cannabinoid mainly responsible for cannabis's psychoactive effects -- one of over sixty the plant produces.

name: Coca
fact: Andean peoples have chewed its leaf, buffered with lime to raise its pH, for a documented 5,000 years without the dependence refined cocaine produces.

name: Cocaine
fact: The coca leaf's alkaloid, isolated and concentrated: it blocks the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine at the nerve synapse.

name: Tobacco
fact: Nicotiana tabacum manufactures nicotine in its roots as an insect defence; nearly all of the genus's 75 species can do the same.

name: Nicotine
fact: An alkaloid absorbed easily through skin and lung alike. The old 40-60 mg lethal-dose figure was debunked in 2014; the real lower limit is closer to 500-1000 mg.

name: Opium Poppy
fact: Papaver somniferum, not the wild corn poppy. Lancing its unripe seed pod oozes a latex resin that dries into raw opium.

name: Morphine
fact: Isolated from opium in 1803 and named for Morpheus, the god of dreams -- medicine's benchmark analgesic ever since.

name: Peyote
fact: Lophophora williamsii, a spineless button cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert, is the sole source of ceremonial peyote for the Native American Church.

name: San Pedro Cactus
fact: Echinopsis pachanoi, a fast-growing columnar cactus of the high Andes, used ceremonially for a documented 3,000 years.

name: Mescaline
fact: A phenethylamine alkaloid, structurally closer to amphetamines than to most other plant hallucinogens, made independently by peyote and San Pedro.

name: Psilocybin Mushroom
fact: Psilocybe cubensis fruits readily on the dung of grazing cattle in warm pastures, bruising blue-green wherever it is bruised or cut.

name: Psilocybin
fact: A prodrug: the body converts it to psilocin, the compound actually responsible for the hallucinogenic effect.

name: Morning Glory
fact: Ipomoea seeds contain LSA, an ergoline alkaloid related to LSD; the Zapotec used one Mexican species ritually for centuries before its chemistry was known.

name: Betel Nut
fact: Chewed with lime inside a betel leaf, the areca palm's seed is consumed habitually by an estimated 600 million people worldwide.

name: Ayahuasca Vine
fact: Banisteriopsis caapi's bark supplies beta-carboline MAO inhibitors that let an otherwise orally inactive tryptamine survive digestion when brewed together.

name: Salvia Divinorum
fact: Diviner's sage. Its salvinorin A is the only known naturally occurring hallucinogen with no nitrogen atom in its structure at all.

name: Sweet Flag
fact: Calamus. Its aromatic rhizome was chewed by pioneers as a stimulant and thirst-quencher, though its beta-asarone is now banned from US food products.

name: Mescal Bean
fact: Sophora secundiflora's bright red seeds -- red hots -- concentrate cytisine, used in a Native American vision-seeking rite that predates peyote's spread.

name: Meteorite
fact: A meteoroid that survives the trip through the atmosphere and reaches the ground — most don't.

name: Impact Crater
fact: Struck near 20 km/s, rock is compressed past a million bar — melted, vaporized, or turned to coesite.

name: Tektite
fact: Impact-melted terrestrial rock, quenched airborne into glass — no crystals, under 0.02% water by weight.

name: Moldavite
fact: Green tektite glass from one event: the Ries impact, 15 million years ago, its melt landing 450 km away.

name: Australite
fact: Tektite reshaped by a second trip through the atmosphere — the flanged button NASA modeled Apollo capsules on.

name: Krishna
fact: Eighth avatar of Vishnu, raised among Vrindavan's cowherds; plays the bansuri flute, a peacock feather in his crown.

name: Radha
fact: Krishna's foremost consort among the Vrindavan gopis; her own symbol, tradition says, is the Golden Lotus.

name: Yashoda
fact: Krishna's foster mother in Gokul, wife of the chieftain Nanda; credited with two of his best-known childhood miracles.

name: Kansa
fact: Tyrant king of Mathura and Krishna’s uncle, undone by the very prophecy he tried to escape.

name: Rama
fact: Seventh avatar of Vishnu and prince of Ayodhya; broke Shiva's own bow to win Sita's hand, then defeated Ravana.

name: Sita
fact: Found by King Janaka while ploughing a field and raised as his daughter; her own name means ‘furrow.’

name: Ravana
fact: Ten-headed rakshasa king of Lanka and grandson of the sage Pulastya; an ardent devotee of Shiva.

name: Lakshmana
fact: Rama's loyal younger half-brother, who chose fourteen years of exile at his side over life in Ayodhya.

name: Arjuna
fact: Third of the five Pandava brothers and wielder of the celestial bow Gandiva; Krishna served as his charioteer.

name: Chisel
fact: A wedge-shaped steel blade, driven into wood, stone, or metal by a mallet or hammer.

name: Stethoscope
fact: Laennec's 1816 original was a hollow wooden tube; the binaural rubber-tubed design followed in 1851.

name: Dental Drill
fact: Its cutting bur is usually tipped with tungsten carbide or diamond.

name: Compass
fact: A magnetised needle, free to pivot, that aligns itself with Earth's magnetic field.

name: Fire Hose
fact: Amsterdam fire chief Jan van der Heyden sewed the first leather fire hose in 1673.

name: Chalk
fact: Most classroom chalk today is gypsum, not true calcium-carbonate chalk.

name: Carpenter
fact: Trains as an apprentice for three to four years before becoming a journeyman.

name: Electrician
fact: US apprenticeships run three to five years and 4,000 to 6,000 hours of paid on-the-job training.

name: Plumber
fact: Installs and maintains the pipes that carry a building's water in and its waste out.

name: Astronomer
fact: Now more often exposes a CCD camera for minutes than peers through an eyepiece.

name: Meteorologist
fact: Reads pressure, temperature, and wind to forecast weather from local to global scale.

name: Astronaut
fact: A sealed helmet exchanges breathable oxygen and carbon dioxide with the spacecraft.

name: Veterinarian
fact: Completes a dedicated veterinary-medicine degree covering anatomy, pharmacology, and surgery.

name: Farm Manager
fact: Plans the sequence from ploughing and sowing through to harvest.

name: Medical Doctor
fact: Four to five years of medical school, then a supervised residency, before independent practice.

name: Dentist
fact: Earns a B.D.S., D.M.D., or D.D.S. degree before treating patients.

name: Railroad Engineer
fact: US train drivers must be certified, and recertified every two to three years.

name: Ship's Captain
fact: Legally responsible for a ship's safe navigation, seaworthiness, cargo, and crew.

name: Airline Pilot
fact: Captaining an airliner requires an Airline Transport Pilot License, the highest pilot certificate.

name: Firefighter
fact: Trains at a local, regional, or state-approved fire academy before active duty.

name: Paramedic
fact: US certification takes 1,500-plus classroom hours and 500-plus clinical hours.

name: Chef
fact: Typically apprentices for three to four years, mixing classroom instruction with kitchen work.

name: Photographer
fact: Still frames light through a box and a lens, exactly as the first cameras did.

name: Jewelry Designer
fact: Ancient jewelry favored 24-karat gold, more accessible then than silver.

name: Textile Designer
fact: Interlaces a vertical warp yarn with a horizontal weft on a loom to design woven cloth.

name: Teacher
fact: Requires professional qualification, typically including pedagogy -- the science of teaching.

name: Khufu
fact: Commissioned the Great Pyramid; his only surviving portrait is a 3-inch ivory statuette found in 1903.

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
fact: Khufu's tomb at Giza, roughly 2.3 million limestone and granite blocks. The only Wonder still standing.

name: Pheidias
fact: Athenian sculptor (c. 480-430 BC) whose chryselephantine cult statues defined Greek monumental art.

name: Chryselephantine
fact: Greek for 'gold and ivory' -- ivory flesh and gold-leaf robes built over a hidden wooden statue core.

name: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
fact: Pheidias's roughly 12-meter seated, chryselephantine Zeus at Olympia -- lost by the 5th century AD.

name: Nebuchadnezzar II
fact: King of Babylon for forty-three years, who built the Ishtar Gate and destroyed the First Temple.

name: Ziggurat
fact: Stepped Mesopotamian temple tower; Babylon's own, Etemenanki, may underlie the Tower of Babel story.

name: Ishtar Gate
fact: Babylon's processional gate to Marduk's temple, its mudbrick fired under a lapis-blue glaze.

name: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
fact: Legendary terraced gardens; no Babylonian text or excavation confirms they ever stood at Babylon at all.

name: Croesus
fact: Lydian king whose vast wealth gave English the phrase 'rich as Croesus.'

name: Temple of Artemis
fact: Ephesus's great sanctuary to Artemis; its final, marble version had over 127 columns.

name: Herostratus
fact: Burned the Temple of Artemis in 356 BC purely to be remembered -- and still is.

name: Sostratus of Cnidus
fact: Architect credited, though disputedly, with the Lighthouse of Alexandria; Ptolemy let him sign it.

name: Lighthouse of Alexandria
fact: The Pharos, over 100 meters tall on Alexandria's harbor island; stood for more than a thousand years.

name: Mausolus
fact: Carian ruler (377-353 BC) who began his own vast marble tomb while still alive.

name: Artemisia II
fact: Mausolus's sister-wife; ruled Caria alone for two years after his death in 353 BC.

name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
fact: Mausolus's tomb at Halicarnassus -- so famous its name now means any grand tomb.

name: Chares of Lindos
fact: Sculptor of Lindos, on Rhodes, who cast the Colossus of Rhodes over twelve years.

name: Colossus of Rhodes
fact: 108-foot bronze Helios at Rhodes's harbor; stood 56 years before an earthquake felled it.

name: Protostar
fact: A collapsing cloud fragment gathering mass, glowing from infall — no core fusion yet.

name: Brown Dwarf
fact: 13 to 80 Jupiter masses — too little to fuse hydrogen, so it just cools for the rest of time.

name: Supergiant
fact: 8+ solar masses and up to a million times as luminous. Almost every one ends in a supernova.

name: Pulsar
fact: A spinning neutron star sweeping a radio beam past Earth — found by Jocelyn Bell in 1967.

name: Crab Nebula
fact: Wreckage of the supernova Chinese astronomers logged in 1054 CE, still expanding, pulsar at its core.

name: Spectroscope
fact: Splits starlight into a rainbow crossed by dark lines — each line naming an element.

name: Radio Telescope
fact: Karl Jansky's antenna caught radio hiss from the galactic center in 1932, founding the field.

name: Galaxy
fact: Stars, gas, dust and dark matter bound by gravity. Up to 2 trillion of them, by one estimate.

name: Milky Way
fact: Our barred spiral, 100-400 billion stars. The Sun orbits its center once every 240 million years.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
fact: Proved a separate galaxy by Hubble in 1925, using Cepheids. 2.5 million light-years off, and closing.

name: Spiral Galaxy
fact: A rotating disc of stars, gas and dust with arms of active star birth. About 60% of galaxies today.

name: Elliptical Galaxy
fact: Smooth and featureless, red with old stars. The giants of this shape sit at the hearts of clusters.

name: Barred Spiral Galaxy
fact: A spiral with a straight stellar bar through its core. About two-thirds of spirals have one — ours does.

name: Lenticular Galaxy
fact: A lens-shaped hybrid: a disc like a spiral's, but no arms, and gas long used up like an elliptical's.

name: Local Group
fact: Our galaxy group: 100+ members, dominated by two spirals — the Milky Way and Andromeda.

name: Galaxy Cluster
fact: Hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound by gravity — the biggest bound structures in the universe.

name: Supercluster
fact: A group of galaxy clusters and groups. The Local Group sits inside the Laniakea Supercluster.

name: Supermassive Black Hole
fact: Millions to billions of solar masses. Almost every large galaxy has one anchoring its center.

name: Accretion Disc
fact: Gas pulled from a companion star spirals in and heats enough to blaze in X-rays before it falls in.

name: Active Galaxy
fact: A galaxy outshone by its own nucleus — matter falling onto a central supermassive black hole.

name: Quasar
fact: The most luminous class of active galaxy — 3C 273 alone outshines the Milky Way by 100 times.

name: Seyfert Galaxy
fact: An ordinary-looking spiral with an extraordinarily bright core — Carl Seyfert named the class in 1943.

name: Radio Galaxy
fact: A giant elliptical blasting jets of radio-emitting particles for millions of light-years past its disc.

name: Exoplanet
fact: A planet around another star. Mayor and Queloz confirmed the first one, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995.

name: Cepheid Variable
fact: A star that swells and shrinks on a clock — its period reveals its true brightness. Leavitt, 1908-12.

name: Spectrum
fact: Starlight fanned out by wavelength — its dark lines give away a star's elements, heat, and motion.

name: Redshift
fact: Light stretched to longer wavelengths by recession or expansion. Hubble read it as the universe's growth.

name: Dark Energy
fact: About 68% of the universe, and it's speeding up the expansion. Found in 1998 supernova redshifts.

name: Dark Matter
fact: Unseen mass, about 27% of the universe — Vera Rubin found galaxies spinning too fast without it.

name: Cosmic Microwave Background
fact: The universe's first light, redshifted down to 2.7 kelvin. Penzias and Wilson found it by accident in 1965.

name: Globular Cluster
fact: Hundreds of thousands of ancient stars packed in a sphere, up to 12.7 billion years old.

name: Orion Nebula
fact: The nearest big stellar nursery, 1,300 light-years off — naked-eye visible in Orion's sword.

name: Pleiades
fact: The Seven Sisters: an open cluster of 1,000+ young stars, 444 light-years away, naked-eye visible.

name: ALS
fact: Also called Lou Gehrig's disease: a person's motor neurons die while their mind stays intact.

name: Echolocation
fact: Bouncing sound off the world to see it: orcas and other toothed whales click and read back the echoes.

name: Biomimicry
fact: Engineering copies nature's homework: a humpback's bumpy flipper now shapes wind-turbine blades.

name: Frozen Zoo
fact: A bank of frozen sperm, eggs, and cells from over 1,300 endangered species, ready to thaw.

name: Ultraviolet
fact: Light one octave bluer than violet, invisible to us -- it's what sunburns skin and makes minerals glow.

name: Fluorescent Mineral
fact: Drinks invisible UV light and throws visible color back -- fluorite even gave 'fluorescence' its name.

name: Aerogel
fact: Nicknamed 'frozen smoke': a solid that's up to 99.8% air, one of the lightest solids ever made.

name: Lichtenberg Figure
fact: The branching, fractal scar a strong charge burns through an insulator as it discharges -- lightning is one.

name: Fuel Cell
fact: Combines hydrogen and oxygen without burning them, making electricity, heat, and water -- no soot.

name: Afar Triangle
fact: The one place on Earth where seafloor-spreading-style rifting is happening on dry land, not underwater.

name: Aardvark
fact: Its claws tear open termite mounds; a single night's foraging can down 50,000 insects on its sticky tongue.

name: Beaver
fact: A keystone engineer: its dams reshape rivers into wetlands, and its four incisors never stop growing.

name: Naked Mole Rat
fact: A eusocial mammal with one breeding queen per colony, near cold-blooded, and immune to acid-triggered pain.

name: Pronghorn
fact: The fastest land mammal in the Americas -- built to outrun a cheetah species extinct for 12,000 years.

name: Fennec Fox
fact: Its ears are the largest of any canid relative to body size -- radiators for heat, dishes for sound.

name: Vampire Bat
fact: Hunts only in total darkness, reading a warm vein through heat sensors in its nose before its bite.

name: Aye-Aye
fact: Taps wood eight times a second, listens for the echo of a hollow tunnel, then fishes out the grub inside.

name: Star-Nosed Mole
fact: Its 22-tentacled nose carries 25,000+ touch sensors and can identify prey in 120 milliseconds flat.

name: Barn Owl
fact: Its two ears sit at different heights on its skull, letting it strike prey in pitch darkness by sound alone.

name: Satin Bowerbird
fact: The male builds no nest -- he builds a stick bower and decorates it almost entirely in blue to court females.

name: Leatherback Turtle
fact: Holds its core 18°C above cold water via countercurrent heat exchange, and dives deeper than any reptile.

name: Archerfish
fact: Spits a shaped water jet to knock insects off leaves, correcting its aim for light bending at the surface.

name: Electric Eel
fact: Not a true eel: 6,000 stacked cells fire up to 860 volts, and it curls around prey to shock it twice.

name: Mantis Shrimp
fact: Its claw strikes at 23 m/s, fast enough to flash-boil a bubble that hits prey with a second, separate blow.

name: Pistol Shrimp
fact: Snaps a claw shut fast enough to flash-heat a bubble past the Sun's surface temperature, at 218 decibels.

name: Bombardier Beetle
fact: Mixes two stored chemicals to fire a near-boiling, pulsed spray it can aim almost anywhere on its own body.

name: Tardigrade
fact: Dries itself into a glass-like 'tun' to survive years without water, -272°C to 149°C, and the vacuum of space.

name: Coconut Crab
fact: The largest land arthropod alive; adults give up the borrowed shell of their hermit-crab kin entirely.

name: Neith
fact: Warrior-weaver goddess of Sais, worshipped as a creator; crossed bows were her own emblem.

name: Seshat
fact: Goddess of writing and measurement who founded temples with the king in the 'stretching of the cord' rite.

name: Nefertem
fact: Young god who rose from the primordial waters as a lotus at Ra's own nostrils; member of the Memphis triad.

name: Nekhbet
fact: Vulture goddess of Upper Egypt, worshipped at Nekheb; paired with Wadjet as the crown's 'Two Ladies.'

name: Min
fact: Ithyphallic fertility god of Coptos and Akhmim whose festival carried his image to the fields at harvest.

name: Renenutet
fact: Cobra goddess of the grain harvest, name meaning 'to nurse'; guarded granaries and nursed royal infants.

name: Bes
fact: Dwarf protector of households and childbirth, shown facing forward instead of in profile to scare off evil.

name: Mut
fact: Mother goddess of Karnak, wife of Amun and mother of Khonsu in the Theban Triad; wears both of Egypt's crowns.

name: Tefnut
fact: Moisture goddess sneezed or spat into being by Atum-Ra; twin sister and consort of Shu, mother of Geb and Nut.

name: Sokar
fact: Falcon god of the Memphis necropolis, fused into Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, patron of craftsmen and the dead.

name: Wepwawet
fact: Wolf-formed 'opener of the ways' of Asyut, a standard-bearer who led the pharaoh's army and later the dead.

name: Griffon Vulture
fact: A carrion-eating scavenger whose bald head sheds heat, soaring on one of the largest wingspans of any raptor.

name: Sponge
fact: No true tissues, nerves or organs — just specialised cells filtering food from water pumped through its own pores.

name: Comb Jelly
fact: Not a jellyfish — its own animal phylum, swum by eight rows of beating cilia that split light into rainbow bands.

name: Hydra
fact: A freshwater cnidarian that clones a new body off its own side by budding, and barely seems to age.

name: Planarian
fact: Cut it into pieces and each piece can regrow a whole worm — brain included — within a couple of weeks.

name: Leech
fact: A segmented worm related to the earthworm — its bite injects an anticoagulant still used in modern surgery.

name: Ribbon Worm
fact: Fires an eversible, sometimes venom-barbed proboscis at prey — possibly Earth's longest animal.

name: Bryozoan
fact: A colony of thousands of near-identical animals under a millimetre long, sharing one skeleton — long mistaken for moss.

name: Lampshell
fact: Looks like a two-shelled clam, but a brachiopod's valves sit top and bottom, not left and right.

name: Velvet Worm
fact: Ambushes prey by firing two crossing jets of sticky slime from glands beside its jaws.

name: Horseshoe Crab
fact: Its blue, copper-based blood clots on contact with bacterial toxins and still tests every batch of injectable medicine.

name: Sea Spider
fact: Not a true spider — its body is so reduced that its own gut and gonads run out into its legs.

name: Tusk Shell
fact: A tusk-shaped shell open at both ends, buried head-down in sand, catching prey with thread-like tentacles.

name: Sea Cucumber
fact: When threatened, some species eject sticky internal organs through the anus to entangle a predator, then regrow them.

name: Feather Star
fact: A sea-star relative filtering plankton with feathery arms, gripping the reef with claws instead of tube feet.

name: Slug
fact: A land snail that lost its shell, or reduced it to an internal remnant, in several separate lineages.

name: Cuttlefish
fact: Its porous internal cuttlebone works like a submarine's ballast tank, and its pupils are shaped like a W.

name: Foraminifera
fact: A single cell that builds an elaborate calcium-carbonate shell — fossil shells like these built the Great Pyramid.

name: Radiolarian
fact: A single cell in an intricate glassy skeleton, its geometry the inspiration for Ernst Haeckel's illustrations.

name: Dinoflagellate
fact: The single-celled organism behind a glowing night wave — some species flash blue light the instant it's disturbed.

name: Diatom
fact: Encased in two interlocking glass shells fitting like a pillbox — makes a fifth or more of Earth's oxygen.

name: Euglena
fact: Carries a plant's chloroplasts to photosynthesise in light, then swims off to swallow food like an animal in the dark.

name: Paramecium
fact: Covered in thousands of beating hairs that row it through the water and sweep food into a mouth-like groove.

name: Stonewort
fact: A freshwater alga often crusted in limestone, among the closest living algal relatives that land plants have.

name: Cycad
fact: A palm-like gymnosperm older than the dinosaurs — several genera still make sperm cells that swim.

name: Ginkgo
fact: The last living species of its plant order, famous for outliving almost anything thrown at it — even an atomic bomb.

name: Hornwort
fact: Most cells hold just one giant chloroplast — unique among land plants — often housing nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

name: Clubmoss
fact: Not a moss at all — a vascular, spore-dispersing lineage older than ferns, whose oily spores once lit stage magic.

name: Manatee
fact: The gentle "sea cow" grazes seagrass and mangrove leaves in warm shallow water, and can chill to death below 20°C.

name: Dugong
fact: The only truly marine grazing mammal — its seagrass-feeding trails across the seabed likely inspired mermaid legends.

name: Hyrax
fact: A rabbit-sized rock-dweller whose closest living relatives are the elephant and the manatee.

name: Sengi
fact: Not a shrew — its closest relatives are elephants, and it can outrun almost anything its own size.

name: Tenrec
fact: Madagascar's answer to hedgehogs, shrews, and otters all at once — one species "talks" by rubbing its own spines.

name: Golden Mole
fact: Blind and earless, it "swims" through loose sand — some species find prey by sensing vibration through the skull.

name: Colugo
