fact: French mathematician and philosopher whose 1654 letters with Fermat founded probability theory.

name: Baruch Spinoza
fact: Dutch-Jewish rationalist excommunicated in 1656; argued God and Nature are one substance.

name: Gottfried Leibniz
fact: German polymath who argued reality is built from monads, substances that mirror the universe.

name: George Berkeley
fact: Irish idealist philosopher who held that objects exist only insofar as they are perceived.

name: Voltaire
fact: French Enlightenment writer who mocked Leibniz's optimism in Candide after the Lisbon earthquake.

name: David Hume
fact: Scottish empiricist who argued causation is never perceived directly, only inferred from habit.

name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
fact: Genevan philosopher whose Social Contract (1762) argued government must express the general will.

name: Adam Smith
fact: Scottish economist whose Wealth of Nations (1776) founded modern free-market economics.

name: Edmund Burke
fact: Irish statesman whose Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) founded modern conservatism.

name: Jeremy Bentham
fact: English philosopher who founded utilitarianism: the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

name: Mary Wollstonecraft
fact: English writer whose Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued for women's education.

name: Georg Hegel
fact: German idealist who argued reality unfolds through contradiction resolving into higher unity.

name: Arthur Schopenhauer
fact: German philosopher who argued a blind, striving Will underlies all appearance and causes suffering.

name: Ludwig Feuerbach
fact: German philosopher whose Essence of Christianity (1841) argued theology is really anthropology.

name: John Stuart Mill
fact: English philosopher whose On Liberty (1859) argued freedom may only be limited to prevent harm.

name: Søren Kierkegaard
fact: Danish philosopher, father of existentialism, who wrote most major works under pseudonyms.

name: Henry David Thoreau
fact: American writer who lived alone at Walden Pond and argued for civil disobedience.

name: Charles Sanders Peirce
fact: American philosopher and logician who founded pragmatism with his pragmatic maxim.

name: William James
fact: American philosopher and psychologist who developed pragmatism and coined 'stream of consciousness.'

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
fact: German philosopher who proclaimed 'God is dead' and called for humanity to be surpassed.

name: Ferdinand de Saussure
fact: Swiss linguist who founded semiotics, arguing a word's link to its meaning is arbitrary.

name: Edmund Husserl
fact: German philosopher who founded phenomenology, seeking certainty by 'bracketing' every assumption.

name: Henri Bergson
fact: French philosopher who argued an élan vital, a vital impetus, drives creative evolution.

name: John Dewey
fact: American philosopher who argued we only think when we are confronted with problems.

name: George Santayana
fact: Spanish-American philosopher: 'those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.'

name: Miguel de Unamuno
fact: Spanish philosopher whose Tragic Sense of Life (1913) grounded existence in awareness of death.

name: W. E. B. Du Bois
fact: American sociologist and first Black Harvard PhD; named 'double consciousness' and the color line.

name: Bertrand Russell
fact: British philosopher, co-founder of analytic philosophy, who argued for working less and living fuller.

name: Chernobog
fact: Named by a 12th-century monk as the 'bad god' Slavs invoked over a shared bowl -- blamed for every misfortune.

name: Belobog
fact: The 'White God' has no ancient source -- first appearing in the 1500s, invented as Chernobog's opposite.

name: Baba Yaga
fact: A witch of Slavic folklore who lives in a hut on chicken legs and travels by wooden mortar and pestle.

name: Dievas
fact: The Baltic sky god of light -- said to walk the earth disguised as a beggar, testing people's kindness.

name: Rainbow Serpent
fact: Known by dozens of names across Aboriginal Australia, it carved mountains and lives in the waterholes it made.

name: Baiame
fact: Sky father of southeastern Aboriginal Australia, who came down and shaped its rivers, mountains and forests.

name: Ta'aroa
fact: Tahitian creator god who broke out of a cosmic shell alone and built the sky and earth from its two halves.

name: Tane
fact: God of forests and birds who forced his sky father and earth mother apart, letting light into the world.

name: Rangi
fact: The Maori sky father, held in an embrace with earth mother Papa so tight their children grew up in darkness.

name: Papa
fact: The Maori earth mother -- the ground itself, wife to sky father Rangi until their son forced them apart.

name: Tawhirimatea
fact: The only child of Rangi and Papa who protested their separation, and answered it with an army of storms.

name: Tu
fact: Maori god of war, the only brother who stood against Tawhirimatea's storm rather than flee.

name: Maui
fact: Polynesian trickster hero who fished up islands with a magic hook and lassoed the sun to slow it down.

name: Makemake
fact: Creator god of Rapa Nui's birdman cult, carved into the island's rock as a face with huge eyes.

name: Haua
fact: Goddess who shared Makemake's place at the heart of Rapa Nui's birdman cult and its seabird rites.

name: Spider Woman
fact: Hopi and Navajo Spider Grandmother, credited with bringing the spindle, the loom, and weaving to the people.

name: Raven Spirit
fact: The Haida credit this shapeshifting trickster with finding the first humans hidden inside a clam shell.

name: Sedna
fact: The Inuit sea goddess, who holds the animals people hunt and withholds them when wronged.

name: Iktomi
fact: Lakota trickster, first-born son of Inyan the Rock, turned into a spider as punishment for his cunning.

name: Nanabozho
fact: Ojibwe trickster called Michabo, 'the Great Hare who created the Earth,' credited with inventing fishing.

name: Kiviuq
fact: An Inuit hero said to travel eternally by kayak and sled across the Arctic, from Alaska to Greenland.

name: Inua
fact: The spirit the Inuit believe lives in every person, animal, lake and mountain -- one life-force per kind.

name: Viracocha
fact: Andean creator god who rose from Lake Titicaca in darkness and made humankind by breathing into stones.

name: Ngai
fact: Creator god of the Kikuyu, Maasai and neighboring peoples, addressed as 'possessor of brightness.'

name: Amma
fact: Dogon sky god whose union with the earth goddess was blocked by a termite mound standing in her place.

name: Nommo
fact: The first living beings Amma made -- hermaphroditic water spirits with a human body and a fish's tail.

name: Papa Legba
fact: Guardian of the crossroads in Haitian Vodou, tracing back to Yoruba and Fon gods carried over the Atlantic.

name: Cicero
fact: Exposed the Catiline conspiracy to overthrow the Republic with four fiery Senate speeches.

discovered.note: Uncovers and denounces Catiline's plot to overthrow the Roman Republic.

name: Charlemagne
fact: Crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800, reviving the title in the West.

discovered.note: Crowned emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III at St. Peter's Basilica.

name: William the Conqueror
fact: Won the English crown at Hastings in 1066, then surveyed his new kingdom in the Domesday Book.

discovered.note: Defeats and kills Harold II at the Battle of Hastings, taking the English throne.

name: Leonardo da Vinci
fact: Painted The Last Supper and the Mona Lisa, and filled notebooks with anatomy and invention sketches.

discovered.note: Begins painting the Mona Lisa, which he kept reworking until his death.

name: Michelangelo
fact: Carved David from a single marble block, then spent four years frescoing the Sistine ceiling.

discovered.note: Completes the Sistine Chapel ceiling after four years painting it from scaffolding.

name: Henry VIII
fact: Broke from Rome to divorce his first wife; married six times, beheading two of them.

discovered.note: The Act of Supremacy makes him head of the Church of England.

name: Elizabeth I
fact: Presided over the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 during her 44-year reign.

discovered.note: English fire ships scatter the Spanish Armada off Gravelines.

name: Nicolaus Copernicus
fact: Placed the Sun, not Earth, at the center of the universe in a book published as he lay dying.

discovered.note: Publishes De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, proposing a Sun-centered universe.

name: Galileo Galilei
fact: Turned a telescope on Jupiter and was later tried by the Inquisition for saying Earth moves.

discovered.note: Publishes Sidereus Nuncius, revealing Jupiter's moons and the Moon's craters.

name: Isaac Newton
fact: United gravity and planetary motion in the Principia after reportedly watching an apple fall.

discovered.note: Publishes Principia Mathematica, unifying gravity with the laws of motion.

name: Louis XIV
fact: France's 'Sun King' ruled for 72 years and built the Palace of Versailles.

discovered.note: Begins his personal rule of France after Cardinal Mazarin's death.

name: Oliver Cromwell
fact: Led Parliament's cavalry to victory in the Civil War, then signed the king's death warrant.

discovered.note: Signs the death warrant of Charles I, who is beheaded outside the Banqueting House.

name: George Washington
fact: Crossed the icy Delaware for a surprise victory, then stepped down after two presidential terms.

discovered.note: Becomes the first President of the United States.

name: Thomas Jefferson
fact: Drafted the Declaration of Independence, then doubled the nation's size via the Louisiana Purchase.

discovered.note: Drafts the Declaration of Independence, adopted 4 July 1776.

name: Benjamin Franklin
fact: Flew a kite in a thunderstorm to prove lightning is electric, then signed all three founding documents.

discovered.note: Flies a kite in a thunderstorm, showing lightning is an electrical phenomenon.

name: Napoleon
fact: Crowned himself Emperor in 1804, then met final defeat at Waterloo eleven years later.

discovered.note: Crowns himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame.

name: Karl Marx
fact: Co-wrote The Communist Manifesto, then spent decades in London writing Das Kapital.

discovered.note: Publishes The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels.

name: Charles Darwin
fact: Collected Galápagos finches on a five-year voyage, then explained their variety through natural selection.

discovered.note: Publishes On the Origin of Species, presenting evolution by natural selection.

name: Otto von Bismarck
fact: Vowed to settle great questions with 'iron and blood,' then unified Germany within a decade.

discovered.note: Has Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor in Versailles' Hall of Mirrors.

name: Mohandas Gandhi
fact: Walked 240 miles to the sea to make illegal salt, leading India's independence movement.

discovered.note: Leads the Salt March, a 24-day walk to the sea to defy Britain's salt tax.

name: William Shakespeare
fact: Wrote Hamlet for the Globe Theatre, which later burned down when a stage cannon misfired.

discovered.note: His company builds the Globe Theatre on the south bank of the Thames.

name: Johann Sebastian Bach
fact: Directed Leipzig's church music for 27 years and once improvised a fugue for a king on the spot.

discovered.note: Becomes Thomaskantor, director of church music in Leipzig, a post he holds until his death.

name: Uruk
fact: The world's first true city, on the Euphrates around 3200 BC -- temples and walls of sun-dried mud brick.

discovered.note: Reaches its peak as the world's first true city, with monumental mudbrick temple architecture and organized urban life.

name: Epic of Gilgamesh
fact: The world's oldest surviving narrative literature -- a Sumerian king's quest for immortality, in cuneiform.

discovered.note: The earliest Sumerian poems about Uruk's king Gilgamesh are set down in writing.

name: Sargon of Akkad
fact: Conquered Uruk and the Sumerian city-states around 2334 BC to found history's first known empire.

discovered.note: Conquers Uruk and the Sumerian city-states, founding the Akkadian Empire -- history's first known empire.

name: Battle of Kadesh
fact: Ramesses II's Egyptians clashed with the Hittites in 1274 BC in the largest chariot battle ever fought.

discovered.note: Egyptian and Hittite chariot armies fight the largest chariot battle in recorded history, to a stalemate.

name: Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty
fact: Sealed in silver 15 years after Kadesh -- the oldest peace treaty with both sides' copies still surviving.

discovered.note: Egypt and the Hittites exchange silver treaty tablets, the oldest surviving peace treaty with both parties' own copies intact.

name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
fact: The Germanic king Odoacer deposed Rome's last western emperor in 476 AD, ending the empire.

discovered.note: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor, ending the Western Roman Empire.

name: Battle of Hastings
fact: William of Normandy's ship-borne cavalry defeated King Harold's army in a day, 14 October 1066.

discovered.note: William of Normandy defeats King Harold's English army, the last successful invasion of England.

name: Domesday Book
fact: William the Conqueror's survey of nearly every landholder in England, completed in 1086.

discovered.note: William the Conqueror's survey of every manor and landholder in England is completed.

name: Magna Carta
fact: Sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215 under baronial revolt -- the first charter to bind the king to law.

discovered.note: King John seals the Great Charter at Runnymede, the first document to put the English crown under the law.

name: Marco Polo
fact: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant who set off along the Silk Road in 1271 to reach Kublai Khan's court.

discovered.note: The teenage Venetian merchant sets off along the Silk Road toward Kublai Khan's court in China.

name: Fall of Constantinople
fact: Ottoman cannons breached 800-year-old walls, taking Constantinople in 1453 and ending Byzantium.

discovered.note: Sultan Mehmed II's gunpowder cannons breach Constantinople's ancient walls after a 53-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire.

name: Liquorice
fact: A legume root, not a herb — three to five years underground before it's dug up, cleaned, and dried.

name: Caryophyllene
fact: One of the few plant compounds confirmed to directly activate a cannabinoid receptor (CB2) — and it's in cinnamon, cloves, and black pepper, all classed safe to eat by the FDA.

name: Coumarin
fact: Smells of sweet hay and fresh-cut grass, and builds up in the liver at high, sustained doses — the reason cassia and true cinnamon carry different safe limits.

name: Anethole
fact: About 13 times sweeter than table sugar to the tongue, and made independently by three unrelated plant families — aniseed, star anise, and fennel all converged on the same molecule.

name: Shikimic Acid
fact: The starting molecule for synthesizing the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — a 2005 shortage of it, drawn almost entirely from star anise pods, tightened world Tamiflu supply during a flu scare.

name: Myristicin
fact: Nutmeg's own defensive chemical, and a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that clears certain neurotransmitters — a high-quality seed can carry up to 13mg of it per gram.

name: Sabinene
fact: A woody, peppery terpene shared by nutmeg's seed and mace, its own seed coat — one reason the two spices from the same fruit still taste distinct.

name: Safrole
fact: The sweet-shop smell in old-fashioned root beer, and a liver carcinogen in rodents at high dose — the US banned it as a food additive in 1960.

name: Cineole
fact: Cardamom's medicinal, cooling edge — up to 70 percent of some cardamom oils — and the same molecule that makes up most of eucalyptus oil itself.

name: Cuminaldehyde
fact: The molecule responsible for cumin's whole identity — spicy, green, a little sweaty — and the reason cumin doesn't smell like any of its carrot-family relatives.

name: Fenchone
fact: A bitter, camphor-toned compound sitting beneath fennel's aniseed sweetness — structurally in the same family as camphor itself.

name: Mastic
fact: Resin scored from a Chios shrub's bark, hardening into brittle amber tears over two to three weeks. The word 'masticate' comes from chewing it.

name: Rose Petal
fact: Dried buds and petals of the damask rose, the species behind most rose flavouring in Western and Middle Eastern kitchens.

name: Ajwain
fact: A parsley-family seed whose oil is mostly thymol — the compound that makes thyme taste like thyme.

name: Barberry
fact: A thorny shrub's tart berries, dried and sold across Iran as zereshk — the thorns are exactly why they are still mostly hand-harvested.

name: Amchoor
fact: Unripe green mangoes, peeled, sliced, and sun-dried, then ground — the sourness comes mostly from citric acid, the same acid that makes lemon juice sharp.

name: Lemon Myrtle
fact: An Australian tree whose leaf oil runs 90 to 98 percent citral, a higher concentration than lemongrass and the most citral-rich natural source known.

name: Grains of Selim
fact: Dried pods of a West African evergreen tree in the same family as custard apple and soursop — in Senegal the unripe pods are smoked before drying.

name: Dried Lime
fact: A whole lime left drying mostly out in the sun until it hardens black — the sun exposure is what actually darkens it, not the boiling step some recipes add first.

name: Wattle
fact: Roasted, ground acacia seed with a coffee, chocolate and hazelnut flavour — specialised seed-grinding tools for it date back at least 1,000 years in Australia.

name: Anardana
fact: Whole pomegranate seeds and pulp, sun-dried to reddish brown — used across North India as a souring agent the way lemon is used elsewhere.

name: Germacrene
fact: Annatto seed's single most abundant flavour compound at nearly 18 percent of the essential oil — the reason the spice smells faintly of pine and wood despite being famous only for its red dye.

name: Pinene
fact: The scent molecule behind pine resin and turpentine — mastic gum has been measured at up to 79 percent alpha-pinene, more concentrated than the pine trees it smells like.

name: Thymoquinone
fact: Nigella seed's main aromatic compound — also what thyme and oregano's own thymol slowly oxidises into.

name: Nigellone
fact: Two thymoquinone molecules fused together by sunlight during oil extraction — discovered early enough that it kept its own name instead of its chemical one, dithymoquinone.

name: Paradol
fact: Grains of paradise's slow-building pepper heat — structurally a close cousin of ginger's own gingerol.

name: Picrocrocin
fact: Saffron's bitter-tasting compound, up to 4 percent of the dried spice's weight — bound to a sugar molecule until drying breaks the two apart.

name: Safranal
fact: Saffron's aroma, freed only once heat and enzymes split picrocrocin apart during drying — it can make up 70 percent of the dried spice's volatile oil.

name: Sedanolide
fact: One of two compounds — alongside butylphthalide — credited with celery's entire smell and taste.

name: Phenylethanethiol
fact: Curry leaf's most distinctive odour molecule — sulphurous and meaty, sitting in the same leaf oil as the citrus-scented linalool it shares nothing in common with.

name: Pentylfuran
fact: Poppy seed's primary flavour compound — a furan ring with a five-carbon tail, and most of what a raw poppy seed actually tastes of.

name: Turmerone
fact: A sesquiterpene from turmeric's essential oil, entirely separate from curcumin — turmeric's colour and its characteristic smell come from two different molecules.

name: Ocimene
fact: One of the terpenes found in dried unripe mango, alongside myrcene and limonene — part of why amchoor smells faintly floral under all that sourness.

name: Panch Phoran
fact: Bengal's whole five-seed blend — fenugreek, cumin, nigella, black mustard, and fennel — used unground, unlike almost every other spice mix.

name: Chaat Masala
fact: North India's tangy street-food seasoning, built around amchoor and black salt rather than any single heat source.

name: Bok Globule
fact: A small, dark, cold pocket of dust and gas — first described by Bart Bok in 1947 — that usually collapses into a double or multiple star system rather than one star alone.

name: Cometary Globule
fact: A Bok globule with one side stripped away by a nearby hot star's ultraviolet light, left with a bright rim and a trailing dark tail.

name: Herbig–Haro Object
fact: A glowing knot where a young star's jet slams into surrounding gas at hundreds of kilometres a second — over a thousand are now catalogued, each lasting only tens of thousands of years.

name: T Tauri Star
fact: A pre-main-sequence star under 10 million years old and under 2 solar masses, still contracting toward the main sequence — named for the prototype star in Taurus.

name: Herbig Ae/Be Star
fact: The heavier, hotter counterpart to a T Tauri star — 2 to 8 solar masses, still wrapped in its birth disc, first identified by George Herbig in 1960.

name: FU Orionis Star
fact: A young star caught mid-outburst as its own disc suddenly dumps material onto it, brightening by several magnitudes for decades at a time — the average young star does this 10 to 20 times.

name: Actin Filament
fact: A helical polymer of ATP-bound actin subunits, 7 nm across, that grows faster at one end than the other — the asymmetry is what lets a motor protein read a direction.

name: Myosin
fact: A two-headed motor protein whose tails bundle into thick filaments and whose heads walk along actin, one ATP hydrolyzed per step.

name: Intermediate Filament
fact: A 10 nm rope, midway in width between actin and microtubules, built purely for toughness — it has no polarity and drives no motor.

name: Integrin
fact: A transmembrane receptor with one foot in the matrix outside the cell and one hand on the actin cytoskeleton inside — a literal handshake with its surroundings.

name: Muscle Contraction
fact: Thick and thin filaments never shorten themselves — they slide past each other, millions of tiny myosin strokes firing at once.

name: Cell Migration
fact: Crawling is push and grip: actin polymerization extends the front edge, integrins anchor it to the ground, and the cell body follows.

name: G Protein-Coupled Receptor
fact: Seven passes through the membrane and one job: turn an outside signal into an inside shape-change that swaps GDP for GTP on a G protein.

name: Receptor Tyrosine Kinase
fact: Ligand binding pairs two receptors up, and each spends ATP phosphorylating the other's tail — a handshake that builds its own docking sites.

name: Adenylyl Cyclase
fact: The enzyme a hormone reaches through a G protein to turn ordinary ATP into a completely different kind of message.

name: Cyclic AMP
fact: ATP with its tail looped back to bite its own phosphate — that loop is what turns fuel into a signal.

name: Protein Kinase A
fact: Cyclic AMP doesn't do the phosphorylating itself — it just pulls the pin that releases PKA's catalytic half.

name: Phospholipase C
fact: One enzyme, one cut through a membrane lipid, and two different second messengers come out of the same reaction.

name: Inositol Trisphosphate
fact: The water-soluble half of a split membrane lipid, carrying three phosphates — light enough to swim through the cytosol to the ER.

name: Diacylglycerol
fact: The greasy half of the same split lipid — too fat-soluble to leave the membrane, so it waits there for calcium to arrive.

name: Protein Kinase C
fact: Needs two second messengers at once, a lipid and a calcium spike, before it will touch a substrate.

name: Ras
fact: GTP-bound means on, GDP-bound means off — Ras is a molecular switch, and its stuck-on mutants drive up to 90% of some cancers.

name: MAPK Cascade
fact: Three kinases in a row, each one switching on the next, turn a single Ras signal into a wave that reaches the nucleus.

name: Cortisol
fact: A stress hormone built from cholesterol, small and greasy enough to walk straight through a cell membrane instead of knocking on it.

name: Nuclear Receptor
fact: A receptor that skips the relay entirely — it binds its hormone and the DNA it regulates in the very same protein.

name: Continent
fact: Continental crust is thick but light, so it floats higher than the seafloor — billions of years old in places.

name: Ocean
fact: One of five basins holding 97% of Earth's water, still widening where mid-ocean ridges add new seafloor.

name: Peninsula
fact: Land joined to the mainland on one side only, water on the rest — often via a narrow isthmus.

name: Archipelago
fact: A chain or cluster of islands, like Hawaii or the Azores — most often volcanic in origin.

name: Strait
fact: A narrow channel joining two seas; Gibraltar's separates Europe from Africa.

name: Isthmus
fact: A narrow land bridge between two larger landmasses, sea on both sides — the mirror of a strait.

name: Equator
fact: The imaginary line at 0° latitude, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

name: Hemisphere
fact: Half of Earth's surface — the Equator splits north from south, a meridian splits east from west.

name: Latitude
fact: Circles parallel to the Equator, 0° there to 90° at either pole — north-south position.

name: Longitude
fact: Meridians running pole to pole, perpendicular to latitude — east-west position.

name: Prime Meridian
fact: The longitude fixed at 0° by international agreement in 1884, running through Greenwich, England.

name: Time Zone
fact: A region sharing one standard time, its offset from UTC set relative to the Prime Meridian.

name: Tropic of Cancer
fact: Latitude 23.4°N — the northernmost point where the Sun sits directly overhead, on the June solstice.

name: Tropic of Capricorn
fact: Latitude 23.4°S — the southernmost point where the Sun sits directly overhead, on the December solstice.

name: Steppe
fact: Dry, treeless, temperate grassland — too dry for forest, not dry enough to be desert.

name: Savanna
fact: Tropical grassy woodland, trees spaced too far apart for the canopy to close — a fifth of Earth's land.

name: Border
fact: The line where one state's sovereign territory ends and another's begins — natural or drawn.

name: Country
fact: A political entity or its territory — sovereign state, dependent territory, or something between.

name: Nation-State
fact: A sovereign, bordered state whose population shares a common national identity.

name: Capital City
fact: The city holding a country's seat of government — not always its largest.

name: Population Density
fact: People per unit of land area — Monaco packs in over 18,000/km²; Mongolia has about two.

name: Supply Chain
fact: The network of facilities that turns raw materials into finished products and moves them on to customers.

name: Logistics
fact: Moving goods from origin to consumption — a word the military took from the French for lodgings.

name: Supply Chain Management
fact: Procurement, operations, logistics and marketing, from raw material to customer, run as one system.

name: Sales Forecasting
fact: Using past sales figures to predict short- or long-term performance for financial planning.

name: Demand Planning
fact: Predicting future customer demand so a business holds the right inventory, not too much or too little.

name: Sales & Operations Planning
fact: A monthly process, credited to consultant Richard Ling in the 1980s, that balances demand against supply.

name: Warehouse
fact: A building for storing goods, used by manufacturers, importers, wholesalers and transport firms alike.

name: Inventory
fact: The goods and materials a business holds on hand for resale, production or use.

name: Inventory Management
fact: Tracking stock with software; retail barcode scanning began in 1974, computerized records in the 1980s.

name: Safety Stock
fact: Extra inventory held on purpose, as insurance against uncertain demand, supply or forecasts.

name: Economic Order Quantity
fact: The order size that minimizes total holding and ordering costs — a formula Ford W. Harris derived in 1913.

name: Bullwhip Effect
fact: Small swings in retail demand get amplified into big swings in orders further up a supply chain.

name: Just-in-Time Manufacturing
fact: Receiving goods only as needed, to cut cost and waste — Toyota modeled it on supermarket restocking.

name: Kanban
fact: 'Signboard' in Japanese — a card that authorizes production only after the next step pulls from it.

name: Lean Manufacturing
fact: Produce only what's needed, fix problems immediately, let workers improve the process — named 'Lean' in 1988.

name: Material Requirements Planning
fact: A production and inventory scheduling system Joseph Orlicky developed in 1964.

name: Enterprise Resource Planning
fact: Integrated business-process software; research firm Gartner coined the acronym 'ERP' in the 1990s.

name: Vendor-Managed Inventory
fact: The supplier, not the buyer, decides how much stock to ship and hold — a model Walmart and P&G made famous.

name: Distribution Requirements Planning
fact: Applies MRP-style time-phased planning to a distribution network, tracking parameters like safety stock.

name: Fire Lance
fact: A bamboo tube of gunpowder and slow match lashed to a spear — the ancestor of every gun.

name: Composite Bow
fact: Horn belly for compression, sinew backing for tension, wood core between — far more pull per draw.

name: Chariot
fact: A cart built light around spoked wheels, so horses could pull it fast enough for war.

name: War Elephant
fact: An elephant armored in iron plate and scale, sent to trample ranks and break cavalry charges.

name: Horse Archer
fact: A rider firing a compact recurve bow at a gallop — the steppe's answer to heavy infantry.

name: Stirrup
fact: A foot loop hung from the saddle; a rigid paired version let riders fight without falling off.

name: Greek Fire
fact: A petroleum-based incendiary sprayed from a shipboard siphon; the Byzantines never revealed the recipe.

name: Flintlock Musket
fact: Flint struck steel to spark the priming pan — cheaper and steadier than a smoldering match cord.

name: Machine Gun
fact: Hiram Maxim's recoil-operated, water-cooled gun fired 600 rounds a minute, one crew for sixty riflemen.

name: Torpedo
fact: A self-propelled, compressed-air-driven shell of steel or bronze that runs to its target underwater.

name: Zeppelin
fact: A rigid, aluminum-framed airship lifted by hydrogen gas cells; Germany used them to bomb Britain.

name: AK-47
fact: A steel-bodied rifle that bleeds propellant gas to cycle its own bolt, built to run caked in mud.

name: Atomic Bomb
fact: A weapon of nuclear fission; the Manhattan Project bred its plutonium fuel inside a reactor.

name: Poison Gas
fact: Chlorine drifting downwind from opened cylinders — chemical warfare's first mass battlefield use.

name: Sodium Channel
fact: A membrane protein selective for sodium ions, opening on depolarization to drive the action potential's rise.

name: Potassium Channel
fact: Opens just after a sodium channel does, letting potassium leave and pulling the voltage back down.

name: Refractory Period
fact: The brief window after a spike when a sodium channel sits inactivated and a second one can't fire.

name: Node of Ranvier
fact: The bare gap between two segments of myelin, where the axon is exposed and sodium channels cluster densely.

name: Saltatory Conduction
fact: The impulse jumps from one exposed node to the next in a myelinated axon, far faster than a bare one allows.

name: Schwann Cell
fact: The peripheral nervous system's myelin-maker — the PNS counterpart to the oligodendrocyte, one axon each.

name: Mechanoreceptor
fact: A sensory nerve ending built to fire when pressed, stretched, or deformed rather than by light or chemicals.

name: Nociceptor
fact: A sensory ending tuned to potentially damaging stimuli, in skin and just as often deep in muscle and joints.

name: Pacinian Corpuscle
fact: A mechanoreceptor wrapped in 20 to 70 onion-like layers, buried deep in skin to catch vibration and pressure.

name: Muscle Spindle
fact: A stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptor inside the muscle itself, reporting how long the muscle currently is.

name: Retina
fact: Technically brain tissue, budded outward before birth — the only piece of CNS visible without surgery.

name: Photoreceptor
fact: Rods and cones share a mechanism: an opsin pigment absorbs a photon and changes shape, starting the signal.

name: Cornea
fact: The eye's clear front window, built from ~200 stacked layers of collagen fibers spaced to not scatter light.

name: Lens
fact: Over 90% protein by weight — crystallins, packed dense enough to bend light with no blood supply of its own.

name: Iris
fact: A pigmented ring of muscle around the pupil — one set of fibers narrows it, another set widens it.

name: Oculomotor Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve III: moves the eyeball with one set of fibers, shrinks the pupil with another.

name: Hair Cell
fact: Stereocilia-tufted cells turning motion into signal — the same design serves both hearing and balance.

name: Cochlea
fact: A fluid-filled spiral making almost three full turns, lined with hair cells to catch sound at every pitch.

name: Eardrum
fact: A thin cone of tissue turning air-pressure changes into vibration, passed on to three tiny bones.

name: Vestibular System
fact: The inner ear's other job besides hearing — sensing balance and orientation, via the same cranial nerve.

name: Glossopharyngeal Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve IX: taste from the tongue's back third, and the order that starts the parotid gland salivating.

name: Taste Bud
fact: Taste receptor cells clustered on the tongue — the ones at the very back use a different cranial nerve.

name: Olfactory Epithelium
fact: The nasal lining is a sense organ itself — its receptor neurons' axons bundle straight into a cranial nerve.

name: Motor Neuron
fact: A neuron whose cell body sits in the spinal cord's ventral horn, its axon running out to control a muscle.

name: Reflex Arc
fact: The simplest circuit in the body: a stretched muscle spindle synapses onto a motor neuron, no brain required.

name: Basal Ganglia
fact: Nuclei buried inside the cerebral hemispheres, shaping voluntary movement from beneath the cortex.

name: Substantia Nigra
fact: A basal-ganglia nucleus that makes dopamine; losing enough of these neurons causes Parkinson's disease.

name: Epinephrine
fact: One methyl group away from noradrenaline — the same fight-or-flight chemical, tuned by a single enzyme step.

name: Endorphin
fact: The body's own painkiller: binds the same receptors opioid drugs do, at the nerve endings that report pain.

name: Electroencephalogram
fact: Scalp electrodes eavesdropping on the cortex — mostly picking up summed postsynaptic potentials, not spikes.

name: Alpha Wave
fact: An 8-to-13-hertz rhythm on a relaxed, eyes-closed EEG, thought to arise from a thalamic pacemaker circuit.

name: REM Sleep
fact: The dreaming stage, run on acetylcholine — the same neurotransmitter active in waking, with noradrenaline off.

name: Wernicke's Area
fact: The temporal lobe's language-comprehension hub, wired to the ear's own cranial nerve to hear what it parses.

name: Broca's Area
fact: The frontal lobe's speech hub, linked to Wernicke's comprehension area by one dedicated fiber tract.

name: Sword
fact: A straight double-edged blade with a crossguard, standard among Norman knights from the 11th century.

name: Dagger
fact: A short, sharply tapered double-edged blade -- a sword scaled down to a size worn at the belt.

name: Misericorde
fact: A long, narrow dagger known from the 12th century -- thin enough to slide through a visor or armor joint.

name: Longsword
fact: An 80-110 cm double-edged blade with a two-handed grip, built to thrust through gaps in plate armor.

name: Gambeson
fact: A quilted jacket of stitched wool or linen padding -- armor by itself, or worn under mail to cushion it.

name: Chain Mail
fact: Wire rings, each riveted shut and linked through four others -- a hauberk worn in Europe for 1,900 years.

name: Shield
fact: Light wood boards faced with leather, centered on a riveted metal boss that guards the holding hand.

name: Kite Shield
fact: Almond-shaped and elongated to a point, covering a mounted rider's leg where a round shield could not.

name: Plate Armor
fact: Well-tempered steel plates, articulated joint by joint -- complete suits existed in Europe by about 1420.

name: Halberd
fact: An axe blade, a spike, and a hook for pulling riders down, all mounted on one long shaft.

name: Pike
fact: A spearhead on a shaft 3 to 7 meters long, reinforced with metal strips -- a wall against cavalry.

name: War Hammer
fact: A blunt hammer face balanced by a spike on the reverse -- stun with one side, then punch with the other.

name: Poleaxe
fact: An axe blade, a hammer, and a spearhead on one ash shaft -- three chances to find a gap in plate armor.

name: War Mace
fact: A flanged steel head riveted to a tapered handle -- ridges that focus a blow's force enough to dent plate.

name: Flail
fact: An iron-shod striking head swinging off a wooden shaft on a chain -- a threshing tool turned to war.

name: Crossbow
fact: A bow locked crosswise onto a wooden stock, cocked and released by a trigger -- common in Europe by 1100.

name: Longbow
fact: A six-foot bow made specifically of yew -- the weapon behind English victories at Crecy and Agincourt.

name: Battering Ram
fact: An iron- or steel-capped log slung on chains inside a wheeled frame, swung again and again at a gate.

name: Siege Tower
fact: A wheeled wooden tower faced in iron or wet hide against fire, rolled to a wall to drop a gangplank.

name: Katar
fact: A South Indian push-dagger with an H-shaped grip so a punching thrust lands the whole arm's weight.

name: Kris
fact: A Javanese dagger pattern-welded from layered iron and nickel-rich iron, sometimes meteoric.

name: Shotel
fact: An Ethiopian sword curved into a near semicircle, built to hook around an opponent's shield.

name: Takouba
fact: A meter-long, straight double-edged sword carried across the Sahel by Tuareg, Hausa and Fulani.

name: Tulwar
fact: A curved single-edged saber of the Indian subcontinent, known by its all-metal disc-pommel hilt.

name: Flyssa
fact: A narrow single-edged Algerian blade of the Kabyle Iflissen, pommel capped in an animal head.

name: Iklwa
fact: Shaka's short Zulu stabbing spear, its shaft cut down and its blade widened for close combat.

name: Shamshir
fact: A Persian saber curved into a radical arc; the name literally means 'lion's fang.'

name: Yataghan
fact: An Ottoman forward-curving blade with no guard, its hilt flared into two 'ears' at the pommel.

name: Repeating Crossbow
fact: A Chinese crossbow with a gravity-fed magazine of bolts, worked by one lever for rapid fire.

name: Sling
fact: A pouch on two cords, whirled overhead and released to hurl a stone farther than a bare throw.

name: Macuahuitl
fact: An Aztec wooden sword lined with obsidian blades sharper than steel, but brittle against armor.

name: Vexillum
fact: Cloth hung from a horizontal crossbar on a spear, carried by Roman cavalry -- root of the word 'vexillology'.

name: Saltire
fact: A diagonal cross. Andrew, by tradition, was crucified on one -- giving Scotland's flag its white saltire.

name: Oriflamme
fact: France's medieval royal battle standard: a blood-red banner on a gilded lance. Its name means 'golden flame.'

name: Ensign
fact: A national flag flown by a ship. Britain keeps three: White for the Navy, Blue for government, Red for trade.

name: Tricolour
fact: Three solid colour bands. France's blue-white-red, fixed in 1794, became a liberty-movement template.

name: Union Flag
fact: James I's 1606 flag overlaid Scotland's saltire on England's red cross -- Ireland's cross joined only in 1801.

name: Dannebrog
fact: Denmark's flag, said to have fallen from the sky in 1219. Official since 1625, the oldest one still flown.

name: Flag of Norway
fact: Added a blue cross to Denmark's pattern in 1821, to match the French, Dutch, and American 'flags of freedom.'

name: Flag of Sweden
fact: Blue and gold trace to Sweden's Three Crowns coat of arms, in use since at least 1364.

name: Flag of Finland
fact: Adopted at independence in 1918: blue for Finland's thousands of lakes, white for winter snow.

name: Flag of Iceland
fact: Blue for mountains and sea, white for ice, red for fire. Finalised 1915, official with the 1944 republic.

name: Flag of Germany
fact: Black, red, and gold trace to the Lützow Free Corps' Napoleonic-era uniforms -- Germany's colours since 1848.

name: Flag of Poland
fact: White and red come from the coat of arms' White Eagle on red -- national colours by 1831, flag by 1919.

name: Flag of Argentina
fact: Light blue and white from the 1810 May Revolution cockade; the gold Sun of May was added in 1818.

name: Flag of Uruguay
fact: Nine stripes for Uruguay's original nine departments, under a Sun of May shared with Argentina. Adopted 1828.

name: Flag of Brazil
fact: 27 stars map the sky over Rio on 15 Nov 1889, the day the republic was proclaimed -- one per federal unit.

name: Flag of Chile
fact: A lone white star for Venus over Andes-snow white and sky blue. Adopted 1817, decades before Texas's version.

name: Wiphala
fact: A 49-square rainbow checkerboard used by Andean Quechua and Aymara -- Bolivia's official co-flag since 2009.

name: Flag of Venezuela
fact: Francisco de Miranda's yellow-blue-red tricolour, first flown 12 March 1806 at Jacmel, Haiti.

name: Flag of Costa Rica
fact: The coat of arms shows three volcanoes between two oceans, ringed by seven stars for seven provinces.

name: Flag of El Salvador
fact: Five volcanoes for the five states of the old Central American federation, under a biblical rainbow of peace.

name: Flag of Panama
fact: A blue star for the Conservative party and a red star for the Liberal party, designed in 1903.

name: Flag of Jamaica
fact: A gold saltire quarters green and black: 'hardships there are, but the land is green and the sun shineth.'

name: Flag of Cuba
fact: A Masonic red triangle behind a white 'Lone Star,' first raised by rebels at Cardenas on 19 May 1850.

name: Flag of Mexico
fact: The coat of arms' eagle devouring a serpent on a cactus is the Aztec omen that marked Tenochtitlan's site.

name: Flag of Canada
fact: An 11-point maple leaf, adopted 15 Feb 1965 -- the point count chosen for staying sharp in wind-tunnel tests.

name: Flag of the United States
fact: 13 stripes for the original colonies, 50 stars for the states -- current design flown since July 1960.

name: Immortals
fact: Persia's elite 10,000-man guard, kept at exactly that number by instantly replacing any casualty.

name: Hoplite
fact: Greek citizen-soldiers who fought shoulder to shoulder in the phalanx behind a bronze-faced shield.

name: Sarissa
fact: Philip II's 5-7 meter Macedonian pike, longer than the Greek dory, that let phalanx rows overlap.

name: Gladius
fact: Rome's short stabbing sword, adopted from Celtiberian designs during the Punic Wars.

name: Pilum
fact: A Roman javelin with a soft iron shank that bent on impact, jamming an enemy's shield.

name: Lorica Segmentata
fact: Roman body armor of overlapping iron bands, buckled over a padded tunic from the 1st century AD.

name: Testudo
fact: Roman legionaries locked shields into a moving wall and roof, shrugging off missiles during a siege.

name: Cataphract
fact: Cavalry armored from head to hoof -- rider and horse both -- charging home with heavy lances.

name: Varangian Guard
fact: Byzantine emperors' bodyguard, deliberately recruited from Norse and later Anglo-Saxon outsiders.

name: Berserker
fact: Norse warriors said to fight in a trance-like fury; a 9th-century poem calls them 'wolf-skin men.'

name: Housecarl
fact: Paid professional soldiers of Scandinavian kings; Harold's housecarls held the line at Hastings.

name: Knight
fact: A mounted, armored warrior who owed a lord roughly 40 days of yearly service in exchange for land.

name: Trebuchet
fact: A pivoting siege beam that hurled stones at castle walls; Chinese crews once pulled its ropes by hand.

name: Chainmail
fact: Interlocking iron rings woven into mesh armor, first made by the Celts around the 3rd century BC.

name: Rapier
fact: A slender 16th-century thrusting sword born in Spain and Italy for civilian dueling, not the battlefield.

name: Scimitar
fact: A light, curved slashing sword built for mounted warfare across Persia, Arabia and the Ottoman world.

name: Janissary
fact: Ottoman infantry levied as Christian boys from the Balkans; among Europe's first troops issued firearms.

name: Landsknecht
fact: German Renaissance mercenary pikemen, known for outlandish slashed-and-puffed dress.

name: Winged Hussar
fact: Polish heavy cavalry, active 1503-1702, famed for lance charges and feathered wings on their backs.

name: Naginata
fact: A Japanese polearm with a curved blade, prized for dismounting cavalry and later favored by noblewomen.

name: Parthian Shot
fact: Firing backward at a full gallop while feigning retreat -- the Parthians' signature cavalry trick.

name: Milgram Obedience Experiments
fact: Experiments Stanley Milgram ran at Yale from 1961, testing how far people would go in obeying orders to harm someone else.

name: Asch Conformity Experiments
fact: Experiments Solomon Asch ran from 1951, testing whether people would echo an answer they knew was wrong to match a unanimous group.

name: Narcissism
fact: Personality trait of grandiosity, a constant need for admiration, and low empathy, from an ordinary style to narcissistic personality disorder.

name: Machiavellianism
fact: Personality trait for a cynical, manipulative style: deceiving and exploiting others, with little regard for conventional morality.

name: Psychopathy
fact: Personality construct of shallow emotion, low empathy and remorse, and impulsive antisocial behavior, often masked by charm.

name: Dark Triad
fact: Construct grouping narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy as three distinct, overlapping traits sharing a callous, manipulative style.

name: D-Factor
fact: Proposed common core beneath dark traits: a general tendency to maximize one's own gain at others' expense, dressed in self-justifying beliefs.

name: Cognitive Dissonance
fact: Discomfort felt when holding two contradictory beliefs, or when belief and behavior don't match, that motivates changing one of them.

name: Classical Conditioning
fact: Learning process where a neutral stimulus, paired repeatedly with a meaningful one, comes to trigger that stimulus's own response.

name: Principles of Persuasion
fact: Six patterns Robert Cialdini identified as reliably raising compliance: reciprocity, consistency, social proof, liking, authority, scarcity.

name: Foot-in-the-Door Technique
fact: Compliance pattern where agreeing to a small request raises the odds of later agreeing to a larger, related one.

name: Door-in-the-Face Technique
fact: Compliance pattern where refusing an extreme request raises the odds of accepting a smaller one that follows it.

name: Groupthink
fact: Pattern where a group's push for harmony overrides real appraisal of alternatives, steering it toward a bad decision.

name: Neuro-Linguistic Programming
fact: Techniques and a communication theory introduced by Richard Bandler and John Grinder in the 1970s; controlled studies have found no scientific support for its central claims.

name: Milton H. Erickson
fact: American psychiatrist, 1901–1980, founder of the indirect, conversational style of clinical hypnosis known as Ericksonian hypnosis.

name: M2 Bradley
fact: An aluminum-armored troop carrier armed like a tank, carrying a 25mm cannon and TOW missiles since 1981.

discovered.note: The M2 Bradley enters U.S. Army service, with fleet-wide fielding beginning in 1983.

name: UH-60 Black Hawk
fact: Two General Electric T700 turboshaft engines replace the single engine of the Huey it succeeded in 1979.

discovered.note: The UH-60A enters U.S. Army service, built with a long, low profile so it can be carried inside a C-130 Hercules.

name: CH-47 Chinook
fact: Two counter-rotating rotors cancel each other's torque, so the Chinook needs no tail rotor at all.

discovered.note: The CH-47 Chinook enters service after its first flight on September 21, 1961.

name: AH-64 Apache
fact: Its AN/APG-78 'Longbow' radar, mounted above the rotor, tracks up to 128 targets at once.

discovered.note: The AH-64D Apache Longbow is delivered to the Army in March 1997.

name: Kiowa Warrior
fact: A sensor ball above the rotor — crews call it the beach ball — packs a camera, thermal imager and laser designator.

discovered.note: The armed OH-58D Kiowa Warrior configuration enters production in May 1991.

name: M109 Paladin
fact: A 155mm howitzer on a tracked, diesel-powered chassis that moves under its own power instead of being towed.

discovered.note: The M109 self-propelled howitzer enters U.S. Army service in the early 1960s.

name: M270 MLRS
fact: One launcher firing all twelve rockets blankets a square kilometer — troops nicknamed it the 'grid square removal system.'

discovered.note: The first M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System launchers are delivered to the U.S. Army.

name: HIMARS
fact: The same launcher as the M270 MLRS, but with one rocket pod on a wheeled truck instead of tracks.

discovered.note: HIMARS first enters service in June 2005 with the 27th Field Artillery at Fort Bragg.

name: Patriot Missile System
fact: Its AN/MPQ-53 phased-array radar tracks both target and missile, radioing steering corrections back in flight.

discovered.note: The Patriot system begins replacing Nike Hercules as the Army's primary high-to-medium air defense system.

name: Javelin Missile
fact: Its onboard infrared seeker locks on before launch, so the gunner can take cover immediately — no wire or laser needed.

discovered.note: The FGM-148 Javelin enters operational service, replacing the wire-guided M47 Dragon.

name: TOW Missile
fact: Two hair-thin wires spool out behind it, carrying the gunner's steering commands to the target.

discovered.note: The BGM-71 TOW enters U.S. Army service after first production in 1968.

name: Hellfire Missile
fact: It homes in on a laser spot someone else paints on the target, rather than carrying its own radar or camera.

discovered.note: The Hellfire II variant enters U.S. Army service.

name: HMMWV
fact: Portal-axle hubs raise the drivetrain above the wheel centers, nearly doubling an SUV's ground clearance.

discovered.note: The first Humvees enter U.S. Army service.

name: Stryker
fact: An 8x8 wheeled armored vehicle trades off-road ability and armor for road speed and easy maintenance.

discovered.note: The Stryker family enters U.S. Army service, named for two Medal of Honor recipients named Stryker.

name: MRAP
fact: A V-shaped hull, first built for South Africa's Casspir in 1979, throws a mine blast sideways instead of straight up.

discovered.note: The Cougar, one of the first mass-fielded MRAP-type vehicles, enters production.

name: M16 Rifle
fact: Its aluminum-alloy receiver made it far lighter than the steel-and-walnut rifles it replaced in 1964.

discovered.note: The U.S. military adopts the M16, deploying it to Vietnam the following year.

name: M4 Carbine
fact: A shortened M16: 80% of parts interchange, but a 14.5-inch barrel makes it far easier to handle indoors.

discovered.note: The M4 carbine is officially adopted; the Army begins replacing M16s fleet-wide starting in 2010.

name: M249 SAW
fact: Adapted from Belgium's FN Minimi, its belt feed fires the M16's own round in bursts no magazine could sustain.

discovered.note: The M249 Squad Automatic Weapon enters U.S. Army service, adapted from the Belgian FN Minimi.

name: M2 Browning
fact: Designed by John Browning around 1918, it's been in continuous U.S. service since 1933 — longer than any firearm but his own M1911.

discovered.note: The M2 Browning enters continuous U.S. military service, a run unmatched except by Browning's own M1911 pistol.

name: Amyloid Precursor Protein
fact: A membrane protein encoded on chromosome 21, clipped by secretase enzymes into fragments including amyloid-beta.

name: Amyloid Beta
fact: A 36-to-43-amino-acid peptide cut from APP; the main component of the amyloid plaques found in Alzheimer's brains.

name: Amyloid Plaque
fact: Extracellular deposits of misfolded amyloid-beta in the brain's grey matter — one of Alzheimer's two hallmark lesions.

name: Tau Protein
fact: A protein that normally stabilizes the microtubule tracks running down a neuron's axon.

name: Neurofibrillary Tangle
fact: Intracellular tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, twisted into paired helical filaments — Alzheimer's other hallmark lesion.

name: Alpha-Synuclein
fact: A presynaptic protein that regulates synaptic vesicle recycling; its misfolded form builds Lewy bodies.

name: Lewy Body
fact: A round inclusion of misfolded alpha-synuclein inside a neuron, first described in 1902.

name: Apolipoprotein E
fact: A fat-transport protein whose ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.

name: Neurodegeneration
fact: The progressive loss of neurons' structure and function, ending in cell death — the process behind every dementia.

name: Dementia
fact: A syndrome of progressive cognitive decline severe enough to interfere with daily life — not one disease, but many.

name: Alzheimer's Disease
fact: The most common cause of dementia, marked by amyloid plaques and tau tangles; first described in 1906.

name: Vascular Dementia
fact: The second most common form of dementia, caused by strokes or other damage that restricts blood flow to the brain.

name: Lewy Body Dementia
fact: Dementia marked by fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and REM sleep behavior disorder.

name: Frontotemporal Dementia
fact: A family of disorders degenerating the frontal and temporal lobes, changing personality and language before memory.

name: Alois Alzheimer
fact: German psychiatrist and neuropathologist (1864–1915) who first described the disease that bears his name.

name: Friedrich Lewy
fact: German-American neurologist (1885–1950) who identified the brain inclusions later named Lewy bodies.

name: Arnold Pick
fact: Czech-German psychiatrist (1851–1924) whose 1892 case report first described what became frontotemporal dementia.

name: Auguste Deter
fact: Alzheimer's first documented patient; her 1906 autopsy revealed the plaques and tangles that define the disease.

name: Otto Kernberg
fact: Vienna-born psychiatrist who fled Nazi Austria for Chile in 1939 and later built the object relations model of personality disorders.

name: Marsha Linehan
fact: Psychologist whose 1993 book, decades after her own adolescent hospitalization, introduced dialectical behavior therapy.

name: John Gunderson
fact: Harvard psychiatrist whose 1975 paper helped define borderline personality disorder as a distinct diagnosis.

name: Peter Fonagy
fact: Psychologist who, with Anthony Bateman, built mentalization-based treatment from attachment theory's caregiver-mirroring research.

name: Jeffrey Young
fact: Psychologist trained under Aaron Beck who founded schema therapy, extending CBT to personality disorders.

name: Theodore Millon
fact: Psychologist who founded the Journal of Personality Disorders and built a biosocial theory of personality pathology.

name: Robert Cloninger
fact: Psychiatrist-geneticist who modeled personality as four temperament dimensions plus three character dimensions.

name: Mary Zanarini
fact: Harvard researcher who has followed roughly 300 hospitalized borderline personality disorder patients for decades.

name: Thomas Widiger
fact: Clinical psychologist on the DSM-III-R advisory committee and DSM-IV's first research coordinator.

name: Object Relations Theory
fact: Psychoanalytic theory holding that early caregiving relationships form lasting internalized images of self and others.

name: Splitting
fact: Defense mechanism of experiencing people as wholly good or wholly bad, with no stable middle ground.

name: Transference-Focused Psychotherapy
fact: Structured psychodynamic therapy working through a patient's contradictory feelings as they surface toward the therapist.

name: Dialectical Behavior Therapy
fact: Therapy pairing CBT technique with mindfulness and acceptance skills drawn from Zen practice.

name: Mentalization-Based Treatment
fact: Therapy building the capacity to read mental states, one's own and others', often impaired by disorganized attachment.

name: Schema Therapy
fact: Integrative therapy targeting 'early maladaptive schemas' — self-defeating patterns formed in childhood.

name: Good Psychiatric Management
fact: Less-intensive borderline personality disorder treatment that began as a drug-trial control condition.

name: Alternative DSM-5 Personality Disorder Model
fact: DSM-5 model rating personality on continuous trait and functioning scales instead of categories alone.

name: Temperament and Character Inventory
fact: 240-item questionnaire from Cloninger's model, scoring seven temperament and character dimensions.

name: McLean Study of Adult Development
fact: Decades-long study that overturned the assumption that borderline personality disorder rarely improves.

name: Ivan Pavlov
fact: Russian physiologist whose dogs' unexpected salivating led him to describe the conditioned reflex.

name: John B. Watson
fact: American psychologist who conditioned an infant, 'Little Albert,' to fear a white rat.

name: B. F. Skinner
fact: American psychologist who studied how consequences shape behavior with an operant conditioning chamber.

name: Sigmund Freud
fact: Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis after early research into cocaine's medical uses.

name: Carl Jung
fact: Swiss psychiatrist who broke from Freud in 1913 to found analytical psychology.

name: Abraham Maslow
fact: American psychologist who arranged human needs into a hierarchy topped by self-actualization.

name: Carl Rogers
fact: American psychologist who pioneered person-centered therapy built on empathy and acceptance.

name: Wilhelm Wundt
fact: German physiologist who opened the first laboratory devoted purely to psychological research.

name: Clinical Psychology
fact: Branch treating psychological problems through diagnosis, therapy, and prevention.

name: Biological Psychology
fact: Branch studying how the brain, nervous system, and neurotransmitters produce behavior.

name: Educational Psychology
fact: Branch studying how people learn, from childhood learning disorders to adult education.

name: Cognitive Psychology
fact: Branch studying mental processes like memory, perception, and problem-solving.

name: Forensic Psychology
fact: Branch applying psychology to law, from eyewitness memory to criminal evaluation.

name: Social Psychology
fact: Branch studying how others' presence, real or imagined, shapes thought and behavior.

name: Industrial-Organizational Psychology
fact: Branch applying psychology to the workplace, from hiring to employee well-being.

name: Health Psychology
fact: Branch studying how behavior, biology, and social context shape illness and health.

name: Experimental Psychology
fact: Branch using controlled laboratory methods to uncover the causes of behavior.

name: Developmental Psychology
fact: Branch studying how the human mind and behavior change across the lifespan.

name: Abnormal Psychology
fact: Branch studying atypical patterns of behavior, emotion, and thought.

name: Behaviorism
fact: School holding that only observable behavior, not introspection, belongs in psychology.

name: Psychoanalysis
fact: School holding that unconscious conflict, often from childhood, drives behavior.

name: Analytical Psychology
fact: Jung's school centered on the collective unconscious and universal archetypes.

name: Humanistic Psychology
fact: Psychology's 'third force,' emphasizing human potential over pathology or conditioning.

name: Child
fact: Between infancy and puberty — no longer a baby, not yet an adolescent.

name: Jean Piaget
fact: Swiss psychologist who mapped four stages of children's thinking, built from watching his own three kids.

name: Erik Erikson
fact: Psychoanalyst who trained as a wandering artist before Anna Freud recruited him into psychoanalysis.

name: John Bowlby
fact: British psychiatrist whose WHO report on homeless postwar children shaped his theory of infant attachment.

name: Mary Ainsworth
fact: American-Canadian psychologist whose Uganda fieldwork led her to design the Strange Situation.

name: Lev Vygotsky
fact: Soviet psychologist who argued a child's thinking is shaped by language and social interaction.

name: Harry Harlow
fact: American psychologist whose infant-monkey experiments showed contact comfort, not feeding, drives attachment.

name: Sensorimotor Stage
fact: Piaget's first stage, birth to about two, when infants learn through senses and motor action alone.

name: Object Permanence
fact: Understanding a hidden object still exists — the sensorimotor stage's key achievement.

name: Preoperational Stage
fact: Piaget's second stage, roughly ages two to seven, when symbols and words emerge before logic does.

name: Egocentrism
fact: A preoperational child's difficulty grasping that others see things differently.

name: Conservation
fact: Recognizing that quantity stays the same despite a change in shape or container.

name: Concrete Operational Stage
fact: Piaget's third stage, ages seven to eleven, when logical thought works only on concrete things.

name: Formal Operational Stage
fact: Piaget's final stage, from about age eleven, when abstract, hypothetical reasoning becomes possible.

name: Attachment Theory
fact: The claim that infants have an innate drive to bond with a primary caregiver for safety.

name: Strange Situation
fact: Ainsworth's lab test revealing an infant's attachment style through staged separations and reunions.

name: Secure Attachment
fact: The most common Strange Situation pattern — a child uses the caregiver as a secure base.

name: Avoidant Attachment
fact: An insecure pattern where a child shows little distress and avoids the caregiver on reunion.

name: Ambivalent Attachment
fact: An insecure pattern where a distressed child can't be settled even by the caregiver's return.

name: Disorganized Attachment
fact: A fourth pattern Mary Main added — contradictory, freezing behavior toward the caregiver.

name: Contact Comfort
fact: Harlow's finding that infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth surrogate over a wire one that fed them.

name: Maternal Deprivation
fact: Bowlby's hypothesis that losing a stable attachment figure causes lasting emotional harm.

name: Trust vs. Mistrust
fact: Erikson's first stage, roughly the first year, resolved by hope when caregiving is consistent.

name: Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt
fact: Erikson's second stage, roughly ages one to two, resolved by will as toddlers assert self-control.

name: Initiative vs. Guilt
fact: Erikson's third stage, ages three to six, resolved by purpose through self-started activities.

name: Industry vs. Inferiority
fact: Erikson's fourth stage, roughly ages seven to ten, resolved by competence through school success.

name: Identity vs. Role Confusion
fact: Erikson's fifth stage, adolescence, resolved by fidelity as teens search for a stable self.

name: Intimacy vs. Isolation
fact: Erikson's sixth stage, young adulthood, resolved by love through committed relationships.

name: Generativity vs. Stagnation
fact: Erikson's seventh stage, middle adulthood, resolved by care for the next generation.

name: Integrity vs. Despair
fact: Erikson's eighth and final stage, late life, resolved by wisdom through accepting a life as lived.

name: Zone of Proximal Development
fact: Vygotsky's gap between what a child can do alone and what she can do with a skilled partner's help.

name: Scaffolding
fact: Wood, Bruner, and Ross's term for support that fades as a learner gains skill.

name: Private Speech
fact: Vygotsky's term for a young child's audible self-talk, later internalized as silent inner speech.

name: Sociocultural Theory
fact: Vygotsky's claim that a child's cognitive growth is shaped by social interaction and language.

name: Babbling
fact: Repeated consonant-vowel sounds like 'bababa' that infants produce from about six months old.

name: One-Word Stage
fact: The holophrastic stage in which a single word like 'up' stands in for a whole sentence.

name: Telegraphic Speech
fact: Terse two-word combinations like 'want juice', dropping articles, from about 18 months.

name: Overregularization
fact: A child's error of over-applying a grammar rule, like saying 'goed' instead of 'went'.

name: Critical Period Hypothesis
fact: Lenneberg's claim that native language must be learned before a window closes near puberty.

name: Theory of Mind
fact: The capacity to grasp that other people hold beliefs and knowledge different from one's own.

name: False-Belief Task
fact: A test for theory of mind: does a child know Sally will look where she left her marble?

name: Meissner's Corpuscle
fact: A rapidly-adapting mechanoreceptor packed into fingertip and lip skin, tuned to light touch and flutter near 10-50 Hz.

name: Dermatome
fact: The strip of skin whose sensation runs back through one spinal nerve's dorsal root alone; 31 such strips tile the body.

name: Spinothalamic Tract
fact: The pain and temperature pathway that crosses sides within the spinal cord itself, then climbs uninterrupted to the thalamus.

name: Periaqueductal Gray
fact: A sleeve of gray matter ringing the midbrain's cerebral aqueduct that switches on the brain's own pain-suppressing opioid circuitry.

name: Olfactory Receptor Neuron
fact: A bipolar neuron in the nasal lining whose unmyelinated axon threads the skull's cribriform plate to join cranial nerve I.

name: Olfactory Bulb
fact: A forebrain structure tucked beneath the frontal lobe, wired directly to roughly ten million olfactory receptor neurons.

name: Anosmia
fact: Lost sense of smell: a skull-base blow shearing the olfactory nerve, viral damage to receptor neurons, or nasal blockage.

name: Seizure
fact: A sudden burst of excessive, synchronized action potentials firing together across neurons, hijacking behavior.

name: Epilepsy
fact: The chronic diagnosis reached once seizures keep recurring unprovoked, two or more, more than a day apart.

name: Oxytocin
fact: A hormone synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary to drive labor, milk letdown, and bonding.

name: Vasopressin
fact: An antidiuretic hormone the hypothalamus releases when osmoreceptors or autonomic blood-pressure signals detect too little water.

name: Locus Coeruleus
fact: A pons nucleus, literally 'blue spot' in Latin, the brain's principal norepinephrine source, driving sympathetic arousal.

name: Raphe Nuclei
fact: A midline chain of brainstem nuclei supplying most of the brain's serotonin, setting sleep-wake cycles and mood.

name: Ventral Tegmental Area
fact: A midbrain cluster of dopamine neurons projecting to the amygdala and other limbic targets, the origin of reward circuitry.

name: Amnesia
fact: Memory loss traced to hippocampal or medial-temporal-lobe damage: inability to recall the past, form new memories, or both.

name: Henry Molaison
fact: The 1953 patient known as H.M., whose bilateral hippocampus removal for epilepsy left him unable to form new long-term memories.

name: Korsakoff Syndrome
fact: Amnesia and confabulation from thiamine deficiency, usually chronic alcoholism, damaging the mammillary bodies near the hypothalamus.

name: Long-Term Potentiation
fact: A lasting strengthening of a synapse after brief high-frequency firing, the leading explanation for how hippocampal memories form.

name: CREB
fact: A gene-transcription factor that must switch on before a burst of long-term potentiation can harden into lasting memory.

name: Striatum
fact: The basal ganglia's main input hub, its neurons studded with synapses from the substantia nigra's dopamine axons.

name: Optic Chiasm
fact: The X-shaped point below the hypothalamus where each optic nerve's inner-retina fibers cross to the opposite hemisphere.

name: Lateral Geniculate Nucleus
fact: The thalamic relay station that takes the crossed signal straight from the optic chiasm and forwards it to the visual cortex.

name: Golgi Tendon Organ
fact: A tension sensor braided from a tendon's own collagen fibers at the muscle-tendon junction, reading force, not length.

name: Stretch Reflex
fact: The monosynaptic reflex where a muscle spindle's stretch signal synapses straight onto a spinal motor neuron.

name: Purkinje Cell
fact: The cerebellar cortex's sole output neuron, its dendritic tree fanned out flat like one vast net catching every input.

name: Charles Bell
fact: The anatomist who showed a spinal nerve's ventral root drives movement and its dorsal root carries sensation, by severing each.

name: Francois Magendie
fact: The physiologist whose rigorous root-severing experiments confirmed Bell's sensory-motor split, amid a bitter priority dispute.

name: Aplysia
fact: A sea slug with only about 20,000 neurons, many single cells so large and identifiable they can be mapped one by one.

name: Eric Kandel
fact: Won the 2000 Nobel Prize for showing serotonin, acting through cAMP, physically reshapes an Aplysia synapse to store memory.

name: Schizophrenia
fact: A psychotic disorder linked to dopamine signaling running hot in the striatum, the same receptors antipsychotics are built to block.

name: Neuromuscular Junction
fact: The chemical synapse where a motor neuron meets a skeletal muscle fiber, releasing acetylcholine to trigger contraction.

name: Unconditioned Stimulus
fact: A stimulus, like food, that triggers a reflexive response automatically, with no learning required.

name: Unconditioned Response
fact: The innate, unlearned reflex — like salivating at food — that an unconditioned stimulus reliably triggers.

name: Conditioned Stimulus
fact: A once-neutral stimulus that, through classical conditioning, has learned to predict and trigger a response.

name: Conditioned Response
fact: The learned response — like salivating to a bell alone — that a conditioned stimulus now triggers.

name: Conditioned Extinction
fact: A conditioned response fades when its stimulus keeps appearing without ever being paired with reward again.

name: Spontaneous Recovery
fact: An extinguished conditioned response can briefly reappear on its own after a rest period.

name: Stimulus Generalization
fact: Stimuli similar to a conditioned one trigger the same response too, weaker the less alike they are.

name: Stimulus Discrimination
fact: The learned ability to respond to one stimulus while ignoring similar ones — generalization's reverse.

name: Operant Conditioning
fact: Learning in which a behaviour's likelihood changes based on the consequences that follow it.

name: Positive Reinforcement
fact: Presenting a pleasant consequence after a behaviour, which raises the odds it happens again.

name: Negative Reinforcement
fact: Removing or escaping an unpleasant stimulus after a behaviour, which also raises its likelihood.

name: Positive Punishment
fact: Presenting an unpleasant stimulus right after a behaviour, which lowers the odds it happens again.

name: Negative Punishment
fact: Removing a pleasant stimulus right after a behaviour, which also lowers its likelihood.

name: Shaping
fact: Building a complex behaviour by reinforcing ever-closer approximations of it, one step at a time.

name: Observational Learning
fact: Picking up a new behaviour simply by watching someone else perform it, with no direct reward needed.

name: Vicarious Reinforcement
fact: Becoming more likely to copy a behaviour after seeing someone else get rewarded for it.

name: Sensory Memory
fact: A split-second, near-total echo of what the eyes and ears just took in, before attention picks any of it out.

name: Working Memory
fact: The system that holds information briefly while also actively manipulating it, not just storing it.

name: Memory Encoding
fact: Converting perceived information into a form the memory system can actually store — memory's first stage.

name: Memory Storage
fact: Retaining encoded material over time — memory's second stage, ranging from seconds to a lifetime.

name: Memory Retrieval
fact: Locating a stored memory and bringing it back into conscious awareness — memory's third stage.

name: Serial Position Effect
fact: Items at the start and end of a list are recalled better than items in the middle.

name: Declarative Memory
fact: Long-term memory for facts and experiences that can be consciously recalled and stated outright.

name: Procedural Memory
fact: Implicit long-term memory for how to perform a skill, used without conscious effort.

name: Semantic Memory
fact: Declarative memory for general facts and concepts, detached from the moment they were learned.

name: Episodic Memory
fact: Declarative memory for personally experienced events, tied to a specific time and place.

name: Proactive Interference
fact: Older memories already in storage make it harder to learn or recall newer, similar material.

name: Retroactive Interference
fact: Newly learned material makes it harder to recall older memories that came before it.

name: Drive Reduction Theory
fact: Behaviour is pushed by biological deficits, like thirst, that motivate action until the deficit shrinks.

name: Hierarchy of Needs
fact: Abraham Maslow's ranked ladder of human needs, from basic survival up to self-actualization.

name: James-Lange Theory
fact: Holds that bodily arousal comes first, and the felt emotion is the brain's read on those bodily changes.

name: Cannon-Bard Theory
fact: Holds that bodily arousal and the felt emotion fire at the same time, neither one causing the other.

name: Laryngoscope
fact: Robert Macintosh's 1943 curved blade lifts the epiglottis indirectly; still the most-used laryngoscope shape.

discovered.note: Robert Macintosh introduces the curved laryngoscope blade.

name: Gigli Saw
fact: A flexible twisted-wire saw Leonardo Gigli devised around 1894 to cut bone during obstructed labour.

discovered.note: Leonardo Gigli develops the wire saw for lateral pubiotomy.

name: Trocar
fact: A sharp-pointed obturator inside a hollow cannula; its name comes from French trocart, 'three-sided point.'

name: Mouth Gag
fact: Walter Whitehead's 1877 ratcheted steel frame forces the jaws apart to hold the mouth open.

discovered.note: Walter Whitehead introduces his ratcheted mouth gag.

name: DeBakey Forceps
fact: Michael DeBakey's atraumatic vascular forceps grip vessels with fine ridged jaws that won't crush them.

name: Magill Forceps
fact: Ivan Magill's 1920 angled forceps guide a breathing tube past the vocal cords without blocking the view.

discovered.note: Ivan Magill introduces the forceps for nasotracheal intubation.

name: Ear Syringe
fact: A rubber bulb drives warmed water along the ear canal's roof to flush softened wax back out its floor.

name: Otoscope
fact: The handle holds the light; an 8-diopter lens gives roughly 3x magnification of the eardrum.

name: Tuning Fork
fact: John Shore's 1711 steel fork also became a bedside tool for the Weber and Rinne hearing tests.

discovered.note: John Shore invents the tuning fork.

name: Bulldog Clamp
fact: A spring-loaded steel clamp with serrated jaws that grips a vessel shut without crushing it.

name: Deaver Retractor
fact: A thin curved steel blade hooked against an incision's edge to hold organs like the lungs clear.

name: Bone Rongeur
fact: French for 'gnawer' -- spring-loaded steel jaws that bite bone away in small, controlled bites.

name: Umbilical Cord Clamp
fact: A plastic clip left on the cord stump until the compressed tissue dries and seals on its own.

name: Vaginal Speculum
fact: Edward Cusco's 1870 two-bladed steel cylinder opens like a hinged duck's bill to reveal the vaginal walls.

discovered.note: Edward Gabriel Cusco patents the modern bivalve speculum.

name: Tenaculum
fact: A sharp locking hook Samuel Pozzi adapted from Civil War bullet forceps to steady the cervix.

name: Rectal Speculum
fact: A rigid steel tube 50-100mm long that opens the anal canal for direct inspection of the lower rectum.

name: Hemostat
fact: Emil Kocher's 1882 ratcheted steel clamp locks onto a bleeding vessel and stays shut hands-free.

discovered.note: Emil Theodor Kocher introduces his ratcheted hemostatic clamp.

name: Suction Tube
fact: A vacuum pump draws blood and fluid out through tubing -- Potain's hand-operated aspirator came first.

name: Cervical Dilator
fact: A graduated series of rods, each wider than the last, is passed in turn to gradually stretch the cervix.

name: Allis Forceps
fact: Oscar Allis's 1883 forceps use inward-curving serrated teeth to grip fascia without letting go.

discovered.note: Oscar Huntington Allis introduces the forceps for abdominal surgery.

name: Scalpel
fact: A separate steel blade clicks onto the reusable B.P. handle patented in 1915, then is thrown away.

discovered.note: The B.P. handle is patented, standardising the detachable-blade scalpel.

name: Needle Holder
fact: A ratcheted steel forceps, jaws often tipped in tungsten carbide, locks a suture needle for pushing through tissue.

name: Surgical Suture Needle
fact: A curved steel needle swaged onto its thread -- no eye to load, unlike the reusable needles it replaced.

name: Thumb Forceps
fact: A one-piece steel spring squeezed between thumb and finger -- forceps without a hinge or a ratchet.

name: Surgical Scissors
fact: Mayo scissors have semi-blunt ends for general cutting; Metzenbaum scissors are lighter, for delicate tissue.

name: Emil Kraepelin
fact: German psychiatrist who split psychosis into dementia praecox and manic-depressive insanity in 1893.

name: Ernst Kretschmer
fact: German psychiatrist who linked body build to temperament in 1921, coining the term 'schizoid.'

name: Kurt Schneider
fact: German psychiatrist whose 1923 book Psychopathic Personalities founded the modern study of PD.

name: Hervey Cleckley
fact: American psychiatrist whose 1941 The Mask of Sanity gave psychopathy its first clinical portrait.

name: Heinz Kohut
fact: Psychoanalyst who held that a caregiver's admiring 'mirroring' builds a child's self-esteem.

name: Robert Hare
fact: Canadian forensic psychologist whose Psychopathy Checklist became psychiatry's gold-standard test.

name: Personality Disorder
fact: An enduring, pervasive pattern of behavior and inner experience that departs from cultural norms.

name: Paranoid Personality Disorder
fact: Pervasive distrust that reads other people's ordinary motives as malevolent.

name: Schizoid Personality Disorder
fact: Detachment from relationships paired with a narrow, restricted range of emotion.

name: Schizotypal Personality Disorder
fact: Acute discomfort in close relationships plus odd beliefs and eccentric behavior.

name: Antisocial Personality Disorder
fact: A chronic disregard for other people's rights, without remorse, rooted in conduct before age 15.

name: Borderline Personality Disorder
fact: Unstable relationships, self-image, and emotion, with a deep fear of abandonment.

name: Histrionic Personality Disorder
fact: Excessive emotionality and attention-seeking across nearly every social context.

name: Narcissistic Personality Disorder
fact: Grandiosity, a hunger for admiration, and a marked lack of empathy for others.

name: Avoidant Personality Disorder
fact: Social inhibition and feelings of inadequacy driven by fear of criticism.
