name: Dependent Personality Disorder
fact: Excessive need to be cared for, producing submissive, clinging behavior.

name: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder
fact: Preoccupation with orderliness and control that crowds out flexibility.

name: Cold War
fact: The nuclear-armed standoff between the US-led West and Soviet-led East that never became a direct war.

discovered.note: Truman Doctrine speech marks the conventional start of the Cold War rivalry between the US and USSR.

name: NATO
fact: Founded in 1949 by the US, Canada, and ten Western European states as a Cold War defense pact.

discovered.note: The North Atlantic Treaty is signed by twelve founding member states.

name: Warsaw Pact
fact: The Soviet bloc's counter-alliance, formed in 1955 the same week West Germany joined NATO.

discovered.note: The USSR and its Eastern European satellites sign the Warsaw Treaty days after West Germany's admission to NATO.

name: Nuclear Deterrence
fact: Preventing an attack by threatening unbearable retaliation, rather than by physically blocking it.

name: Mutual Assured Destruction
fact: MAD: once both superpowers could annihilate each other after surviving a first strike, neither dared attack.

name: Massive Retaliation
fact: Eisenhower-era doctrine: answer any Soviet aggression, however small, with overwhelming nuclear force.

discovered.note: Secretary of State John Foster Dulles announces the doctrine of massive retaliation.

name: Extended Deterrence
fact: The US pledge to defend non-nuclear allies with its own arsenal -- NATO's 'nuclear umbrella.'

name: Tactical Nuclear Weapon
fact: Not a design category but a mission one: built for the battlefield, not the enemy's homeland.

name: Strategic Nuclear Weapon
fact: The counterpart to tactical weapons: aimed at an enemy's home territory, not its forces in the field.

name: NATO Nuclear Sharing
fact: US nuclear weapons based on non-nuclear NATO soil -- American-controlled in peace, allied-delivered in war.

discovered.note: The US begins moving nuclear weapons onto allied European territory, first the UK, then West Germany.

name: Nuclear Planning Group
fact: NATO's standing forum for nuclear policy, open to every member but France, meeting since 1966.

discovered.note: NATO establishes the Nuclear Planning Group after the rejected Multilateral Force proposal.

name: Flexible Response
fact: Graduated response -- conventional, then tactical, then strategic -- replacing automatic nuclear escalation.

discovered.note: NATO formally adopts flexible response as strategic concept MC 14/3.

name: Cuban Missile Crisis
fact: 1962 stand-off defused partly by a secret US pledge to remove its own missiles from Turkey.

discovered.note: The US discovers Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, opening a thirteen-day crisis.

name: Non-Proliferation Treaty
fact: 1968 treaty limiting nuclear weapons to five states, reconciled with NATO sharing only on a technicality.

discovered.note: The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons opens for signature.

name: NATO Double-Track Decision
fact: 1979 decision to deploy Pershing II and cruise missiles in Europe unless the Soviets withdrew their SS-20s.

discovered.note: NATO foreign and defense ministers adopt the Double-Track Decision.

name: INF Treaty
fact: 1987 Reagan-Gorbachev treaty eliminating an entire class of missiles -- the US withdrew from it in 2019.

discovered.note: Reagan and Gorbachev sign the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in Washington.

name: Aaron Beck
fact: American psychiatrist (1921–2021) who founded cognitive therapy from patients' automatic negative thoughts.

name: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy
fact: Merges Beck's cognitive therapy with behaviourism, treating distorted thoughts and habits directly.

name: Family Systems Therapy
fact: Treats the family, not the individual, as the unit of therapy, targeting interaction patterns.

name: Evidence-Based Practice
fact: Bases clinical decisions on the best available research rather than tradition or intuition.

name: Positive Psychology
fact: Studies what makes life flourish, not just what causes illness; founded by Martin Seligman in 1998.

name: Personal Construct Psychology
fact: Kelly's theory that people interpret events through personal constructs, like naive scientists.

name: Unconscious Mind
fact: The part of the psyche unavailable to introspection, often pictured as a submerged iceberg.

name: Transference
fact: Redirecting feelings for a childhood figure onto a present-day person, often the therapist.

name: Defence Mechanism
fact: An unconscious strategy — repression, displacement, projection — that shields against anxiety.

name: Exposure Therapy
fact: Deliberately confronting a feared stimulus, without danger, until the anxiety response fades.

name: Systematic Desensitization
fact: Joseph Wolpe's 1950s technique pairing relaxation with a graded hierarchy of feared situations.

name: Hierarchy Of Evidence
fact: Ranks research designs by reliability, from case reports up to meta-analyses of controlled trials.

name: Meta-Analysis
fact: Statistically pooling results from many studies into one combined estimate of an effect.

name: Dodo Bird Verdict
fact: Saul Rosenzweig's 1936 claim that rival therapies produce roughly equal outcomes.

name: Case Formulation
fact: A clinician's working hypothesis about what caused and now maintains a client's problem.

name: Structured Clinical Interview
fact: SCID: a semi-structured interview guide clinicians use to diagnose disorders against DSM criteria.

name: Beck Depression Inventory
fact: Aaron Beck's 1961 self-report scale — 21 questions scored 0 to 3 each — for rating depression severity.

name: Global Assessment Of Functioning
fact: A 1-to-100 clinician-rated scale of a patient's social, occupational and psychological functioning.

name: Transtheoretical Model
fact: Prochaska and DiClemente's model of behaviour change moving from precontemplation to maintenance.

name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
fact: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday events, persisting at least six months.

name: Panic Disorder
fact: Recurring unexpected panic attacks along with ongoing fear of having another.

name: Agoraphobia
fact: Anxiety about places or situations where escape or help might not be available if panic strikes.

name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
fact: Intrusive obsessions relieved only briefly by repeated compulsions, reinforcing the cycle.

name: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
fact: Intrusive memories, avoidance and heightened arousal persisting more than a month after trauma.

name: Major Depressive Disorder
fact: At least two weeks of pervasive low mood or loss of interest; no laboratory test confirms it.

name: Bipolar Disorder
fact: Mood swings between depressive episodes and abnormally elevated mania or hypomania.

name: Seasonal Affective Disorder
fact: Depressive episodes tied to season, usually winter, that fully lift the rest of the year.

name: Sociopathy
fact: Popular but non-clinical term for chronic antisocial, remorseless behavior.

name: Photic Zone
fact: The ocean's sunlit surface layer, thinning out wherever light fades below 1% of its surface strength — around 200 meters down in open water, sometimes just 15 in murky coastal seas.

name: Aphotic Zone
fact: Permanent darkness below roughly 1,000 meters, making up most of the ocean's total volume — no sunlight ever reaches it.

name: Twilight Zone
fact: The dim band roughly 200 to 1,000 meters down, also called the dysphotic zone — too faint for photosynthesis, but still lit enough for some animals to hunt by sight.

name: Pelagic Zone
fact: The open water column itself, away from shore and seafloor — some 1.33 billion cubic kilometers, with about 90% of marine life crowded into its topmost layer.

name: Benthic Zone
fact: The sea floor and the sediment beneath it, home to over a million known animal species — far more than the roughly 5,000 species of zooplankton adrift in the water above it.

name: Continental Shelf
fact: A continent's shallow, flooded edge, rarely deeper than 100 meters — under a tenth of the ocean's area, yet responsible for 15 to 20% of all its biological productivity.

name: Hydrothermal Vent
fact: Seawater that seeped into a crack near volcanic seafloor, was superheated underground to as much as 464°C, and rushes back out into water only a couple degrees above freezing.

name: Chemosynthesis
fact: Building organic matter by oxidizing inorganic chemicals instead of using sunlight — bacteria and archaea near hydrothermal vents run this on hydrogen sulfide, leaving solid sulfur behind instead of oxygen.

name: Whale Fall
fact: A whale carcass on the deep seafloor can feed a local ecosystem for 50 to 100 years, as its lipid-rich bones are broken down anaerobically by sulfur-reducing bacteria.

name: Phytoplankton
fact: Drifting, autotrophic algae and cyanobacteria that photosynthesize near the surface — together responsible for roughly half of the oxygen produced on Earth.

name: Zooplankton
fact: Tiny drifting animals and protozoans — copepods, larvae, and more — that eat phytoplankton and each other, unable to swim against a current.

name: Plankton
fact: Anything that drifts with the current rather than swimming against it, split between the photosynthesizing phytoplankton and the zooplankton that eat them.

name: Krill
fact: Shrimp-like crustaceans whose single Antarctic species alone totals some 379 million tonnes of biomass — over half of it eaten every year by whales, seals, penguins, and fish.

name: Osmoregulation
fact: A marine bony fish loses water to the sea by osmosis, so it drinks seawater and pumps the excess salt back out through its gills — a freshwater fish runs the same process in reverse.

name: Countershading
fact: A dark back and a pale belly cancel out an animal's own shadow, hiding it from below against the bright surface and from above against the dark deep — seen in sharks, dolphins, and penguins alike.

name: Bioluminescence
fact: Light made by a luciferin-luciferase reaction rather than a bulb — common enough that roughly 76% of deep-sea animal groups below 200 meters can produce it.

name: Upwelling
fact: Wind pushes surface water aside and cold, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it — just five such zones, covering 5% of the ocean, yield a quarter of the world's fish catch.

name: Marine Snow
fact: A slow, continuous fall of dead plankton, feces, and mucus-bound debris sinking from the sunlit surface — the main food supply for animals living where sunlight never reaches.

name: Pinniped
fact: Seals, sea lions, and walruses — fin-footed carnivorans that still haul out on land or ice to mate, give birth, and molt, unlike fully aquatic whales and dolphins.

name: Walrus
fact: Its tusks are canine teeth up to a meter long, used for fighting and for hauling out onto ice — not, as once thought, for digging clams from the seafloor; the snout does that.

name: Narwhal
fact: Its famous spiral tusk is really an elongated left canine tooth laced with millions of nerve endings — footage shows narwhals using it to tap and stun small Arctic cod before eating them.

name: Sea Lion
fact: An "eared seal" whose external ear flaps and forward-rotating hind flippers let it walk on all fours on land, unlike a true seal.

name: Seal
fact: A true seal has no external ear flap and can't rotate its hind flippers forward, so on land it must "galumph" on its belly — but in the water it swims more efficiently than an eared sea lion.

name: Nudibranch
fact: A shell-less sea slug named for its exposed "naked gills" — some species eat anemones and hydroids, then repurpose the stinging cells for their own defense instead of digesting them.

name: Tunicate
fact: A sea squirt's tadpole-like larva has a notochord and nerve cord like any other chordate's, but after it settles and undergoes metamorphosis it loses them all, becoming a sessile filter feeder wrapped in a tough "tunic."

name: Epipelagic Zone
fact: The sunlit surface layer, 0-200 m deep — the only zone with light for photosynthesis.

name: Mesopelagic Zone
fact: The 'twilight zone,' 200-1,000 m down — too dim for photosynthesis, lit by bioluminescence.

name: Bathypelagic Zone
fact: The 'midnight zone,' 1,000-4,000 m down — pitch black but for the odd bioluminescent flash.

name: Abyssopelagic Zone
fact: From about 4,000 m to the seafloor — crushing pressure and near-total absence of life.

name: Hadal Zone
fact: Below 6,000 m, mostly inside ocean trenches, under roughly 1,100 atmospheres of pressure.

name: Continental Slope
fact: The steep drop-off beyond the continental shelf, often cut by submarine canyons.

name: Abyssal Plain
fact: A near-perfectly flat, sediment-buried seafloor, 3,000-6,000 m down, over half of Earth.

name: Wave
fact: An oscillation of water raised by wind dragging across the surface.

name: Rogue Wave
fact: A wave over twice the surrounding sea's height — once dismissed as sailors' myth.

name: Trade Winds
fact: Steady easterlies toward the equator — northeast in the north, southeast in the south.

name: Thermocline
fact: The layer where ocean temperature drops sharply, separating warm surface from cold deep water.

name: Dermal Denticle
fact: Tooth-like scales covering shark skin, structurally the same as vertebrate teeth.

name: Ampullae of Lorenzini
fact: Jelly-filled pores on a shark's snout that sense prey's faint electric fields.

name: Claspers
fact: Paired male reproductive organs on sharks and rays, formed from the pelvic fins.

name: Spiracle
fact: A hole behind a shark or ray's eye that draws water to the gills without swimming.

name: Gill Raker
fact: Comb-like projections on a fish's gill arches that strain food from the water.

name: Otolith
fact: A calcium-carbonate ear stone in a fish's inner ear, laid down in yearly growth rings.

name: Nematocyst
fact: A jellyfish stinging cell that fires a venom-tipped thread in under a millionth of a second.

name: Siphon
fact: A cephalopod's funnel, jetting water from the mantle for rapid bursts of speed.

name: Ink Sac
fact: A cephalopod organ storing near-pure melanin, squirted out as a body-shaped decoy cloud.

name: Chromatophore
fact: A muscle-ringed pigment sac in cephalopod skin that can change color in a fraction of a second.

name: Radula
fact: A mollusk's chitinous, tooth-covered ribbon for scraping food, regrown at the back.

name: Operculum
fact: A trapdoor-like plate that seals a sea snail into its shell when it retreats.

name: Byssus
fact: Sticky protein threads a mussel spins to anchor itself to rock, unweakened by water.

name: Blowhole
fact: A whale or dolphin's nostril, relocated to the top of the head.

name: Melon
fact: A fatty organ in a toothed whale's forehead that focuses its echolocation clicks.

name: Fluke
fact: A cetacean's horizontal tail fin, made of connective tissue with no bone inside.

name: Porpoise
fact: A small cetacean with flat, spade-shaped teeth and no pronounced beak, unlike a dolphin.

name: Copepod
fact: Barely 1-2 mm long with a single median red eye — possibly the largest animal biomass on Earth.

name: Crayfish
fact: A freshwater crustacean in the same infraorder as lobsters, with feather-like gills.

name: Prawn
fact: Not a distinct scientific group from shrimp, just a common name for the larger catch.

name: Fiddler Crab
fact: The male grows one claw far larger than the other, waving it to court mates and warn off rivals.

name: Spiny Lobster
fact: No large claws on its walking legs, unlike a true lobster; it rasps its antennae instead.

name: Giant Isopod
fact: A deep-sea scavenger in a rigid, segmented shell; one captive specimen went five years without eating.

name: Amphipod
fact: A crustacean flattened side-to-side, found from fresh water to the deepest ocean trench.

name: Molt
fact: Shedding an entire rigid exoskeleton is the only way a crustacean can grow.

name: Matchlock
fact: A smoldering cord lowered into the flash pan by a lever pull -- the first trigger-fired gun mechanism.

name: Wheellock
fact: A spring-wound steel wheel spun against pyrite showers sparks into the pan -- fireable with one hand.

name: Flintlock
fact: Flint struck against a hinged steel plate showers sparks into the pan in a single motion.

name: Arquebus
fact: A matchlock bolted to a shoulder stock -- the first firearm ever built with a trigger.

name: Musket
fact: A flintlock-fired shoulder gun that became Europe's standard infantry firearm by the 1700s.

name: Pistol
fact: A wheellock handgun short enough to fire one-handed and hide under a cloak.

name: Flanged Mace
fact: Curved steel flanges brazed around the head bite into armor instead of glancing off like a club.

name: Gauntlet
fact: Overlapping steel plates riveted over a glove -- a stiff mitten form, or a fingered one for full grip.

name: Maximilian Armor
fact: Steel hammered into close-set parallel flutes for rigidity without extra weight, named for Maximilian I.

name: Proof Armor
fact: A breastplate shot with a pistol on purpose -- the dent left behind was the maker's guarantee.

name: Sallet
fact: A smooth steel skull flared into a tail over the neck, replacing the older bascinet helmet.

name: Barbute
fact: An Italian open-faced helmet, its T-shaped opening deliberately echoing the ancient Corinthian helmet.

name: Armet
fact: Two hinged cheek-pieces lock together at the chin, closing completely around the wearer's head.

name: Close Helmet
fact: Visor and bevor share the skull's own pivots, so the whole face defense swings open in one motion.

name: Burgonet
fact: An open-faced cavalry helmet with a peak over the brow -- lighter than a close helmet, easier to see in.

name: Morion
fact: A crested skull and wide brim with no face defense at all, worn by pikemen packed shoulder to shoulder.

name: Zweihander
fact: A sword scaled up past six feet, wielded two-handed by the Landsknechte's double-paid Doppelsoldner.

name: Katzbalger
fact: A short, sturdy sword with a distinctive S-shaped guard -- the Landsknecht's signature sidearm.

name: Schiavona
fact: A basket hilt of leaf-shaped iron bars fully enclosing the hand, named for the Doge of Venice's guard.

name: Smallsword
fact: A light triangular-bladed sword for the thrust alone -- no 18th-century gentleman dressed without one.

name: Main Gauche
fact: A parrying dagger for the off hand, its ring-guard curved to trap an opponent's blade point.

name: Plug Bayonet
fact: A dagger's handle jammed into the musket's muzzle -- turning an empty gun into a spear, but blocking it.

name: Socket Bayonet
fact: An iron sleeve fits around the outside of the barrel, so the musket can fire with the blade still fixed.

name: Mold Fossil
fact: A cavity left in rock after a buried shell or bone dissolves away completely, preserving only the negative impression of its outer surface.

name: Cast Fossil
fact: The positive replica left when minerals carried by water later fill a mold, reproducing an organism's original shape in stone.

name: Law of Superposition
fact: In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock, the oldest layer sits at the bottom and each layer above it is younger.

name: Index Fossil
fact: A fossil species that lived briefly but spread widely enough that finding it in two rock layers, however far apart, proves those layers formed at the same time.

name: Isotope
fact: A variant of an element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons — identical chemistry, different mass, sometimes different stability.

name: Half-Life
fact: The fixed time it takes for half of a radioactive isotope's atoms to decay, unchanged no matter how much of the isotope is present.

name: Radiometric Dating
fact: Dating a rock by measuring the ratio of a radioactive isotope trapped inside it to the stable element it has decayed into over time.

name: Geologic Time Scale
fact: Earth's 4.5-billion-year history divided into eons, eras, periods and epochs, pinned down by fossil correlation between rock layers and radiometric ages of the rock itself.

name: Burgess Shale
fact: A middle Cambrian rock formation in the Canadian Rockies whose fine mud buried an entire seafloor community in low oxygen, preserving soft tissue that almost never fossilizes.

discovered.note: Charles Walcott, secretary of the Smithsonian, finds the deposit near Field, British Columbia, and collects over 65,000 specimens from it before 1924.

name: Lagerstätte
fact: German for "storage place": a sedimentary deposit with exceptional fossil richness or preservation, from soft-tissue Konservat sites like the Burgess Shale to dense bone-bed Konzentrat sites.

name: Sclerochronology
fact: Reading the growth bands laid down in coral, shell or bone the way tree rings are read, to recover daily, tidal, and seasonal cycles from millions of years ago.

name: Jaw
fact: Evolved from a pair of gill-arch supports, repurposed from holding gill slits open into a biting hinge.

name: Lobe-Finned Fish
fact: Paired fins on a fleshy, muscular stalk with internal bones, not a ray-finned fish's thin bony rays.

name: Tiktaalik
fact: A 375-million-year lobe-finned fish with a mobile neck and wrist bones inside its fin — a real 'fishapod'.

name: Acanthostega
fact: An early tetrapod with eight digits per limb, yet still gilled and too weak-ribbed to leave the water.

name: Ichthyostega
fact: An early tetrapod with sturdier overlapping ribs, dragging itself more like a seal than a salamander.

name: Tetrapod
fact: Any four-limbed vertebrate descended from lobe-finned fish — a group that still includes limbless snakes.

name: Amniotic Egg
fact: A membrane-wrapped, fluid-buffered egg that develops away from water, unlike a naked jelly-coated one.

name: Amniote
fact: A tetrapod whose amniotic egg let it complete development entirely on dry land for the first time.

name: Synapsid
fact: An amniote with one temporal opening behind each eye for jaw muscle — the branch leading to every mammal.

name: Sauropsid
fact: The amniote branch of every reptile and bird; it excretes nitrogen waste as uric acid, not urea.

name: Therapsid
fact: A synapsid with teeth split into incisors, canines and postcanines, legs set beneath the body, not sprawled.

name: Cynodont
fact: Greek for 'dog tooth'; later forms had one large snout foramen marking a muscular, likely whiskered face.

name: Auditory Ossicles
fact: Malleus, incus, stapes — three tiny middle-ear bones found only in mammals; reptiles make do with one.

name: Endothermy
fact: Making body heat from metabolism rather than sunlight — the trait that makes mammals and birds warm-blooded.

name: Bat
fact: The only mammal built for true powered flight — a skin membrane stretched across four long finger bones.

name: Diaphragm
fact: The dome of muscle below the lungs that pulls air in by expanding the chest when it contracts.

name: Reticulum
fact: The honeycomb-walled second stomach chamber that works with the rumen as one fermentation vat.

name: Omasum
fact: The 'book stomach' — leaf-like folds that wring water and fatty acids out of digesta before the true stomach.

name: Abomasum
fact: The ruminant's 'true stomach' — the chamber that secretes acid and enzymes like an ordinary mammal's.

name: Blubber
fact: Vascularized fat under the skin, up to half a marine mammal's weight, that insulates even under pressure.

name: Canine Tooth
fact: The pointed tooth for gripping and tearing — so prominent in dogs that the family Canidae is named for it.

name: Molar
fact: A flat back tooth for grinding — one part of the differentiated dentition reptiles never evolved.

name: Incisor
fact: The front cutting tooth — in rodents like beavers it never stops growing, worn down only by gnawing.

name: Opposable Thumb
fact: A thumb that rotates to press pulp-to-pulp against the fingers — true opposition is rare outside primates.

name: Hibernation
fact: Months of minimal heartbeat and near-freezing body heat that let a mammal outlast a winter with no food.

name: Ocean Current
fact: A large-scale drift of surface seawater, set moving by wind dragging across it hour after hour.

name: Coriolis Effect
fact: Earth's spin bends the path of anything moving freely across its surface — right up north, left down south.

name: Ocean Gyre
fact: A basin-wide loop of surface current, curved by the Coriolis effect into a slow rotating wheel.

name: El Niño
fact: Trade winds slacken every few years, Pacific upwelling stalls, and warm water spreads over cold.

name: Thermohaline Circulation
fact: The ocean's slow deep-water conveyor, driven by cold, salty water sinking at the poles.

name: Halocline
fact: A sharp boundary in salinity — commonly a lens of river water resting on denser seawater in an estuary.

name: Pycnocline
fact: The layer where density changes fastest — set by temperature near the equator, salinity near the poles.

name: Internal Wave
fact: A wave that rolls along a hidden boundary between water layers of different density, not along the surface.

name: Spring Tide
fact: Sun and Moon lined up at new or full moon, their pulls adding together for the month's largest tidal range.

name: Ocean Wave
fact: Wind stress rippling the sea into a moving shape that carries energy forward while the water mostly stays put.

name: Swell
fact: Waves that have outrun their storm and sorted themselves by wavelength into smooth, evenly spaced rollers.

name: Breaker
fact: A wave steepened past the point of stability in water shallower than about half its own wavelength.

name: Seamount
fact: An undersea volcanic mountain, often born near a mid-ocean ridge, that never breached the surface.

name: Sonar
fact: Sound, not light or radio, for seeing underwater — it travels farther and faster through water.

name: Echo Sounder
fact: Times a ping's round trip to the seafloor, times the speed of sound in water, for a depth reading.

name: Giant Tube Worm
fact: An adult with no mouth, gut, or anus. It feeds bacteria in its plume, then digests them from inside.

name: Lanternfish
fact: Up to 65% of deep-sea fish biomass. Its light-organ pattern is a signature to spot rival or mate in the dark.

name: Hatchetfish
fact: Erases its own silhouette: belly photophores dim or brighten to match the faint light falling from above.

name: Sea Ice
fact: Frozen ocean water that rejects nearly all its salt as it forms, leaving the ice itself almost fresh.

name: Salt Marsh
fact: A tidal wetland whose grasses trap sediment so well it rivals a rainforest for net productivity per acre.

name: Utahraptor
fact: The largest known dromaeosaurid at up to 7 m long, with a sickle claw around 24 cm — a 2001 sandstone block held seven individuals together, hinting at gregarious behavior.

discovered.note: Named by Kirkland, Gaston and Burge after a large claw find prompted excavation of Utah's Gaston Quarry.

name: Troodon
fact: Named for its serrated 'wounding teeth', with an enlarged braincase for its size — a 2023 study found females shared communal nests, laying eggs at a steep incline like modern megapodes.

name: Albertosaurus
fact: A smaller tyrannosaurid than T. rex at 8-9 m — a bonebed along Alberta's Red Deer River, excavated 1997-2008, yielded 26 individuals of mixed ages, fueling debate over pack behavior.

discovered.note: Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn for the province where the first remains were found.

name: Yutyrannus
fact: At roughly 1,400 kg, the largest dinosaur known with direct evidence of feathers — 40 times heavier than the previous record holder — its filaments preserved as imprints up to 20 cm long in fine volcanic ash.

discovered.note: Named by Xu Xing and colleagues from three specimens in China's Yixian Formation.

name: Deinocheirus
fact: Known for nearly 50 years only from 2.4 m arms found in 1965, a mystery solved by two 2013-2014 skeletons revealing a sail-backed, duck-billed ornithomimosaur with fish scales among its stomach stones.

discovered.note: Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska finds its giant forelimbs in Mongolia, a mystery unsolved until nearly-complete skeletons turn up in 2013-2014.

name: Majungasaurus
fact: A Madagascan abelisaurid with a rounded horn on its fused frontal bones — the only non-avian theropod with direct fossil evidence of cannibalism, its own tooth-mark spacing matching bite marks on other Majungasaurus bones.

name: Cryolophosaurus
fact: The first carnivorous dinosaur described from Antarctica, excavated from Mount Kirkpatrick in 1990-91 — nicknamed 'Elvissaurus' for a crest that rises perpendicular to the skull just above the eyes, then fans sideways.

discovered.note: Formally described from Mount Kirkpatrick remains, the first non-avian dinosaur officially named from Antarctica.

name: Sinosauropteryx
fact: The first non-avian dinosaur ever found with feathers, described in 1996 — preserved melanosomes show a banded tail and a countershaded body, dark above and light below, and one specimen's gut held a small lizard.

discovered.note: A Liaoning farmer's find, recognized by Phil Currie as the first dinosaur outside Avialae shown to have feathers.

name: Argentinosaurus
fact: Known only from fragmentary vertebrae and limb bones, scaled against more complete relatives to estimate 30-35 m long and 65-80 tonnes — among the largest land animals ever to walk the earth.

discovered.note: Formally described by Bonaparte and Coria from bones a farmer found near Plaza Huincul, Argentina, in 1987.

name: Mamenchisaurus
fact: A Chinese sauropod whose 18-19 lightly built, highly pneumatic neck vertebrae made up nearly half its total body length, among the longest necks, relative to body size, of any known animal.

discovered.note: First discovered at a highway construction site in Sichuan Province, China.

name: Amargasaurus
fact: A small sauropod with a double row of tall, bifurcated neural spines down its neck and back, the tallest reaching 60 cm — Sharpey's fibers found in 2022 suggest ligaments spanned them, skin-covered, as a sail.

discovered.note: Its only known skeleton is found in Argentina's La Amarga Formation, led by José Bonaparte.

name: Edmontosaurus
fact: One of the largest known hadrosaurids at up to 12 m, known from several 'mummified' specimens whose fossilized skin preserves a broad, beaked snout used to crop tough gymnosperm browse.

name: Corythosaurus
fact: A hadrosaur with a tall, helmet-shaped bony crest resembling a cassowary's or a Corinthian helmet, its internal chambers thought to have resonated calls like a wind instrument when the animal exhaled.

discovered.note: Barnum Brown finds the first skeleton, complete with skin impressions, along Alberta's Red Deer River.

name: Torosaurus
fact: Named by Marsh in 1891 during the Bone Wars, its perforated frill gave it the longest skull of any known land animal — long debated as a mature Triceratops, though a 2022 study again supports it as a separate genus.

discovered.note: Named by Othniel Charles Marsh from skulls John Bell Hatcher collected in Wyoming.

name: Centrosaurus
fact: A single-horned ceratopsian behind Alberta's Hilda mega-bonebed, believed the largest dinosaur bonebed ever found — thousands of individuals, read by most as a herd drowned attempting to cross a flooded river.

name: Kentrosaurus
fact: A Tanzanian stegosaur with short plates toward the shoulders grading into long spikes toward the tail and hips — most of Hennig's original 1,200 bones from some 50 individuals were later destroyed in WWII bombing.

discovered.note: Edwin Hennig describes it from Tendaguru, Tanzania, expedition material; most of the original bones are later destroyed in WWII bombing of Munich.

name: Borealopelta
fact: A nodosaur that sank upside-down onto a seafloor and fossilized in three dimensions, skin and armor intact — melanosomes show reddish countershading, and its gut still held fern fragments and wildfire charcoal.

discovered.note: A miner finds it at an oil sands operation near Fort McMurray, Alberta; six years of preparation follow.

name: Heterodontosaurus
fact: A small South African ornithischian, barely over a metre long, with three distinct tooth types in one jaw — cone-shaped incisors, enlarged canine-like tusks, and chisel-like cheek teeth for cutting vegetation.

discovered.note: Its holotype skull is found at Tyinindini in South Africa's Transkei.

name: Pteranodon
fact: Not a dinosaur — a pterosaur with a toothless, spear-like beak; males reached wingspans of 5.6-7.6 m with a tall, forward-projecting crest, while smaller females carried only a small, rounded one.

discovered.note: O.C. Marsh names it from Kansas chalk fossils, for its complete lack of teeth.

name: Mosasaurus
fact: Not a dinosaur — a marine squamate related to monitor lizards and snakes, up to 12 m long, with a second row of teeth on the roof of its mouth. An 1808 Cuvier identification of it helped establish extinction as real.

discovered.note: Georges Cuvier identifies a Maastricht skull as an extinct marine reptile, bolstering the then-controversial idea of extinction.

name: K-Pg Extinction
fact: The event that ended the non-avian dinosaurs 66 Mya, tied to a 10-15 km asteroid striking Chicxulub, Mexico — the 1980 Alvarez hypothesis pointed to a worldwide layer of iridium, an element rare on Earth but common in asteroids.

discovered.note: Luis and Walter Alvarez propose the impact hypothesis after finding iridium spiking 20-160 times normal levels at the boundary layer worldwide.

name: Coprolite
fact: Fossilized dung, a trace fossil rather than a body part — named in 1829 by William Buckland, who found spiral markings and undigested fragments inside that reveal what an extinct animal actually ate.

discovered.note: William Buckland coins the term, from Greek for 'dung' and 'stone'.

name: Bone Wars
fact: The 1877-1892 rivalry between Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, who between them named 142 new dinosaur species from a starting point of nine — using bribery, sabotage and stolen workers along the way.

discovered.note: Rivalry between Cope and Marsh intensifies into open competition, peaking through 1892.

name: Arandaspis
fact: One of the oldest known vertebrates: a small armoured jawless fish from Ordovician Australia.

name: Sacabambaspis
fact: An armoured jawless fish the length of a forearm, named for the Bolivian village that yielded it.

name: Astraspis
fact: A jawless fish armoured in star-shaped tubercles, among the oldest vertebrates known from North America.

name: Cephalaspis
fact: A bottom-feeding jawless fish; its helmet-like head shield held sensors for prey buried in mud.

name: Pteraspis
fact: A small armoured jawless fish with a horned snout, filtering plankton in Devonian seas.

name: Birkenia
fact: A jawless fish under 10 cm, its trunk covered in chevron-patterned rod-shaped scales.

name: Conodont
fact: Known 150+ years only from tiny tooth-like elements; the eel-like animal itself surfaced in the 1980s.

name: Placoderm
fact: The first jawed vertebrates: fish armoured in bony plates, jaws evolved from forward gill arches.

name: Dunkleosteus
fact: An armoured apex predator with no teeth — bony jaw blades sharpened themselves as it bit.

name: Bothriolepis
fact: The most widespread Devonian vertebrate genus: an armoured bottom-dweller on jointed fins.

name: Coccosteus
fact: A small armoured predator whose neck joint let its skull tip back for a wider bite.

name: Climatius
fact: A finger-length 'spiny shark' bristling with fifteen spines, one before nearly every fin.

name: Cladoselache
fact: An early shark so well preserved in Ohio's Cleveland Shale its muscle and kidneys survive.

name: Stethacanthus
fact: A Carboniferous shark relative whose males alone grew an anvil-shaped brush on the back.

name: Xenacanthus
fact: An eel-bodied freshwater shark with a fin down its back and a spine jutting from its head.

name: Cheirolepis
fact: One of the earliest ray-finned fish, first known with the skull bones later seen across the group.

name: Eusthenopteron
fact: A Devonian lobe-fin nicknamed 'the Prince of Miguasha,' its fin bones matching a tetrapod's arm.

name: Panderichthys
fact: A flat-headed Devonian lobe-fin with wrist-like fin bones and a chamber that may have gulped air.

name: Osteolepis
fact: A lobe-fin from a Scottish lake prone to oxygen crashes, scaled in sensory-laced cosmine.

name: Hagfish
fact: The only living animal with a skull but no vertebral column; its slime gels seawater in a flash.

name: Lamprey
fact: One of two living jawless vertebrate lineages, feeding through a toothed sucking disc, not a jaw.

name: Queensland Lungfish
fact: Barely changed in 100+ million years: a single lung it uses when its river runs low on oxygen.

name: Coelacanth
fact: Thought extinct since the dinosaurs, until a curator found one in a trawler's catch in 1938.

name: Morganucodon
fact: A shrew-sized mammaliaform from around 205 million years ago, still carrying the old reptile-style jaw joint alongside the new mammal one. Its teeth show it grew a first set as a juvenile and replaced them once, the same pattern every mammal alive uses today.

name: Monotreme
fact: The only mammals that lay eggs instead of bearing live young — the platypus and four echidna species are all that's left. They still nurse the hatchlings on milk, which is what keeps them classified as mammals at all.

name: Multituberculate
fact: Small, rodent-like mammals named for the rows of cusps on their molars. They ran alongside the dinosaurs and outlasted them by tens of millions of years, persisting from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Eocene — over 130 million years, longer than any other mammal lineage — before losing out to competition from early rodents.

name: Marsupial
fact: Pregnancy lasts as little as 12 to 33 days — too short for a proper placenta to develop — so a blind, furless joey crawls out and finishes growing latched to a teat in the pouch, fed on milk instead of blood.

name: Placental Mammal
fact: In a placental pregnancy the fetal tissue sits directly in a pool of the mother's blood inside the placenta, exchanging oxygen and nutrients through a membrane that keeps the two bloodstreams from actually mixing — letting the fetus develop in the womb far longer than any marsupial's joey does.

name: Baiji
fact: A freshwater dolphin found only in China's Yangtze River, nearly blind and reliant on sonar — a disability that left it colliding with boat propellers on one of the world's busiest waterways. Declared functionally extinct in 2006, it was the first cetacean species driven extinct by human activity.

name: Hispaniolan Solenodon
fact: One of the very few venomous mammals: venom from modified salivary glands runs down grooves in its second lower incisors and into the bite. Its lineage split off before the dinosaurs went extinct, changing so little since that it's considered a living fossil.

name: Sumatran Rhinoceros
fact: The smallest living rhinoceros, and the only Asian rhino with two horns instead of one — and the only one covered in a coat of reddish-brown hair. Fewer than 80 mature individuals remain, in scattered pockets of Sumatra and Borneo.

name: Laotian Rock Rat
fact: First found for sale as meat in a Laotian market in 1996 and described as a new species in 2005 — until a 2006 study placed it in Diatomyidae, a rodent family known only from fossils and presumed extinct for 11 million years. It looks like a cross between a rat and a squirrel, with a limp, furred tail.

name: Indri
fact: The largest living lemur, with only a rudimentary stub of a tail, unlike every other lemur. Unusually for a lemur it's active by day, and family groups sing loud, coordinated duets that can last over three minutes and carry for kilometers through Madagascar's forest.

name: Mountain Pygmy Possum
fact: Known only from fossils and presumed extinct until a live one turned up at a Victorian ski resort in 1966. It's the only small Australian mammal that truly hibernates, sleeping up to seven months a year under boulder fields, fattened beforehand mostly on migrating bogong moths.

name: Red Panda
fact: Not closely related to the giant panda at all — its nearest kin are raccoons, weasels, and skunks, and it's the sole living member of its own family, Ailuridae. It grips bamboo stalks with a 'false thumb' formed from an enlarged wrist bone, an adaptation the giant panda evolved separately.

name: Pygmy Hippopotamus
fact: About a quarter the weight of a common hippopotamus, and built for a different life — solitary and mostly nocturnal in West African forest and swamp, rather than gregarious in open rivers. Fewer than 2,500 are estimated to remain in the wild.

name: Numbat
fact: A termite specialist that laps up to 20,000 termites a day with a long, sticky tongue — its up to 50 teeth are too small and blunt to bother chewing them. It's the only marsupial that's active exclusively in daylight.

name: Eukaryote
fact: A cell with a true, membrane-bound nucleus, and — with very few exceptions — mitochondria inside it.

name: Endosymbiotic Theory
fact: Mitochondria and chloroplasts both descend from free-living bacteria that an ancestral cell engulfed and kept.

name: Choanoflagellate
fact: A single-celled or colonial protist with one collared flagellum — the closest living relative of animals.

name: Multicellularity
fact: Many cells cooperating as one body with a division of labor — it evolved independently at least 25 times.

name: Body Plan
fact: The blueprint of symmetry, layers, and limb layout shared by every member of an animal phylum.

name: Hox Gene
fact: Tells an embryo which body part belongs where, along the head-to-tail axis — conserved 550 million years.

name: Evo-Devo
fact: Comparing how different animals build their bodies, gene by gene, to see how development itself evolved.

name: Sexual Reproduction
fact: Two gametes, each halved by meiosis, fuse into one zygote carrying a full set mixed from both parents.

name: Asexual Reproduction
fact: Offspring from one parent, no gametes fused — mitosis and binary fission both get there without a partner.

name: Coevolution
fact: Two species reshaping each other by natural selection — flower and pollinator as often as parasite and host.

name: Red Queen Hypothesis
fact: A species must keep adapting just to hold its ground against rivals who keep adapting too.

name: Gregor Mendel
fact: An Augustinian friar who bred and counted some 28,000 pea plants, and worked out the rules of inheritance.

name: Alfred Russel Wallace
fact: Sketched out natural selection during a malarial fever in the Malay Archipelago, then mailed it to Darwin.

name: Lynn Margulis
fact: Argued mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free bacteria — about fifteen journals rejected the paper.

name: Ernst Mayr
fact: Defined a species as a group that breeds only among itself, and tied speciation to geographic isolation.

name: J.B.S. Haldane
fact: Proposed in 1949 that carrying one sickle-cell gene resists malaria — confirmed five years later.

name: Microbead
fact: Polyethylene beads melted for scouring grit in face scrubs -- banned from US rinse-off cosmetics, 2015.

name: Synthetic Microfiber
fact: Shed from synthetic clothing in the wash — fleece garments alone shed over 170% more than other fabrics.

name: Tire Wear Particle
fact: Ground off tire tread by road friction -- one of the largest single sources of microplastic pollution.

name: Weathered Plastic Debris
fact: Sunlight and wear crumble litter like plastic bags into fragments once loose in the environment.

name: Primary Microplastic
fact: Manufactured at microscopic size from the start, not fragmented from something larger.

name: Secondary Microplastic
fact: Formed when a larger plastic item weathers and fragments after it is already out in the environment.

name: Microplastic
fact: A plastic particle under 5 millimetres across -- the size line drawn for primary and secondary alike.

name: Moth
fact: The domesticated silkmoth has been bred for so many generations that it can no longer fly and no longer exists in the wild.

name: Wasp
fact: Its black-and-yellow warning pattern is mimicked by many harmless insects for protection, a phenomenon called Batesian mimicry.

name: Aphid
fact: For much of the year a colony is entirely female, cloning itself asexually generation after generation before switching to sexual reproduction in autumn.

name: Earwig
fact: Its name comes from an old, essentially undocumented belief that earwigs crawl into people's ears.

name: Stick Insect
fact: Heteropteryx dilatata, native to Malaysia, Sumatra and Thailand, is the heaviest known stick insect species, weighing up to 65 grams.

name: Silverfish
fact: One of the few insects that keeps moulting after reaching adulthood — it may shed its cuticle 17 to 66 times over its life.

name: Bristletail
fact: When disturbed, it can spring up to 30 centimetres into the air — a huge leap for an insect usually under 2.5 centimetres long.

name: Mayfly
fact: Its lineage stretches back to the Late Carboniferous, some 320 million years ago, making it one of the most ancient winged insect groups alive today.

name: Springtail
fact: Estimated at up to 100,000 individuals per square metre of soil, it may be among the most abundant macroscopic animals on Earth.

name: Exoskeleton
fact: Grown as chitin fibers embedded in a protein matrix, then stiffened by cross-linking reactions called sclerotization.

name: Compound Eye
fact: Built from thousands of individual lens units called ommatidia, each aimed in a slightly different direction.

name: Tracheal System
fact: Delivers oxygen straight to tissues through branching tubes — insects have no lungs and don't rely on blood to carry oxygen.

name: Insect Spiracle
fact: A valved opening into the tracheal system; insects can hold it shut between breaths to cut water loss.

name: Hemolymph
fact: An insect's version of blood, but it usually carries no oxygen at all — that job belongs entirely to the tracheal system.

name: Malpighian Tubule
fact: Filters waste from the hemolymph and concentrates it into uric acid, which needs almost no water to excrete.

name: Ecdysis
fact: A rigid exoskeleton can't stretch, so growth requires splitting the old cuticle open and stepping out of it entirely.

name: Complete Metamorphosis
fact: Larva and adult can look so different they barely seem related — the whole body is rebuilt inside a pupa between them.

name: Incomplete Metamorphosis
fact: No pupal stage — each nymph already looks like a small, wingless version of the adult, changing a little more at every molt.

name: Imaginal Disc
fact: Pouches of cells folded up inside a caterpillar-like larva, already fated to become a wing, leg, or eye once the pupa unfolds them.

name: Hardy–Weinberg Principle
fact: The null model: absent selection, mutation, migration or drift, allele frequencies hold exactly steady.

name: Stabilizing Selection
fact: Natural selection that trims both extremes of a trait, keeping the population near the average.

name: Directional Selection
fact: Natural selection that favours one extreme of a trait, shifting the population's average toward it.

name: Disruptive Selection
fact: Natural selection that favours both extremes of a trait over the middle, hollowing out the average.

name: Allopatric Speciation
fact: Speciation driven by a geographic barrier that blocks gene flow between two halves of a population.

name: Sympatric Speciation
fact: Speciation with no geographic split at all — reproductive isolation arises within a shared range.

name: Founder Effect
fact: A new population founded by only a few individuals starts with a skewed, incomplete slice of the gene pool.

name: Population Bottleneck
fact: A catastrophic crash in numbers that leaves a survivors' gene pool shaped mostly by chance.

name: Analogous Structure
fact: Same job, unrelated build — a structure that converged on a similar form without a shared ancestor.

name: Convergent Evolution
fact: Unrelated lineages, facing the same kind of problem, independently evolving similar solutions.

name: Divergent Evolution
fact: Lineages sharing a common ancestor growing less alike as each adapts to its own environment.

name: Atavism
fact: An ancestral trait, thought lost, reappearing when a mutation switches its dormant genes back on.

name: Biogenetic Law
fact: Haeckel's discredited claim that embryonic development visibly replays a species' evolutionary history.

name: Spontaneous Generation
fact: The superseded theory that living things — maggots from meat, mice from rags — arise from non-living matter.

name: Biogenesis
fact: Life comes only from existing life — the principle that finally displaced spontaneous generation.

name: Panspermia
fact: The fringe, untested hypothesis that life could hitch a ride between worlds on a comet or meteoroid.

name: Darwin's Finches
fact: About 18 Galápagos songbird species, all descended from one ancestral finch, each with a beak shaped by diet.

name: On the Origin of Species
fact: Darwin's 1859 book laying out evolution by natural selection and descent with modification.

discovered.note: Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species, the founding text of evolutionary biology.

name: Molecular Evidence
fact: DNA comparison as evidence for evolution: humans and chimpanzees differ across less than 2% of their genome.

name: Rhizosphere
fact: Soil reshaped by root secretions — plants leak 20-40% of their fixed sugars and acids straight into it.

name: Microbiome
fact: The community of microbes sharing one habitat, plus everything they are doing there.

name: Biofilm
fact: Microbes glued to a surface in their own slime — sugars, proteins and DNA they secrete themselves.

name: Endophyte
fact: A bacterium or fungus living inside a plant, causing it no visible harm, sometimes real benefit.

name: Holobiont
fact: A host plus every symbiont living in or on it, treated as one ecological and evolutionary unit.

name: Probiotic
fact: A live microbe that, in the right numbers, actually benefits the host who eats it — the WHO's definition.

name: Frankia
fact: A nitrogen-fixing filamentous bacterium partnering with non-legumes like alder, in nodules of its own kind.

name: Martinus Beijerinck
fact: Isolated the nodule bacterium in 1888; traced tobacco mosaic disease to something smaller than a cell.

discovered.note: Filters tobacco mosaic sap and finds it still infectious, naming the agent contagium vivum fluidum.

name: Sergei Winogradsky
fact: Found in 1887 that a bacterium could live on sulfur alone; invented the column showing soil's hidden layers.

discovered.note: Shows the sulfur bacterium Beggiatoa oxidizes hydrogen sulfide for energy, discovering chemolithotrophy.

name: Ilya Metchnikoff
fact: Watched cells swarm a thorn pushed into a starfish larva in 1882, and named the process phagocytosis.

discovered.note: Discovers phagocytosis in transparent starfish larvae; shares the 1908 Nobel Prize for the work.

name: Pestalotiopsis microspora
fact: The first fungus shown to subsist on polyurethane plastic with no oxygen at all.

name: Chewing Gum
fact: Its base is synthetic rubber, not tree resin — U.S. makers dropped chicle for it by the 1960s.

name: Wallace Line
fact: A faunal boundary through the Malay Archipelago, between Bali and Lombok and through the Makassar Strait, with Asian placental mammals to its west and Australian marsupials to its east.

discovered.note: Wallace draws the boundary from his own field observations; Thomas Henry Huxley names it 'Wallace's Line' in 1868.

name: Georges Cuvier
fact: Compared fossil mammoth and mastodon bones to living elephants and concluded species had ceased to exist entirely — the first rigorous proof that extinction was real.

discovered.note: Presents comparative anatomy of fossil elephant remains, establishing extinction as an accepted scientific fact.

name: Catastrophism
fact: Cuvier's proposal that Earth's past was shaped by sudden, short-lived, sometimes violent upheavals that wiped out whole faunas, rather than by the slow grind uniformitarians preferred.

name: Charles Lyell
fact: Argued in Principles of Geology that slow, everyday processes — erosion, sedimentation, uplift — given enough time, could explain all of Earth's geology; Darwin carried volume one aboard the Beagle.

discovered.note: Publishes the first volume of Principles of Geology.

name: James Hutton
fact: Read Scotland's rock cycle as proof Earth was inconceivably old, closing his 1788 theory with 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end.'

discovered.note: Publishes Theory of the Earth in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh.

name: Uniformitarianism
fact: The principle that the same gradual processes at work today — erosion, sedimentation, uplift — have always operated; Hutton proposed it, Lyell systematized it, and it gave Darwin the deep time evolution needed.

name: Punctuated Equilibrium
fact: Eldredge and Gould's 1972 model: most species show long stretches of stasis in the fossil record, punctuated by comparatively brief bursts of change concentrated around speciation events.

discovered.note: Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould propose the model, building on Ernst Mayr's geographic model of speciation.

name: Cambrian Explosion
fact: Beginning about 538 million years ago, nearly every major living animal phylum appears in the fossil record within a geological eyeblink of 13 to 25 million years.

name: LUCA
fact: The single population of cells, estimated around 4.2 billion years old, from which every living thing — bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes alike — descends.

name: Molecular Clock
fact: Zuckerkandl and Pauling's 1962 observation that differences between species' proteins accumulate roughly linearly with time, letting calibrated DNA differences estimate a divergence date.

discovered.note: Émile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling introduce the concept from hemoglobin comparisons.

name: Vicariance
fact: A population's range split by a new geographic barrier — a rising mountain range, a spreading sea, a closing isthmus — rather than by any organism traveling to a new place.

name: Background Extinction Rate
fact: The steady, low-level baseline pace of species loss between mass extinctions, roughly one species per million species-years — today's extinction rate runs far above it.

name: Chicxulub Crater
fact: A 180-kilometer-wide scar buried under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, left by a roughly 10-kilometer asteroid about 66 million years ago; found in 1978, but not confirmed as an impact structure until 1991.

discovered.note: Alan Hildebrand and colleagues confirm rock samples link the buried crater to the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary.

name: Single-Use Plastic
fact: Designed to be thrown away after one use — 20 companies make half the world's supply of it.

name: Plastic Pollution
fact: About 368 million tonnes of plastic are made worldwide each year; only 9% of it has ever been recycled.

name: Marine Debris
fact: Manufactured waste adrift at sea; about four-fifths of it starts on land, carried out mostly by rivers.

name: Great Pacific Garbage Patch
fact: A drifting Pacific debris patch twice the size of Texas, mostly fishing gear by weight.

name: Ghost Net
fact: A lost or abandoned fishing net that keeps trapping fish and other animals for years afterward.

name: Photodegradation
fact: Sunlight snapping a polymer's carbon bonds; a bag can shatter into 2,000 pieces after 3 months outdoors.

name: Plastic Recycling
fact: Melting plastic waste down and remolding it — of all plastic ever made, only about 9% has been recycled.

name: Pyrolysis
fact: Heating plastic past 250 °C with no oxygen breaks it back into oil, gas and char instead of burning it.

name: Bioplastic
fact: Plastic made from biomass like corn starch or sugarcane instead of petroleum — still 2% of output.

name: Landfill
fact: An engineered waste site with liners to contain leachate; still the world's third-largest methane source.

name: Incineration
fact: Burning waste to ash and flue gas, cutting its volume by 95% or more while recovering heat as energy.

name: Container Deposit Legislation
fact: A refunded deposit on containers — schemes like Denmark's return over 90% of what's sold.

name: Waste Picker
fact: Someone who earns a living salvaging recyclables from waste; an estimated 1-2% of people worldwide do.

name: Extended Producer Responsibility
fact: A policy making manufacturers, not just consumers, financially responsible for a product's end of life.

name: Circular Economy
fact: An economy built to keep materials circulating by design, rather than 'take, make, dispose'.

name: Thomas Robert Malthus
fact: Argued population grows faster than food supply — the essay that sparked Darwin's idea of natural selection.

discovered.note: Publishes An Essay on the Principle of Population.

name: Peppered Moth
fact: Soot-blackened bark flipped the odds: dark moths went from rare to 98% of Manchester's population.

name: Gradualism
fact: Darwin's own view: species transform continuously in small steps, no sharp line between one form and the next.

name: Microevolution
fact: Allele frequencies shifting generation to generation within one population — evolution's fastest scale.

name: Macroevolution
fact: Patterns visible only above the species level — speciation, extinction, radiations — over deep time.

name: Gene Duplication
fact: A copying error leaves two versions of a gene — one keeps the old job, the other is free to evolve a new one.

name: Pseudogene
fact: A duplicated gene's spare copy, disabled by mutations nothing selects against — a fossil in the genome.

name: Comparative Anatomy
fact: Lining up skeletons across species — a whale's flipper bones match a human arm, bone for bone.

name: Biogeography
fact: Where a species lives, and where its relatives live, often says more about history than habitat does.

name: Polyploidy
fact: An error in cell division leaves extra full sets of chromosomes — instant isolation from the parent species.

name: Frost Wedging
fact: Water in a crack freezes and expands 9% — with enough force at -22°C to split any rock.

name: Exfoliation
fact: Rock peels off in curved sheets as buried pressure releases — it rounded Half Dome's face.

name: Stalactite
fact: Calcium carbonate deposited drop by drop from a cavern's ceiling — about 0.13 mm a year.

name: Stalagmite
fact: Grows upward from a cave floor, drip by drip, fed by the same water dripping off a stalactite.

name: Cave Column
fact: A stalactite and stalagmite that finally met in the middle — floor to ceiling in one piece.

name: Karst
fact: Limestone terrain gone to holes: sinkholes above, caves and vanishing rivers below.

name: Permafrost
fact: Ground frozen continuously for two years or more. The oldest known has stayed frozen 700,000 years.

name: Frost Heave
fact: Ice lenses growing underground shove the surface up a foot or more as the ground freezes.

name: Thermokarst
fact: Thawing ice-rich permafrost collapses the ground into karst-like hollows — no limestone involved.

name: Solifluction
fact: Waterlogged summer soil creeping slowly downhill over ground still frozen underneath.

name: Laterite
fact: Tropical wet-dry cycling leaches silica from soil, concentrating iron and aluminium instead.

name: Podzol
fact: Boreal-forest soil leached ash-grey on top by acids. The name is Russian for 'under-ash'.

name: Chernozem
fact: Black steppe and prairie earth, 4-16% humus — some of the most productive farmland on Earth.

name: Gley Soil
fact: Waterlogged soil gone blue-grey as anaerobic microbes strip oxygen from its iron instead of air.

name: Black Cotton Soil
fact: Basalt weathered under wet-dry monsoon seasons into cracking, swelling black clay.

name: Splash Erosion
fact: Raindrop impact on bare soil throws particles up to 1.5 m — water erosion's mildest stage.

name: Sheet Erosion
fact: A thin, even film of runoff strips soil off bare ground — up to 100 tons an acre in one storm.

name: Rill Erosion
fact: Runoff concentrates into narrow channels a few centimetres deep, erased each ploughing season.

name: Gully Erosion
fact: A rill left too long deepens into a channel metres deep — beyond anything a plough can undo.

name: Badland
fact: Soft, impermeable rock cut by so many gullies that only bare ridges stand between them.

name: Ventifact
fact: Sandblasted by wind-driven grains into flat, polished facets — one facet, or up to three.

name: Desert Pavement
fact: Wind blows a desert's fine sand and dust away, leaving pebbles behind as an interlocking lag.

name: Barchan Dune
fact: A crescent dune with horns trailing downwind — scarce sand, one steady wind direction.

name: Constellation
fact: A pattern of stars grouped by an observer -- 88 are formally recognized today.

name: Ecliptic
fact: The Sun's apparent yearly path across the sky, tilted 23.4 degrees to the equator.

name: MUL.APIN
fact: Babylonian star catalogue on clay tablets naming 66 stars and constellations, c. 1000 BCE.

name: Zodiac
fact: Belt of constellations along the ecliptic, split into 12 equal signs by Babylonian astronomers.

name: Aries
fact: Zodiac's first sign; Babylonians saw these stars as a farmhand before they became a ram.

name: Taurus
fact: Named 'the Bull of Heaven' in Babylon's MUL.APIN -- the bull Ishtar sent against Gilgamesh.

name: Gemini
fact: Named for the mythological twins Castor and Pollux, its two brightest stars.

name: Cancer (constellation)
fact: Faintest zodiac constellation; Babylonian boundary stones show it as a turtle, not a crab.

name: Leo
fact: Called UR.GU.LA, 'the Great Lion,' in Babylonian astronomy; its star Regulus means 'little king.'

name: Virgo
fact: Its star Spica means 'ear of grain'; Babylonians linked the constellation to grain goddess Shala.

name: Scale
fact: A pivoted beam with a pan at each end; Egyptian weighing stones survive from c. 2600 BCE.

name: Libra
fact: Once 'the Scorpion's Claws'; its stars are still named for the southern and northern claw.

name: Scorpio
fact: Named MUL.GIR.TAB by Babylonians; placed opposite Orion, the hunter it killed in Greek myth.

name: Sagittarius
fact: Depicted as a centaur archer, its arrow aimed at Scorpius's red star Antares.

name: Capricorn
fact: Pictured as a goat-fish hybrid since the Bronze Age; a symbol of the Babylonian god Ea.

name: Aquarius
fact: Called GU.LA, 'the Great One,' by Babylonians and identified with the water god Ea.

name: Pisces
fact: Its two fish are tied by a cord -- Aphrodite and Eros in disguise, fleeing the monster Typhon.

name: Capsid
fact: Repeating protein subunits called capsomeres, self-assembling into whatever shape has the lowest free energy.

name: Viral Envelope
fact: A patch of the host's own membrane, stolen on the way out through budding, studded with viral proteins.

name: Nucleocapsid
fact: The capsid plus the genome and core proteins it holds, counted as one packaged unit.

name: Tobacco Mosaic Virus
fact: The first virus ever identified, in 1892 — infectious sap that passed straight through a bacteria-proof filter.

name: Baltimore Classification
fact: David Baltimore's 1971 scheme: seven classes of virus, sorted by the route each genome takes to become mRNA.

name: Reverse Transcriptase
fact: Writes DNA from an RNA template, running the usual direction of molecular biology backward.

name: Retrovirus
fact: An RNA virus that copies itself into DNA and splices that copy permanently into a host chromosome.

name: RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase
fact: Copies RNA straight from RNA. No uninfected cell keeps this enzyme around — only an RNA virus's genome encodes it.

name: Polyprotein
fact: One long chain translated from a single reading frame, cut apart afterward into several working proteins.

name: Bacteriophage T7
fact: A 40,000-base-pair genome and a self-made DNA polymerase, fast enough to burst E. coli in about 25 minutes.

name: Bacteriophage Lambda
fact: The model for the lysis-or-lysogeny decision: its CI repressor and rival Cro protein form a genetic coin flip.

name: Bacteriophage ΦX174
fact: The first DNA genome ever fully sequenced, in 1977 — 5,386 bases with genes that overlap each other.

name: HIV
fact: A retrovirus that infects the CD4+ helper T cells meant to organize the immune response, then destroys them.

name: Influenza A Virus
fact: Its genome comes in eight separate RNA segments — exactly why two flu strains in one cell can swap parts.

name: Rabies Virus
fact: Bullet-shaped and neurotropic, riding nerve endings to the brain. Once symptoms start, it is almost always fatal.

name: Poliovirus
fact: A bare icosahedral shell around 7,500 bases of RNA, spread mouth-to-gut through water fouled by sewage.

name: Adenovirus
fact: 240 hexon proteins build the shell; twelve fiber-tipped spikes at the corners grab onto a new cell.

name: Herpes Simplex Virus
fact: Its DNA genome can go quiet inside a sensory neuron for a lifetime, flaring up whenever something disturbs it.

name: SARS-CoV
fact: The coronavirus behind the 2002-2004 SARS outbreak, docking onto the ACE2 receptor on lung cells to get in.

name: Human Papillomavirus
fact: An 8,000-base circular DNA genome in a small bare shell. Two of its types cause seven in ten cervical cancers.

name: Hemagglutinin
fact: The influenza spike that grabs sialic acid on a host cell, then flips shape at low pH to fuse the envelope in.

name: Neuraminidase
fact: Cuts the sialic acid that would otherwise glue freshly budded flu virions in place. Tamiflu jams this enzyme.

name: Integrase
fact: Splices a retrovirus's DNA copy into a host chromosome. HIV's version is a target of antiretroviral drugs.

name: Sirius
fact: The brightest star in the night sky — its return each July, just ahead of the Nile's flood, anchored the ancient Egyptian calendar.

name: Betelgeuse
fact: A red supergiant marking Orion's shoulder, big enough that swapped in for the Sun it would swallow the inner planets.

name: Rigel
fact: Orion's foot star, a blue supergiant near 12,000 kelvin — hotter, bluer, and more luminous than Betelgeuse.

name: Deneb
fact: The tail star of Cygnus, over 1,400 light-years off — bright enough at that range to be one of the most luminous stars known.

name: Vega
fact: Lyra's brightest star and the first star besides the Sun ever photographed — the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE.

name: Altair
fact: Aquila's brightest star, only 17 light-years off — it spins so fast the star bulges visibly at its equator.

name: Arcturus
fact: The brightest star north of the celestial equator — found by following the arc of the Big Dipper's handle.

name: Procyon
fact: Canis Minor's brightest star, Greek for 'before the dog' — it rises just ahead of Sirius from most northern latitudes.

name: Aldebaran
fact: Taurus's brightest star, a red giant 45 times the Sun's width marking the bull's eye — Arabic for 'the follower' of the Pleiades.

name: Regulus
fact: Leo's brightest star, Latin for 'the little king' — it sits so near the ecliptic that the Moon and planets cross in front of it.

name: Antares
fact: Scorpius's brightest star, a red supergiant 680 times the Sun's radius — Greek for 'rival of Mars,' after its ember-red glow.

name: Capella
fact: Auriga's brightest star, 'the goat star' — named for Amalthea, the mythical she-goat that nursed the infant Zeus.

name: Castor
fact: One of Gemini's twin stars, named for the mortal horseman of Greek myth — Homer called him 'the horse breaker.'

name: Pollux
fact: Gemini's other twin star, named for the immortal son of Zeus — a champion boxer who beat a king in the ring.

name: Polaris
fact: The current North Star, under a degree from the north celestial pole, at the tip of Ursa Minor's tail.

name: Ursa Major
fact: The Great Bear, third-largest of the 88 constellations — Callisto, turned into a bear, swept into the sky by Zeus.

name: Ursa Minor
fact: The Little Bear, home to Polaris at the tip of its tail — ancient Phoenician sailors steered by it, not the larger bear.

name: Cassiopeia
fact: The vain queen's constellation, a W of five bright stars — Poseidon condemned her to circle the pole, upside-down half the time.

name: Cepheus
fact: Andromeda's father and Cassiopeia's husband, King of Aethiopia — five stars tracing a child's drawing of a house.

name: Orion
fact: The hunter, one of the sky's most recognizable figures — his three-star belt points the way to half a dozen neighboring stars.

name: Canis Major
fact: The Greater Dog, Orion's hunting companion — home to Sirius, found by extending Orion's Belt southeast.

name: Canis Minor
fact: The Lesser Dog — just two bright stars, but Procyon, its lead star, always rises moments before the Dog Star itself.

name: Scorpius
fact: The scorpion that killed Orion — placed on the sky's opposite side, so the hunter forever flees as it rises.

name: Ophiuchus
fact: The Serpent Bearer, depicted grappling a snake while treading on Scorpius — sometimes miscalled a '13th zodiac sign.'

name: Serpens
fact: The only one of the 88 constellations split into two disconnected halves, divided by Ophiuchus, who holds it.

name: Cygnus
fact: The swan, its brightest star Deneb marking the tail — ancient myths disagree on whose transformation it commemorates.

name: Lyra
fact: The lyre of Orpheus, placed in the sky by Zeus after the musician's death — its music had nearly won his wife back from Hades.

name: Aquila
fact: The eagle, its brightest star Altair marking the bird's head — Arabic for 'the flying eagle.'

name: Canes Venatici
fact: The Hunting Dogs, a 1687 invention of Johannes Hevelius born from a translation error — Ptolemy's 'club' became 'dogs.'

name: Boötes
fact: The herdsman, appearing to drive the Great Bear around the pole — home to Arcturus, the brightest northern star.

name: Corona Borealis
fact: The Northern Crown, a half-circle of stars — Ariadne's wedding gift from Dionysus, set in the heavens to mark their marriage.

name: Auriga
fact: The charioteer, cradling the she-goat Amalthea and her Kids — Capella marks the goat that nursed the infant Zeus.

name: Big Dipper
fact: Seven stars of Ursa Major forming a ladle, not a constellation of its own — two of them point straight at Polaris.

name: Winter Triangle
fact: Sirius, Betelgeuse, and Procyon, one from each of three neighboring constellations — an almost-equilateral triangle.

name: Summer Triangle
fact: Vega, Deneb, and Altair, the brightest star of Lyra, Cygnus, and Aquila — each a corner of the same wide triangle.

name: Cigar Galaxy
fact: A starburst galaxy near Ursa Major forging stars ten times faster than the Milky Way, stretched cigar-thin by a neighbor's pull.

name: Whirlpool Galaxy
fact: The first galaxy ever recognized as spiral-shaped, its arms stirred by a smaller companion galaxy merging into it.

name: Ring Nebula
fact: A dying sun-like star's outer layers, shed into a glowing ring around the white dwarf core left behind.

name: Gnomon
fact: A vertical rod that tells time and season by its shadow — the working part of every sundial.

name: Sundial
fact: The earliest known sundials are Egyptian and Babylonian shadow clocks, dated to around 1500 BCE.

name: Water Clock
fact: Kept time by a steady drip when the sun wasn't visible -- by night, or under cloud.

name: Armillary Sphere
fact: Nested rings modelling the sky's great circles -- equator, ecliptic, meridians -- around a central Earth.

name: Antikythera Mechanism
fact: At least 30 meshing bronze gears turned by hand, predicting eclipses and planetary positions decades out.

name: Astrolabe
fact: A flat brass model of the sky that tells time, finds latitude, and casts a horoscope from one reading.

name: Merkhet
fact: A plumb line on a wooden bar -- Egypt's simplest tool for finding north and telling the hour by starlight.

name: Eratosthenes
fact: Chief librarian at Alexandria who measured Earth's circumference from two shadows, to within a few percent.

name: Hipparchus
fact: Catalogued roughly 850 stars, then found by comparing older records that the equinoxes slowly creep.

name: Claudius Ptolemy
fact: His Earth-centered Almagest, circles turning on circles, stood as astronomy's last word for over 1,400 years.

name: Eudoxus of Cnidus
fact: Nested 27 invisible spheres around the Earth, around 370 BCE, to reproduce every planet's looping path.

name: Aristarchus of Samos
fact: Proposed the Sun stood still and Earth moved around it -- some 1,800 years before Copernicus dared the same.

name: Zhang Heng
fact: Han-dynasty polymath who set his armillary sphere turning on its own, driven by a water clock, around 125 CE.

name: Nabta Playa
fact: A ring of megaliths in Egypt's desert, raised around 4800 BCE, its gates facing summer solstice sunrise.

name: Eclipse
fact: The Moon crossing directly between Sun and Earth, or Earth's shadow falling across the Moon.

name: Saros Cycle
fact: 223 lunar months, about 18 years and 11 days, after which nearly the same eclipse comes round again.

name: Ionic Bond
fact: Na+ and Cl- locked by opposite charge — melting the crystal apart takes 801°C.

name: Covalent Bond
fact: Shared electrons, not traded ones. Diamond is one giant covalent molecule.

name: Hydrogen Bond
fact: Weak, fast, and constant — each water molecule holds about 3.6 of them at once.

name: Van der Waals Force
fact: The faintest attraction in chemistry — too weak to liquefy helium without deep cold.

name: Hydrophobic Effect
fact: Water pushes oily molecules together — it isn't the oil doing the reaching.

name: NADH
fact: NAD+ carrying two electrons it picked up while a nutrient was being oxidised.

name: Quaternary Structure
fact: Separately folded chains assembled into one machine — hemoglobin's four subunits.

name: Protein Domain
fact: A 50-to-250-residue stretch that folds into its own shape wherever it ends up.

name: Actin
fact: 1 to 5 percent of a cell's protein by weight — one of the cytoskeleton's three filaments.

name: Kinesin
fact: Walks hand-over-hand toward a microtubule's plus end, cargo in tow.

name: Dynein
fact: Walks the other way — toward a microtubule's minus end, back to the cell's centre.

name: Motor Protein
fact: Spends one ATP hydrolysis per step to walk a filament, not just to fold.

name: Antibody
fact: Y-shaped, and the immune system can build roughly 10 billion different versions.

name: Lysozyme
fact: Fleming named it in 1922 — an enzyme that bursts bacteria by cutting their wall.

name: Histone
fact: Small, positively charged, rich in lysine and arginine — DNA's own spool.

name: Nucleosome
fact: 146 base pairs of DNA wound 1.65 times around eight histone proteins.

name: Telomere
fact: TTAGGG, repeated, capping a chromosome — and a little shorter after every division.

name: Telomerase
fact: Rebuilds the chromosome-end repeats most cells let shrink. Nobel Prize, 2009.

name: Mismatch Repair
fact: Catches base-pairing errors that slipped past DNA polymerase's own proofreading.

name: G Protein
fact: On when it holds GTP, off once its own enzyme activity clips that to GDP.

name: GTP
fact: ATP's cousin with guanine instead of adenine — fuel and a signal both.

name: Phosphorylation
fact: A phosphate tag that flips a protein's shape, and its job, on or off.

name: Allosteric Regulation
fact: One binding site changes another — hemoglobin's four seats talk to each other.

name: Five Themes of Geography
fact: Location, place, human-environment interaction, movement, region — the NCGE/AAG's 1984 teaching framework.

name: Antarctica
fact: The only continent no country owns — an international treaty holds every territorial claim in abeyance.

name: Arctic Ocean
fact: The smallest, shallowest of the five oceans, and the only one covered in drifting sea ice most of the year.

name: China
fact: Capital Beijing. Sericulture began here 8,500 years ago; China guarded the silk monopoly for a thousand more.

name: Japan
fact: Capital Tokyo. An archipelago of four main islands and 14,000+ smaller ones, set on the Pacific Ring of Fire.

name: India
fact: Capital New Delhi. Independent since 15 August 1947, when British India split into India and Pakistan.

name: Mongolia
fact: Capital Ulaanbaatar. Nomadic life on the steppe has centred on the felt-covered ger for thousands of years.

name: Kazakhstan
fact: The Botai, in northern Kazakhstan, left the earliest strong evidence of horse domestication, c. 3500 BCE.

name: Nepal
fact: Capital Kathmandu. Everest sits on its China border, and Nepal holds parts of all 14 of the world's 8,000m peaks.

name: Sri Lanka
fact: Formerly Ceylon, and still the source of 'true cinnamon' — Cinnamomum verum, named Ceylon cinnamon after it.

name: Maldives
fact: Capital Malé. The world's lowest-lying country, its 1,192 coral islands averaging just 1.5 m above the sea.

name: Indonesia
fact: Capital Jakarta. More than 17,000 islands make it the world's largest archipelagic state.

name: Philippines
fact: The golden South Sea pearl, farmed here, was declared the Philippines' national gem in 1996.

name: Thailand
fact: Capital Bangkok. Briefly the world's top rice exporter in 2011, and consistently among the top three since.

name: Cambodia
fact: Angkor Wat, built here by the Khmer Empire from 1113-1150 CE, is the largest religious monument on Earth.

name: Laos
fact: Capital Vientiane. Prince Fa Ngum founded its precolonial kingdom, Lan Xang — 'a million elephants' — in the 1300s.

name: Vietnam
fact: Capital Hanoi. Reunified as one state on 2 July 1976, a year after the Vietnam War ended.

name: Malaysia
fact: Capital Kuala Lumpur. Its share of Borneo carries a rainforest estimated at 140 million years old.

name: Singapore
fact: Independent 9 August 1965 — not by choice, but by a 126-0 vote expelling it from the Federation of Malaysia.

name: Taiwan
fact: Capital Taipei. Its tea shops gave the world bubble tea in the 1980s, tapioca pearls dropped into cold tea.

name: Brunei
fact: Capital Bandar Seri Begawan. A 1929 oil strike turned a small Bornean sultanate into one of the richest states.

name: North Korea
fact: Capital Pyongyang. Its border with the South, fixed by the 1953 armistice, is among the most militarised on Earth.

name: South Korea
fact: Capital Seoul. Along with China and Russia, one of the world's three major sources of cultivated ginseng.

name: Afghanistan
fact: Capital Kabul. Grew over 90% of the world's illicit opium for two decades, until cultivation fell 95% in 2023.

name: Uzbekistan
fact: Soviet cotton irrigation — Uzbekistan was top exporter by 1988 — shrank the Aral Sea 60% in under 40 years.

name: Pakistan
fact: Independent 14 August 1947. Its capital moved from Karachi to purpose-built Islamabad, completed in 1967.

name: Bangladesh
fact: 80% of the country lies within the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, the largest river delta in the world.

name: Australia
fact: The Great Barrier Reef off its northeast coast is the largest coral reef system on Earth, visible from space.

name: New Zealand
fact: Home to the flightless kiwi, the bird whose name New Zealanders themselves have worn ever since.

name: Papua New Guinea
fact: Shares New Guinea, the world's 2nd-largest island, with Indonesia — and speaks 840 languages, more than anywhere.

name: Fiji
fact: Capital Suva. Taveuni's Rainbow Reef has earned Fiji's waters the name 'soft coral capital of the world.'

name: Samoa
fact: Jumped the International Date Line in Dec 2011, skipping 30 December to trade with Australia in real time.

name: Reflecting Telescope
fact: Newton's 1668 design swapped the lens for a curved mirror, killing the color-fringing that plagued refractors.

discovered.note: Isaac Newton builds the first working reflecting telescope.

name: Sextant
