fact: Two mirrors double the measured angle, so a 60° arc can read up to 120° of sky.

discovered.note: John Hadley and Thomas Godfrey independently develop the double-reflection principle behind the sextant.

name: Adaptive Optics
fact: A laser fakes a star in the sky so a mirror can flex fast enough to cancel the atmosphere's twinkle.

name: Coronagraph
fact: An occulting disk in the telescope blots out a star's glare so instruments can see what's hiding beside it.

discovered.note: Bernard Lyot introduces the coronagraph.

name: Spectrograph
fact: Same prism as a spectroscope, but a camera behind it instead of an eye — the spectrum gets recorded.

name: Astronomical Interferometer
fact: Link two telescopes and their combined light resolves detail as fine as the gap between them.

name: Hubble Space Telescope
fact: A reflecting telescope orbiting above the blur of Earth's atmosphere, riding up on Discovery in 1990.

discovered.note: Space Shuttle Discovery launches the Hubble Space Telescope on mission STS-31, April 24.

name: James Webb Space Telescope
fact: 18 hexagonal beryllium mirrors, gold-plated to reflect the infrared light the telescope was built to see.

discovered.note: JWST launches on an Ariane 5 rocket, December 25.

name: Voyager Program
fact: Powered by decaying plutonium, not sunlight — why it still transmits from interstellar space 45+ years on.

discovered.note: Voyager 1 and 2 launch atop Titan IIIE-Centaur rockets.

name: Sputnik 1
fact: A 58cm metal sphere that did nothing but broadcast a radio beep — and started the Space Race doing it.

discovered.note: The USSR launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, October 4.

name: Apollo 11
fact: Two astronauts walked on the Moon while a third circled alone overhead in the command module.

discovered.note: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon, July 20; Armstrong and Aldrin walk the surface.

name: International Space Station
fact: Continuously crewed since November 2000 — the longest unbroken human presence off Earth.

discovered.note: The ISS begins continuous human occupation, November 2.

name: Curiosity Rover
fact: Its ChemCam fires a laser at rock from 7m away and reads the flash of vaporized plasma to tell what it is.

discovered.note: Curiosity lands in Gale Crater on Mars, August 6.

name: New Horizons
fact: A spare part built for the Cassini mission — its plutonium power generator — carried it past Pluto in 2015.

discovered.note: New Horizons flies by Pluto, July 14.

name: Cassini-Huygens
fact: Launched to Saturn in 1997, it dropped a probe onto Titan in 2005 — the only landing ever made past Mars.

discovered.note: Cassini-Huygens launches for Saturn, October 15.

name: Alpha Centauri
fact: Three stars, one system, and the nearest neighbors our Sun has — the closest just 4.2 light-years off.

name: Proxima Centauri
fact: The single closest star to the Sun — and it has a roughly Earth-mass planet sitting in its habitable zone.

discovered.note: Proxima b, an exoplanet orbiting Proxima Centauri, is confirmed, August 24.

name: Virgo Cluster
fact: Not close enough to hold onto us, but massive enough to slow our galaxy's drift away by about a tenth.

name: Halley's Comet
fact: Edmond Halley used Newton's laws to prove this comet keeps returning — and predicted the exact year it would.

discovered.note: Halley's Comet returns as predicted, confirmed by Johann Palitzsch, December 25.

name: Stellar Parallax
fact: Wait six months for Earth to cross its orbit, and a nearby star visibly shifts against the background sky.

discovered.note: Friedrich Bessel publishes the first reliable stellar parallax measurement, for 61 Cygni.

name: Settlement
fact: A permanent home base, no longer struck and carried onward after the harvest.

name: Cultural Hearth
fact: The place a cultural trait or practice is first invented, from which it then spreads outward.

name: Distance Decay
fact: Interaction between two places fades the farther apart they are — Tobler's First Law of Geography.

name: Culture Region
fact: An area unified by one shared cultural trait, strongest at its core and fading toward its edge.

name: Contagious Diffusion
fact: A practice spreading outward person to person, like a disease, with no regard for city size.

name: Hierarchical Diffusion
fact: An innovation leapfrogging straight to the biggest cities first, only later reaching small towns.

name: Stimulus Diffusion
fact: The core of a practice spreads, but gets reshaped to fit each new place it lands in.

name: Relocation Diffusion
fact: A practice carried to a new place in person, by someone who actually moved there.

name: Migration
fact: A permanent change of home, whether across town or across an ocean.

name: Push Factor
fact: A hardship at home — war, drought, no jobs — that drives people to migrate away.

name: Pull Factor
fact: An opportunity elsewhere — jobs, safety, freedom — that draws migrants toward it.

name: Urbanization
fact: The rising share of a population living in cities rather than the countryside.

name: Unitary State
fact: A country where the central government holds supreme power over every region.

name: Federalism
fact: Power split geographically between a central government and self-governing regions.

name: Separatist Movement
fact: An organized push by a minority group to fully break away from the larger country.

name: Self-Determination
fact: The principle that a people has the right to choose its own political status.

name: Census
fact: An official count of everyone living in a territory, ideally taken once a decade.

name: Electoral District
fact: A slice of territory whose voters elect their own representative to a legislature.

name: Gerrymandering
fact: Drawing electoral district lines to favor one party — named for an 1812 salamander-shaped map.

name: Primary Sector
fact: The part of an economy that extracts raw material straight from land or sea.

name: Secondary Sector
fact: The part of an economy that manufactures raw material into a finished product.

name: Tertiary Sector
fact: The service economy — retail, healthcare, transport — now most of US employment.

name: Quaternary Sector
fact: The knowledge economy split off from services around 1970: software, R&D, finance.

name: Factors of Production
fact: Land, labor and capital: the classic inputs every business must pay for.

name: Comparative Advantage
fact: The principle that a place should make what it produces most efficiently, and trade for the rest.

name: Footloose Industry
fact: A factory so cheap to relocate it can chase wherever labor is cheapest.

name: Gini Coefficient
fact: A single number from 0 to 1 measuring how unequally income is shared across a population.

name: Break of Bulk
fact: The point where cargo switches transport modes and must be unloaded and reloaded by hand.

name: Agglomeration
fact: The economic payoff of clustering close together — the basic reason cities exist at all.

name: Central Place Theory
fact: Christaller's model of how villages, towns and cities space themselves evenly across a plain.

name: Suburbanization
fact: The mid-20th-century population shift from city centers into car-dependent suburbs.

name: Redlining
fact: Government maps that outlined minority neighborhoods and marked them too risky for loans.

name: White Flight
fact: The mass departure of white residents as a neighborhood or city grows more diverse.

name: Gentrification
fact: Wealthier newcomers moving into a once-abandoned inner-city area, raising rents as they arrive.

name: Urban Sprawl
fact: Low-density development leapfrogging outward from a city with little planning.

name: Edge City
fact: A suburban node with more office space than downtown, that didn't exist before the 1960s.

name: Ghetto
fact: A district where one ethnic or religious group is confined, a term dating to 16th-century Venice.

name: Restriction Enzyme
fact: An enzyme that cuts DNA at one exact sequence — a bacterium's chemical scissors against invading viruses.

name: Cloning Vector
fact: A plasmid cut open at one site, ready to accept and carry a foreign piece of DNA.

name: Recombinant DNA
fact: DNA stitched together from two different sources into one molecule.

name: Bacterial Transformation
fact: A bacterium taking up foreign DNA from its surroundings and replicating it as its own.

name: Taq Polymerase
fact: A DNA polymerase from a hot-spring bacterium, stable enough to survive PCR's near-boiling step.

name: PCR
fact: Repeated heating and cooling that doubles a target DNA sequence millions of times over.

name: Gel Electrophoresis
fact: An electric field pulling DNA through a gel's mesh, sorting fragments from small to large.

name: DNA Hybridization
fact: Heat splits a DNA double strand apart; cooling lets matching sequences find each other again.

name: Southern Blot
fact: DNA sorted by gel, blotted onto a membrane, then probed to find one sequence in the mix.

name: Sahara
fact: The world's largest hot desert, roughly the size of the contiguous US, across North Africa.

name: Nile
fact: At 6,650 km, among Earth's longest rivers; its yearly flood built Ancient Egypt's farmland.

name: Amazon River
fact: Carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers combined, draining the Amazon rainforest.

name: Andes
fact: The world's longest continental mountain range -- 8,900 km along South America's Pacific edge.

name: Alps
fact: Europe's youngest, highest range, thrust up where the African and Eurasian plates collided.

name: Mediterranean Sea
fact: Nearly landlocked; it reaches the Atlantic only through the 14-km-wide Strait of Gibraltar.

name: Argentina
fact: Stretches from the Andes to the Atlantic; independence declared 1816 at the Congress of Tucuman.

name: Brazil
fact: Holds most of the Amazon basin and rainforest; the only Portuguese-speaking nation in the Americas.

name: Chile
fact: A ribbon of land between the Andes and the Pacific -- over 4,300 km long, rarely 350 km wide.

name: Peru
fact: Once the heart of the Inca Empire, whose ruins at Machu Picchu still crown the Andes.

name: Colombia
fact: One of only two South American countries with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.

name: Venezuela
fact: Home to the world's largest known oil reserves, which have shaped its economy for a century.

name: Bolivia
fact: The largest landlocked country in the Southern Hemisphere; a third of it lies in the Andes.

name: Ecuador
fact: Named for the equator itself, which its capital Quito sits almost exactly on.

name: Paraguay
fact: Landlocked and split into two regions by the Paraguay River, which flows past its capital.

name: Uruguay
fact: The only South American country lying entirely south of the Tropic of Capricorn.

name: Nigeria
fact: Africa's most populous country, from northern savanna to southern coastal rainforest.

name: Egypt
fact: Ancient civilization arose along the Nile's fertile floodplain, cutting through the Sahara.

name: South Africa
fact: Where the Atlantic meets the Indian Ocean; uniquely among nations it has three capitals.

name: Kenya
fact: Named for Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest peak, whose slopes the equator crosses.

name: Ethiopia
fact: One of only two African countries never colonized; fossils here rank among the oldest human ancestors.

name: Morocco
fact: Separated from Spain by just 14 km at the Strait of Gibraltar.

name: Algeria
fact: Africa's largest country by area; the Sahara covers most of its territory.

name: Ghana
fact: The first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, on 6 March 1957.

name: Tanzania
fact: Home to Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, and the Serengeti's migrating herds.

name: Senegal
fact: Its capital Dakar sits on the westernmost point of mainland Africa.

name: DR Congo
fact: Centered on the Congo, the world's deepest river, under Earth's second-largest rainforest.

name: Madagascar
fact: The world's fourth-largest island; over 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else.

name: France
fact: The 1789 Revolution overthrew the monarchy and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

name: Germany
fact: Unified into a single empire in 1871 under Prussian leadership, with Berlin as capital.

name: Italy
fact: Unified as a kingdom in 1861 on the peninsula that was once the heart of the Roman Republic.

name: Spain
fact: Spans most of the Iberian Peninsula, which it shares only with Portugal.

name: Portugal
fact: Borders barely changed since 1297, making it one of Europe's oldest stable nation-states.

name: United Kingdom
fact: Great Britain, part of Ireland, and thousands of smaller islands -- an archipelago nation.

name: Netherlands
fact: More than a quarter of the country lies below sea level, reclaimed from the sea since the 1300s.

name: Switzerland
fact: The Alps cover most of this landlocked country, neutral and war-free since 1815.

name: Poland
fact: Named for its flat terrain along the North European Plain -- from 'pole,' open field.

name: Russia
fact: The largest country on Earth by area, so vast it spans eleven time zones.

name: Greece
fact: Birthplace of Athenian democracy, scattered across thousands of Mediterranean islands.

name: Sweden
fact: Stretches roughly 1,600 km along the Scandinavian Peninsula, from 55N to 69N latitude.

name: Glycolysis
fact: Ten enzyme steps split one glucose into two pyruvate, right in the cytosol, no oxygen required. Net gain: two ATP, two NADH.

name: Pyruvate
fact: Glycolysis's three-carbon output, sitting at a metabolic fork: burn it for more ATP with oxygen, or ferment it to lactate without.

name: Krebs Cycle
fact: Pyruvate's carbons get stripped away one by one in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO2 and stacking up NADH and FADH2 to spend later.

name: Electron Transport Chain
fact: A relay of protein complexes in the mitochondrion's inner membrane passes electrons down an energy staircase to oxygen, pumping protons across as it goes.

name: ATP Synthase
fact: A molecular turbine: protons flowing back down the gradient the electron transport chain built spin its rotor, and each turn bolts a phosphate onto ADP.

name: Cellular Respiration
fact: Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain running in sequence — about 30 to 32 ATP squeezed from one glucose molecule with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

name: Homeostasis
fact: Steady internal conditions held constant by active correction — blood sugar spikes, the pancreas releases insulin, and the level comes back down.

name: Diabetes
fact: Insulin production fails or cells stop responding to it, and glucose piles up in the blood instead of getting taken up for fuel.

name: Apoptosis
fact: Programmed cell death: mitochondria release cytochrome c, an apoptosome assembles, and a cascade of caspase enzymes dismantles the cell from the inside out.

name: Cell Cycle
fact: G1, S, G2, then M: growth, DNA replication, more growth, then division — checkpoints at each border refuse to let a damaged cell proceed.

name: Carbohydrate
fact: Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen roughly one-two-one. Starch and cellulose are both just glucose chained together — wired two different ways.

name: Nucleic Acid
fact: DNA and RNA — both built from repeating nucleotides, each one a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogen base.

name: Centrosome
fact: Two centrioles at right angles, wrapped in pericentriolar material — the cell's main microtubule organizing center, doubling before mitosis so each pole gets one.

name: Operon
fact: A cluster of genes run by one shared promoter, switched on or off together — E. coli's lac operon turns on only when there's lactose around to digest.

name: Transcription Factor
fact: A protein built to grab one specific DNA sequence, usually near a gene's start, and turn that gene's transcription up or down.

name: Oncogene
fact: A mutated or overactive version of a normal growth gene — push the cell cycle's accelerator hard enough and a tumor is what you get.

name: Nondisjunction
fact: Chromosomes fail to separate cleanly during meiosis, leaving one gamete with an extra copy and another one short — trisomy 21 is the most common survivable result.

name: Horizontal Gene Transfer
fact: Bacteria hand a plasmid straight to a neighbor through direct contact, no reproduction required — the main route antibiotic resistance spreads between species.

name: Endosymbiosis
fact: Mitochondria keep their own circular DNA and divide by binary fission — strong evidence they were once free-living bacteria engulfed over a billion years ago.

name: Tonicity
fact: Whether the outside of a cell is saltier (hypertonic), more dilute (hypotonic), or matched (isotonic) — tonicity decides which way osmosis pushes the water.

name: Turgor Pressure
fact: Water pushes the plant cell's membrane hard against its rigid wall from the inside — the pressure that keeps a plant upright without a single bone.

name: Pinocytosis
fact: Cell drinking: the membrane dimples around a droplet of fluid and pinches off as a vesicle, taking in whatever happens to be dissolved in it — no target required.

name: Quorum Sensing
fact: A bacterial population senses its own chemical signal building up; once it crosses a threshold, every cell switches behavior at once.

name: Genotype
fact: The specific alleles an organism actually carries — its genetic parts list, as opposed to what those parts end up building.

name: Phenotype
fact: What a genotype actually becomes once development and environment get involved — the traits you can see, measure, or catch a disease from.

name: Auxin
fact: A plant hormone made at the shoot tip. Darwin showed in 1881 that the tip senses light while the bend happens lower down; Frits Went isolated the chemical itself decades later.

name: Phototropism
fact: Auxin builds up on a stem's shaded side, making those cells stretch more than the sunlit side — the whole stem curves toward the light.

name: Ireland
fact: Britain ceded Dublin Castle, its seat of rule here for 700 years, to the new state in 1922.

name: Austria
fact: Full sovereignty was restored 15 May 1955, when Allied powers signed a treaty at Vienna's Belvedere Palace.

name: Türkiye
fact: In 2022 its government asked the world to use 'Türkiye' instead of 'Turkey', partly to avoid the bird's name.

name: Israel
fact: Independence was declared 14 May 1948; its Star of David was adopted by Zionists in Basel in 1897.

name: Lebanon
fact: Became a republic when French Mandate rule ended in 1943, choosing the ancient cedar as its emblem.

name: Saudi Arabia
fact: Ibn Saud's 1902 raid retaking Riyadh's Masmak fort began the conquest that unified the kingdom by 1932.

name: Iran
fact: Its Lion and Sun emblem, official since the Safavid era, was dropped after the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

name: Flag of the Netherlands
fact: Started orange-white-blue for William of Orange; orange faded to red, fixed by decree in 1937.

name: Flag of Ireland
fact: Green for Catholics, orange for Protestants, white between for peace; standardized in 1848.

name: Flag of Switzerland
fact: White couped cross on red, from the war flag of Schwyz; one of only two square national flags.

name: Flag of Austria
fact: Red-white-red, recorded on a 1230 abbey seal, is among the oldest state symbols still flown.

name: Flag of Greece
fact: Nine stripes spell 'Freedom or Death' in syllables; the cross recalls Greek Orthodox Christianity.

name: Flag of Türkiye
fact: The star and crescent flew on Ottoman flags by the 1840s; the Republic kept it unchanged in 1923.

name: Flag of Israel
fact: Blue stripes echo the tallit, the Jewish prayer shawl; the flag was adopted 28 October 1948.

name: Flag of Lebanon
fact: A cedar tree on red-white stripes, adopted 7 December 1943, days before independence.

name: Flag of Saudi Arabia
fact: Bears the Shahada above a sword, printed identically on both sides so the text always reads right.

name: Flag of Iran
fact: 'Allahu Akbar' repeats 22 times along its bands, marking the date of the 1979 revolution.

name: Flag of Japan
fact: The Hinomaru sun-disc is centuries old, but only became Japan's legal flag by statute in 1999.

name: Flag of South Korea
fact: Red-blue taegeuk for cosmic balance, with four trigrams; first flown under Joseon in 1883.

name: Flag of China
fact: Four small stars for the people's classes orbit one large star for the Communist Party.

name: Flag of Indonesia
fact: Nearly identical to Monaco's flag; Monaco's later objection to the resemblance was ignored.

name: Flag of Australia
fact: Its Commonwealth Star gained a seventh point in 1908, for the Territory of Papua.

name: Flag of New Zealand
fact: Four red Southern Cross stars on a Blue Ensign; voters chose to keep it in a 2016 referendum.

name: Flag of Papua New Guinea
fact: Designed by 15-year-old Susan Karike; adopted 1971, sharing the Southern Cross with Australia.

name: Metonic Cycle
fact: Almost exactly 19 years and 235 lunar months, after which the Moon's phases fall on the same calendar dates again.

name: Tumor Suppressor Gene
fact: The real stop signal: halts a damaged cell, or forces it to self-destruct. p53 is disabled in a third of cancers.

name: Tumor
fact: An uncoordinated mass of tissue growth. Most stay contained — invading nearby tissue is what makes one cancer.

name: Metastasis
fact: Cancer cells breaking off to colonize a distant organ — over 90% of cancer deaths trace to this.

name: Glioma
fact: Grows from the brain's glial support cells, not its neurons — about 80% of malignant brain tumors.

name: Melanoma
fact: Grows from melanocytes, the skin's pigment cells. Caused mainly by UV — the deadliest skin cancer.

name: Leukemia
fact: Begins in bone marrow and floods the bloodstream with abnormal cells, instead of forming one solid mass.

name: Nitrification
fact: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonium to nitrite, and Nitrobacter finishes the job by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate.

name: Denitrification
fact: Bacteria reduce nitrate back to nitrogen gas once oxygen runs out — the nitrogen cycle's only way back to air.

name: Nitrogen Cycle
fact: Fixation, nitrification and denitrification move one element between air, soil and every living cell.

name: Carbon Cycle
fact: Photosynthesis pulls CO2 from the air; respiration, decay and methanogenesis put it back in other forms.

name: Sulfur Cycle
fact: Bacteria oxidize hydrogen sulfide to sulfate, and others reduce sulfate back to hydrogen sulfide.

name: Methanogen
fact: An archaeon that combines CO2 and hydrogen for energy; methane is the only waste product it can make.

name: Extremophile
fact: Life that doesn't merely survive extreme heat, cold, acid, pressure or salt — it needs the extreme to grow.

name: Thermophile
fact: An organism whose growth optimum sits between 41°C and 122°C — hot springs and geysers are full of them.

name: Halophile
fact: Needs salt to grow, not just tolerates it — some strains require water several times saltier than the sea.

name: Eutrophication
fact: Nutrient overload: algae bloom on the surplus, then die and rot, and the rotting uses up the water's oxygen.

name: Biomagnification
fact: A pollutant too stable to break down concentrates further at every step up the food chain.

name: Wastewater
fact: Everything that flows from a drain, plus whatever else households, industry or storms send after it.

name: Primary Treatment
fact: The physical stage: screens catch trash, then gravity settles most of the solids out in a couple of hours.

name: Activated Sludge
fact: Aerobic bacteria clump into flocs in an aeration tank, and part of every batch reseeds the next one.

name: Trickling Filter
fact: Wastewater trickles over a bed of rock or plastic coated in a living biofilm a few millimetres thick.

name: Secondary Treatment
fact: The biological stage: microbes finish what settling couldn't, converting dissolved waste to cells and CO2.

name: Anaerobic Digestion
fact: Sludge fed to anaerobic microbes in sequence — acids first, then acetate, then methanogens finish it as gas.

name: Septic System
fact: A tank does the anaerobic work solids need; a soil drain field does the aerobic work the liquid needs next.

name: Indicator Organism
fact: Testing every pathogen in water isn't practical, so labs test for E. coli as a stand-in for all of them.

name: Water Treatment
fact: Coagulate, settle, filter, then disinfect — four stages turning raw river water into safe tap water.

name: Bioremediation
fact: Using microbes already living in a polluted site — sometimes sped with nutrients — to break it down in place.

name: Water Activity
fact: Pure water rates 1.0; jam sits near 0.85 since its water is chemically bound to sugar, not free for microbes.

name: Food Spoilage
fact: Not the same as foodborne illness: spoilage bacteria make food taste and smell bad without being dangerous.

name: Clostridium botulinum
fact: An anaerobic, endospore-forming soil bacterium whose toxin is the most potent one known — nanograms can kill.

name: Staphylococcus aureus
fact: Lives harmlessly on human skin and in the nose, but the toxin it makes in food survives cooking.

name: Listeria monocytogenes
fact: One of the few foodborne pathogens that keeps growing in the refrigerator, dividing even down near 0°C.

name: Campylobacter
fact: The most common bacterial cause of foodborne illness in the US, and most of it traces back to poultry.

name: Aflatoxin
fact: A carcinogen made by Aspergillus flavus on stored peanuts and grain; the FDA limits it strictly by law.

name: Pasteurization
fact: Heat a food just enough to kill the microbes troubling it, not enough to cook it or ruin its flavour.

name: Food Irradiation
fact: Ionizing radiation kills microbes by breaking their DNA, without heating the food — 'cold pasteurization.'

name: Sake
fact: Koji's mould enzymes turn rice starch to sugar and yeast ferments that sugar to alcohol — both at once.

name: Single-Cell Protein
fact: Growing yeast or bacteria on an industry's leftover waste, then eating the microbial biomass as protein.

name: Attenuated Vaccine
fact: A live pathogen weakened by growth in a foreign host until it can no longer cause disease at home.

discovered.note: Louis Pasteur produces the first artificially attenuated vaccine, from a stale chicken cholera culture.

name: Inactivated Vaccine
fact: Killed by heat or chemicals — unable to replicate, but intact enough to still teach the immune system.

discovered.note: Jonas Salk's formaldehyde-inactivated poliovirus vaccine is licensed for use.

name: Toxoid
fact: A bacterial toxin disarmed by formaldehyde — poison gone, shape the immune system still learns intact.

name: Subunit Vaccine
fact: Only the antigenic fragment of a pathogen, not the whole organism — nothing left alive to cause disease.

discovered.note: The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine, made by yeast engineered with the viral surface-antigen gene, is approved — the first human vaccine made this way.

name: Conjugate Vaccine
fact: A bacterial sugar antigen bolted to a carrier protein so a young immune system finally notices it.

discovered.note: The Hib conjugate vaccine is approved, cutting Haemophilus influenzae type b infection rates by over 90% in four years.

name: mRNA Vaccine
fact: Genetic instructions, not the pathogen itself — host cells read the mRNA and build the antigen on their own.

discovered.note: The UK's MHRA becomes the first regulator worldwide to approve an mRNA vaccine, authorising the Pfizer-BioNTech shot.

name: Adjuvant
fact: Added to a vaccine to make the immune system take a weak antigen more seriously.

discovered.note: Alexander Glenny describes aluminium salts boosting antibody response when mixed into a vaccine — the origin of 'alum' adjuvant.

name: Hybridoma
fact: An antibody-making B cell fused to an immortal cancer cell — one cell, one target, dividing forever.

discovered.note: Georges Kohler and Cesar Milstein fuse a B cell with a myeloma cell, inventing hybridoma technology; Nobel Prize, 1984.

name: Monoclonal Antibody
fact: Every molecule identical — descended from one B cell, so every copy has the same shape, same target.

name: ELISA
fact: An enzyme-tagged antibody turns a colourless liquid visibly colored wherever its target is present.

discovered.note: ELISA is developed independently in Sweden and the Netherlands as a safer replacement for radioactive immunoassays.

name: Incidence
fact: The count of brand-new cases of a disease in a population over a set stretch of time.

name: Prevalence
fact: Every existing case of a disease at one moment — old cases and new ones both, all counted together.

name: Pandemic
fact: An epidemic that has crossed borders and continents, no longer confined to one region.

name: Endemic Disease
fact: Constantly present in a population at a fairly steady baseline, neither spiking nor vanishing.

name: Epidemic
fact: A sharp, unusual rise in a disease's incidence above its normal baseline in one population.

name: Herd Immunity
fact: Once enough of a population is immune, a pathogen can't find hosts fast enough to keep spreading.

name: Basic Reproduction Number
fact: R0 — how many new infections one case causes, on average, in a population with no immunity at all.

name: Zoonotic Disease
fact: An infection that jumps from a non-human animal into humans — roughly 75% of emerging diseases start this way.

name: Disease Vector
fact: A living carrier of a pathogen from one host to another — sometimes just a ride, sometimes a second home.

name: Fomite
fact: A doorknob, a glass, a railing — an inanimate object carrying infection between people who never touched.

name: John Snow
fact: London physician who traced 1854's cholera to a single water pump, a decade before germ theory existed.

name: Nosocomial Infection
fact: An infection picked up during treatment in a healthcare facility, not the illness the patient arrived with.

name: Notifiable Disease
fact: A disease physicians are legally required to report, so health authorities can spot an outbreak forming.

name: Beta-Lactamase
fact: A bacterial enzyme that snaps open the ring at the heart of every penicillin-family drug, destroying it.

discovered.note: Penicillinase, the first beta-lactamase, is isolated from E. coli by Abraham and Chain — before penicillin had reached a single patient.

name: Cephalosporin
fact: A beta-lactam antibiotic family bred to dodge the enzymes that destroy natural penicillins.

discovered.note: Giuseppe Brotzu isolates the fungus Acremonium (then Cephalosporium) near a Sardinian sewer outfall; the drug reaches patients in 1964.

name: Vancomycin
fact: Binds the cell-wall building block itself, not an enzyme — medicine's antibiotic of last resort.

discovered.note: Isolated from a Borneo soil sample sent to Eli Lilly by a missionary, from what was then called Streptomyces orientalis.

name: Tetracycline
fact: Jams the ribosome's 30S subunit so incoming tRNA can't dock — pumped into bacterial cells, not animal ones.

discovered.note: Benjamin Duggar isolates chlortetracycline from Streptomyces aureofaciens in a Missouri soil sample.

name: Macrolide
fact: Binds the ribosome's 50S subunit, stopping the growing protein chain — standard swap for penicillin allergy.

discovered.note: Erythromycin, the first macrolide, is cultured from a Streptomyces relative found in a Philippine soil sample.

name: Sulfonamide
fact: A structural mimic of PABA that jams folate synthesis — bacteria need to make their own, human cells don't.

discovered.note: Gerhard Domagk's red dye Prontosil is shown to cure streptococcal infection in mice, later traced to its breakdown product sulfanilamide.

name: Fluoroquinolone
fact: Jams DNA gyrase mid-unwind, stopping bacterial DNA from replicating or being read.

discovered.note: Nalidixic acid, the first quinolone, turns up as an unintended byproduct while George Lesher's team is trying to synthesize chloroquine.

name: MRSA
fact: Staph aureus with an altered cell-wall protein that keeps working even with methicillin bound everywhere else.

discovered.note: The first documented MRSA isolates appear in a British hospital study.

name: Azole
fact: Blocks the enzyme that finishes building ergosterol, the molecule holding a fungal cell membrane together.

name: Protease Inhibitor
fact: Jams the enzyme that cuts HIV's one long protein chain into working pieces — the virus keeps assembling junk.

discovered.note: Saquinavir, approved 6 December, is the first HIV protease inhibitor; US annual AIDS deaths fall by roughly 60% within two years.

name: Chloroquine
fact: Concentrates in Plasmodium-infected blood cells, blocking disposal of digested hemoglobin's toxic waste.

discovered.note: Hans Andersag synthesizes chloroquine at Bayer as a synthetic answer to quinine, initially dismissed as too toxic to use.

name: Paul Ehrlich
fact: Coined the 'magic bullet' idea — a chemical that kills a pathogen and leaves the patient untouched.

discovered.note: Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata's compound 606, arsphenamine, is marketed as Salvarsan — the first modern chemotherapeutic drug, for syphilis.

name: Oseltamivir
fact: Blocks neuraminidase, the enzyme new flu particles need to cut themselves free of the cell that made them.

discovered.note: The FDA approves oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — the first neuraminidase inhibitor available as a pill.

name: Endospore
fact: A bacterium's dormant, armoured backup copy of itself. Some have woken up after 25 million years.

name: Growth Curve
fact: Lag, then exponential doubling, then a stationary plateau, then death — a closed culture's whole biography.

name: Sterilization
fact: Not mostly dead — completely. The one microbial control standard tough enough to also take out endospores.

name: Autoclave
fact: Steam under pressure hits 121°C, hot enough to kill even endospores.

name: Disinfectant
fact: Kills most microbes on a countertop, not a body. Endospores may still walk away.

name: Antiseptic
fact: The disinfectant gentle enough to put on skin instead of just a countertop.

name: HEPA Filter
fact: Certified to trap 99.97% of particles at 0.3 micrometres — the size that slips past filters easiest.

name: Germicidal UV
fact: UV-C at 254 nanometres welds a microbe's own DNA bases together in pairs they were never meant to share.

name: Lyophilization
fact: Freeze it, then drop the pressure until the ice skips melting and sublimates straight to vapour.

name: Triclosan
fact: Once in 3 of every 4 liquid soaps sold in the US — banned from them by the FDA in 2016.

name: Coenzyme
fact: An enzyme's reusable organic sidekick, usually cut straight from a vitamin.

name: Cofactor
fact: Not every enzyme works alone. Some need a bound metal ion or organic helper just to hold their shape.

name: Competitive Inhibition
fact: A sulfa drug fits a bacterial enzyme's active site because it is built to resemble the real substrate, PABA.

name: Iron Bacteria
fact: Lives on oxidizing dissolved iron, leaving reddish-brown slime in wells, streambeds and pipes.

name: Anaerobic Respiration
fact: Still runs an electron transport chain, just not with oxygen at the end — nitrate or sulfate stands in.

name: Photosystem I
fact: Named first, works second — it re-boosts spent electrons high enough to finally make NADPH.

name: Carbon Fixation
fact: Turning CO2 into something with a carbon skeleton. About 250 billion tonnes of it happens every year.

name: Calvin Cycle
fact: Fixes carbon, spends ATP and NADPH to reduce it, then rebuilds its own starting material to run again.

name: Rubisco
fact: Probably the most abundant enzyme on Earth — up to half of all soluble protein in a leaf is this one molecule.

name: Beta-Oxidation
fact: A fatty acid chain gets chewed down two carbons at a time, each bite handed off as a fresh acetyl-CoA.

name: Cellulase
fact: Almost nothing alive makes this enzyme — a problem, since cellulose is Earth's most abundant organic polymer.

name: Ion
fact: An atom that has gained or lost an electron. Hydrogen gaining one becomes hydride, H⁻; losing its only one leaves a bare proton.

name: Purine
fact: The double-ring nucleobases, adenine and guanine — the bulkier half of DNA and RNA's four-letter alphabet.

name: Pyrimidine
fact: The single-ring nucleobases — cytosine, thymine, and uracil — the smaller half of the genetic alphabet.

name: Sucrose
fact: Table sugar: one glucose and one fructose locked together by a glycosidic bond.

name: Chitin
fact: A tough polymer of nitrogen-bearing glucose units — fungal cell walls, insect and crustacean shells.

name: Triglyceride
fact: Glycerol with three fatty-acid tails, each attached by an ester bond that releases a water molecule.

name: Saturated Fat
fact: A fat with no carbon=carbon double bonds — every carbon holds its maximum hydrogen and packs solid at room temperature.

name: Unsaturated Fat
fact: A fat with at least one carbon=carbon double bond — the kink stops it packing tightly, so it stays liquid as oil.

name: Steroid
fact: Four fused carbon rings — the shared skeleton of cholesterol, testosterone, and cortisone alike.

name: Sterol
fact: A steroid with a hydroxyl group on its ring — cholesterol in animal membranes, ergosterol doing the same job in fungi.

name: Lipoprotein
fact: A protein shell around a fat cargo — the only way something as water-fearing as cholesterol travels through blood.

name: ADP
fact: Adenosine with two phosphates instead of three — what's left of ATP after the cell spends its last one.

name: Denaturation
fact: Heat or extreme pH unravels a protein's shape without breaking a single peptide bond — cooked, not digested.

name: Buffer Solution
fact: A weak acid paired with its conjugate base, holding pH nearly steady even as acid or base is added.

name: Germ Theory
fact: The idea that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease — it displaced miasma theory by the 1880s.

name: Koch's Postulates
fact: Four criteria for proving a microbe causes a disease: present in every case, grown pure, reproduces disease, recovered unchanged.

name: Louis Pasteur
fact: French chemist, 1822–1895, who proved germ theory, invented pasteurization, and produced the first rabies vaccine.

name: Robert Koch
fact: German physician, 1843–1910, who identified the anthrax bacterium in 1876 and the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882.

name: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
fact: Dutch draper who ground his own glass lenses to about 275x and in 1676 was first to see a living bacterium.

name: Prion
fact: A misfolded protein that forces normal copies of itself to misfold too — no DNA or RNA involved, and the disease still spreads.

name: Helicobacter pylori
fact: A spiral bacterium that neutralizes stomach acid with its own urease enzyme — and turned out to cause most peptic ulcers.

name: Light Microscope
fact: Two glass lens systems in series, magnifying to about 1000x before visible light's own wavelength blurs any more detail.

name: Transmission Electron Microscope
fact: An electron beam through a wafer-thin specimen resolves single columns of atoms — a thousand times finer than light allows.

name: Scanning Electron Microscope
fact: Scans a beam across a metal-coated surface and reads the scattered electrons back — a 3D-looking image down to 0.4 nanometers.

name: Phase-Contrast Microscope
fact: Converts the invisible phase shifts light makes in a transparent cell into visible brightness — no stain, no dead cells.

name: Fluorescence Microscope
fact: Shines one wavelength at a specimen and captures only the longer wavelength it fluoresces back — labeled structures glow.

name: Confocal Microscope
fact: A laser and a pinhole that rejects light from outside the focal plane — stack the slices and reconstruct a 3D image.

name: Gram Stain
fact: Crystal violet, then iodine, then alcohol, then safranin — thick-walled cells stay purple, thin-walled ones wash out pink.

name: Acid-Fast Stain
fact: Carbolfuchsin steamed into a waxy mycolic-acid wall, rinsed with acid-alcohol strong enough to strip a plain Gram stain.

name: Negative Stain
fact: An acidic dye colors the background, not the cell — both are negatively charged and repel, leaving a pale silhouette.

name: Endospore Stain
fact: Malachite green steamed through a spore coat nothing else penetrates — spores stay green, safranin turns the rest red.

name: Peptidoglycan
fact: Alternating sugar rings cross-linked by short amino acid chains into a mesh — the load-bearing wall unique to bacteria.

name: Teichoic Acid
fact: Glycerol-phosphate polymers threaded through a Gram-positive wall, gripping magnesium and calcium ions.

name: Lipopolysaccharide
fact: Lipid A anchoring a core sugar and a variable O-antigen chain — the outer coat of Gram-negative bacteria, and their endotoxin.

name: Outer Membrane
fact: A second, asymmetric membrane found only in Gram-negative bacteria — phospholipid inside, lipopolysaccharide facing out.

name: Periplasm
fact: The gel-filled gap between a Gram-negative cell's two membranes — up to 40% of its volume, packed with enzymes.

name: Porin
fact: Barrel-shaped protein channels through the outer membrane, letting molecules under about 600 daltons pass and nothing bigger.

name: Mycoplasma
fact: A bacterium with no cell wall at all, among the smallest free-living cells — and naturally immune to penicillin.

name: Coccus
fact: A spherical bacterium, dividing into the pairs, chains, or grape-like clusters that name Strepto- and Staphylococcus.

name: Spirochete
fact: A corkscrew-shaped bacterium that moves with flagella wound inside its own periplasm instead of trailing outside the cell.

name: Proton Motive Force
fact: A proton gradient built across a membrane — stored energy driving ATP synthase, transport proteins, and the flagellum alike.

name: Bacterial Flagellum
fact: A protein propeller run by a rotary motor in the cell envelope — powered by proton flow, not ATP, up to 100,000 rpm.

name: Chemotaxis
fact: Counterclockwise flagella bundle into a smooth run; clockwise, they fly apart into a tumble — attractants just lengthen the runs.

name: Pilus
fact: A thin protein filament, 3–10 nanometers across, for gripping surfaces or — as the sex pilus — pulling two bacteria together.

name: Bacterial Conjugation
fact: A sex pilus reels a recipient in, then a plasmid crosses the bridge as a single strand — the fastest way resistance spreads.

name: Transduction
fact: A bacteriophage mispackages bacterial DNA instead of its own and delivers it into the next cell it infects.

name: Nucleoid
fact: The unbound tangle where a bacterium's DNA sits — compacted a thousandfold, with no membrane around it at all.

name: Bacterial Capsule
fact: A gelatinous polysaccharide coat outside the wall, thick enough to stop a phagocyte from getting a grip.

name: Polyhydroxybutyrate
fact: A carbon-storage granule bacteria stockpile when food is abundant but another nutrient is scarce — today, a compostable plastic.

name: Peroxisome
fact: A tiny organelle that dismantles fatty acids and disarms hydrogen peroxide with its own catalase enzyme.

name: Aquaporin
fact: A membrane channel built for one job — passing about a billion water molecules a second while blocking every ion.

name: Epidermis
fact: Keratin-filled dead cells at the surface, replaced about every 48 days — the body's real barrier.

name: Dermis
fact: Collagen and elastic fibers beneath the epidermis, threaded with blood vessels and nerve endings.

name: Plant Epidermis
fact: One cell layer covering a leaf's surface. Almost no chloroplasts — except in its own guard cells.

name: Plant Cuticle
fact: A waxy film the epidermis secretes over itself — the reason water beads on a leaf instead of soaking in.

name: Three-Domain System
fact: Woese split all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eucarya in 1990, using ribosomal RNA alone.

name: Bergey's Manual
fact: The reference microbiologists check first: every characterized bacterial species, catalogued since 1923.

name: Binomial Nomenclature
fact: Two italicized Latin words, genus then species — Linnaeus's fix for a world of clashing common names.

name: Carl Woese
fact: Compared ribosomal RNA across life and found a whole missing domain hiding in plain sight: Archaea.

discovered.note: Woese and Fox publish evidence that Archaea form a third, distinct domain of life.

name: Phylogenetic Tree
fact: Branches trace divergence, nodes mark a common ancestor — Darwin's only diagram in Origin of Species.

name: Extreme Halophile
fact: Needs at least 2 molar salt and often grows in fully saturated brine — home is the Dead Sea, not the sea.

name: Hyperthermophile
fact: Thrives above 80°C; the record holder grows at 122°C, hotter than any home oven reaches.

name: Nitrogen Fixation
fact: Nitrogenase yanks N2 apart into usable ammonia — and stops working the instant oxygen touches it.

name: Heterocyst
fact: A thick-walled cell some cyanobacteria build just to fix nitrogen inside an oxygen-free bubble.

name: Rickettsia
fact: Can't survive outside a living cell; ticks and lice inject it, and spotted fever follows.

name: Chlamydia Bacterium
fact: Lives only inside host cells, alternating an infectious spore-like form with a growing one.

name: Myxobacteria
fact: Hunts in swarms nicknamed 'wolf packs,' then starves into a fruiting body built of its own cells.

name: Deinococcus Radiodurans
fact: Shrugs off 5,000 grays of gamma radiation — roughly a thousand times the dose that kills a human.

name: Thermus Aquaticus
fact: Found thriving in a scalding Yellowstone spring; its heat-proof enzyme now runs every PCR machine.

name: Bdellovibrio
fact: Rams another bacterium at 100 body-lengths a second, then eats it alive from inside its own wall.

name: Clostridium
fact: Anaerobic and spore-forming, behind three of history's nastiest toxins: tetanus, botulism, gas gangrene.

name: Bacillus Anthracis
fact: Its spores can wait in soil or wool for decades, then cause anthrax the moment they're inhaled.

name: Mycobacterium Tuberculosis
fact: A waxy cell wall shrugs off Gram stain entirely — only an acid-fast dye reveals it in the lungs.

name: Pseudomonas Aeruginosa
fact: Smells faintly of grapes, glows blue-green, and sits on the WHO's own list of resistance threats.

name: Legionella
fact: Normally lives inside amoebae in water pipes; a 1976 hotel outbreak in Philadelphia gave it its name.

name: Chytrid
fact: The only fungus with a swimming spore — one species has driven whole frog populations extinct.

name: Zygomycete
fact: Black bread mold in a nutshell: sporangia bursting with spores, plus a tough dormant zygospore.

name: Ascomycete
fact: Sac fungi, over 64,000 species strong — includes the mold that gave the world penicillin.

name: Basidiomycete
fact: Club fungi: every mushroom, plus the rusts and smuts that quietly wreck grain harvests.

name: Apicomplexan
fact: Nearly every species is a parasite, armed with an apical complex built to drill into a host cell.

name: Oomycete
fact: Looks like a fungus, isn't one — its cellulose walls helped trigger the Irish Potato Famine.

name: Trypanosoma
fact: Swaps its surface coat again and again to dodge the immune system — the trick behind sleeping sickness.

name: Leishmania
fact: Rides in a sandfly's gut as a whip-tailed cell, then hides inside human immune cells once bitten in.

name: Naegleria Fowleri
fact: Warm-freshwater amoeba that enters through the nose; the resulting brain infection kills over 97%.

name: Nematode
fact: Roundworms may be the most numerous animals on Earth; one species mapped its every single neuron.

name: Tapeworm
fact: Has no gut of its own — it just soaks up the host's pre-digested food through its entire skin.

name: Trematode
fact: A flatworm with two suckers that needs a snail, then a vertebrate, in sequence, to complete its life.

name: Proto-Oncogene
fact: The normal growth gene every cell carries — one mutation away from becoming an oncogene.

name: Mimivirus
fact: Once mistaken for a purple-staining bacterium; its genome tops a million base pairs, rivaling real cells.

name: Plaque Assay
fact: Each clear ring in a bacterial lawn is one phage's descendants — count rings, know the virus titer.

name: Restriction-Modification System
fact: Shreds any incoming phage DNA on sight, while methyl tags keep the bacterium's own DNA safe from itself.

name: Cytokine
fact: Stanley Cohen coined the term in 1974, after showing production wasn't limited to immune cells.

name: Interferon
fact: Discovered in 1957 by Isaacs and Lindenmann: a virus-infected cell's chemical warning to its neighbors.

name: Complement System
fact: About 50 blood proteins, three separate pathways in, but always the same three jobs on the invader.

name: Dendritic Cell
fact: Named in 1973 by Ralph Steinman, who won a 2011 Nobel for showing it bridges innate and adaptive immunity.

name: Toll-Like Receptor
fact: Named for a 1985 exclamation — “Das ist ja toll!” — at a mutant fruit fly with the same broken gene.

name: Natural Killer Cell
fact: Carries no antigen receptor at all — it kills any cell that fails to show a normal MHC class I badge.

name: Mast Cell
fact: Loaded with histamine and heparin; emptying every granule at once is what anaphylaxis actually is.

name: Inflammation
fact: Redness, heat, swelling and pain — Celsus wrote down all four around the time of Christ.

name: Fever
fact: The hypothalamus's thermostat gets reset upward; 38.3°C is the line doctors call a fever.

name: Antigen
fact: Short for “antibody generator” — though plenty of antigens never actually trigger one.

name: Epitope
fact: The one small patch of an antigen an antibody actually touches — the rest is just scaffolding.

name: B Cell
fact: Named for the bursa of Fabricius, a bird organ — even though human B cells mature in bone marrow.

name: T Cell
fact: Named simply for the thymus, the organ where it learns to recognize a fragment riding on MHC.

name: Helper T Cell
fact: Carries the CD4 marker HIV also grabs onto — exactly why the virus targets this cell first.

name: Cytotoxic T Cell
fact: Carries the CD8 marker and delivers perforin and granzymes — a chemical order to self-destruct.

name: Plasma Cell
fact: A B cell's factory form: several thousand identical antibody molecules leave it every second.

name: Memory Cell
fact: Can sit quiet in the blood for decades, then outrace a naive cell the moment its antigen returns.

name: MHC Class I
fact: Every nucleated cell wears one, showing cytoplasmic protein fragments to any passing cytotoxic T cell.

name: MHC Class II
fact: Only a few cell types make this one — dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells — to brief helper T cells.

name: Clonal Selection
fact: Burnet's 1957 theory: an antigen picks out — doesn't teach — the one lymphocyte that already matches it.

name: IgM
fact: A five-unit pentamer, first responder of the primary response, too big to ever leave the bloodstream.

name: IgG
fact: Three in every four antibodies in your blood, and the only class that crosses the placenta.

name: IgA
fact: More of this is made than every other antibody class combined — most never even reaches the blood.

name: IgE
fact: Under 0.0001% of your antibodies, bound tight to mast cells, and enough to trigger anaphylactic shock.

name: Normal Microbiota
fact: Roughly 10,000 microbial species have been catalogued living across the healthy human body.

name: Adhesin
fact: Often just one minor protein riding the tip of a pilus — it decides which host cell a bacterium can grab.

name: Exotoxin
fact: A secreted bacterial protein, sometimes potent enough that heat alone turns it into a safe vaccine.

name: Endotoxin
fact: Lipid A, the toxic core of a Gram-negative cell's own outer membrane, released only when the cell dies.

name: Virulence Factor
fact: Adhesins, capsules, enzymes, toxins — whatever trait actually lets a microbe make a healthy host sick.

name: Opportunistic Pathogen
fact: Candida albicans lives in you harmlessly for years, until something tips its numbers out of balance.

name: Hypersensitivity
fact: Gell and Coombs sorted every kind of damaging immune overreaction into just four types, in 1963.

name: Allergy
fact: Cow's milk, soy, egg, wheat, peanut, tree nut, fish and shellfish cause 90% of food allergies.

name: Anaphylaxis
fact: Richet's 1902 coinage means the opposite of protection — and the Nobel committee agreed in 1913.

name: Autoimmune Disease
fact: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system's own T cells are what destroy the insulin-making cells.

name: Immunodeficiency
fact: AIDS has one hard number attached to it: a CD4+ T cell count below 200 per microliter of blood.

name: Transplant Rejection
fact: T cells reading a donor organ's HLA proteins as foreign is exactly what immunosuppressants exist to blunt.

name: Promoter
fact: DNA just upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase, sigma factor in hand, docks to start transcription.

name: Terminator
fact: A GC-rich hairpin, or the Rho protein pulling along the mRNA, knocks RNA polymerase off the DNA.

name: Operator
fact: Sits between the promoter and an operon's genes; a repressor parked here blocks RNA polymerase.

name: Repressor
fact: A protein that clamps an operator shut; the lac repressor lets go the moment allolactose binds it.

name: Sigma Factor
fact: Swapping RNA polymerase's sigma subunit retargets it — E. coli's sigma-32 turns on heat-shock genes.

name: Two-Component System
fact: A membrane sensor autophosphorylates on cue, then hands the phosphate to a partner that flips genes on.

name: RNA Interference
fact: Small RNA loaded into RISC finds and shreds a matching mRNA; Fire and Mello won the 2006 Nobel for it.

name: Open Reading Frame
fact: DNA from a start codon to a stop codon with none between; long runs get flagged as candidate genes.

name: Bioinformatics
fact: BLAST checks a new sequence against a database of hundreds of billions of nucleotides to guess its job.

name: Metagenomics
fact: Sequencing soil or seawater DNA directly finds microbes culturing misses; under 1% of species grow in a dish.

name: Catabolite Repression
fact: Glucose keeps E. coli's lac operon off despite lactose; cAMP and CAP switch it on once glucose runs out.

name: Antigenic Variation
fact: N. gonorrhoeae swaps which pilin gene it expresses, altering its surface protein so old antibodies miss it.

name: Phase Variation
fact: E. coli pili genes flip on and off by inverting a promoter inside them — no new mutation needed.

name: Auxotroph
fact: A microbe that lost the ability to make a compound, like an amino acid, and needs it supplied to grow.

name: Thymine Dimer
fact: UV light fuses two adjacent thymine bases on a DNA strand, kinking the helix and blocking replication.

name: Photoreactivation
fact: An enzyme, absent in humans, uses visible light to break a UV thymine dimer's bonds, undoing the damage.

name: Excision Repair
fact: Snips out a DNA segment with a lesion like a thymine dimer; polymerase and ligase refill and seal the gap.

name: SOS Response
fact: A bacterial last resort: an error-prone polymerase copies past DNA damage, trading accuracy for survival.

name: Ames Test
fact: Screens chemicals for mutagenicity using a histidine-starved Salmonella strain that reverts back to growth.

name: Transposon
fact: A DNA segment that jumps to a new spot in the genome, often disrupting whatever gene it lands in.

name: F Plasmid
fact: Carries the genes for its own pilus and transfer; spliced into the chromosome it makes an Hfr cell.

name: R Plasmid
fact: A resistance plasmid stacking genes for several antibiotics at once, often ten on one loop of DNA.

name: Genomic Island
fact: A stretch of chromosome over 10 kilobases whose GC content betrays that it came from another species.

name: Replica Plating
fact: Stamping a velvet-pressed copy of a colony plate onto fresh media to spot mutants without poisoning them.

name: DNA Library
fact: A whole genome, cut into fragments by restriction enzymes and cloned one fragment per host cell.

name: cDNA
fact: DNA copied from mature mRNA, so it skips introns entirely — bacteria can read it without splicing.

name: Selectable Marker
fact: A resistance gene on a vector that lets only successfully transformed cells survive antibiotic selection.

name: Green Fluorescent Protein
fact: A jellyfish protein that glows green under blue light, fused to genes to reveal exactly when they switch on.

name: Colony Blotting
fact: Colonies pressed onto a membrane, lysed in place, then probed to find which ones carry a target gene.

name: DNA Probe
fact: A labeled single strand of DNA that seeks out and binds its exact complementary sequence.

name: FISH Probe
fact: A glowing probe that lights up a target sequence right inside an intact cell on a microscope slide.

name: DNA Microarray
fact: A chip dotted with thousands of DNA probes that lights up to show every gene a cell was expressing at once.

name: Transgenic Plant
fact: A plant carrying a gene inserted from another species, often delivered by a bacterium's own plasmid.

name: Bt Toxin
fact: An insect gut-rupturing protein made by a sporulating soil bacterium; engineered into crops as a built-in pesticide.

name: Golden Rice
fact: Rice engineered to make beta-carotene in its grain, fighting vitamin A deficiency where rice is a staple.

name: Ti Plasmid
fact: A soil bacterium's plasmid that inserts its T-DNA into a plant's chromosome, causing crown gall tumors.

name: Electroporation
fact: A brief electric pulse punches temporary pores in a cell membrane, letting DNA slip inside.

name: Streptococcus pyogenes
fact: Clears a wide zone on blood agar — it lyses red blood cells completely, not just partially.

name: Strep Throat
fact: Streptococcal pharyngitis: S. pyogenes in the throat, spread on the coughs and sneezes of someone already infected.

name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
fact: Club-shaped rods lined up like a wooden fence. Most often enters through the nose, tonsils, or throat.

name: Diphtheria
fact: A grey pseudomembrane clogs the tonsils while its toxin rides the blood to the heart, kidneys, and nerves.

name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
fact: An encapsulated diplococcus, cells found in pairs, and the top cause of pneumonia in children and the elderly.

name: Pneumococcal Pneumonia
fact: The most common bacterial pneumonia in adults. Fluid fills the lung's own tiny air sacs and blocks oxygen from crossing in.

name: Bordetella pertussis
fact: A tiny, encapsulated coccobacillus that attaches to ciliated cells lining the airway with proteins built for exactly that.

name: Whooping Cough
fact: Pertussis: paroxysms of coughing end in a sharp, high-pitched gasp as the next breath forces its way back in.

name: Tuberculosis
fact: Initially infects the lungs. Most infections stay silent for years, latent rather than active, before a few progress.

name: Rhinovirus
fact: Grows best at 33°C, noticeably colder than the body's core — exactly why it sets up in the nose and not deeper down.

name: Common Cold
fact: Rhinoviruses cause up to 40% of colds on their own — over 100 known types of just that one genus.

name: Folliculitis
fact: Infection and inflammation of a hair follicle. Most boils and carbuncles trace back to S. aureus.

name: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
fact: An exfoliative toxin cleaves the protein holding two skin layers together, and the skin separates like a scald.

name: Impetigo
fact: A contagious infection of the skin's outer layer, typically Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

name: Rickettsia rickettsii
fact: Rides into the blood on a tick's saliva, then invades the cells lining small and medium blood vessels.

name: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
fact: A rash of small spots of bleeding starts at the wrists and ankles, then works its way toward the trunk.

name: Measles Virus
fact: An enveloped RNA virus with no known animal reservoir. Humans are its only natural host.

name: Measles
fact: Nine in ten non-immune people sharing a home with a case will catch it — among the most contagious diseases known.

name: Rubella Virus
fact: An enveloped RNA virus in its own genus, Rubivirus. Found in the blood five to seven days after infection.

name: Rubella
fact: German measles: a pink, lighter rash than measles proper. Crossing the placenta in pregnancy is the real danger.

name: Dermatophyte
fact: A group of fungi that feed on keratin itself, which is why they only ever colonize skin, hair, and nails.

name: Ringworm
fact: Tinea: a red, itchy, scaly, circular rash, from the Latin for worm. No worm is actually involved.

name: Wart
fact: Human papillomavirus infecting skin through the smallest of breaks — a wound is the virus's actual entrance.

name: Clostridium tetani
fact: An anaerobe that cannot grow around oxygen at all. Its toxin travels the nerves it reaches, not the blood.

name: Tetanus
fact: Lockjaw starts it: the toxin blocks the nerve signals that normally tell a muscle to relax, not just contract.

name: Clostridium perfringens
fact: The shortest reported generation time of any known organism — 6.3 minutes — an anaerobic spore-former.

name: Gas Gangrene
fact: Myonecrosis: muscle tissue dies outright, gas collects in it, and it can turn to shock within hours.

name: Pseudomonas Infection
fact: The single most common cause of infection in burn injuries — needs only a breach to get in.

name: Actinomyces israelii
fact: A normal colonizer of the mouth, vagina, and colon — harmless as long as it stays in those anoxic pockets.

name: Actinomycosis
fact: Slow, spreading tissue infection after trauma opens a way in — dental work, a broken jaw, a bite.

name: Bartonella henselae
fact: Carried by domestic and feral cats, passed on by their scratches, bites, and the fleas that ride them.

name: Cat Scratch Disease
fact: Most often passed on by a scratch or bite from a kitten rather than an adult cat.

name: Streptobacillus moniliformis
fact: Nearly every wild and domestic rat carries it, almost always without symptoms of its own.

name: Rat-Bite Fever
fact: High fevers, shivering, headache, and joint pain, days after a bite or scratch from a colonized rodent.

name: Peptic Ulcer
fact: One in five to one in ten people infected go on to develop an ulcer; most never notice a thing.

name: Mumps Virus
fact: An enveloped RNA paramyxovirus. Humans are its only host, and it travels on respiratory secretions and saliva.

name: Mumps
fact: Parotitis — painful swelling of the salivary glands in front of the ears — is the single most common symptom.

name: Hepatitis A Virus
fact: A non-enveloped RNA picornavirus, fecal-oral in spread — water or food fouled by infected feces.

name: Hepatitis A
fact: Usually resolves completely on its own, with no ongoing liver disease left behind once it's over.

name: Clostridioides difficile
fact: Held in check by a healthy gut microbiome. Let an antibiotic clear out the competition and it grows unopposed.

name: C. diff Infection
fact: Ranges from mild diarrhea to severe, life-threatening colon inflammation — a pseudomembrane can even form.

name: Norovirus
fact: As few as ten virions are enough to start an infection — among the most contagious viruses known.

name: Norovirus Gastroenteritis
fact: Spread by the fecal-oral route — through contaminated food or water, or straight person to person.

name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
fact: Oocysts shed in feces aren't infectious yet — sporulation takes one to several weeks outdoors first.

name: Cyclosporiasis
fact: A diarrheal disease rarely spread person-to-person, because the parasite needs weeks outdoors first.

name: Cryptosporidiosis
fact: Infects the small intestine's brush border, producing watery diarrhea — sometimes with a cough alongside it.

name: Typhoid Fever
fact: Unlike other Salmonella strains, this one is a human-only pathogen — no animal reservoir carries it at all.

name: Urethra
fact: A short mucosa-lined tube from bladder to skin surface — about 4 cm in women, roughly 20 cm in men.

name: Vagina
fact: A muscular, mucosa-lined canal kept acidic, pH 3.8–4.5, by resident Lactobacillus fermenting glycogen.

name: Leptospira interrogans
fact: A hook-ended spirochete living in the kidneys of carrier rodents, shed continuously in their urine.

name: Gardnerella vaginalis
fact: A small gram-variable rod that signals a vagina's shift away from its normal Lactobacillus.

name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
fact: A coffee-bean-shaped diplococcus whose pilin genes reshuffle into over a hundred antigenic variants.

name: Chlamydia trachomatis
fact: An obligate intracellular bacterium, alternating an infectious form with a dividing form inside the host cell.

name: Treponema pallidum
fact: A corkscrew-shaped spirochete too thin to Gram-stain — visible only by dark-field microscopy.

name: Haemophilus ducreyi
fact: True to its genus name, 'blood-loving' — it grows only on blood-enriched chocolate agar.

name: Tampon
fact: A compressed core of cotton, rayon, or both; the most absorbent 1970s blends soaked up nearly 20x their weight.

name: Cystitis
fact: Bladder infection, usually uropathogenic E. coli climbing the urethra and attaching to bladder cells.

name: Pyelonephritis
fact: A bladder infection that climbed the ureters into the kidneys — 1 to 2 women per 1,000 get it yearly.

name: Leptospirosis
fact: A biphasic zoonosis from water fouled by infected urine — about a million cases and 58,900 deaths yearly.

name: Bacterial Vaginosis
fact: The most common vaginal condition in reproductive-age women — thin discharge, strong fishy odor, no inflammation.

name: Vulvovaginal Candidiasis
fact: Candida albicans overgrowth causing itching and thick white discharge; about 75% of women get it once.

name: Toxic Shock Syndrome
fact: A Staphylococcus aureus superantigen touching off a cytokine storm and a dangerous blood-pressure crash.

name: Gonorrhea
fact: Often silent — about half of infected women show no symptoms — yet it can still scar the fallopian tubes.

name: Chlamydia
fact: The most-reported bacterial STI in the US; about 70% of infected women never notice a symptom.

name: Syphilis
fact: 'The great imitator' — a painless chancre, then a rash, then years of silence before possible late damage.

name: Chancroid
fact: Painful soft genital ulcers, unlike syphilis's painless chancre, with tender, pus-filled groin nodes.

name: Botulism
fact: Clostridium botulinum's toxin blocks the neuromuscular junction's go signal — the opposite of tetanus.

name: Meningitis
fact: Inflammation of the meninges, from infection — bacterial cases are far deadlier than viral ones.

name: Meningococcemia
fact: Neisseria meningitidis in the bloodstream, releasing endotoxin at up to 1,000 times normal levels.

name: Poliomyelitis
fact: In under 1% of infections, poliovirus destroys motor neurons, causing lopsided flaccid paralysis.

name: Arbovirus
fact: A virus amplified in a wild bird or rodent host, then carried between them by a biting mosquito or tick.

name: West Nile Virus
fact: Introduced to North America in 1999; birds are its real host, humans an accidental dead end.

name: Encephalitis
fact: Inflammation of the brain itself, not just its coverings — likelier than meningitis to kill or disable.

name: Rabies Encephalitis
fact: Once rabies virus reaches the brain by riding motor-neuron transport backward, death is over 99% certain.

name: Lymph Node
fact: Bean-shaped and strung along the lymph vessels — packed with B and T cells that filter what drains in.

name: Spleen
fact: Fist-sized, behind the stomach — red pulp filters worn blood cells, white pulp mounts immune responses.

name: Lymphocyte
fact: A white blood cell born in bone marrow — as a B cell, T cell, or NK cell, each with a different job in immunity.

name: Yersinia pestis
fact: Grows in a flea's gut until it blocks the foregut, so the starving flea keeps biting and regurgitating bacteria.

name: Plague
fact: Called the Black Death — bacteria dumped into a flea bite reach a lymph node and swell it into a tender bubo.

name: Francisella tularensis
fact: So infectious that a lab exposure alone can cause tularemia — a handful of organisms is enough by some routes.

name: Tularemia
fact: An ulcer marks where it got in, and the lymph node draining that spot swells and turns tender within days.

name: Brucella
fact: Each species keeps mainly to one host — melitensis in goats and sheep, abortus in cattle, suis in pigs.

name: Brucellosis
fact: Undulant fever — from raw milk or a slaughterhouse cut, temperature spikes and fades in waves for weeks.

name: Sepsis
fact: The body's own inflammatory response to infection does the damage here, not the microbe alone.

name: Septic Shock
fact: Sepsis whose blood pressure won't hold even with fluids — roughly 4 in 10 who reach this stage do not survive.

name: Infective Endocarditis
fact: Bacteria seed a clot already sitting on a damaged heart valve — a valve with no blood supply to fight back.

name: Epstein-Barr Virus
fact: A herpesvirus that infects the throat, then quietly settles into B cells for good — most adults carry it.

name: Infectious Mononucleosis
fact: Kissing disease — weeks of fatigue and fever from a virus spread almost entirely through saliva.

name: Yellow Fever Virus
fact: A flavivirus that cycles between Aedes mosquitoes and forest monkeys long before it ever reaches a person.

name: Yellow Fever
fact: Named for the jaundice it causes — in severe cases, black vomit and bleeding, fatal up to half the time.

name: Acute Retroviral Syndrome
fact: Fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes 2 to 4 weeks after HIV exposure, as the virus floods the bloodstream.

name: Clinical Latency
fact: HIV keeps replicating for years while CD4+ T cell counts slowly fall, even with no symptoms yet.

name: AIDS
fact: Diagnosed once the CD4+ T cell count drops below 200 cells per microliter, or a defining opportunistic disease appears.

name: Needle-Borne HIV Transmission
fact: A needlestick from HIV-positive blood infects a health worker about 0.3% of the time, far below hepatitis B's roughly 10%.

name: Perinatal HIV Transmission
fact: Untreated, HIV passes from mother to child around birth or through breastfeeding in a fifth to a third of cases; treatment cuts that below 5%.

name: Human Herpesvirus 8
fact: Identified in Kaposi's sarcoma tissue in 1994, this double-stranded DNA herpesvirus usually persists for life without symptoms.

name: Kaposi's Sarcoma
fact: Purple-to-black nodules from HHV-8-infected blood vessel cells; it became an AIDS-defining illness once the epidemic began.

name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
fact: A fungus so adapted to mammal lungs it has never been grown outside one; healthy people carry it without knowing.

name: Pneumocystis Pneumonia
fact: Once the most common AIDS-defining illness in the US; risk climbs sharply once CD4+ counts fall under 200 per microliter.

name: Toxoplasmic Encephalitis
fact: Latent Toxoplasma cysts reactivate in the brain once immunity collapses, an AIDS-defining condition.

name: Cytomegalovirus
fact: A herpesvirus with the largest genome of any known human herpesvirus; infected cells swell with an 'owl's eye' nucleus.

name: CMV Retinitis
fact: Reactivated cytomegalovirus infects the retina in 15% to 40% of people with AIDS, once a leading cause of AIDS-related blindness.

name: HIV Wasting Syndrome
fact: Cachexia from chronic, uncontrolled HIV infection; it was the presenting sign of AIDS in about a fifth of early cases.

name: Zidovudine
fact: AZT: a thymidine look-alike missing the 3' hydroxyl group reverse transcriptase needs to extend the DNA chain, so it just stops.

name: HAART
fact: Combining antiretrovirals from different drug classes suppresses HIV for years — it lowers viral load but never clears the provirus.

name: Big Bang
fact: The universe expanding from an initial hot, dense state, 13.8 billion years ago.

name: Universe
fact: All space, time, matter and energy — 68% dark energy, 27% dark matter, under 5% ordinary matter.

name: Microbe
fact: An organism too small to see unaided — most of the tree of life, by species count and by mass.

name: Pathogen
fact: A microbe that causes disease — most microbes don't, which is why this needed its own word.

name: Infection
fact: A pathogen established and multiplying in a host — the event, before any symptom shows.

name: Disease
fact: The harm an infection does made visible — the same infection can stay silent or become this.

name: Iceland
fact: Capital Reykjavík. The only large island sitting astride a mid-ocean ridge at sea level, straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between the North American and Eurasian plates.

name: Norway
fact: Capital Oslo. Its coast measures about 29,000 km with its roughly 1,200 fjords counted in, but only about 2,500 km without them.

name: Finland
fact: Capital Helsinki. Over 180,000 lakes have been recorded within its borders, and in 1906 it became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage.

name: Estonia
fact: Capital Tallinn. Estonian is a Finnic language, not Indo-European, and the country takes in more than 2,300 Baltic islands and islets.

name: Lithuania
fact: Capital Vilnius. On 11 March 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to declare the restoration of its independence.

name: Latvia
fact: Capital Riga. It first declared independence from the Russian Empire on 18 November 1918 and restored it on 21 August 1991.

name: Denmark
fact: Capital Copenhagen. Its highest natural point, Møllehøj, reaches only 170.86 m — the country is the Jutland peninsula plus an archipelago of 406 islands.

name: Belgium
fact: Capital Brussels. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and Brussels is now the de facto capital of the European Union.

name: Luxembourg
fact: Capital Luxembourg City. The world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy, and in 2020 the first country anywhere to make all public transport free.

name: Liechtenstein
fact: Capital Vaduz. One of only two doubly landlocked countries on Earth — landlocked, and ringed entirely by other landlocked states.

name: Andorra
fact: Capital Andorra la Vella, at 1,023 m the highest capital city in Europe. The country is a co-principality with two heads of state.

name: San Marino
fact: Capital City of San Marino. Traditionally founded in AD 301, it claims to be the oldest extant sovereign state and the oldest constitutional republic.

name: Monaco
fact: A city-state whose capital is itself. At 2.08 km² it is the second-smallest sovereign state after Vatican City, and the most densely populated country in the world.

name: Malta
fact: Capital Valletta. Its megalithic temples, begun around 3500 BC, are among the oldest free-standing structures in the world.

name: Cyprus
fact: Capital Nicosia. A 9,500-year-old cat burial found on the island is older than ancient Egyptian civilisation.

name: Bulgaria
fact: Capital Sofia. The Cyrillic script was developed in the First Bulgarian Empire's capital Preslav, and the Varna culture left the world's oldest known gold jewellery, over 6,000 years old.

name: North Macedonia
fact: Capital Skopje. Landlocked, drained by the Vardar, and holding part of ancient Lake Ohrid; it covers roughly the northern third of the Macedonia region.

name: Albania
fact: Capital Tirana. In the 15th century Skanderbeg's campaigns held off Ottoman advances for more than two decades.

name: Montenegro
fact: Capital Podgorica. Its name is a Venetian translation of Crna Gora, 'Black Mountain', after the dark evergreen forests of Mount Lovćen.

name: Serbia
fact: Capital Belgrade. Seventeen Roman emperors were born on its territory, more than anywhere outside Italy.

name: Croatia
fact: Capital Zagreb. Its Adriatic coast is fringed by more than a thousand islands and islets, the largest such archipelago on that sea.

name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
fact: Capital Sarajevo. It has a tripartite presidency, with one member each from the Bosniak, Serb and Croat communities serving at once.

name: Slovenia
fact: Capital Ljubljana. Its Karst Plateau gave geology the word 'karst', and the Ljubljana Marshes Wheel found here is the world's oldest wooden wheel.

name: Czechia
fact: Capital Prague. It was the only country in Central and Eastern Europe to stay a parliamentary democracy through the entire interwar period.

name: Slovakia
fact: Capital Bratislava. It is the world's largest per-capita producer of cars, with the automotive industry making up about 44% of industrial output.

name: Hungary
fact: Capital Budapest. Hungarian is Uralic, one of the few languages in Europe outside the Indo-European family.

name: Romania
fact: Capital Bucharest. Romanian is a Romance language descended from the Latin of Roman Dacia, conquered in Trajan's Dacian Wars.

name: Ukraine
fact: Capital Kyiv. At 603,628 km² it is the largest country lying wholly within Europe, and its chernozem black earth feeds a major grain export trade.

name: Moldova
fact: Capital Chișinău. Landlocked until 1999, when a small frontage on the Danube gave it access to the sea; its name comes from the Moldova River.

name: Belarus
fact: Capital Minsk. About 70% of the fallout from the 1986 Chernobyl explosion in neighbouring Ukraine settled on Belarusian soil.

name: Georgia
fact: Capital Tbilisi. Georgian is a Kartvelian language with no known relation to any other language family in the world.

name: Armenia
fact: Capital Yerevan. In AD 301 it became the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, and its alphabet was invented around AD 405 by Mesrop Mashtots.

name: Azerbaijan
fact: Capital Baku, on the Caspian Sea. The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic of 1918–1920 was the first modern parliamentary republic in the Muslim world.

name: Sudan
fact: Capital Khartoum, where the Blue Nile and the White Nile meet. Africa's third-largest country by area, holding the Nubian pyramids of Meroë.

name: South Sudan
fact: Capital Juba. Independent on 9 July 2011 after 98.83% of referendum voters chose separation from Sudan, making it the world's most recent sovereign state.

name: Eritrea
fact: Capital Asmara, whose Italian-era modernist and art deco centre became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017. Independent from Ethiopia in 1993 after a referendum.

name: Djibouti
fact: Capital Djibouti City. Independent from France on 27 June 1977; Lake Assal within its territory is the lowest point on the African continent.

name: Somalia
fact: Capital Mogadishu. Formed on 1 July 1960 when the newly independent British Somaliland and Italian Somaliland united; it has the longest coastline on mainland Africa.

name: Uganda
fact: Capital Kampala. Named for the Buganda kingdom, and home to Mount Stanley in the Rwenzori range, which at 5,109 m is its highest peak.

name: Rwanda
fact: Capital Kigali, sitting at 1,567 m. Called the land of a thousand hills, it holds Lake Kivu, one of the twenty deepest lakes in the world.

name: Burundi
fact: Political capital Gitega, with Bujumbura the largest city and economic capital. One of Africa's smallest countries at 27,834 km².

name: Malawi
fact: Capital Lilongwe. Lake Malawi, nicknamed the Calendar Lake for being about 365 miles long and 52 miles wide, has one of the richest lake fish faunas on Earth.

name: Zambia
fact: Capital Lusaka. Independent from the United Kingdom on 24 October 1964, taking its name from the Zambezi river after six decades as Northern Rhodesia.

name: Zimbabwe
fact: Capital Harare. Named after Great Zimbabwe, the medieval stone city whose Shona name means 'houses of stones'.

name: Mozambique
fact: Capital Maputo. Independent from Portugal on 25 June 1975; the Zambezi crosses it and divides the country into two contrasting topographic halves.

name: Eswatini
