fact: Executive capital Mbabane, legislative capital Lobamba. In April 2018 the king renamed the Kingdom of Swaziland to Eswatini; it remains Africa's last absolute monarchy.

name: Lesotho
fact: Capital Maseru. The only independent state lying entirely above 1,000 m; its lowest point, around 1,400 m, is the highest low point of any country.

name: Botswana
fact: Capital Gaborone. Independent from the United Kingdom on 30 September 1966, and today it produces more diamonds than any other country.

name: Namibia
fact: Capital Windhoek. Independent from South Africa on 21 March 1990; the Namib along its coast is the oldest desert in the world.

name: Angola
fact: Capital Luanda. Independent from Portugal on 11 November 1975; before colonisation the territory held the Kingdom of Kongo and the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba.

name: Comoros
fact: Capital Moroni. Mount Karthala on Ngazidja rises 2,361 m and is one of the most active volcanoes in the world.

name: Mauritius
fact: Capital Port Louis. The dodo was endemic to this island alone, with the last widely accepted sighting in 1662.

name: Seychelles
fact: Capital Victoria. Africa's smallest and least populous sovereign state; the coco de mer palm grows only on Praslin and Curieuse and bears the world's heaviest seed.

name: Cabo Verde
fact: Capital Praia. Ten volcanic islands lying 600 to 850 km west of Cap-Vert, continental Africa's westernmost point, and uninhabited before settlement from the 1460s.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe
fact: Capital São Tomé. The equator passes through its islet of Ilhéu das Rolas, and by 1905 the islands were the world's largest producer of cocoa.

name: Gabon
fact: Capital Libreville. About 89.3% of its land is forested, and at Oklo a natural nuclear fission reactor ran inside the uranium ore two billion years ago.

name: Republic of the Congo
fact: Capital Brazzaville, the only national capital that grew up on the opposite bank of a river from another capital, Kinshasa, within sight across the Congo.

name: Equatorial Guinea
fact: Capital Ciudad de la Paz, a purpose-built city that replaced Malabo in 2026. Independent from Spain in 1968, it is the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa.

name: Cameroon
fact: Capital Yaoundé, with Douala the largest city. Called 'Africa in miniature' because coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna all occur within its borders.

name: Central African Republic
fact: Capital Bangui. The Ubangi, a tributary of the Congo, drains about two-thirds of the country, while the Chari in the north flows away into Lake Chad.

name: Chad
fact: Capital N'Djamena. Named after Lake Chad, the remnant of a lake that covered some 330,000 km² of the Chad Basin 7,000 years ago.

name: Niger
fact: Capital Niamey, on the Niger River. Africa's sixth-largest country, with more than 80% of its land inside the Sahara.

name: Burkina Faso
fact: Capital Ouagadougou. Renamed from Upper Volta on 4 August 1984 by Thomas Sankara, combining the Mooré word for 'upright' with the Dyula word for 'fatherland'.

name: Togo
fact: Capital Lomé. Less than 115 km wide between Ghana and Benin, with only 56 km of lagoon-backed coast on the Gulf of Guinea.

name: Benin
fact: Capital Porto-Novo, with the seat of government at Cotonou. Known as Dahomey until 1975, when it was renamed after the Bight of Benin on its southern coast.

name: Mali
fact: Capital Bamako. Named for the medieval Mali Empire, which peaked in the 14th century as Africa's wealthiest state under Mansa Musa.

name: Mauritania
fact: Capital Nouakchott, on the Atlantic coast. Africa's eleventh-largest country, with roughly 90% of its territory inside the Sahara.

name: The Gambia
fact: Capital Banjul. The smallest country in continental Africa, less than 50 km wide at its widest point and shaped around the lower Gambia River.

name: Guinea
fact: Capital Conakry. The Guinea Highlands contain the sources of the Niger, the Gambia and the Senegal rivers, and the country is the world's second-largest bauxite producer.

name: Guinea-Bissau
fact: Capital Bissau. Independence from Portugal was declared on 24 September 1973 and recognised in 1974; offshore lie the 88 islands and islets of the Bijagós Archipelago.

name: Sierra Leone
fact: Capital Freetown, founded in 1792 by about 1,200 Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia. Independent from the United Kingdom on 27 April 1961.

name: Liberia
fact: Capital Monrovia. Settlement began in 1822 under the American Colonization Society and independence was declared on 26 July 1847, making it Africa's oldest continuously independent country.

name: Tunisia
fact: Capital Tunis. Cape Angela on its northern shore is the northernmost point of mainland Africa, and the country holds the eastern end of the Atlas Mountains.

name: Libya
fact: Capital Tripoli. Africa's fourth-largest country at almost 1.8 million km², with the tenth-largest proven oil reserves in the world.

name: Antigua and Barbuda
fact: Capital St. John's. Independent from Britain on 1 November 1981; its 440 km² of territory makes it one of the Caribbean's smallest states, yet one of the few with an air force.

name: Bahamas
fact: Capital Nassau. Some 700 islands and over 2,500 cays strung across 800 km of the Atlantic, whose highest point, Mount Alvernia on Cat Island, reaches only 64 m.

name: Barbados
fact: Capital Bridgetown. Independent 30 November 1966, and exactly 55 years later, on 30 November 2021, it replaced the monarchy with a president and became a republic.

name: Belize
fact: Capital Belmopan. Independent 21 September 1981, and the only country in Central America whose sole official language is English.

name: Canada
fact: Capital Ottawa. Formed by Confederation on 1 July 1867, it has the longest coastline of any country, touching the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic Oceans.

name: Costa Rica
fact: Capital San José. It abolished its military on 1 December 1948 and wrote the ban into the 1949 constitution, making it one of the few sovereign states with no standing army.

name: Cuba
fact: Capital Havana. The largest country in the Caribbean by area, it became the Republic of Cuba on 20 May 1902 after the Spanish–American War and US occupation.

name: Dominica
fact: Capital Roseau. The youngest island of the Lesser Antilles volcanic arc and still volcanically active, it holds Boiling Lake, the world's second-largest hot spring.

name: Haiti
fact: Capital Port-au-Prince. Independent on 1 January 1804, it is the only known country in history established by a successful slave revolt, and the first in the Americas to abolish slavery.

name: Dominican Republic
fact: Capital Santo Domingo. It occupies the eastern five-eighths of Hispaniola and contains both the Caribbean's highest peak, Pico Duarte, and its lowest point, Lake Enriquillo.

name: El Salvador
fact: Capital San Salvador. At 21,041 km² it is the smallest and most densely populated country in Central America, and the only one with no Caribbean coastline.

name: Grenada
fact: Capital St. George's. Independent 7 February 1974; nutmeg planted here from 1843 earned it the name Island of Spice, and in 1983 US forces invaded in Operation Urgent Fury.

name: Guatemala
fact: Capital Guatemala City. Independent from Spain on 15 September 1821, and with about 17.6 million people it is the most populous country in Central America.

name: Guyana
fact: Capital Georgetown. Independent from the United Kingdom on 26 May 1966, it is the only country in mainland South America with English as its official language.

name: Honduras
fact: Capital Tegucigalpa. Independent from Spain in 1821; the writer O. Henry coined the phrase 'banana republic' in 1904 from his time here.

name: Jamaica
fact: Capital Kingston. Independent 6 August 1962; the third-largest island of the Greater Antilles, and the birthplace of reggae music and the Rastafari movement.

name: Mexico
fact: Capital Mexico City. Its name comes from Mēxihko, the Nahuatl term for the Aztec heartland; independence was declared on 27 September 1821.

name: Nicaragua
fact: Capital Managua. The largest country by area in Central America, known as the land of lakes and volcanoes; Momotombo's 1610 eruption destroyed the city of León.

name: Panama
fact: Capital Panama City. It seceded from Colombia in November 1903, and the 83 km canal across its isthmus was completed by the United States in 1914.

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
fact: Capital Basseterre. At 261 km² and roughly 48,000 people, it is the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere in both area and population.

name: Saint Lucia
fact: Capital Castries. Independent 22 February 1979, it has the highest ratio of Nobel laureates to population of any sovereign country, with Arthur Lewis and Derek Walcott.

name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
fact: Capital Kingstown. Independent 27 October 1979; its volcano La Soufrière erupted explosively in April 2021, forcing about 16,000 people to evacuate.

name: Suriname
fact: Capital Paramaribo. Independent from the Netherlands on 25 November 1975, it is the only state outside Europe where Dutch is the official language.

name: Trinidad and Tobago
fact: Capital Port of Spain. Independent 31 August 1962; it is the birthplace of the steelpan, the limbo, and calypso and soca music.

name: United States
fact: Capital Washington, D.C. The Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776; the federation now spans 50 states, including non-contiguous Alaska and Hawaii.

name: Epithelial Tissue
fact: Cells packed into continuous sheets with almost no matrix and no blood vessels at all — every epithelium is fed by diffusion through the basement membrane beneath it.

name: Connective Tissue
fact: Cells marooned in a matrix they secreted themselves — bone, cartilage, fat, tendon and even blood all qualify, and type I collagen alone is about a quarter of all mammalian protein.

name: Muscle Tissue
fact: Actin and myosin in three arrangements: striated skeletal fibers you command, striated cardiac muscle you cannot, and smooth muscle in the walls of your organs.

name: Nervous Tissue
fact: Grey matter is the cell bodies and synapses doing the processing; white matter is the myelinated axons carrying the results between them.

name: Organ
fact: Several tissue types joined into one structural unit for one job — the intestinal wall alone stacks epithelium, smooth muscle and connective tissue, and a human body holds roughly 79 of them.

name: Organ System
fact: Organs ganged onto a shared job — the human body runs eleven, and the respiratory system alone recruits nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, lungs and diaphragm.

name: Metabolism
fact: Catabolism tears molecules apart and anabolism builds them up, both trading through ATP — a human turns over roughly their own body weight in ATP each day while holding only grams of it at any instant.

name: Digestion
fact: Breaking food into pieces small enough to cross a gut wall — salivary amylase takes about 30% of the starch before you swallow, then gastric juice at pH 1–3 starts on protein.

name: Circulatory System
fact: Heart, vessels and about five litres of blood on a closed double circuit — the muscle capillaries alone in a 70 kg body run somewhere between 9,000 and 19,000 km.

name: Respiratory System
fact: Nose to alveoli, driven by a diaphragm that flattens 12 to 16 times a minute — 300 million air sacs give roughly 145 m² of surface for gas to cross.

name: Digestive System
fact: About nine metres of tube from mouth to anus, with salivary glands, liver and pancreas feeding in — the small intestine does most of the chemistry, the large intestine takes 30 to 40 hours over the leftovers.

name: Skeletal System
fact: Roughly 270 bones at birth fuse to about 206 by adulthood — 80 axial, 126 appendicular — and haematopoiesis in the marrow makes blood inside them.

name: Muscular System
fact: More than 600 skeletal muscles, around 40% of body mass, each hauling on bone through a tendon while cardiac and smooth muscle work the heart and organ walls unasked.

name: Endocrine System
fact: Glands releasing hormones straight into the bloodstream — slower than nerve signals but far longer-lasting, with the hypothalamus sitting on top as the neural control centre for the lot.

name: Urinary System
fact: Kidneys take about 20% of cardiac output and strain 180 litres of filtrate a day, then claw back 99% of it — the 0.8 to 2 litres left over is urine.

name: Lymphatic System
fact: Around 800 lymph nodes on a one-way network with no pump at all — muscle contraction alone squeezes the roughly 3 litres a day that leaks out of capillaries back into the blood.

name: Immune System
fact: Layered defence: skin, mucus and stomach acid first, then innate cells that answer any invader on sight, then B and T cells that learn one specific antigen and remember it.

name: Reproductive System
fact: The one organ system an individual can live without — gonads make the gametes, testicles the sperm and ovaries the ova, and the rest is plumbing to bring them together.

name: Integumentary System
fact: Skin, hair, nails and glands as one system — 1.5 to 2 m² of covering that is 12 to 15% of body weight, the largest organ system there is.

name: Kidney
fact: The pair filters about 180 litres of plasma a day through roughly a million nephrons each, then takes nearly all of it back.

name: Liver
fact: Around 500 separate jobs in one 1.5 kg organ, and three quarters of its blood arrives already used, straight from the gut.

name: Gallbladder
fact: A 50 ml pear that makes no bile of its own — it concentrates the liver's three to tenfold and squeezes when fat arrives.

name: Oesophagus
fact: About 25 cm long, striated muscle at the top and smooth muscle at the bottom, with a sphincter ring closing each end.

name: Trachea
fact: Sixteen to twenty rings of hyaline cartilage hold it open, every one of them incomplete — open at the back, where the trachealis muscle joins the ends.

name: Bronchus
fact: The right one is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, which is why an inhaled object usually ends up in the right lung.

name: Artery
fact: Everything leaving the heart, through a middle wall layer of elastin and smooth muscle. The pulmonary artery is the exception that carries blood with no oxygen in it.

name: Vein
fact: Thin walls, wide lumen, low pressure — and nearly 70% of all the blood in the body is sitting in them right now.

name: Capillary
fact: Five to ten micrometres across and one endothelial cell thick — the only place oxygen, glucose and urea actually cross.

name: Alveolus
fact: About 480 million of them, 70 to 80 square metres of surface, and a membrane 0.2 micrometres thick at its thinnest where air meets blood.

name: Uterus
fact: Pear-shaped, 7.6 cm long and about 60 grams until a blastocyst implants in its lining — then the muscle wall grows to several times that.

name: Ovary
fact: The female gonad: about a million oocytes are present at birth, and only some 500 of them — one a cycle — are ever ovulated.

name: Testis
fact: Held at about 34.4 °C, some 2.3 degrees below the rest of the body, because sperm production is impeded above 36.7.

name: Placenta
fact: Half a kilo of organ the fetus builds and then discards — mother and fetus trade oxygen across it with no intermingling of their blood.

name: Skull
fact: Twenty-two bones — eight cranial, fourteen facial — locked at immovable sutures. Only the mandible moves.

name: Joint
fact: Fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial — and only the synovial kind has a fluid-filled cavity, so those bones are never directly joined at all.

name: Femur
fact: The longest and thickest bone in the body, and reliably about 26.7% of a person's height — which is how a bare skeleton gives away how tall it stood.

name: Rib
fact: Twelve pairs: seven joined to the sternum by their own cartilage, three sharing the cartilage above them, and the last two attached to nothing in front.

name: Thyroid Gland
fact: A 25-gram butterfly of a gland below the Adam's apple, releasing 80–90% T4 and only 10–20% T3 and storing the rest outside its cells as colloid.

name: Adrenal Gland
fact: Two organs fused into one cap on each kidney — 7 to 10 grams the pair — a steroid-making cortex wrapped around a medulla that is really a sympathetic ganglion.

name: Glucagon
fact: Twenty-nine amino acids from the islets' alpha cells, named a portmanteau of 'glucose agonist' by Kimball and Murlin in 1922.

name: Testosterone
fact: Over 95% of a man's comes from the testes' Leydig cells, and 5α-reductase turns it into DHT, which grips the same receptor about five times harder.

name: Estrogen
fact: Three main forms counted by their hydroxyl groups — estrone one, estradiol two, estriol three — and estradiol is roughly ten times stronger than estrone.

name: Progesterone
fact: About 30 mg a day from the corpus luteum, and 250 mg a day from the placenta by the end of a pregnancy it exists to hold.

name: Growth Hormone
fact: One chain of 191 amino acids, released in pulses with the biggest during deep sleep — too much of it after childhood gives acromegaly rather than height.

name: Blood Clotting
fact: Thirteen numbered factors, each a zymogen waking the next, ending with thrombin cutting fibrinogen into fibrin and factor XIII stitching the strands crosswise.

name: Wound Healing
fact: Four overlapping phases that can run past a year, and the scar still tops out at 80% of unwounded skin's strength.

name: Thermoregulation
fact: Holding a core near 36.8 °C by trading sweat and vasodilation against shivering and brown fat — a losing fight above a sustained 35 °C wet bulb.

name: Menstrual Cycle
fact: A median 28 days, but only the follicular half really varies — the luteal phase runs about 14 days, the working lifespan of the corpus luteum.

name: Puberty
fact: It begins in the brain, with pulses of GnRH resuming after a decade of quiet, one to two years before anything is visible from outside.

name: Bile
fact: 400 to 800 mL a day, 97–98% water, colored yellow-green by bilirubin and its oxidised form biliverdin.

name: Pineal Gland
fact: A grain-of-rice gland wedged between the two halves of the thalamus — Descartes called it the principal seat of the soul, and it calcifies with age into 'brain sand'.

name: Circadian Rhythm
fact: Left to itself the human clock free-runs at about 24 hours and 11 minutes; the 2017 Nobel went to Hall, Rosbash and Young for the genes that make it tick.

name: Melatonin
fact: Blood levels run 80–120 pg/mL at night against 10–20 pg/mL by day; Aaron Lerner isolated it in 1958 while chasing whatever in pineal extract lightened tadpole skin.

name: Nucleus Accumbens
fact: About 95% of its neurons are GABAergic medium spiny cells carrying D1- or D2-type dopamine receptors — and it is a deep-brain-stimulation target for treatment-resistant OCD.

name: Sound
fact: A pressure wave running through a medium — the human ear answers from about 20 Hz up to 20 kHz, and to nothing at all in a vacuum.

name: Pitch
fact: Not a physical property but a judgement: the ear ordering sounds high to low, anchored since 1939 on A above middle C at 440 Hz.

name: Octave
fact: Two notes an octave apart stand at exactly 2:1 in frequency — halve a vibrating string and the pitch jumps by one.

name: Musical Scale
fact: A run of notes from one pitch up to its octave: seven in the major scale, twelve in the chromatic, each chromatic step the twelfth root of two apart.

name: Chord
fact: Two or more notes at once; the commonest is the triad — root, third and fifth — and each triad takes its name from the scale degree it stands on.

name: Rhythm
fact: From Greek rhythmos, 'any regular recurring motion' — accented beats set against unaccented ones, fixing when each sound lands.

name: Tempo
fact: Counted in beats per minute, and only pinned down after Maelzel's metronome — Beethoven published BPM marks for his first eight symphonies in the 1810s.

name: Melody
fact: A linear succession of tones the listener takes as a single entity — at its most literal, nothing more than pitch plus rhythm.

name: Harmony
fact: Music's vertical axis — notes stacked rather than strung out, and moving in progression; modern tonal harmony in the West begins around 1600.

name: Music
fact: Sound arranged into form, harmony, melody and rhythm; the oldest surviving instruments are the Geissenklösterle bone flutes, c. 43,150–39,370 years before present.

name: Musical Notation
fact: Neumes appeared in European monasteries by the mid-9th century, and Guido of Arezzo (c. 991 – after 1033) turned them into the ruled staff still read today.

name: Orchestra
fact: Seventy to over a hundred players in four sections — named for the orchestra, the floor in front of an ancient Greek stage where the chorus stood.

name: Symphony
fact: An extended orchestral work in three or four movements, the first in sonata form; Haydn wrote at least 106 of them across 36 years.

name: Opera
fact: Drama whose roles are sung: Peri's lost Dafne of about 1597 came first, and Monteverdi's L'Orfeo of 1607 is the earliest still regularly staged.

name: Jazz
fact: Out of Black New Orleans at the turn of the 20th century — swung time, blue notes, and a soloist who never plays the same composition twice.

name: Human Voice
fact: Vocal folds 17–25 mm long in adult men and 12.5–17.5 mm in adult women chop the lungs' airflow into pulses the mouth then filters.

name: Cello
fact: Tuned C2–G2–D3–A3, an octave below the viola; Adrien Servais added the floor spike around 1845, before which players gripped it between their calves.

name: Harp
fact: Its strings rise nearly perpendicular from the soundboard, which is what makes it a harp and not a zither; the Chogha Mish harps of Iran date to 3300–3100 BCE.

name: Language
fact: Estimates of the number of human languages run between 5,000 and 7,000. Every one pairs a grammar with a vocabulary, and can build an unlimited number of new sentences from a finite set of rules.

name: Phoneme
fact: The smallest sound unit that can change a word's meaning. Every spoken language has both consonant and vowel phonemes.

name: Word
fact: Speakers know one when they hear it, but linguists have never agreed on a definition -- phonological, grammatical and orthographic criteria each give different answers.

name: Grammar
fact: The system of rules governing clauses, phrases and words, studied through phonology, morphology and syntax.

name: Writing System
fact: A conventional set of symbols for representing a language. The earliest appeared in the late 4th millennium BC, each emerging from proto-writing that could not yet encode a full language.

name: Alphabet
fact: A writing system whose letters stand for phonemes -- the smallest sound segments that distinguish one word from another. A syllabary instead gives a symbol to each syllable, a logography to each word or morpheme.

name: Script
fact: The concrete set of characters a language is actually written in. ISO 15924 gives each script both a four-letter code and a numeric one.

name: Dialect
fact: A variety of a language marked off by its phonology, morphology, syntax and vocabulary -- standardised or not, written or not.

name: Lingua Franca
fact: A bridge language used between people with no native language in common -- often a third language belonging to neither side.

name: Language Family
fact: A group of languages descended from one common ancestor, the proto-language. The word 'family' is borrowed from biology, and historical linguists draw the tree the same way.

name: Pidgin
fact: A stripped-down contact language with a limited vocabulary and grammar drawn from several sources, usually improvised for trade.

name: Creole
fact: A pidgin grown up: expanded into a full language with native speakers, a consistent grammar and a large stable vocabulary, all within a fairly short period.

name: Sign Language
fact: Full natural languages in the visual-manual modality, with their own grammar and lexicon. They are not universal, and different sign languages are usually not mutually intelligible.

name: Loanword
fact: A word at least partly assimilated from one language into another. Linguists call it borrowing even though nothing is taken away and nothing is ever returned.

name: Literacy
fact: UNESCO data has the world's adult literacy rate climbing about five percentage points every decade since 1950, when it stood at 55.7%.

name: Esperanto
fact: The most widely spoken constructed language, published in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto -- a pen name its early adopters liked so much they gave it to the language.

name: Indo-European
fact: Eight branches still have living speakers, four of them with hundreds of millions of native speakers each. Two further branches are extinct.

name: Sino-Tibetan
fact: More than 400 languages and around 1.4 billion speakers -- 1.3 billion of them native speakers of the Sinitic branch alone.

name: Afroasiatic
fact: About 400 languages and over 500 million native speakers, split into six branches: Berber, Chadic, Cushitic, Egyptian, Omotic and Semitic.

name: Niger-Congo
fact: Ethnologue lists 1,540 Niger-Congo languages -- more member languages than any other family on Earth.

name: Austronesian
fact: About 386 million speakers and some 1,257 languages -- the second-largest count of any family -- reaching from Taiwan to Madagascar to the Pacific.

name: Dravidian
fact: 250 million speakers, mostly in South India, with outlying pockets as far away as Afghanistan and Iran.

name: Turkic
fact: More than 35 documented languages spread from Southeastern Europe to Siberia, forming a dialect continuum rather than a set of sharp boundaries.

name: Greek Alphabet
fact: The earliest known alphabetic script to write vowels systematically as well as consonants. The 24-letter Ionic version became standard by the end of the 4th century BC.

name: Latin Alphabet
fact: Also called the Roman script. Several Latin-script alphabets exist, differing in graphemes, collation and sound values from the classical original.

name: Cyrillic
fact: The designated national script across Slavic, Turkic, Mongolic, Uralic, Caucasian and Iranic-speaking countries of Eurasia, and used by many minority languages besides.

name: Devanagari
fact: A left-to-right abugida of 48 primary characters -- 14 vowels and 34 consonants -- used for over 120 languages, the largest of them Hindi.

name: Chinese Characters
fact: Logographs that stand for morphemes rather than sounds. Everyday text needs 3,500 to 5,000 of them; over 100,000 have been identified and encoded in Unicode.

name: Hangul
fact: 24 basic letters, called jamo, stacked into syllable blocks of an initial consonant, a vowel and an optional final consonant.

name: Kana
fact: Syllabaries writing the morae of Japanese. Hiragana and katakana are the two in current use.

name: Ge'ez Script
fact: An abugida that began as a consonant-only abjad. Amharic and Tigrinya speakers call it fidal, meaning 'script' or 'letter'.

name: Latin
fact: A classical Italic language of the Indo-European family, and the source of much of the technical vocabulary of theology, science, medicine and law.

name: English
fact: The world's most spoken language at about 1.5 billion speakers, yet only 372 million of them are native speakers -- it is only the third-largest native language.

name: Mandarin
fact: Natively spoken by 70% of all Chinese speakers, over a range so wide that Southwestern and Lower Yangtze varieties are not mutually intelligible with Beijing's.

name: Hindi
fact: Modern Standard Hindi has 347 million native speakers and another 264 million who speak it as a second language.

name: Spanish
fact: 519 million native speakers and official status in 21 countries. The largest population of native speakers is in Mexico, not Spain.

name: Arabic
fact: ISO assigns codes to 32 varieties of Arabic. The shared standard, Modern Standard Arabic, has essentially no native speakers -- everyone learns it in school.

name: French
fact: 258 million people speak French as a second language -- more than three times the 75 million who speak it natively.

name: Bengali
fact: Over 242 million native speakers as of 2025, making it the sixth most spoken native language in the world.

name: Portuguese
fact: About 267 million native speakers -- the fifth-most spoken native language, and the most widely spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere.

name: Russian
fact: The de facto official language of the Soviet Union, still official in Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

name: Urdu
fact: The national language and lingua franca of Pakistan, and also an official Eighth Schedule language in India.

name: Indonesian
fact: The 2020 census found over 97% of Indonesians fluent in it, though most of them speak it as a second language, not a mother tongue.

name: German
fact: The majority and official language of Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, and a recognised national language in Namibia.

name: Japanese
fact: Around 123 million speakers. Japan is the only country where it is the national language.

name: Swahili
fact: Counting second-language speakers, estimates run from 150 to 200 million; most native speakers live in Tanzania and Kenya.

name: Korean
fact: About 81 million speakers. It is Hangugeo in the south and Chosono in the north.

name: Turkish
fact: Around 90 million speakers make it the most widely spoken Turkic language, and the 18th-most spoken language in the world.

name: Vietnamese
fact: Around 86 million native speakers -- several times as many as the entire rest of the Austroasiatic family combined.

name: Tamil
fact: Attested since about 300 BCE, one of the longest-surviving classical languages in the world.

name: Persian
fact: A pluricentric language with three mutually intelligible standards -- Iranian, Afghan and Tajiki -- written in an Arabic-derived alphabet, except in Tajikistan, which uses a Cyrillic-derived one.

name: Italian
fact: About 64 million native speakers as of 2024, and between 68 and 85 million speakers in total.

name: Thai
fact: Its abugida has 44 consonant symbols, 16 vowel symbols that combine into at least 32 forms, and four tone marks.

name: Polish
fact: Over 39.7 million native speakers in 2024, the sixth-most-spoken language of the European Union, with strict T-V distinctions and obligatory honorifics.

name: Dutch
fact: About 25 million first-language speakers and 5 million second-language speakers, the third most spoken Germanic language.

name: Greek
fact: The longest documented history of any Indo-European language: at least 3,400 years of written records, and 2,800 years of the Greek alphabet.

name: Hebrew
fact: The only successful large-scale revival of a language: a sacred tongue with no native speakers that regained several million of them.

name: Amharic
fact: An Ethio-Semitic language: the first language of the Amhara people and the lingua franca of Ethiopia's metropolitan populations.

name: Hausa
fact: Over 94.5 million speakers, and the lingua franca of most of northern Nigeria, southern Niger, northern Cameroon and parts of Chad and Sudan.

name: Tagalog
fact: First language of about a quarter of Filipinos. Its standardised form, Filipino, is the national language and one of two official languages, alongside English.

name: Yoruba
fact: Roughly 50 million speakers, only about 2 million of whom are second-language speakers.

name: Punjabi
fact: Approximately 150 million native speakers -- one of the most widely spoken native languages in the world.

name: Javanese
fact: More than 68 million native speakers, on the central and eastern parts of Java plus pockets on the north coast of western Java.

name: Telugu
fact: About 100 million speakers make it the most widely spoken member of the Dravidian family, with a recorded history of at least 2,000 years.

name: Sanskrit
fact: The sacred language of Hinduism and of the historical texts of Buddhism and Jainism, and a link language across ancient and medieval South Asia.

name: Arabic Script
fact: The second-most widely used alphabetic writing system in the world, and second by the number of countries that use it.

name: Carnivore
fact: An obligate carnivore like a cat cannot synthesise its own taurine, arginine or retinol, so flesh is a requirement rather than a preference — and a hypercarnivore takes more than 70% of its diet as meat.

name: Herbivore
fact: Cross-linked plant cellulose is far harder to break down than meat, so most herbivores do not digest their own food — mutualistic gut bacteria and protozoans do it for them.

name: Omnivore
fact: Not a trophic level but a strategy: one bear's diet can run from almost entirely herbivorous to almost entirely carnivorous depending on what is available locally and seasonally.

name: Predator
fact: What makes it predation is that the food dies — an animal browsing leaves is not a predator, because the plant usually survives the assault.

name: Prey
fact: Predator and prey numbers chase each other: across Alaska and Canada, snowshoe hare populations swing on a near-synchronous 10-year period and lynx numbers follow, a cycle read off fur-trade records from 1845 to 1935.

name: Pollination
fact: The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma — about 80% of flowering plants have an animal do it, and some 98% of the remainder is done by wind.

name: Pollinator
fact: The animal that actually carries the pollen: at least 80% of the world's crop species need one, and cacao's flowers are pollinated by biting midges small enough to get inside them.

name: Nocturnal
fact: Gordon Walls' 1942 nocturnal bottleneck: mammals spent roughly 160 million years confined to the dark by diurnal dinosaurs, and modern mammals still carry the limited colour vision and acute hearing they bought with it.

name: Diurnal
fact: Most animals began day-active and some retreated into the night — geckos alone have switched back about 20 separate times, producing roughly 430 diurnal species.

name: Mimicry
fact: Three parties, not two — a mimic, the model it resembles, and the dupe that is fooled; Henry Walter Bates described the harmless-copies-the-defended version in 1862, Fritz Müller the honest mutual kind in 1878.

name: Venom
fact: The line between venom and poison is delivery, not chemistry: venom is driven through a wound by a bite or sting, and it has evolved independently at least 104 times across 8 phyla.

name: Endoskeleton
fact: Mineralised frame on the inside, overlaid by soft tissue — it grows with its owner, which is how a human goes from about 270 bones at birth to about 206 without ever moulting.

name: Gestation
fact: An African bush elephant carries a calf for 22 months and delivers it at 100 to 120 kg; a human birth normally comes at about 40 weeks.

name: Larva
fact: A juvenile built so unlike its adult that it lives somewhere else and eats something else — which is the point, since it is then sheltered from different predators and competes with neither its parents nor itself.

name: Habitat
fact: Species-specific, not a place on a map: rotting wood in Britain is habitat to over 1700 invertebrate species, each keyed to its own microhabitat of light, humidity and temperature.

name: Ecosystem
fact: Arthur Tansley put the word in print in 1935 — Arthur Roy Clapham coined it at his request — to insist that organisms and their physical surroundings are one system, linked by nutrient cycles and energy flows.

name: Ecological Niche
fact: Hutchinson's 1957 version is an n-dimensional hypervolume of every condition a species can live in — and the realized niche is always narrower than that, because competitors hold the rest.

name: Biome
fact: Plot average annual precipitation against average annual temperature, as Whittaker did, and the world's vegetation sorts itself out — 14 major terrestrial biomes in the most-used scheme.

name: Scavenger
fact: Living on carrion alone is rare among vertebrates because finding enough of it costs more energy than it returns — vultures manage it on gliding flight, toxin-proof guts and expandable intestines.

name: Homologous Structure
fact: Richard Owen named it in 1843 — 'the same organ in different animals under every variety of form and function' — so a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a horse's foreleg are one structure, while an insect's wing and a bird's are not.

name: Dominant Allele
fact: One copy is enough to show — but dominant never meant common or better; dominance is a relationship between two alleles, and the same allele can be dominant to one and recessive to a third.

name: Punnett Square
fact: Reginald Punnett's 1905 grid: one parent's gametes along the top, the other's down the side, and the four cells give 1:2:1 genotypes and Mendel's 3:1 phenotypes.

name: Antibiotic Resistance
fact: Natural selection running in a petri dish — the bacteria a course of antibiotics leaves behind are, by definition, the ones it failed to kill, and in 2019 that arithmetic was directly responsible for 1.27 million deaths.

name: Domestication
fact: A long-term relationship in which humans take over the care of another organism for a predictable supply of a resource — the dog was first, and the only large carnivore ever to go through it.

name: Fitness
fact: Nothing to do with strength, health or lifespan — it is the average number of offspring left by carriers of a genotype, which is why the term 'Darwinian fitness' exists at all; Haldane put the maths on it in 1924.

name: Psychology
fact: The scientific study of mind and behaviour — a laboratory science only since 1879, when Wundt started measuring conscious experience instead of arguing about it.

name: Parkinson's Disease
fact: By the time the first tremor shows, 50-80% of the substantia nigra's dopamine neurons are already gone; James Parkinson described the condition in 1817.

name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
fact: A highly heritable neurodevelopmental condition present from early childhood — about 1 in 100 children by WHO estimate — that DSM-5 made one spectrum in 2013.

name: ADHD
fact: Inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity present from before age 12; heritability runs 70-80%, and stimulants treat it by raising dopamine and noradrenaline signalling.

name: Anorexia Nervosa
fact: Eating restricted to a dangerously low body weight alongside intense fear of gaining it; about 5% die within ten years, the highest mortality of any psychiatric diagnosis.

name: Addiction
fact: A persistent urge to use despite substantial harm, running on the ventral tegmental area's dopamine neurons — and not the same thing as physical dependence.

name: Placebo Effect
fact: An inert sugar pill can genuinely reduce pain: since 1978 it has been known that placebo analgesia depends on the brain's own opioids, and naloxone blocks it.

name: Confirmation Bias
fact: The pull toward evidence that fits what you already think — Peter Wason's 1960 subjects tested only the number triples their guess predicted, never one that could refute it.

name: Gestalt Psychology
fact: Wertheimer, Koffka and Kohler's school, dated to 1912: perception delivers organized wholes, and breaking them into smaller parts explains nothing.

name: Structuralism
fact: Titchener's attempt to classify the mind's structures the way chemists classify elements, sorting experience into sensations, images and affections by trained introspection.

name: Phrenology
fact: A pseudoscience: Gall's claim from 1796 that skull bumps reveal mental traits was discredited by the 1840s, but not before it was used to argue for slavery.

name: Lobotomy
fact: A discredited operation severing the prefrontal cortex's connections; roughly 40,000 Americans underwent it, and Moniz took a Nobel Prize for it in 1949.

name: Id
fact: In Freud's 1923 structural model, the wholly unconscious part: uncoordinated instinctual needs and desires, running on the pleasure principle and demanding satisfaction now.

name: Ego
fact: Freud's mediator — the part of the id modified by direct contact with the outside world, trading the pleasure principle for the reality principle.

name: Super-Ego
fact: The parent taken inside: Freud built it on the model not of the parents themselves but of the parents' own super-ego, which is how a culture's rules outlive it.

name: Multiple Intelligences
fact: Gardner's 1983 proposal that intelligence is eight independent kinds — beloved in classrooms, and still without a published study demonstrating its validity.

name: Habituation
fact: The simplest learning there is: a response fades to a repeated harmless stimulus, and fades only for that stimulus — which is what separates it from a sense organ tiring.

name: Mnemonic
fact: A hook that makes recall cheap — 'Richard of York gave battle in vain' carries seven colours in order, and HOMES carries all five Great Lakes.

name: Mantle
fact: 2,900 km of peridotite between crust and core — 84% of Earth's volume, solid rock that still creeps like a fluid given geological time.

name: Crust
fact: 5–10 km thick under the oceans, 25–70 km under the continents, and less than 1% of the planet's volume either way.

name: Earth's Core
fact: Below 2,890 km the rock gives out and iron takes over: a liquid outer core that makes the magnetic field, around a solid inner ball 1,221 km in radius.

name: Rock Cycle
fact: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic are not three kinds of rock so much as three stages of one loop, turned by plate tectonics and running water.

name: Evaporation
fact: Molecules leaving a liquid's surface at any temperature at all — no boiling required; humid air slows it, moving air speeds it up.

name: Water Cycle
fact: About 505,000 km³ of water leaves the surface and falls back every year, and any given molecule spends only around nine days in the air.

name: Pangaea
fact: Assembled around 335 million years ago and rifting apart by 200 million, ringed by a single superocean, Panthalassa.

name: Continental Drift
fact: Wegener's 1912 claim that the continents move: right about the fact, wildly wrong about the speed, and dismissed for fifty years because he had no mechanism.

name: Plate Tectonics
fact: Seven or eight major plates creeping along at 0–10 cm a year; geologists only accepted it once seafloor spreading was confirmed in the mid-1960s.

name: Subduction
fact: One plate sliding beneath another at up to 11 cm a year — some slabs have sunk the whole way to the core-mantle boundary at 2,890 km.

name: Fault
fact: A fracture whose two sides have actually moved: friction locks it, strain piles up, and the slip when it finally fails is the earthquake.

name: Landslide
fact: Gravity taking a slope apart — rockfall, mudflow, debris flow — usually after rain saturates the ground or shaking loosens it.

name: Avalanche
fact: A slab avalanche needs a weak layer buried under cohesive snow; human-triggered ones peak on 35–45° slopes, and dry powder flows can exceed 300 km/h.

name: Aquifer
fact: Rock that both holds water and lets it move — pore space alone is not enough, which is why permeable sandstone and fissured limestone qualify.

name: Geode
fact: A cavity in lava or in limestone, lined inward over ages by mineral-laden water: dull on the outside, walled with quartz on the inside.

name: Ice Age
fact: Not one cold snap but 2.58 million years of them — at the last maximum, ice 3–4 km thick held sea level about 110 m below today's.

name: Stratovolcano
fact: The steep layered cone of a subduction zone: silica-rich lava too sticky to flow far, stacked with tephra — Fuji, Rainier, Vesuvius.

name: Shield Volcano
fact: Basalt runny enough to run for miles before it freezes, so the slopes stay at 2–10° — Mauna Loa is about 100 km across at the base.

name: Kimberlite
fact: Melt from 150–450 km down, erupted violently on its own carbon dioxide up a carrot-shaped pipe 75 m to 1.5 km wide.

name: Richter Scale
fact: Richter and Gutenberg, 1935: the base-10 logarithm of the largest trace a standard seismometer draws, so one whole number is about 31.6 times the energy.

name: God
fact: Traditions divide sharply over the word: Judaism, Christianity and Islam hold that one God exists, polytheists that many do, and deists that a creator exists but never intervenes — while the attributes usually argued over are omnipotence, omniscience and perfect goodness.

name: Worship
fact: From Old English weorthscipe, 'worth-ship' — ascribing worth to what is honoured; Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox theology further separates latria, the adoration held due to God alone, from dulia, the honour offered to saints.

name: Prayer
fact: Muslims are obliged to pray at fixed times each day facing Mecca and Jews three times daily, Hindus join the palms in pranam, and Buddhists lean on repeated mantra — the shared element is deliberate address to an object of worship.

name: Scripture
fact: Latin scriptura means simply 'writing': the Rigveda of about 1500 BCE is among the oldest religious texts still in use, and while Christianity fixed its canon by councils, Hinduism and Buddhism never settled on one at all.

name: Religion
fact: Scholars count roughly 10,000 distinct religions worldwide, though Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism together account for over 73% of the world's people; the Latin religiō originally meant conscientiousness or obligation, not belief in gods.

name: Faith
fact: Named differently in each tradition — pistis in Greek Christianity, iman in Islam, emunah in Judaism, saddhā in Buddhism — and disputed in kind: adherents generally describe it as trust grounded in warrant, critics as belief held without evidence.

name: Sin
fact: Judaism frames sin as 'missing the mark' of God's law, Christianity adds original sin inherited from Adam, Islam grades it from minor dhanb to grave, and Buddhism has no offended deity at all, treating wrong acts as karma with natural consequences.

name: Afterlife
fact: Egyptians weighed the heart against Maat's feather of truth to decide entry to the Fields of Aaru; Abrahamic traditions expect resurrection and judgement, while Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions expect rebirth steered by karma.

name: Heaven
fact: The word is Old English heofon, 'sky', as are Hebrew shamayim and Arabic samāʾ — but Christianity and Islam describe it as a permanent reward, while Hindu svarga and the Buddhist deva realms are temporary stops before rebirth resumes.

name: Prophet
fact: From Greek prophētēs, one who speaks for a god: the Talmud counts 48 prophets and seven prophetesses, the Quran names 25 while Islamic tradition puts the total near 124,000, and Islam calls Muhammad the seal — the last — of them.

name: Sacrament
fact: Augustine's definition — an outward sign of an inward grace — is shared by traditions that count them very differently: the Catholic and Orthodox churches recognise seven, a number fixed at the Council of Trent, while most Protestants keep only baptism and the Eucharist.

name: Priest
fact: A figure authorised to perform a religion's sacred rites and mediate between people and the divine — Catholic and Orthodox priests are ordained to celebrate the sacraments, while Jewish kohanim hold their standing by inherited lineage rather than ordination.

name: Pope
fact: Bishop of Rome, head of a church of about 1.4 billion Catholics and sovereign of Vatican City since 1929, elected by a conclave of cardinals under 80.

name: Hajj
fact: The pilgrimage to Mecca asked once of every Muslim who can afford and physically manage it, held on the 8th to 12th of Dhu al-Hijjah: about 1.8 million people circle the Kaaba seven times, walk between Safa and Marwah, and stand at Arafat.

name: Ramadan
fact: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, running 29 or 30 days from one crescent sighting to the next, in which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset — eating suhur before first light and breaking the fast at iftar, traditionally with dates.

name: Kaaba
fact: A stone cube about 12.9 by 11 metres at the centre of Mecca's Masjid al-Haram, draped each year in the gold-embroidered black kiswah, with the Black Stone set in its eastern corner; every mosque on Earth points its prayer toward it.

name: Sabbath
fact: Jewish Shabbat runs from just before Friday sunset until three stars appear on Saturday night, with 39 categories of creative work set aside; most Christians moved the day of rest to Sunday, though Seventh-day Adventists and others kept Saturday.

name: Gospel
fact: Old English gōdspel, 'good news', translating Greek euangelion: Mark was written around AD 70 and Matthew, Luke and John over the following thirty years, all four anonymous and only later attached to the names they now carry.

name: Hadith
fact: Reports of what Muhammad said, did or silently approved, each carried by an isnad — a named chain of transmitters — and graded sahih, hasan or da'if; the 9th-century collections of Bukhari and Muslim are the most authoritative for Sunnis, while Shia Islam relies on its own Four Books.

name: Miracle
fact: An event held to lie beyond natural explanation: Catholic canonisation still requires verified miracles, Islamic theology treats the Quran's own inimitability as the miracle, and David Hume argued no testimony could ever make one likelier than a mistaken witness.

name: Angel
fact: Greek angelos and Hebrew mal'akh both mean simply 'messenger'; belief in angels is an article of faith in Islam, whose Quran describes them with wings in twos, threes and fours, and named figures such as Gabriel and Michael were fixed in Christian tradition by the 3rd to 5th centuries.

name: Jerusalem
fact: Its 0.9-square-kilometre Old City holds the Western Wall below the Temple Mount, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Al-Aqsa compound with the Dome of the Rock — holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam at once, and claimed as capital by both Israel and Palestine.

name: Electricity
fact: Named after amber — Greek elektron — because a rubbed lump of it lifts dust; Gilbert coined electricus for the effect in 1600.

name: Factory
fact: Machines too big to keep in a cottage, gathered under one roof: Arkwright ran his Cromford mills day and night on two twelve-hour shifts from 1772.

name: Industrial Revolution
fact: Britain from about 1760, reaching Europe and the US by 1840; steam there supplied some 10,000 horsepower in 1800 and 210,000 by 1815.

name: Interchangeable Parts
fact: Honore Blanc was building muskets from swappable flintlock parts by about 1778; Whitney reassembled ten guns from mixed piles before Congress in July 1801.

name: Assembly Line
fact: Ford's moving line started at Highland Park on 7 October 1913 and split the Model T into 45 steps — 12.5 hours of work down to 93 minutes.

name: Mass Production
fact: Standardised goods in constant flow; the term was popularised by a 1926 Encyclopaedia Britannica supplement written from correspondence with Ford.

name: Algorithm
fact: Named for al-Khwarizmi of Baghdad's House of Wisdom: the Latin version of his arithmetic opens Dixit Algoritmi, 'thus spoke al-Khwarizmi'.

name: Binary Code
fact: Leibniz published it in 1703 as Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire — arithmetic using only the characters 1 and 0.

name: Wind Turbine
fact: Scottish academic James Blyth had one charging batteries to light his Marykirk holiday home in July 1887.

name: Power Grid
fact: Generation and consumption must stay balanced across the whole grid, because the energy is consumed as it is produced.

name: Abacus
fact: Two hardwood beads above the bar and five below on every rod — that is the Chinese suanpan, in written records by the 2nd century BC.

name: Atom
fact: Over 99.94% of its mass sits in a nucleus a few femtometres wide, inside an electron cloud around a hundred picometres across.

name: Chemical Element
fact: A species of atom defined by nothing but its proton count — IUPAC recognises 118, and only the first 94 occur naturally on Earth.

name: Chemical Bond
fact: Electrons and nuclei pulling on each other electrostatically — Lewis worked out the shared-pair version in 1916.

name: Molecule
fact: Two or more atoms held by chemical bonds; the smallest, H2, spans 0.74 ångströms, while a single DNA molecule can run to macroscopic length.

name: Chemical Compound
fact: Different elements bonded in a fixed ratio — water is 2:1 hydrogen to oxygen every time, which is exactly what a mixture never is.

name: Mixture
fact: Substances stirred together without bonding, in any ratio you like, and separable again by filtering, distilling or freezing.

name: Solution
fact: A mixture gone homogeneous — the solute breaks down to single molecules or ions, so there is one phase and nothing ever settles out.

name: Colloid
fact: Particles between 1 nanometre and 1 micrometre: too big to dissolve, too small to settle, and big enough to scatter a light beam — Graham named them in 1861.

name: Chemical Reaction
fact: Only electrons move; the nuclei come through untouched, and every atom that went in comes out again somewhere.

name: Catalyst
fact: Lowers the activation energy and comes out unchanged — Berzelius named it in 1835, and around 90% of commercial chemicals now pass through one.

name: Acid
fact: A proton donor: it hands over H+, tastes sour, turns litmus red, and drops the pH below 7.

name: Base (Chemistry)
fact: The chemical opposite of an acid — a proton acceptor, slippery to the touch, pH above 7, and it turns red litmus blue.

name: pH
fact: The negative log of hydrogen ion activity, so each whole number is a tenfold change — Sørensen invented the scale at the Carlsberg laboratory in 1909.

name: Oxidation
fact: Lavoisier named it for oxygen, but it is really just the loss of electrons — an atom's oxidation state going up, oxygen present or not.

name: Corrosion
fact: Metal dissolving into its own surroundings: it cost the United States about $276 billion in 1998, some 3.2% of GDP.

name: Combustion
fact: High-temperature exothermic redox with oxygen — coal's adiabatic flame reaches about 2,200°C, and starved of air it makes carbon monoxide instead.

name: Hydrocarbon
fact: Hydrogen and carbon and nothing else — methane, benzene, paraffin wax and polyethylene are all the same two elements at different chain lengths.

name: States of Matter
fact: Solid keeps shape and volume, liquid keeps only volume, gas keeps neither — and plasma, the fourth, is about 99% of ordinary matter in the universe.

name: Crystal
fact: A unit cell repeated in every direction; every arrangement there is falls into just seven crystal systems.

name: Allotrope
fact: Same element, different architecture — diamond and graphite are both nothing but carbon, and Berzelius named the idea in 1840.

name: Mineral
fact: Naturally formed, solid, of definite composition and ordered crystal structure — the IMA lists 6,228 species, and a rock is just an aggregate of them.

name: Metal
fact: Positive ions sitting in a shared sea of loose electrons — that sea is the shine, the conduction and the bending, and it covers about three quarters of the periodic table.

name: Nonmetal
fact: Seventeen brittle, poorly conducting, electronegative elements — and five of them, H, C, N, O and Si, make up 93% of all biomass.

name: Metalloid
fact: The six on the staircase — boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium — that look like metals and behave like weak nonmetals.

name: Alkali Metal
fact: Group 1, one electron in the outer s-orbital: soft enough to cut with a knife, stored under oil, and caesium melts at 28.44°C, below body heat.

name: Noble Gas
fact: Full outer shells, so group 18 mostly refuses to react — until Bartlett made xenon hexafluoroplatinate in 1962 and ended the word 'inert'.

name: Halogen
fact: Group 17, seven valence electrons and one short — the only group that offers a gas, a liquid and a solid at room temperature.

name: Alloy
fact: Metal dissolved in metal, still metallically bonded and with no fixed formula — the mismatched atoms strain the lattice and stop it slipping.

name: Amalgam
fact: Any alloy with mercury in it; iron is one of the few metals that refuses, which is why mercury was shipped in iron flasks.

name: Polymer
fact: One small monomer repeated thousands of times — Staudinger argued in 1920 that these really were single giant molecules, and was doubted for years.

name: Plastic
fact: Mouldable synthetic polymer, mostly from oil and gas — over 400 million tonnes were made in 2023, and more than half of all plastic ever made came after 2004.

name: Ceramic
fact: Inorganic, non-metallic and hardened by fire — the oldest are Gravettian figurines of 29,000–25,000 BC, made long before anyone fired a pot.

name: Composite Material
fact: Two materials that stay chemically separate inside one part — wattle and daub has been doing it for over 6,000 years.

name: Semiconductor
fact: Conducts better as it warms, which no metal does, and its conductivity can be dialled by parts-per-million of a deliberate impurity.

name: Galvanization
fact: A zinc coat that corrodes on purpose, named for Luigi Galvani — good for about 40–50 years in a water pipe.

name: Vulcanization
fact: Sulfur bridges stitched between rubber's polymer chains — Hancock patented it on 21 November 1843, eight weeks before Goodyear.

name: Graphene
fact: One atom thick, 130 GPa tensile strength, and it absorbs just 2.3% of the light passing through it.

name: Nuclear Fission
fact: Splitting one uranium-235 nucleus gives about 200 MeV — roughly a hundred million times what burning a single carbon atom yields.

name: Nuclear Fusion
fact: The Sun fuses 620 million tonnes of hydrogen a second, and about 0.7% of that mass leaves as energy.

name: Dragon
fact: Everywhere a serpent, but the two halves of the world disagree on what it is for: Europe made it a fire-breathing hoarder to be killed, China a rain-giver whose five-clawed form only the emperor could wear.

name: Phoenix
fact: Herodotus was told at Heliopolis that it came once in 500 years; Tacitus heard 1,461, which is exactly Egypt's Sothic cycle.

name: Griffin
fact: A lion's body and hind legs with an eagle's head, wings and front talons — the oldest Egyptian one is painted on a cosmetic palette from Hierakonpolis, c. 3300–3100 BC.

name: Unicorn
fact: Ctesias, writing from Persia, described it as a white, red and black wild ass with a horn a cubit and a half long — not a horse at all.

name: Mermaid
fact: The Syrian goddess Atargatis was venerated at Ashkelon with a woman's face and a fish's body — Ctesias reports it in the 5th century BC, long before mermaids reached northern Europe.

name: Werewolf
fact: Old English werwulf, 'man-wolf'. Accusations peaked alongside the witch trials — Peter Stumpp was executed as one at Bedburg in 1589.

name: Golem
fact: Write אמת, emet, 'truth', on its forehead and it moves; rub out the first letter and מת, met, 'dead', stops it.

name: Banshee
fact: Irish bean sí, 'woman of the fairy mound' — she keens for a death in the family even when it happens far away. First recorded in the Cathréim Thoirdhealbhaigh in 1380.

name: Troll
fact: Scandinavian folklore has them turn to stone in sunlight, which is why particular boulders across Norway have troll names attached to them.

name: Underworld
fact: Hades, Duat, Mictlan, Yomi, Sheol, Diyu, Xibalba — the idea of a world of the dead below this one turns up in almost every civilisation there has been.

name: Mount Olympus
fact: A real mountain on the Thessaly–Macedonia border whose summit, Mytikas, is 2,917 m — the highest ground in Greece, and not climbed in the modern era until 2 August 1913.

name: Elysium
fact: Homer's version has no snow, no storm and no rain, only the west wind; Virgil gave it a sun and stars of its own.

name: Asgard
fact: Old Norse Ásgarðr, literally 'enclosure of the Æsir' — a walled stronghold, which is why the story of who built the wall matters so much.

name: Yggdrasil
fact: An ash with three roots reaching three wells — Urðarbrunnr, Mímisbrunnr and Hvergelmir — and the name probably means 'Odin's horse', a kenning for gallows.

name: Trickster
fact: The boundary-crosser: a figure who breaks the rules of the world and, in breaking them, resets them. Loki, Anansi, Coyote, Eshu and Hermes are all filed here.

name: Moirai
fact: Clotho spins the thread, Lachesis measures it out, Atropos cuts it and picks the manner of death — and the Delphic priestess held that Zeus was subject to them too.

name: Tartarus
fact: Hesiod gave it a measurement: a bronze anvil would fall nine days from heaven to earth, and nine more from earth to Tartarus.

name: Nüwa
fact: Chinese creator goddess with a human face and a snake's body who made people from yellow clay — nobles shaped by hand, everyone else flicked from a cord dragged through mud.

name: Pangu
fact: Chinese first being, hatched from a cosmic egg: for 18,000 years the sky rose ten feet a day, the earth sank ten feet, and he grew ten feet to hold them apart.

name: Perun
fact: Slavic thunder god of the oak. The Primary Chronicle records his Kiev idol — silver head, gold moustache — pulled down and thrown in the Dnieper when Vladimir converted in 988.

name: The Dagda
fact: Father-figure of the Tuatha Dé Danann, with a club that kills at one end and revives at the other, and a cauldron no assembly ever left unsatisfied.

name: Photosynthesis
fact: It captures about 130 terawatts — roughly eight times all human power use — and locks 100 to 115 billion tonnes of carbon into living matter every year.

name: Angiosperm
fact: A flowering plant, its seeds shut inside an ovary rather than naked on a scale — some 300,000 species, and the whole group only appeared around 130 million years ago.

name: Gametophyte
fact: The haploid half of a plant's life, and it makes its gametes by ordinary mitosis — in a flowering plant it is down to a few cells hidden inside a pollen grain.

name: Sporophyte
fact: The diploid half, and the one you actually notice: every tree, every fern frond and every blade of grass is a sporophyte.

name: Alternation of Generations
fact: Every plant lives two lives in turn, haploid then diploid — and which one you see flips completely between a moss and an oak.

name: Double Fertilization
fact: Two sperm, two fusions: one builds the embryo, the other builds the triploid endosperm that will feed it — found independently by Nawaschin and Guignard in the 1890s.

name: Endosperm
fact: Tissue with three chromosome sets instead of two — and it is most of a wheat grain, all of white flour, and both the meat and the water of a coconut.

name: Sepal
fact: The outermost whorl, collectively the calyx — usually the only green part of a flower, and it does photosynthesise, just slowly, having few stomata.

name: Petal
fact: The advertising hoarding — and much of the advertising is invisible to us: a buttercup that looks plain yellow has a dark bullseye under ultraviolet.

name: Stamen
fact: A filament with an anther on top. The whole whorl of them is the androecium, from the Greek for 'man's house'.

name: Anther
fact: Four pollen sacs on a stalk, which split open — dehisce — by lengthwise slits, by pores, or by little hinged valves, depending on the family.

name: Stigma (Flower)
fact: The sticky or feathery pad where pollen has to land. Saffron is nothing but these, three crimson ones per crocus, about 150 flowers to the gram.

name: Style (Flower)
fact: The stalk a pollen tube must grow down. Every silk on an ear of maize is one style, and the tube travels it at over a centimetre an hour.

name: Carpel
fact: Stigma, style and ovary as one unit — and morphologically it is a leaf, folded around the ovules and sealed.

name: Ovary (Flower)
fact: The swollen base of the carpel holding the ovules. Its wall becomes the fruit, so the flesh of a tomato is an ovary wall.

name: Meristem
fact: Plant stem cells: undifferentiated, totipotent, and never finished — which is why a root or shoot can keep growing for as long as it is alive.

name: Apical Meristem
fact: The dome of dividing cells at a shoot or root tip. The shoot's makes every leaf and flower, and floods auxin down the stem to hold the side buds shut.

name: Cytokinin
fact: The first one, kinetin, was crystallised in 1954 out of autoclaved herring sperm DNA — a plant hormone found in a fish, and not made by plants at all.

name: Abscisic Acid
fact: Named for abscission, which it turns out to barely cause — ethylene does that. Its real jobs are shutting the stomata and enforcing seed dormancy.

name: Gravitropism
fact: Roots grow down, shoots grow up, and the sensor is a pile of starch grains heavy enough to sink.

name: Thigmotropism
fact: Growth aimed by touch: the side of a tendril that meets a support grows slower than the free side, so the tendril winds itself around.

name: Parenchyma
fact: The plant's general-purpose cell — thin primary wall, still alive, still able to divide. Potato flesh, fruit pulp and a leaf's green layer are all parenchyma.

name: Collenchyma
fact: Alive, and thickened only in the primary wall with cellulose and pectin — stiff enough to hold a stem up, soft enough to let it keep elongating.

name: Sclerenchyma
fact: Lays down a lignified secondary wall and then dies. Flax and hemp fibres are sclerenchyma, and so are the gritty stone cells in a pear.

name: Mesophyll
fact: A leaf's middle layer: a palisade of upright chloroplast-packed cells sitting over a spongy layer that is mostly air space.

name: Companion Cell
fact: A sieve tube dissolves its own nucleus to keep the pipe clear; the companion cell alongside keeps a nucleus, extra ribosomes and extra mitochondria, and runs it.

name: Tracheid
fact: Long, tapered, lignified and dead at maturity — conifer wood is made almost entirely of these, and contains no vessels at all.

name: Transpiration
fact: 97 to 99.5% of the water a plant lifts out of the ground is simply lost again — a large oak throws away around 150,000 litres a year.

name: Self-Pollination
fact: Guarantees seed with no pollinator at all — some plants never even open the flower — but it concentrates every harmful recessive the plant is carrying.

name: Cross-Pollination
fact: About half of all flowering plant species refuse their own pollen outright: the S-locus recognises it and stops the pollen tube dead.

name: Seed Dispersal
fact: Getting away from the parent is the whole point, since seedlings under their own tree are eaten and outgrown. The sandbox tree just fires its seeds 100 m.

name: Xerophyte
fact: Built to lose as little as possible: a waxy cuticle leaks water about 25 times more slowly than open stomata do.

name: Succulent
fact: Tissue that can be 90 to 95% water — and the habit has evolved independently in around 60 unrelated plant families.

name: Epiphyte
fact: Rents the perch, never the food: about 24,000 species, 89% of them flowering plants, and roughly a third of all fern species do it too.

name: Halophyte
fact: Only about 2% of plant species manage it. Dwarf glasswort grows in 70 g/L of dissolved salts — close to twice the strength of seawater.

name: Seed Dormancy
fact: Abscisic acid holds the seed shut and gibberellin lets it go. A date seed from Masada was still willing after nearly 2,000 years.

name: Seed Stratification
fact: One to three months at about 1–3 °C and damp: winter, faked in a bag of moist sand at the back of a fridge.

name: Vernalization
fact: Weeks at 1–7 °C silence the FLC gene that blocks flowering — which is how autumn-sown winter wheat knows to wait until spring.

name: Senescence
fact: Not wearing out — dismantling. The leaf breaks down its chlorophyll, uncovering carotenoids that were there all along, and ships its nitrogen back into the plant.

name: Secondary Growth
fact: Growth in girth rather than in length: the vascular cambium adds a layer of xylem inward every year, and those layers are a tree's rings.

name: Vascular Bundle
fact: Xylem and phloem run together in one strand, xylem on the inner face and phloem on the outer. Every vein in a leaf is one of these.

name: Pith
fact: The soft parenchyma core of a stem. It often dries out and disintegrates into a hollow — and elder pith is still used to clean watch parts.

name: Artillery
fact: Ranged guns that outreach any infantry weapon — and the cause of most combat deaths in the Napoleonic Wars and both World Wars.

name: Trench Warfare
fact: Firepower outran mobility: by the end of October 1914 the whole front in Belgium and France had solidified into trench lines that lasted until the war's last weeks.

name: Tank
fact: Armour, a gun and continuous tracks, specified to cross a four-foot trench; the British Mark I first went into action at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916.

name: World War I
fact: 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918. An estimated 15 to 22 million people died, soldiers and civilians together.

discovered.note: Fighting begins on 28 July 1914; the Western Front freezes into trench lines within months.

name: Dreadnought
fact: HMS Dreadnought, commissioned 2 December 1906, carried ten uniform 12-inch guns and steam turbines, and made every battleship then afloat obsolete.

discovered.note: HMS Dreadnought is commissioned, the first all-big-gun, turbine-powered battleship.

name: Aircraft Carrier
fact: HMS Argus, 1918, was the first ship able to both launch and recover aircraft; within a generation its aircraft outranged every naval gun.

discovered.note: HMS Argus becomes the first carrier able to both launch and recover naval aircraft.

name: U-boat
fact: Unterseeboot, undersea boat. In the First World War alone they sank 5,708 merchant and fishing vessels — 11,108,865 gross register tons.

name: Blitzkrieg
fact: Armour concentrated at one point and steered by radio. The Wehrmacht never adopted the word as doctrine; Hitler called it a completely idiotic term.

name: World War II
fact: 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945. Between 60 and 75 million people died, a majority of them civilians.

discovered.note: Germany invades Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declare war two days later.

name: Manhattan Project
fact: Nearly $2 billion and some 130,000 people, with over 80 percent of the cost going to nothing but making the fissile material. Trinity fired on 16 July 1945.

discovered.note: The US Army establishes the Manhattan Engineer District to build an atomic weapon.

name: Hydrogen Bomb
fact: A fission bomb used only as a match: Ivy Mike, 1952, imploded liquid deuterium and yielded 10.4 megatons, over 450 times the Nagasaki bomb.

discovered.note: Ivy Mike, the first full-scale thermonuclear test, yields 10.4 megatons.

name: ICBM
fact: A ballistic missile ranging beyond 5,500 km: roughly 25 minutes of suborbital coast, apogee near 1,200 km, then re-entry faster than any defence.

discovered.note: The Soviet R-7 flies 6,000 km on 21 August 1957, the first intercontinental ballistic missile.

name: Feudalism
fact: Land held from a lord in return for military service and an oath of fealty — and a word coined in the 18th century, long after anyone lived under it.

name: Napoleonic Wars
fact: 18 May 1803 to 20 November 1815, about 2.8 million military dead. Over 450,000 men crossed into Russia in June 1812; some 120,000 came back.

name: Sun Tzu
fact: Master Sun, credited with the thirteen chapters of the Art of War — a text long doubted until bamboo slips sealed by 118 BC turned up at Yinqueshan in 1972.

name: Flamethrower
fact: Compressed nitrogen pushes heated oil down a hose to a pilot flame at the nozzle. First used against French troops outside Verdun on 26 February 1915.

discovered.note: First used in war on 26 February 1915, against French troops outside Verdun.

name: Iraq
fact: Capital Baghdad. Its plains between the Tigris and Euphrates are ancient Mesopotamia, the cradle of civilisation that produced Sumer and Babylon.

name: Syria
fact: Capital Damascus, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and the seat of the Umayyad Caliphate.

name: Jordan
fact: Capital Amman. Holds Petra, whose Al-Khazneh is believed to be the mausoleum of the Nabataean king Aretas IV, 1st century AD.

name: Kuwait
fact: Capital Kuwait City. Sits on the world's sixth-largest oil reserves, and the Kuwaiti dinar is the world's most valuable currency.

name: Bahrain
fact: Capital Manama. An archipelago of 33 natural islands, famed since antiquity for pearl fisheries reckoned the finest in the world into the 19th century.

name: Qatar
fact: Capital Doha, home to over 80% of the population. A peninsula holding the world's third-largest natural gas reserves.

name: Oman
fact: Capital Muscat. The oldest independent state in the Arab world, ruled continuously by the Al Bu Said dynasty since 1744.

name: United Arab Emirates
fact: Capital Abu Dhabi. A federation of six emirates formed on 2 December 1971, joined by Ras al-Khaimah on 10 January 1972.

name: Yemen
fact: Capital Sanaa. Its port of Mocha exported coffee when Yemen was the world's sole producer, and it holds the Socotra archipelago.

name: Bhutan
fact: Capital Thimphu. Its Gangkhar Puensum, 7,570 m, is the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.

name: Myanmar
fact: Capital Naypyidaw. Its Mogok valley yields the 'pigeon's blood' rubies behind roughly 90% of world ruby production.

name: Timor-Leste
fact: Capital Dili. Portuguese until 1975, then occupied by Indonesia; sovereign on 20 May 2002 as the first new state of the 21st century.

name: Kyrgyzstan
fact: Capital Bishkek. The Tian Shan covers over 80% of it, and every river drains into a closed basin that never reaches the sea.

name: Tajikistan
fact: Capital Dushanbe. Mountains of the Pamir range cover more than 90% of it, and most of the country lies above 3,000 metres.

name: Turkmenistan
fact: Capital Ashgabat. Over 80% is Karakum Desert, one of the driest on Earth, and it holds the world's fifth-largest natural gas reserves.

name: Micronesia
fact: Capital Palikir, on Pohnpei. Four states spread across 607 islands; on Pingelap atoll about 5% of people have complete colour blindness.

name: Palau
fact: Capital Ngerulmud. Its 1981 constitution was the world's first nuclear-free constitution, banning such weapons without a 75% referendum majority.

name: Marshall Islands
fact: Capital Majuro. 29 atolls and five islands, where the United States conducted 67 nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958.

name: Kiribati
fact: Capital Tarawa. 32 atolls plus the raised coral island of Banaba; it shifted the date line in 1995 to greet the third millennium first.

name: Nauru
fact: De facto capital Yaren. At 21 square kilometres it is the world's third-smallest country, and the smallest member of the Commonwealth.

name: Tuvalu
fact: Capital Funafuti. Three reef islands and six atolls whose highest point, on Niulakita, is 4.6 metres above the sea.

name: Tonga
fact: Capital Nuku'alofa. The only extant indigenous monarchy in the Pacific; it never relinquished its sovereignty to a foreign power.

name: Vanuatu
fact: Capital Port Vila. Britain and France ran it jointly from 1906 as the New Hebrides Condominium, with two parallel legal systems, until independence on 30 July 1980.

name: Solomon Islands
fact: Capital Honiara. Six major islands and over 1,000 smaller ones; Admiral Halsey credited its coastwatchers with saving Guadalcanal.

name: Animal
fact: A multicellular eukaryote with muscle cells that grows from a hollow ball of cells, the blastula — over 1.5 million living species described, about 1.05 million of them insects.

name: Chordate
fact: Defined by five traits held at some stage of life — notochord, hollow dorsal nerve cord, endostyle, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail — even if only by the larva.

name: Vertebrate
fact: The chordates that grew a vertebral column around the nerve cord and a cranium around the brain — roughly 65,000 species out of 1.5 million animals.

name: Invertebrate
fact: Not a group so much as everything left over: every animal without a vertebral column, by one estimate 97% of all animal species.

name: Mammal
fact: Milk from mammary glands, hair, and three bones in the middle ear — around 6,640 living species sorted into 27 orders.

name: Reptile
fact: Ectothermic amniotes in four surviving orders — turtles, crocodilians, squamates, and the single lonely tuatara — about 12,000 species listed.

name: Amphibian
fact: The four-limbed vertebrates that stopped short of the amniotic egg: frogs, salamanders and caecilians, most hatching as gilled aquatic larvae.

name: Arthropod
fact: A chitin cuticle that has to be shed to grow, a segmented body, and paired jointed limbs — up to ten million species.

name: Mollusk
fact: 86,600 living species, second only to the arthropods — and in every one, the mantle over the back is what secretes the shell.

name: Crustacean
fact: Mandibulate arthropods carrying two pairs of antennae — crabs, krill, copepods, barnacles, and the woodlouse that made it onto land.

name: Arachnid
fact: Eight legs on a cephalothorax, and never antennae or wings — over 110,000 named species, 51,000 of them spiders.

name: Echinoderm
fact: Bilateral as a larva, then five-fold radial as an adult, walking on tube feet run by a water vascular system — about 7,600 species, every one marine.

name: Cnidarian
fact: Over 11,000 species built of jelly mesoglea between two thin cell layers, with no brain at all — just a nerve net and stinging cnidocytes.

name: Annelid
fact: The segmented worms: over 22,000 species, from earthworms and leeches to ragworms living at hydrothermal vents.

name: Insect
fact: Three body sections, six jointed legs, one pair of antennae — over a million described species, more than half of all animal species known.

name: Primate
fact: An order that arose 74 to 63 million years ago in tropical forests — big brains, forward-facing eyes, grasping hands — with 376 to 524 living species.

name: Rodent
fact: One pair of ever-growing incisors top and bottom, kept in check only by gnawing — about 40% of all mammal species.

name: Shark
fact: Cartilage instead of bone, skin made of tooth-like dermal denticles, five to seven gill slits a side — more than 500 species across thirteen orders.

name: Frog
fact: The order Anura, Greek for 'without tail' — over 7,700 species, about 87% of all amphibians, the larval tail pulled inward into a bony urostyle.

name: Species
fact: The largest group whose members can still interbreed and produce fertile offspring — perhaps 8 to 8.7 million among eukaryotes, only 14% of them described by 2011.

name: Genus
fact: The rank above species, and the first word of every binomial: Panthera leo and Panthera onca are a lion and a jaguar filed under one name.

name: Phylum
fact: The rank below kingdom and above class — Animalia holds about 32 of them, Plantae about 14, Fungi about eight.

name: Kingdom
fact: Linnaeus made it the top rank in 1735; domain was slotted in above it in 1990, leaving kingdom second, and divided into phyla.

name: Domain
fact: The highest rank of all, proposed by Woese, Kandler and Wheelis in 1990 to hold just three groups: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

name: Zoology
fact: The scientific study of animals — structure, embryology, classification, habits, distribution — which begins formally with Aristotle.

name: Ethology
fact: The branch of zoology that studies animal behaviour in the field as much as the lab; its founders Lorenz, Tinbergen and von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize.

name: Homo sapiens
fact: Our own species, emerging in Africa around 300,000 years ago — Linnaeus coined the name in 1758 and is himself the designated type specimen.

name: Ardipithecus
fact: An Ethiopian hominin genus of two named species — A. kadabba at 5.6 million years, A. ramidus at 4.4 — both still carrying an ape's grasping, divergent big toe.

name: Bipedalism
