fact: Moving on the two rear limbs — invented independently by theropod dinosaurs and their bird descendants, by kangaroos and hopping mice, and by hominins.

name: Gene Pool
fact: Every allele carried by a population — Serebrovsky named it the genofond in the 1920s, and Dobzhansky translated it into English as 'gene pool'.

name: Fermentation
fact: Catabolism with the oxygen switched off: roughly 2 ATP per glucose instead of 32, and the carbon that cannot be burned walks out as ethanol or lactate.

name: Gluten
fact: Glutenin and gliadin are 75–85% of bread wheat's protein, but they are not gluten until water and kneading cross-link them by disulfide bonds into one elastic net.

name: Maillard Reaction
fact: Amino acids meeting reducing sugars, running fast from about 140 °C and building the melanoidins that brown a crust — Louis Camille Maillard found it in 1912 while trying to synthesise proteins.

name: Umami
fact: Ikeda named it in 1908 from kombu broth, but the TAS1R1+TAS1R3 receptor that senses it was not found until 2000 — and glutamate with inosinate tastes stronger than the two added up.

name: Emulsion
fact: Droplets of one immiscible liquid held inside another by an amphiphile — thermodynamically doomed the entire time, which is why mayonnaise eventually breaks.

name: Caramelization
fact: Pure sugar pyrolysis with no protein anywhere in it: fructose gives way at 105 °C and sucrose holds out to 170 °C, and the butter smell coming off is diacetyl.

name: Fat
fact: One glycerol carrying three fatty acids, at 9 kcal a gram — more than double sugar or protein — and the only vehicle vitamins A, D, E and K travel in.

name: Roux
fact: Equal weights of flour and fat cooked out together; take it darker for flavour and you lose thickening — a chocolate roux does about a quarter the work of a white one.

name: Sauce
fact: From Latin salsus, 'salted'. Escoffier's Guide culinaire fixed five mothers — espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate, hollandaise — and everything else is a daughter of one of them.

name: Vegetable
fact: A kitchen category, not a botanical one: in Nix v. Hedden (1893) the US Supreme Court taxed the tomato as a vegetable while conceding it is botanically a fruit.

name: Spice
fact: The line against herbs is anatomical: seed, fruit, bark, root or flower bud makes a spice — pepper, cinnamon, ginger, clove — while leaves and stems make a herb.

name: Seasoning
fact: Salt, acid and spice added late or at the table — done properly you cannot taste the seasoning at all, only the ingredient it is sharpening.

name: Condiment
fact: From Latin condire, 'to pickle or season' — it arrives after the cooking so the eater, not the cook, sets the dose. Rome's was garum.

name: Nutrition
fact: The short list a human body cannot build for itself: 9 amino acids, 2 fatty acids, 13 vitamins, 14 minerals and choline. Everything else it makes.

name: Leavening
fact: Three ways to inflate a dough — yeast, an acid-base fizz, or air beaten in — and all three fail unless gluten and gelatinising starch hold the bubble until it sets.

name: Gravy
fact: Built from the juices a roast sheds and leaves welded to the pan, then thickened; the word is in English cookery by the 14th century, from Old French grané.

name: Dairy
fact: Milk from cattle, buffalo, goats or sheep, worked into cheese, butter and yoghurt — Anatolian potsherds put the practice in the seventh millennium BC, long before adults could digest it.

name: Distillation
fact: Not a reaction at all — boil, condense, repeat along a volatility gap. With ethanol the gap shuts at 95.6% by mass and the azeotrope stops you dead.

name: Drying (Food)
fact: The oldest preservation trick there is, about 12,000 BC in the Middle East: take the water activity low enough and bacteria, yeasts and moulds simply cannot grow.

name: Curing (Food)
fact: Near 20% salt to draw water out of any microbe by osmosis, then nitrite to hold back Clostridium botulinum — and the pink is nitric oxide bound to myoglobin, not blood.

name: Smoking (Cooking)
fact: Cold smoke sits at 20–30 °C and never cooks anything; what preserves is chemistry — phenols, formaldehyde and acetic acid at around pH 2.5, with guaiacol supplying the taste.

name: Pickling
fact: Two routes to the same number: lactic bacteria making the acid themselves in 20–40 g of salt per litre, or vinegar poured straight on. Either way, pH 4.6 or under.

name: Mouthfeel
fact: The part of flavour the mouth reports as physics rather than chemistry — viscosity, grain, crunch, the oily film left behind — and viscosity alone changes how full you feel.

name: Food Safety
fact: Between 5 and 60 °C is the danger zone; the WHO counts about 600 million foodborne illnesses and 420,000 deaths a year, and its whole programme fits on five keys.

name: Brewing
fact: Mash the malt at 60–70 °C so amylase can cut its starch into maltose, boil with hops, pitch yeast — Natufians at Raqefet Cave were running a version of it 13,000 years ago.

name: Searing
fact: The surface has to be dry to get past 150 °C, and it does not seal in juices — Justus von Liebig's 1850 claim was already failing tests in the 1930s, and Harold McGee buried it.

name: Braising
fact: Brown it dry, then simmer it covered in a little liquid; the tenderness is collagen melting into gelatin and lubricating the fibres, not water getting in.

name: Culture Medium
fact: Nutrient broth set with agar. Gelatin melted at incubation heat and microbes ate it; agar does neither, so the colonies stay put.

name: Nucleoside
fact: A sugar joined to a base and nothing else. Add one phosphate group and it becomes a nucleotide — that group is the whole difference.

name: Double Helix
fact: Two antiparallel strands wound around a shared axis, bases paired inward like rungs. Watson and Crick published the model in Nature on 25 April 1953.

name: Rosalind Franklin
fact: Her X-ray diffraction work on DNA produced the image that showed it was helical. She died in 1958, four years before the Nobel her data underpinned.

name: War
fact: Armed conflict between organised forces under a command able to sustain operations; the cemetery at Jebel Sahaba in Sudan, about 13,400 years old, held 64 burials, and stone projectile points were found in the bodies of 21 of them.

name: Soldier
fact: The word runs back through Old French soudeour, 'one paid a wage', to the solidus, the late Roman gold coin — a soldier was defined from the start by being paid.

name: Army
fact: A land force organised under command: a modern field army holds three or four corps, each of two or more divisions, down to battalions of 500 to 750 soldiers.

name: Navy
fact: A state's fleet kept for war: Athens voted a silver strike at Laurion into triremes from 483 BC, and that fleet broke the Persian navy in the straits of Salamis three years later.

name: Air Force
fact: A branch that fights in the air rather than a scouting wing of an army: Britain merged the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service into the Royal Air Force on 1 April 1918, fifteen years after the first powered flight.

name: Infantry
fact: Troops who fight on foot, the largest part of almost every army in history; the word reached English in the 1570s from Italian infanteria, men reckoned too junior for the cavalry.

name: Cavalry
fact: Troops who fight mounted, trading numbers for height, speed and mass — and largely converted to tanks and motorised infantry between the world wars.

name: Artillery (Branch)
fact: The guns as a service of their own, with trained officers instead of hired mechanics: artillery caused the majority of combat deaths in the Napoleonic Wars and both world wars.

name: Phalanx
fact: A block of spearmen eight or more ranks deep, each shield covering its owner's left side and his neighbour's right — which left the rightmost file of the line half-exposed.

name: Legion
fact: Rome's infantry formation: 4,200 foot and 300 horse in the manipular Republic, later about 5,200 men in ten cohorts.

name: Fortification
fact: From Latin fortis and facere, to make strong: works built to hold ground — Solnitsata in Bulgaria had stone walls 1.4 m thick by about 4700 BC.

name: City Wall
fact: A town's enclosing defence and usually its first great public work; Jericho had one by the 8th millennium BC, and such walls doubled as toll gates that funnelled all trade through a few watched entrances.

name: Castle Keep
fact: The fortified tower inside a castle, both the lord's residence and the last refuge if the outer walls fell — the White Tower's rag-stone walls run about 7.3 m thick.

name: Motte-and-Bailey
fact: A timber tower on a piled-earth mound with a ditched courtyard below: it needed almost no skilled labour, and about 741 were thrown up across England and Wales after 1066.

name: Portcullis
fact: A latticed grille of wood and metal dropped down grooves cut into the gateway jambs; gatehouses often carried two, to trap attackers in the passage between them.

name: Bastion Fort
fact: Low, thick ramparts sunk behind a ditch, with diamond-shaped bastions at the corners so no stretch of wall lay out of another's fire — worked out in Italy around 1500 once cannon had made high walls indefensible.

name: Siege
fact: The blockade of a city or fortress meant to take it by attrition or prepared assault; the encirclement of Leningrad lasted 872 days, from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944, and killed over a million civilians, most by starvation.

name: Blockade
fact: Force used to cut a whole region off from supply rather than to capture it — and unlawful under modern international law where the purpose is to starve civilians.

name: Attrition
fact: Wearing an opponent down by continuous losses instead of by manoeuvre; at Verdun in 1916 Falkenhayn set out to bleed the French army, and the ten-month battle produced over 700,000 casualties.

name: Conscription
fact: Compulsory military service by law: the Jourdan Law of 1798 held that every Frenchman owed himself to the defence of the nation, and more than 2.6 million men were inducted between 1800 and 1813.

name: Standing Army
fact: Full-time troops kept and paid in peacetime; Tiglath-Pileser III disbanded Assyria's militias for paid professionals around 745 BC, and Charles VII raised the first Christian standing army in the 1430s.

name: Mercenary
fact: A soldier who fights for private gain rather than allegiance; the 1977 Geneva Protocol denies mercenaries combatant status, so a captured one has fewer protections than a captured soldier.

name: Guerrilla Warfare
fact: Small irregular bands using ambush, raid and sabotage instead of pitched battle; the Spanish word means 'little war', and Wellesley carried it into English in 1809.

name: Total War
fact: War in which a whole economy and population are mobilised and the enemy's civilians are counted as legitimate targets — Ludendorff gave it its name in Der totale Krieg in 1935, four years before the war that fit it best.

name: Gravity
fact: By far the weakest of the four forces — two electrons repel electrically 4×10^42 times harder than they attract — yet it alone builds the universe.

name: Orbit
fact: Newton's cannonball: fire it fast enough and the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls, so it never lands.

name: Solar System
fact: Collapsed out of a molecular cloud at least 4.568 billion years ago, and the Sun kept 99.86% of the mass for itself.

name: Escape Velocity
fact: √(2GM/d): 11.186 km/s off Earth, 2.38 off the Moon, 617.7 off the Sun — and it does not depend on what is escaping.

name: Astronomical Unit
fact: Fixed by the IAU in 2012 at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres — sunlight crosses it in 499 seconds.

name: Light-Year
fact: 9,460,730,472,580.8 km — the distance light covers in a Julian year of exactly 365.25 days. A length, not a time.

name: Parsec
fact: The distance at which one AU subtends one arcsecond: 3.26 light-years. Herbert Hall Turner coined the name in 1913.

name: Main Sequence
fact: The band where core hydrogen burns, and where a star spends roughly 90% of its life — the Sun has 6.5 billion years left on it.

name: Red Dwarf
fact: Three-quarters of the Milky Way's fusing stars, not one visible to the naked eye, and none has ever died — they last trillions of years.

name: Planetary Nebula
fact: Nothing to do with planets — Herschel's 1780s misnomer for the roughly 10,000-year glow of gas a dying star sheds.

name: Supernova Remnant
fact: Ejecta at up to 10% of light speed ploughing into interstellar gas — and the main source of the galaxy's cosmic rays.

name: Binary Star
fact: About a third of Milky Way systems, and the only way to weigh a star directly — everything else is inferred from these.

name: Stellar Classification
fact: O B A F G K M, hottest to coolest — Annie Jump Cannon's ordering of the Harvard spectra, on which the Sun comes out G2V.

name: Apparent Magnitude
fact: Backwards and logarithmic: Pogson fixed it in 1856 so five steps is exactly 100× in brightness, and good eyes reach about +6.5.

name: Asteroid Belt
fact: 2.06 to 3.27 AU, and it has lost 99.9% of its original mass — everything left adds up to 3% of the Moon.

name: Meteoroid
fact: The IAU's 2017 size band: 30 micrometres to one metre. Smaller is a micrometeoroid, larger is an asteroid.

name: Meteor
fact: The streak is ram-pressure heating, not friction, between about 120 and 50 km up — 25 million enter the air each day.

name: Heliosphere
fact: The bubble the solar wind inflates against interstellar space — Voyager 1 crossed out of it at 121 AU on 25 August 2012.

name: Magnetosphere
fact: Earth's field holds the solar wind off at 5–10 Earth radii on the day side and trails a magnetotail over 6.3 million km long.

name: Aurora
fact: Atomic oxygen struck by precipitating electrons glows green at 557.7 nm near 100 km up, and red at 630 nm above 150.

name: Sunspot
fact: Magnetic flux strangling convection: the umbra sits at 3,000–4,500 K against a 5,780 K photosphere, so it is dark only by contrast.

name: Coronal Mass Ejection
fact: Around 1.6 billion tonnes of coronal plasma thrown out at an average 489 km/s — one of these blacked out Quebec on 13 March 1989.

name: Solar Eclipse
fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and 400 times farther off, so the discs match — totality never exceeds 7 min 32 s.

name: Lunar Eclipse
fact: Sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere loses its blue to Rayleigh scattering, so the shadowed Moon runs red for up to 107 minutes.

name: Hubble's Law
fact: v = H₀D. Lemaître derived it in 1927, Hubble published in 1929, and the constant still won't agree: 67.7 against 73 km/s/Mpc.

name: Cosmic Inflation
fact: Alan Guth's January 1981 fix — distances doubling every 10⁻³⁷ seconds, which is why opposite sides of the sky match in temperature.

name: Observable Universe
fact: 93 billion light-years across though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old — expansion carried the edge out to 46.5 billion.

name: Event Horizon
fact: The boundary where escape velocity reaches the speed of light — about 3 km out for one solar mass, and one-way in every direction.

name: Gravitational Wave
fact: Einstein predicted them in June 1916; LIGO first caught one on 14 September 2015, as a stretch of a thousandth of a proton's width.

name: Gravitational Lensing
fact: Mass bends light — 1.75 arcseconds past the Sun's limb, twice the Newtonian figure, which is what the 1919 eclipse settled.

name: Antibiotic
fact: Waksman and his collaborators first used the word in 1942 for a substance one microbe makes to stop another — and not one of them works on a virus or a fungus.

name: Antiviral
fact: A virus replicates using your own cells, so there is barely anything to poison that isn't you — aciclovir's trick is to jam the viral DNA polymerase and terminate the chain.

name: Antifungal
fact: A fungus is a eukaryote like you; the one usable difference is that its membrane is built on ergosterol where yours uses cholesterol.

name: Macrophage
fact: One cell type under many names — Kupffer cells in the liver, microglia in the brain, alveolar macrophages in the lung — patrolling tissue by amoeboid movement.

name: Neutrophil
fact: 40 to 70% of your white blood cells, dead within 5 to 135 hours, and able to kill by flinging its own chromatin out as a sticky net.

name: Innate Immunity
fact: It reads molecular patterns shared broadly across pathogens but absent from you — and it is the only immune system plants, fungi, prokaryotes and invertebrates have.

name: Adaptive Immunity
fact: Found only in jawed vertebrates: V(D)J recombination shuffles a small family of genes into a receptor for almost anything, before the body has met a single thing.

name: Pus
fact: Mostly dead neutrophils, killed by bacterial leukocidins and cleared by macrophages — and it goes green when myeloperoxidase, an intensely green antibacterial protein, is in it.

name: Abscess
fact: Pus collected into a pocket inside the tissue — the standard treatment is still to cut it open and drain it, and in most uncomplicated cases adding antibiotics shows no benefit at all.

name: Bone Marrow
fact: About 5% of your body mass, releasing roughly 500 billion new blood cells into circulation every day.

name: Thymus
fact: Grows to 20–50 grams by puberty and then turns to fat — but first it kills, by apoptosis, every T cell whose receptor reacts against the body's own proteins.

name: Parasite
fact: Not a lineage but a living: the roll call runs from malaria's protozoan through hookworms, lice and vampire bats to ringworm fungi and flowering plants like mistletoe.

name: Toxin
fact: Ludwig Brieger's word for a poison a living cell makes — the range runs from a bee sting to botulinum toxin, fatal at doses too small to see.

name: Antitoxin
fact: An antibody grown in an animal against one specific toxin — Behring and Kitasato published serum therapy on 4 December 1890, and The Lancet called diphtheria antitoxin the century's greatest advance in treating acute infection.

name: Passive Immunity
fact: Borrowed antibodies, not your own — protection that starts immediately and is gone in a few weeks to three or four months, because nothing was ever learned.

name: Opsonization
fact: Wright and Douglas named it in 1904 from opsono, "I prepare victuals for" — a coating that makes a microbe appetising to a phagocyte.

name: Airborne Transmission
fact: The old 5 μm line between "airborne" and "droplet" has been abandoned: exhaled particles form a continuum, and only those above about 100 μm reliably fall within 2 metres.

name: Contagion
fact: Once it meant a disease passed only by direct physical contact; the working test now is whether isolating the sick actually slows it down.

name: Quarantine
fact: Ragusa held arrivals 30 days from 1377 — a trentine; Venice stretched it to 40 in 1448, and quaranta gave the practice its name.

name: Outbreak
fact: Cases in excess of what that place and that season normally produce — the count that matters is the baseline you were expecting, not the count itself.

name: Contact Tracing
fact: Smallpox was not finished off by blanket vaccination but by finding every infected person's contacts, isolating them, and immunising the ring around them.

name: Epidemiology
fact: Literally "the study of what is upon the people" — epi, demos, logos — and it works on populations, never on one patient.

name: Incubation Period
fact: The gap between exposure and the first symptom, while the organism multiplies toward the threshold that produces one — and depending on the disease, you may be contagious the whole time.

name: Petri Dish
fact: Koch published a precursor dish in 1881; his assistant Julius Richard Petri made the final modification in 1887, and it has not needed changing since.

name: Pure Culture
fact: Axenic — one species and nothing else, usually clones of a single cell, because the streak plate spread the sample thin enough that each colony grew from one.

name: Aseptic Technique
fact: The goal is to eliminate infection, not to achieve sterility — keep the microbes out of the field rather than fight them once they are in it.

name: Edward Jenner
fact: On 14 May 1796 he cut cowpox pus into the arm of James Phipps, his gardener's eight-year-old son, then gave him smallpox on 1 July and nothing happened.

name: Alexander Fleming
fact: He named lysozyme in 1922 after his own nasal mucus cleared a plate; back from holiday on 3 September 1928 he found a staph plate spoiled by mould and said "That's funny".

name: Joseph Lister
fact: On 12 August 1865 he packed 11-year-old James Greenlees's compound fracture with lint soaked in carbolic acid; four days later there was still no infection.

name: Ignaz Semmelweis
fact: Vienna's First Clinic lost 18.3% of its mothers in April 1847; he made the doctors wash in chlorinated lime from mid-May, and July's figure was 1.2%.

name: Genome
fact: All of it, coding or not: 3.1 billion bases spread over 24 distinct chromosome molecules in a human, and 98% of that never becomes protein.

name: Prokaryote
fact: A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles at all — Bacteria and Archaea, mostly 1 to 10 micrometres, doing their chemistry straight across the cell membrane.

name: Symbiosis
fact: De Bary's 1878 phrase for the living together of unlike organisms — the arrangement, not the verdict, so mutualism, commensalism and parasitism all count.

name: Eusociality
fact: Three tests, all required: reproductive division of labour, overlapping generations, and cooperative care of the brood. Every termite species passes; so does one rodent.

name: Kin Selection
fact: Hamilton's 1964 rule: help a relative when rB exceeds C. Haldane had already made the joke in 1955 — he would die for two brothers or eight cousins.

name: Clade
fact: An ancestor and every last one of its descendants, no branch left out — which is why 'reptile' and 'fish' are not clades. Julian Huxley coined it in 1957.

name: Heredity
fact: Traits passed on as discrete units rather than blended — blending would flatten a population to uniformity in a few generations and leave selection nothing to act on.

name: Mendelian Inheritance
fact: Three laws out of some 28,000 pea plants — dominance, segregation, independent assortment — published in 1866, ignored, and rediscovered by three men independently in 1900.

name: Recessive Allele
fact: It only shows when both copies match. One dominant copy hides it completely, and the carrier never finds out.

name: Heterozygous
fact: Two different alleles at one locus, Rr. The dominant one is what you see; the other rides along silently and gets passed on anyway.

name: Homozygous
fact: Both copies identical, PP or pp — and a recessive trait like Mendel's wrinkled pea turns up in the pp quarter of a cross and nowhere else.

name: Heterozygote Advantage
fact: One sickle-cell allele makes infected red cells sickle and get cleared, which limits malaria; two cause the anaemia. That trade keeps a lethal allele common.

name: Genetic Code
fact: 64 codons for 20 amino acids plus stop, so most amino acids have several spellings. Nirenberg and Matthaei read the first entry in 1961: poly-U gave phenylalanine.

name: Central Dogma
fact: Crick's 1957 claim was about direction, not sequence of steps: once information has passed into protein, it cannot get out again.

name: Gene Expression
fact: Every cell in you carries the same genome; what makes a neuron a neuron is which genes are switched on and how hard.

name: Epigenetics
fact: Waddington's 1942 word, from his landscape of marbles rolling into valleys: changes in which genes run that survive cell division without touching a single base.

name: DNA Methylation
fact: A methyl group parked on carbon 5 of a cytosine. About 75% of CpG sites carry one in mammalian somatic cells, and a methylated promoter goes quiet.

name: Crossing Over
fact: Morgan named it in 1912 for the swap he could only infer; Creighton and McClintock caught it physically in 1931, at the X-shaped chiasmata.

name: Sex Chromosome
fact: The X carries about 1,500 genes and the Y about 78 — and just one of those, SRY, is the switch. Nettie Stevens and E. B. Wilson spotted the pair in 1905.

name: Centromere
fact: The constriction that pinches a chromosome into a short arm and a long one — and the only place a kinetochore will build, because only there does histone CENP-A replace H3.

name: Karyotype
fact: Every chromosome stained and lined up in pairs: 46 in a human, a count only settled by Tjio and Levan in 1956, with G-banding resolving 300 to 400 bands.

name: Exaptation
fact: Gould and Vrba's 1982 replacement for 'preadaptation', which had made evolution sound like it was aiming at something: a part that simply changed jobs.

name: Neoteny
fact: Growing up without growing out of it. Kollmann coined the word in 1885 after the axolotl, and domesticated animals drift the same way.

name: Sexual Dimorphism
fact: Two body plans in one species, and not always the way you expect — in eclectus parrots it is the female who is scarlet and the male who hides in green.

name: Great Oxidation Event
fact: From about 2.46 to 2.06 billion years ago, cyanobacterial oxygen filled the air to roughly a tenth of today's level — and the sulfur isotopes read as a biosphere cut by over 80%.

name: Snowball Earth
fact: Ice all the way to the equator, twice in the Cryogenian — Sturtian 717 to 660 Ma, Marinoan 650 to 635 Ma. Kirschvink named it in 1992.

name: Trilobite
fact: Over 22,000 described species across 270 million years — and every lens in their eyes was a single crystal of calcite, up to 15,000 of them under one cornea.

name: Permian-Triassic Extinction
fact: 251.9 Ma, and 81% of marine species gone in perhaps 60,000 years while the Siberian Traps flooded basalt across a continent — the only mass extinction insects have ever suffered.

name: Stromatolite
fact: Layer on layer of microbial mat cementing sediment into a mound, a metre high or more. They peaked about 1.25 billion years ago, then grazers arrived.

name: RNA World
fact: One molecule holding the message and doing the chemistry, before DNA or protein. Walter Gilbert named it in 1986; the ribosome's catalytic core is still RNA.

name: Hearing
fact: Each pitch shakes its own spot on the basilar membrane — high notes at the cochlea's base, low at its apex — and the brain reads that map, from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

name: Deafness
fact: Diagnosed when an ear cannot detect 25 decibels; profound loss starts above 90 dB, and some 1.33 billion people — a tenth of everyone alive — have some degree of it.

name: Latte
fact: Espresso lost in steamed milk, served in a 230 ml glass with no thick foam layer — 'caffè latte' is attested in English by 1847, decades before the espresso machine.

name: Cappuccino
fact: Equal thirds espresso, steamed milk and foam in a 150-180 ml cup, named not for a hood but for the brown of the Capuchin friars' habits.

name: Masala Chai
fact: Black tea boiled with milk, sugar and spice — the Indian Tea Association, which pushed tea breaks on mills and mines in the early 1900s, at first thought the added spice and milk wasteful.

name: Mont Blanc
fact: The Alps' highest summit, 4,807.3 m in 2025 and a metre lower in the 2023 drought year; first climbed 8 August 1786 by Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard.

name: Soviet Union
fact: Founded 30 December 1922 by treaty as a federal union of national republics under one party, and dissolved on 26 December 1991.

name: Atmosphere
fact: Gas a world holds down with its own gravity: Earth's dry air is 78.08% nitrogen and 20.95% oxygen, pressing 101,325 pascals at sea level.

name: Eruption
fact: Dissolved gas coming out of solution as magma decompresses; the explosivity index runs 0 to 8 and each step is ten times the last, but most eruptions never get past 2.

name: Seismograph
fact: A hanging mass too lazy to move while its frame shakes with the ground — the gap between the two is the whole measurement.

name: Joust
fact: Two riders closing along either side of a tilt barrier with blunt-tipped wooden lances built to shatter; the armour made for it could reach 50 kg, heavier than armour for war.

name: Siege of Jerusalem
fact: Five weeks from 7 June to 15 July 1099, decided by two wheeled towers and an iron-headed ram built from ship timber, and followed by a massacre of the city's Muslims and Jews.

name: Bellerophon
fact: Athena handed him a golden bridle in a dream so he could take Pegasus at Corinth's Pirene spring; he killed the Chimera with a lead-tipped spear, then fell when Zeus set a gadfly on the horse.

name: Fenrir
fact: Loki's wolf son snapped two iron fetters and was held only by the soft ribbon Gleipnir — and Týr paid for the trick with the hand he had left in the wolf's mouth.

name: Norns
fact: Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld draw water and clay from the well at Yggdrasil's root and daub the world tree every day so it will not rot.

name: Rabbi Loew
fact: Judah Loew ben Bezalel, the Maharal, took up his Prague post in 1573 and died there in 1609 — the golem story only attached to him much later, first in print in 1834.

name: Prague
fact: Capital on the Vltava where Charles IV founded Central Europe's oldest university in 1347; the 'city of a hundred spires' actually carries about five hundred.

name: Cauldron
fact: A big pot for boiling over an open fire — the Battersea cauldron is about 2,800 years old, and the word runs back through Norman French caudron to the Latin for 'hot'.

name: Phonograph Record
fact: One modulated spiral groove running inward from the rim — shellac at 78 rpm until Columbia's 1948 LP put 22 minutes a side onto 33⅓.

name: QWERTY
fact: Sholes started from a piano-like alphabetical keyboard and spent five years shuffling it into this order by 1870; the tidy typebar-jamming explanation everyone repeats is disputed.

name: Wireless Telegraphy
fact: Morse dots and dashes carried on damped spark-gap waves instead of copper — broad, interference-prone, and across the Atlantic by 1901.

name: Space Race
fact: The US announced satellite plans on 29 July 1955 and the USSR answered five days later; the contest ran to a handshake in orbit in July 1975.

name: Pesto
fact: From the Genoese pestâ, 'to pound' — garlic and pine nuts crushed to a cream in a marble mortar first, basil and coarse salt next, cheese last, oil only to loosen.

name: Mole
fact: From Nahuatl mōlli, simply 'sauce'; mole poblano averages twenty ingredients and Oaxaca's run past thirty, and both Puebla and Oaxaca claim to have invented it.

name: Marinara
fact: Alla marinara means sailor's style, not seafood — in Italy it is tomatoes, basil, olive oil, garlic and oregano, and the fish stays out.

name: Hemp
fact: Legally it is Cannabis sativa carrying 0.3% delta-9 THC or less on a dry-weight basis — the same species above that line is a controlled drug.

name: Canola
fact: Rapeseed oil once ran to 54% erucic acid, which damages heart muscle; canola is the cultivar group bred under 2%, trademarked by the Canola Council of Canada in 1978.

name: Clover
fact: Domesticated in Spain around 1000 CE, and it was clover in the rotation that replaced the fixed nitrogen European cities ate and never sent back.

name: Chia
fact: A 1–2 mm seed that soaks up twelve times its own weight in liquid and sheathes itself in mucilage; the seed is 25–30% oil, 55% of that omega-3.

name: Jojoba
fact: Its seed is about 54% liquid wax, not oil — straight-chain C36–C46 esters, chemically closer to whale oil than to any vegetable triglyceride.

name: Kenaf
fact: A hibiscus grown for two fibres at once: bast is 40% of the stem and woody core the other 60%, and pulping the whole stalk gives paper of hardwood quality.

name: Jute
fact: Bangladesh calls it the golden fibre — bast strands one to four metres long, retted out of the stem in standing monsoon water.

name: Sisal
fact: One agave gives 200–250 usable leaves over a 7–10 year life, each holding about 1,000 fibres — and the fibre is only 4% of the plant's weight.

name: Abaca
fact: A Philippine banana harvested for its leaf sheaths, not its fruit; stronger than hemp and salt-resistant, it made ships' Manila rope and now makes tea bags and banknotes.

name: Ramie
fact: Six thousand years old and still awkward — alone among bast crops it will not simply ret, and degumming it chemically costs up to a quarter of the fibre's weight.

name: Woad
fact: A mustard-family plant yielding the very same indigo molecule as true indigo, only far less of it — which is why Vasco da Gama's 1498 sea route to India ruined Europe's woad towns.

name: Hop
fact: Only female plants are grown; the lupulin inside their cones holds humulones that are barely bitter until a boil isomerises them into iso-alpha acids.

name: Sugarsnap Pea
fact: Calvin Lamborn crossed a shelling-pea mutant found in 1952 with a snow pea and released the result in 1979 as Sugar Snap; the pod has no membrane, so it never splits open.

name: Mung Bean
fact: Germinates in four to five days, and the sprout is picked at the moment the seed splits and the white root shows — before the plant ever makes a leaf.

name: Fava Bean
fact: Rich in levodopa, and carrying the glycoside vicine — which in people with G6PD deficiency sets off favism, a haemolytic crisis brought on by a plate of beans.

name: Lupin
fact: The seeds are edible only once their bitter alkaloids are brined out — and Australia, where the plant is not native, grows 85% of the world's commercial crop.

name: Poppy Seed
fact: About 3,300 seeds to the gram, and harvesting them well is the opposite of harvesting opium: seed wants a dry ripe pod, latex wants a green one.

name: Amaranth
fact: A C4 pseudocereal whose oil is about 5% squalene, sold as the plant-based stand-in for shark liver oil in cosmetics and supplements.

name: Emmer
fact: The wild spikelet plants itself: its awns spread apart in night humidity and clamp shut by day, and silica hairs act as barbs so it can only travel downward into the soil.

name: Spelt
fact: A hexaploid hulled wheat, most likely a hybrid of emmer with a bread-wheat type, whose grain stays sealed inside its husk even after threshing.

name: Kamut
fact: Khorasan wheat, its kernels twice the size of modern wheat at up to 60 g per thousand — and 'Kamut' is a trademark, held by a Montana company that requires organic growing.

name: Einkorn
fact: German for 'single grain', because each spikelet holds exactly one; diploid, 14 chromosomes, and among the very first wheats farmed.

name: Triticale
fact: Wheat mother, rye father — the cross comes out sterile, and only colchicine doubling its chromosomes makes it breed; the first commercial variety appeared in 1970.

name: Fonio
fact: A Digitaria crabgrass with the smallest seed of any millet and a root over a metre deep; Guinea alone grew more than 75% of the world crop in 2019.

name: Teff
fact: Its Amharic name is thought to mean 'lost' — the seed is under a millimetre across — and Ethiopia grew more than 90% of the world's crop in 2016.

name: Wild Rice
fact: Not rice at all but four species of Zizania, aquatic grasses standing in shallow lake water with only the flowering head above the surface; the Ojibwe name manoomin means 'good grain'.

name: Cinnamon Tree
fact: Cinnamomum verum would reach 15 m but is coppiced to a 3 m bush, first cut at three years old and kept peeling for 40 to 50 more.

name: Clove Tree
fact: An 8–12 m evergreen of the Maluku Islands whose buds are picked at 1.5–2 cm, the moment they turn bright red and before a single petal opens.

name: Nutmeg Tree
fact: Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, and one fruit yields two different spices — nutmeg from the seed, mace from the crimson aril wrapped round it.

name: Turmeric Plant
fact: Commercial turmeric powder averages 3.14% curcumin by weight; curry powder, where turmeric is only one ingredient among many, averages 0.29%.

name: Chilli Pepper
fact: Five domesticated species of Capsicum, a nightshade genus 17 million years in the making, and already in Mexican pottery by 3000 BC.

name: Fennel Plant
fact: A 2.1 m carrot-family perennial whose fruits carry trans-anethole and fenchone; with anise it is one of absinthe's primary ingredients.

name: Star Anise Tree
fact: An evergreen of South China and northern Vietnam whose eight woody carpels are picked just before ripening; until 2012 Roche took up to 90% of the world crop to make Tamiflu.

name: Dill Plant
fact: One Greek word once meant both dill and anise; Latin split it into anethum and anisum, and Anethum is still dill's genus name.

name: Saffron Crocus
fact: A sterile triploid clone — three sets of eight chromosomes, 24 in all, and no viable seed — so every saffron crocus alive was split off a corm by hand.

name: Spearmint
fact: Mentha spicata: square-stemmed, spike-flowered, and one of peppermint's two parents — unlike its sterile hybrid child it still sets seed.

name: Peppermint
fact: Spotted in a Hertfordshire field and published by John Ray in 1696; Linnaeus made it a species in 1753, but it is a hybrid of watermint and spearmint.

name: Tea Plant
fact: Camellia sinensis would grow 20 m tall, but a plantation keeps it clipped to a flat-topped metre so pickers can take nothing but the bud and top leaves.

name: Coffee Plant
fact: Two of Coffea's 120-odd species carry the whole trade — arabica about 55% of world production, robusta about 45% — and a tree takes three to five years to fruit, then bears for fifty.

name: Honeydew Melon
fact: The Inodorus group of Cucumis melo: smooth-rinded and, as the name says, without the musk of a cantaloupe — 90% water, and judged ripe by rind colour rather than size.

name: Kiwifruit
fact: Renamed from Chinese gooseberry in 1959 for the American market; China now grows 55% of the world's crop, more than New Zealand ever did.

name: Date Palm
fact: Runs to 30 m and past 100 years of age, is male or female but never both, and has been farmed in Arabia since the 6th millennium BCE.

name: Passionfruit
fact: Missionaries in Brazil named it around 1700 for the flower, not the fruit — five wounds of the crucifixion read into a vine's blossom, whose fruit is a pepo, a botanical berry.

name: Mangosteen
fact: The inedible purple rind is so loaded with tannins and xanthones that it has been used to tan leather in China.

name: Elderberry
fact: Only the flowers and the ripe berries are safe: everything else on Sambucus nigra, ripe seeds included, carries the cyanogenic glycoside sambunigrin.

name: Boysenberry
fact: A four-way cross of raspberry, blackberry, dewberry and loganberry, traced in the late 1920s to vines Rudolph Boysen had abandoned on a farm in Anaheim.

name: Currant
fact: Ribes bushes are the alternate host white pine blister rust needs, so the United States banned currant growing for most of the 20th century — the federal ban went in 1966 and some state bans still stand.

name: Gooseberry
fact: Same genus as the currant, and the French name is groseille à maquereau — mackerel berry — after the old sauce its sourness was cooked into.

name: Kumquat
fact: The one citrus eaten whole and backwards — the rind is the sweet part, the pulp inside is the sour one — from the Cantonese gām gwāt, 'golden orange'.

name: Quince
fact: Hard, tart and astringent raw, with gritty stone cells right through a fruit that can reach a kilogram, and seeds whose nitriles release hydrogen cyanide in the stomach.

name: Cherimoya
fact: Every flower opens female and turns male within hours, so nothing can pollinate itself — small nitidulid sap beetles do the carrying.

name: Jujube
fact: Its leaves hold ziziphin, which switches off the ability to taste sweetness, and the dried fruit sells as 'red date' with no date palm anywhere in it.

name: Saskatoon Berry
fact: Not a berry but a 5-15 mm purple pome, named from the Cree misâskwatômina, and dried into pemmican as both flavour and preservative.

name: Feijoa
fact: Its perfume is methyl benzoate, and the plant will not set fruit without at least 50 hours of winter chilling.

name: Blood Orange
fact: Anthocyanins are rare in citrus; the crimson only develops when the fruit ripens through cold nights, and it keeps deepening in cold storage after picking.

name: Meyer Lemon
fact: Not a lemon: a citron crossed with a mandarin-pomelo hybrid, collected in China and brought to the USDA in 1908 by the plant explorer Frank N. Meyer.

name: Finger Lime
fact: Its juice vesicles come out as loose spheres that burst between the teeth, which is why it sells as lime caviar.

name: Amla
fact: Called Indian gooseberry but related to no gooseberry at all — a Phyllanthus tree fruit whose bitterness is ellagitannin, emblicanin A alone making up 37%.

name: Medlar
fact: Inedible until it half-rots: a hard frost starts bletting, breaking the cell walls down until the brown flesh can be spooned straight out of the skin.

name: Pawpaw
fact: A custard-fleshed Annonaceae tree that survives eastern US winters, pollinated by beetles drawn to maroon flowers that smell yeasty.

name: Huckleberry
fact: Never domesticated — Idaho's state fruit is still picked wild, resprouts from buried rhizomes after fire, and feeds black and grizzly bears.

name: Lingonberry
fact: It keeps its leaves through winter, tolerates about -45 °C, and runs right across boreal forest and Arctic tundra under insulating snow.

name: Juniper Berry
fact: Not a berry but a female cone whose scales stay fleshy and fuse into a ball called a galbulus — one of the very few spices that come from a conifer.

name: Sea Buckthorn
fact: Its roots partner with nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria, so it colonises bare ground, and the orange fruit runs about 400 mg of vitamin C per 100 g.

name: Parsnip
fact: Frost turns part of the root's starch to sugar, which is why it is left in the ground over winter — but the leaf sap's furanocoumarins blister skin in sunlight.

name: Jerusalem Artichoke
fact: Neither from Jerusalem nor an artichoke: a North American sunflower whose tubers store 8 to 13% inulin, which human digestion cannot touch.

name: Sweetcorn
fact: A recessive mutation stalls the conversion of sugar to starch in the kernel, so it has to be picked at the milk stage — ripening would spend the sugar.

name: Bok Choy
fact: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, which never forms a head; the name is Cantonese baak choi, 'white vegetable', for the pale thick leaf stalks.

name: Endive
fact: A Cichorium crop grown three ways at once: for bitter salad leaves, for roots roasted as a coffee substitute, and for chicons blanched in the dark.

name: Radicchio
fact: The red and white only appear once the light is taken away: plants are lifted and stood in water in dark sheds until chlorophyll stops forming.

name: Swiss Chard
fact: The same species as beetroot and sugar beet, bred for leaf and stalk instead of root — which is why it is also called leaf beet.

name: Collard Greens
fact: Brassica oleracea in the headless Acephala group with kale, on an upright stalk often over two feet and up to six in Portuguese cultivars.

name: Mustard Greens
fact: The leaves of Brassica juncea — the brown mustard whose seeds make the condiment — and sharper than any Brassica oleracea green they get mixed with.

name: Horseradish
fact: The intact root smells of almost nothing; cut it and myrosinase turns sinigrin into allyl isothiocyanate, which goes for the sinuses rather than the tongue.

name: Yam
fact: Dioscorea vines, not sweet potatoes: some 870 species, tubers running 1.5 m down, and the source of the diosgenin used to synthesise progesterone and cortisone.

name: Taro
fact: Toxic raw: the corm's cells are packed with needle-shaped calcium oxalate raphides, which cooking or an overnight soak in cold water defuses.

name: Jicama
fact: A pea-family vine grown for one crisp taproot while the rest of it is poison — the seeds, flowers and pods are heavy with rotenone.

name: Kohlrabi
fact: German Kohl plus Rübe, cabbage plus turnip — but the swollen part is a stem sitting above ground, not a root, and the group name means 'roundish'.

name: Fennel Bulb
fact: Not a root but a stack of swollen leaf bases — 90% water, milder and sweeter than the herb, and mislabelled 'anise' in half the supermarkets in North America.

name: Bamboo Shoot
fact: Raw shoots carry the same cyanogenic glycosides as cassava and must be boiled — giant pandas eat them raw and survive on gut microbes enriched in cyanide-degrading genes.

name: Lotus Root
fact: A rhizome 31.2% starch with almost no taste of its own — Japan grows its own and still imports 18,000 tonnes a year, 15,000 of them from China.

name: Rutabaga
fact: An accidental hybrid that doubled its chromosomes to 2n=38, first recorded by Gaspard Bauhin in 1620 growing wild in Sweden — hence 'swede'.

name: Daikon Radish
fact: A winter radish grown as a long white taproot, and sometimes left unharvested on purpose — rotting in place, it loosens compacted soil and pulls nutrients back up.

name: Water Chestnut
fact: Not a nut but the corm of a flooded-paddy sedge — oligomers of ferulic acid cross-link its cell walls, so it stays crisp even boiled or canned.

name: Chayote
fact: A Mesoamerican gourd holding one flat stone up to 10 cm long — and unusually, its tubers, shoots and leaves are eaten too.

name: Spaghetti Squash
fact: Raw, the flesh is solid like any squash; cooked, it falls away from the rind in strands — and the orange cultivars carry the most carotene.

name: Acorn Squash
fact: Cucurbita pepo var. turbinata — the same species as zucchini and crookneck, just left on the vine until the ridged rind hardens, which is what makes it a winter squash.

name: Snow Pea
fact: An edible-pod pea described in 1825 as having compressed, non-leathery pods — flat and thin-walled, where the snap pea's are round and thick.

name: Yardlong Bean
fact: The pods run 35 to 75 cm — about half a yard, not the one the name promises — and the plant is a cowpea, a different genus from the common bean.

name: Fiddlehead Fern
fact: The still-coiled frond of an ostrich fern, on sale for only a few weeks each spring — boil it 15 minutes, after the CDC traced food-borne illness to undercooked ones in the early 1990s.

name: Sea Kale
fact: William Curtis published on forcing it under blanching pots in 1799; by Mrs Beeton's day a basket of the blanched shoots cost ninepence, among the dearest vegetables in Britain.

name: Samphire
fact: Also called glasswort, because its ashes were burned for the soda ash that made glass and soap — until the Leblanc process replaced plant sources in the early 1800s.

name: Napa Cabbage
fact: A 1 to 3 kg barrel of leaves from near Beijing and the cabbage inside baechu-kimchi — Korean state breeding of it began in 1906, aimed squarely at yield.

name: Tatsoi
fact: Spoon-shaped leaves in a flat ground-hugging rosette, ready in 45 to 50 days and hardy to −10 °C — it is often cut from under the snow.

name: Komatsuna
fact: Japanese mustard spinach: a Brassica rapa leaf variety with mature blades about 30 cm long, grown commercially in Japan and Taiwan and fed to livestock besides.

name: Malabar Spinach
fact: A soft-stemmed vine reaching 10 m whose leaves are 93% water and mucilaginous enough to thicken a soup — its red cultivar once dyed cosmetics and sealing wax in China.

name: New Zealand Spinach
fact: For two centuries the only cultivated vegetable to have come out of Australia and New Zealand — blanch the leaves one minute first to strip the oxalates.

name: Chaya
fact: Simmer it 20 minutes and never in aluminium — raw chaya leaves hold cyanogenic glycosides like cassava's, and the toxins react with aluminium cookware.

name: Alfalfa Sprout
fact: Ready in three to five days at 5 to 8 cm — and both seed and sprout carry L-canavanine, which has produced a lupus-like disease in primates.

name: Mung Bean Sprout
fact: Caught in the four-to-five-day window after the seed splits and a soft white root pushes out — leave it longer and it puts up a green stem and stops being a sprout.

name: Microgreen
fact: Not a sprout: it is grown in a medium and cut above the soil line at 1 to 3 inches, once the cotyledons are open and one pair of true leaves has started.

name: Portobello Mushroom
fact: The same Agaricus bisporus sold as a white button, simply grown on — the cap opens out to 10–15 cm, browns, and the gills go dark.

name: Teak Tree
fact: A mint-family tree whose own oils leave the timber termite-proof and durable with no oil or varnish at all — Myanmar's forests hold nearly half the world's naturally occurring teak.

name: Mahogany Tree
fact: Philip II used it for joinery at El Escorial from 1584 and Havana made it a royal monopoly in 1622; in 2003 big-leaf mahogany became the first high-volume tropical timber on CITES Appendix II.

name: Walnut Tree
fact: Its roots and hulls leak hydrojuglone that oxidises in soil to juglone — apples, tomatoes, pines and birches planted beneath a black walnut yellow and wilt.

name: Cherry Wood Tree
fact: Black cherry's wilted leaves release hydrogen cyanide and are a leading cause of livestock poisoning — while the same tree yields perhaps the premier cabinet timber of the United States.

name: Ash Tree
fact: An olive-family tree, 45 to 65 species, whose elastic wood becomes tool handles and drum shells — and which the emerald ash borer has killed by the tens of millions across 22 US states.

name: Ebony Tree
fact: Heartwood up to 1,200 kg/m³ — twice as hard as oak and dense enough to sink in water — which is why it ends up as piano keys and violin fingerboards.

name: Sandalwood Tree
fact: A thief with roots: haustoria tap up to 300 other species for phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, and the heartwood yields an oil about 90% santalol against 39% in the Australian species.

name: Frankincense Tree
fact: A shallow cut in the trunk bleeds a milky sap that hardens in air into tears collected by hand — the tree died out in Israel and was replanted there in 2012, 1,500 years later.

name: Myrrh Tree
fact: A thorny tree of arid Somalia and Arabia whose dried sap has been in use over 3,000 years — ancient Egypt embalmed with it, and Somalia is still the largest producer.

name: Cork Oak Tree
fact: Once past 25 years old it can be stripped of bark every 9 to 12 years for up to two centuries without harm — and as plastic closures displace cork, its woodlands and the Iberian lynx in them are at risk.

name: Cinchona Tree
fact: Called the fever tree: bark of Cinchona ledgeriana grown in Dutch Java ran 8 to 13% quinine, and nothing else worked against malaria until quinine was synthesised in 1944.

name: Neem
fact: Its seeds hold 0.2 to 0.8 percent azadirachtin by weight, a compound that blocks the insect moulting hormone ecdysone and deters over 600 pest species while barely troubling mammals.

name: Camphor Tree
fact: Camphor was condensed straight out of steam driven through its pulverised wood, a trade lucrative enough that a British naval force bombarded Anping in 1868 to break Taiwan's camphor monopoly.

name: Olive Wood
fact: Hard, dense and strongly patterned, it takes a high polish for bowls and carving, but weather and insect damage rule it out of doors entirely.

name: Agarwood
fact: Aquilaria heartwood is pale and scentless until a Phaeoacremonium mould infects it; the dark resin the tree floods into the wound is oud, one of the costliest raw materials on Earth.

name: Argan
fact: Goats climb up into its thorny branches for the fruit and spit out the nuts, which then have to be cracked by hand between two stones, the slowest step in making argan oil.

name: Shea
fact: Its kernel fat runs 20 to 50 percent stearic acid, which is why shea butter stays solid at room temperature; the tree's old genus name, Butyrospermum, meant 'butter seed'.

name: Spruce
fact: The default soundboard wood for stringed instruments, with long fibres stiff along the grain; the Paneveggio 'Violin Forest' in the Dolomites has been cut for instrument makers for centuries.

name: Fir
fact: Told from the rest of the pine family by needles set singly on round bases, and by cones that stand upright like candles and fall apart on the branch instead of dropping whole.

name: Cypress
fact: Bald cypress heartwood resists rot so thoroughly that swamp-cut timber went into caskets, shingles and fence posts; one tree on North Carolina's Black River rings back to 605 BC.

name: Rosewood
fact: True rosewood is Dalbergia, a genus in the pea family, and CITES now lists every species after rosewood became the most trafficked wild product in the world.

name: White Mulberry
fact: The leaf Bombyx mori silkworms are reared on, cultivated in China for more than 4,700 years, and its flowers release pollen at over half the speed of sound.

name: Almond Tree
fact: Wild almonds are lethally bitter; a point mutation in one bHLH transcription factor shut off two cytochrome P450 genes and produced the sweet kernel the entire crop rests on.

name: Pecan Tree
fact: A hickory of the Mississippi bottomlands and one of the last major crops to be domesticated: wild nuts were gathered for centuries, but commercial orchards only began in the 1880s.

name: Cashew Tree
fact: Its seed shell is loaded with anacardic acid, chemical kin to poison ivy's urushiol; heat decarboxylates it into cardanol, sold as an industrial resin and a termite-proofing for timber.

name: Chestnut Tree
fact: Its wood carries roughly 13 percent tannin, enough that poles coppiced on a 12 to 30 year rotation survive years of ground contact with no treatment at all.

name: Hazel
fact: Cut back to the stump every few years it throws up straight rods, and those coppice wands were the raw material of wattle-and-daub walls and English hedgerow fencing.

name: Alder
fact: It barely rots once submerged, which is why most of Venice stands on alder piles, and its roots carry nodules of nitrogen-fixing Frankia alni that can reach the size of a fist.

name: Linden
fact: Pale, soft and almost grainless, its timber is the classic European carving wood, the material of Riemenschneider's altarpieces and Grinling Gibbons's foliage.

name: Peat Moss
fact: Sphagnum's dead hyaline cells hold 16 to 26 times the plant's dry weight in water, and it sours its own bog by taking up calcium and magnesium and releasing hydrogen ions.

name: Spanish Moss
fact: Neither Spanish nor a moss but a rootless bromeliad, a pineapple relative living on rain and dust; over 10,000 tons were processed in 1939 to pad car seats and mattresses.

name: Papyrus
fact: A sedge with triangular stems whose pith was cut into strips, laid in two crossed layers and hammered damp into a sheet, while its buoyant culms were bundled into boats.

name: Cattail
fact: The US Navy stuffed life vests with its seed down when kapok ran short in the Second World War; the down was still buoyant after 100 hours submerged.

name: Rattan
fact: A climbing palm, and a monocot with no secondary growth, so a cane stays 2 to 5 cm across along its whole length, which can run hundreds of metres through the canopy.

name: Raffia Palm
fact: Raphia regalis grows the longest leaves of any plant, pinnate fronds up to 25 metres long, and raffia fibre is the membrane peeled off their undersides.

name: Coir
fact: One of the few natural fibres saltwater will not rot: lignified cells from the coconut husk, loosened by up to ten months of retting and then beaten free with iron rods.

name: Broomcorn
fact: Sorghum grown for its stiff panicle rather than its grain, after Levi Dickenson of Hadley, Massachusetts tied a broom from the tassels in 1797 and could not keep up with the orders.

name: Gum Arabic Tree
fact: Strip its bark and the acacia seals the wound with a glycoprotein gum; about 70 percent of the world's supply comes from Sudan, where over five million people depend on the trade.

name: Guayule
fact: A Chihuahuan Desert shrub whose latex contains none of the proteins behind Type 1 latex allergy; Bridgestone announced the first all-guayule tyres in 2015.

name: Canaigre
fact: Tanner's dock: a wild rhubarb relative of the American southwest, cultivated for tannin-rich roots that also give a warm medium-brown dye.

name: Sweet Gale
fact: Bog myrtle, the bittering herb of gruit, the pre-hop beer seasoning that Henry IV licensed out in the 11th century as a de facto beer tax.

name: Serpentinite
fact: Mafic and ultramafic rock hydrated by seawater forced deep below the ocean floor, at mid-ocean ridges and in the forearc mantle of subduction zones.

name: Asbestos
fact: Six regulated minerals in two groups: chrysotile, the only serpentine one, and five amphiboles. Around 255,000 people a year are thought to die of diseases it causes.

name: Mesothelioma
fact: A cancer of the lung lining, with a latency of about twenty years from exposure and a life expectancy often under twelve months from diagnosis.

name: Equus
fact: The one surviving horse genus — seven species of horse, ass and zebra. It arose in North America around 4 million years ago, spread into the Old World, and then died out in the Americas about 12,000 years ago; horses only came back in 1519.

name: Wild Dromedary
fact: The wild camel of the southeast Arabian coast that domestic dromedaries were taken from, and were still being bred back to long afterwards. It had a narrow range and died out about 2,000 years after the first domestication.

name: Mongoose
fact: Herpestidae: 34 living species in 14 genera, across southern Europe, Africa and Asia. They are one of at least four mammal groups carrying a mutation in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that blocks snake venom — and the only one that does it by glycosylation.

name: Myriapod
fact: Four living classes — centipedes, millipedes, symphylans and pauropods — about 13,000 species, every one of them terrestrial. Their oldest body fossils are about 427 million years old.

name: Sauropod
fact: Hollow, air-filled bones are a feature of all of them, which is how the necks got so long: some carried as many as 19 cervical vertebrae where almost every mammal is limited to seven.

name: African Wild Ass
fact: Equus africanus, of the deserts and arid country of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia — the wild ancestor of every donkey, and now down to a few hundred animals in the wild.

name: Wild Boar
fact: Sus scrofa, ancestor of nearly every pig breed and one of the widest-ranging mammals alive, from North Africa to Korea and the Sunda Islands. European males run 75 to 100 kg; in northeastern Asia they reach 270.

name: Pipefish
fact: A straight-bodied member of the seahorse family Syngnathidae, armoured in bony plating and feeding through a tube snout. The male carries the eggs, supplying them with nutrients and oxygen through a placenta-like connection.

name: Mackerel
fact: Scombridae, the family that also holds the tunas and bonitos — slim, deeply forked in the tail, with rows of finlets and fins that fold into grooves for streamlining. The vertical stripes work as schooling marks; an Atlantic mackerel cruises at about 0.98 m/s and bursts at 5.5.

name: Fern
fact: Over 10,500 living species of vascular plant that reproduce by spores and have neither seeds nor flowers; the fern crown group goes back about 423 million years.

name: Okapi
fact: The giraffe's only living relative: 1.5 m at the shoulder, 200–350 kg, striped behind like a zebra, and found only north and east of the Congo River.

name: Pterosaur
fact: Flying reptiles of the Mesozoic, 228 to 66 million years ago, on a wing of skin and muscle stretched to one enormously lengthened fourth finger — wingspans from 0.4 m to 10–11 m. Not dinosaurs, but close kin.

name: Areca Palm
fact: Native to the Philippines, growing straight to 20 m on a trunk 10–15 cm across, and carried through the tropics by Austronesian voyagers since at least 1500 BCE for one seed crop.

name: Wild Coca
fact: Erythroxylum gracilipes, the wild shrub from which all four cultivated cocas were domesticated, two or three separate times during the Holocene.

name: Woodland Tobacco
fact: Nicotiana sylvestris, of the Andes of Argentina and Bolivia — one of the two wild parents of the cultivated tobacco plant.

name: Wild Turkey
fact: The ancestor of the domestic bird. A tom weighs 5–11 kg and stands 100–125 cm long, and the flock heads for the trees at twilight to roost well off the ground.

name: Mallard
fact: The wild dabbling duck almost every domestic breed descends from — 50 to 65 cm long, and still more than 17 million mature birds strong.

name: Mouflon
fact: The Asiatic wild sheep, Ovis gmelini, behind every domestic breed; a mature ram's horns curve almost a full revolution, up to 85 cm.

name: Bezoar Ibex
fact: Capra aegagrus, the wild goat the domestic one came from — now held to the Zagros Mountains, formerly widespread across Anatolia.

name: Red Junglefowl
fact: The wild forest bird every chicken descends from, still living from Pakistan east to Vietnam and south into Indonesia.

name: Wild Water Buffalo
fact: Bubalus arnee, ancestor of some 208 million domestic buffalo, is down to fewer than 4,000 mature wild animals, mostly in Assam and Nepal.

name: Grasshopper
fact: About 11,000 species of chewing herbivore in the suborder Caelifera, a lineage reaching back to the early Triassic 250 million years ago.

name: Great Ape
fact: The family Hominidae: eight living species in four genera, the orangutans, the gorillas, the chimpanzee and bonobo, and ourselves.

name: Beetle
fact: About 400,000 described species, a quarter of all known animals, each with its front wings hardened into cases over the flying pair.

name: Crocodilian
fact: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials; with the birds, the only survivors of the archosaurs.

name: Theropod
fact: Hollow-boned, three-toed and ancestrally carnivorous dinosaurs, first appearing 231.4 million years ago; birds came out of the small feathered ones, so about 11,000 species are still alive.

name: Lagomorph
fact: Rabbits, hares and pikas, and not rodents: they carry four upper incisors instead of two, with a small peg pair tucked behind the front ones.

name: Odd-Toed Ungulate
fact: About 17 living species, horses, rhinos and tapirs, bearing weight on the third toe and fermenting plants in the intestine rather than a chambered stomach.

name: Isopod
fact: Crustaceans with seven pairs of thoracic legs and five pairs of branching abdominal appendages used for breathing; the female broods her young in a pouch called a marsupium.

name: Spurge Family
fact: Euphorbiaceae, a cosmopolitan family richest in the tropics; it holds cassava and the rubber tree, and succulents that look like cacti purely through convergent evolution.

name: Scorpionfish
fact: A family of mostly marine fish carrying a sting in sharp spines coated with venomous mucus, widespread in warm seas and richest in the Indo-Pacific.

name: Requiem Shark
fact: Carcharhinidae: migratory sharks of warm seas, from the 69 cm Australian sharpnose to the 4 m oceanic whitetip, every one of them bearing young fully developed.

name: Greylag Goose
fact: Anser anser, the wild goose most domestic breeds descend from - 74 to 91 cm long and around 3.3 kg, and the bird Konrad Lorenz used for his imprinting studies.

name: Wild Silk Moth
fact: Bombyx mandarina, the wild moth of inland China, Korea and Japan that every domesticated silkworm descends from - and unlike its domestic descendant, the males still fly.

name: Africa
fact: The fragment of Pangaea that moved least. It sat near the supercontinent's centre and is still close to where it was, which is why the other continents are described as having rifted away from it rather than the other way round.

name: South America
fact: Rifted from Africa to open the South Atlantic: the split began around 190 million years ago at Falkland latitudes, seafloor spreading took over about 130 to 135 million years ago, and the ocean was fully open by roughly 83 million years ago.

name: Asia
fact: The eastern bulk of Laurasia, which was the northern half of Pangaea from about 335 to 175 million years ago. It grew by collision, welding on one continental block and island arc after another.

name: Europe
fact: Not a separate landmass but the western end of one, divided from Asia by convention along the Urals. The range is the suture of a real collision, and it has never undergone the extensional collapse that flattens most mountains of its age.

name: North America
fact: Separated from Eurasia when the North Atlantic opened about 56 million years ago, the same moment Greenland became a plate of its own across the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay rift.

name: Carcinogen
fact: Any agent that raises the incidence of cancer. The IARC has looked at about 1,060 of them and put 135 in Group 1 — carcinogenic to humans.

name: Mutagen
fact: An agent that pushes the mutation rate above its natural background. Muller showed in 1927 that X-rays do it — the first proof that mutation could be caused rather than waited for.

name: Teratogen
fact: An agent that deforms how an embryo is built rather than what it inherits — the defect is not passed on. Teratogens are held responsible for 2 to 3% of developmental defects in US newborns.

name: Birth Defect
fact: An abnormal condition present at birth, either structural or functional. About 3% of US newborns have one, and roughly 65% of cases have no identifiable cause at all.

name: Chromosomal Aberration
fact: Damage on a scale a point mutation never reaches: a stretch of chromosome deleted, doubled, flipped end for end, or moved onto a different chromosome. One live birth in 160 carries a chromosome abnormality of some kind.

name: Organogenesis
fact: The stretch after gastrulation when three germ layers turn into organs — in humans the internal organs start between weeks three and eight after fertilisation.

name: Angiosarcoma
fact: A cancer of the endothelial cells lining blood and lymph vessels. About one case per million people a year — 1 to 2% of soft-tissue sarcomas, which are themselves under 1% of adult cancer.

name: Free Radical
fact: An atom or molecule carrying an unpaired valence electron, which is the whole reason it is so reactive. Gomberg found the first one, triphenylmethyl, in 1900; ordinary oxygen is a diradical.

name: Hydroxyl Radical
fact: •OH — hydroxide minus an electron, and about the most reactive thing a cell has to cope with. Its half-life in tissue is around a nanosecond, and no enzyme disposes of it the way one does for superoxide.

name: Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon
fact: Benzene rings fused edge to edge into a flat, uncharged sheet. Most of it is made by burning things incompletely: wood and other biofuels alone contribute more than half of annual global emissions.

name: Naphthalene
fact: C10H8: two fused rings, the smallest PAH there is. It melts at 80 °C, the nose picks it up at 0.08 ppm, and it is the main ingredient of traditional mothballs.

name: Anthracene
fact: Three rings in a straight line, C14H10. Colourless in daylight, it fluoresces blue under ultraviolet with a peak at 400–500 nm, which is why particle physicists use it as a scintillator.

name: Phenanthrene
fact: The same fourteen carbons as anthracene with the third ring hung at an angle instead of in line. Its bent skeleton is the core of morphinan, and so of morphine and codeine.

name: Benz[a]anthracene
fact: C18H12, four rings, produced whenever organic matter burns incompletely. It is one of the carcinogenic constituents of tobacco smoke, and IARC lists it in Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans.

name: Dibenz[a,h]anthracene
fact: Five fused rings, C22H14. In 1929 Ernest Kennaway found it was the first pure compound with evidence of cancer-causing activity, and in 1930 he and Izrael Hieger showed single PAHs raise tumours on mouse skin.

name: Benzo[a]pyrene
fact: A benzene ring fused to pyrene, C20H12. In 1933 it became the first single compound picked out of an environmental mixture — coal tar — and shown to cause cancer.

name: Soot
fact: Impure carbon left over from incomplete combustion: clumps of nanoparticles 6 to 30 nm across, carrying polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and sometimes heavy metals such as mercury.

name: Tobacco Smoke
fact: Sidestream smoke — the stream that leaves the burning cone between puffs — carries more than 4,000 chemicals, 69 of them known carcinogens, and is about four times more toxic than the smoke a smoker draws.

name: Chlorinated Hydrocarbon
fact: Any carbon compound carrying a chlorine — chloroform, DDT, PCBs, vinyl chloride. The carbon–chlorine bond is strong and greasy, so the molecule lasts and it collects in fat.

name: Beta-Propiolactone
fact: A four-membered ring strained enough to alkylate nucleic acid, which is how it kills a virus for a vaccine — and why it is not used more widely than that.

name: Ethyleneimine
fact: Aziridine: a nitrogen forced into a three-membered ring, boiling at 56 °C. The strain in that ring is what opens it against DNA.

name: Nitrosamine
fact: R2N–N=O. Nitrite in acid becomes nitrous acid, and nitrous acid nitrosates any secondary amine it meets — which is why these turn up wherever curing salt meets protein.

name: Aflatoxin B1
fact: The B is for the blue it fluoresces under ultraviolet light; the G-group toxins glow green. Of the four, B1 is the most toxic.

name: Thalidomide
fact: Chemie Grünenthal sold it from 1957 in West Germany as Contergan, a sedative mild enough to be given for morning sickness. It was taken off the market in November 1961.

name: Methylmercury
fact: CH3Hg+ — one carbon stuck to a mercury atom, which is the difference between a metal that mostly passes through and one that does not. Its half-life in human blood is about 50 days.

name: Benzoic Acid
fact: E210, named for gum benzoin, whose dry distillation Nostradamus described in 1556. Ripe cranberries and bilberries still carry 0.03–0.13% of it free.

name: BHA
fact: E320, in food since about 1947. Two isomers sold as one antioxidant: the ring stabilises a free radical and sequesters it, so the chain reaction that turns fat rancid never gets going.

name: BHT
fact: E321 — 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol. It hands a hydrogen atom to a peroxy radical, turning it into a hydroperoxide and breaking the autoxidation chain.

name: Cream Cheese
fact: At least 33% milkfat, no more than 55% water, and up to 0.5% of gum to stop it weeping.

name: Soft Serve
fact: Drawn at −4 °C, a third of it air, and 3–6% milkfat where ice cream runs 10 to 18.

name: Gluten-Free Bread
fact: Gluten is 75–85% of the protein in bread wheat, and the reason bread rises. This loaf has none.

name: Carrageen Moss Pudding
fact: The Irish milk pudding that named the additive: carraigín, 'little rock', 55% carrageenan dry.

name: Spherified Pearl
fact: Liquid inside a skin of gel. Unilever documented it in the 1950s; elBulli's kitchen made it famous.

name: Oat Milk
fact: Oat starch, 50–60% of the grain, cut short by amylase. US sales: $4.4m in 2017, $213m in 2020.

name: Fracking Fluid
fact: Shale oil and gas take about 90% of the guar gum India and Pakistan grow, to carry sand into rock.

name: Processed Cheese
fact: Cheese melted with an emulsifying salt so it will melt again. US rules cap that salt at 3% by weight.

name: Coffee Creamer
fact: The pot that whitens coffee without curdling. Carnation had it in 1958 and sold it from 1961.

name: Yellow Mustard
fact: George J. French sold it from 1904 as 'cream salad mustard' — mild seed, heavy vinegar, turmeric yellow.

name: Strawberry Yoghurt
fact: Chilled, short-lived and pink, which is the one thing the cooked fruit in it cannot supply on its own.

name: Cola
fact: Named for the kola nut, coloured by caramel, and acidified with phosphoric acid.

name: Jelly
fact: Gelatin, sugar and water. It sets around 15 °C, melts again in the mouth, and sets colourless.

name: Sweet Wine
fact: Bottled with its sugar unfermented. The sorbate that holds it there is reckoned safe to 1.75 g a day.

name: Cordial
fact: A concentrate for diluting, one part to four or five, and about 30% juice on average.

name: Whitfield's Ointment
fact: 6% benzoic acid and 3% salicylic acid in petrolatum, named for the dermatologist Arthur Whitfield.

name: Dried Apricot
fact: Sulfured, it stays orange on the shelf. The same fruit dried without sulfite goes the brown of leather.

name: Corned Beef
fact: Named for the coarse 'corns' of salt in the brine. Brazil now cans about 80% of the world's supply.

name: Canned Heat
fact: Alcohol held in a gel and sold in a tin. One lit under a chafing dish burns for about twenty minutes.

name: Runway Deicer
fact: Potassium acetate in water, sprayed on airfield pavement. The same salt is the food additive E261.

name: Surimi
fact: Washed fish mince. Freezing wrecked its gel until Nishitani Yosuke froze it with sugars in 1969.

name: Sugar-Free Gum
fact: Sugar alcohols run 40 to 50% of a stick by weight. The sweetener is most of the gum.

name: Diet Soda
fact: Coca-Cola launched Diet Coke in July 1982, a year before aspartame was cleared for fizzy drinks.

name: Tabletop Sweetener
fact: About 1.1% sweetener and the rest bulk, so a spoon of it measures like a spoon of sugar.

name: Instant Mashed Potato
fact: Cooked mash dried on a hot drum into a sheet. Two USDA researchers patented the flake in 1954.

name: Shortening
fact: Procter & Gamble launched Crisco in June 1911 — the name is short for crystallized cottonseed oil.

name: Indium
fact: Half of all indium ends up as indium tin oxide — the transparent conductor on a flat screen.

name: Thallium
fact: Named for the green line in its spectrum. Soluble, tasteless, and absorbed straight through skin.

name: Nihonium
fact: The first element named in Asia — Nihon, for Japan, and for the Riken lab that caught three atoms.

discovered.note: Riken detects a single atom of element 113 after ten months of firing zinc-70 at bismuth.

name: Flerovium
fact: Named for Georgy Flerov, who found spontaneous fission in 1940 and founded the Dubna laboratory.

discovered.note: Dubna fires calcium-48 at plutonium-244 and this time two atoms of element 114 hold up.

name: Moscovium
fact: Named for the Moscow region, home of Dubna — four atoms in 2003, gone in a tenth of a second.

discovered.note: Four atoms made at Dubna, each alpha-decaying to element 113 in about 100 milliseconds.

name: Livermorium
fact: Named for the Livermore lab, which tried the very reaction in 1977 and found nothing at all.

discovered.note: One atom at Dubna on 19 July, identified by the flerovium it decayed into.

name: Praseodymium
fact: The other half of didymium, the element that wasn't. Named for the leek-green colour of its salts.

name: Terbium
fact: Mosander found it in yttria in 1843; its name and erbium's were swapped later and never swapped back.

name: Dysprosium
fact: Named dysprositos, 'hard to get at' — it took Boisbaudran more than thirty goes to get the oxide out.

name: Holmium
fact: Cleve split erbia and got two oxides: brown holmia, named for Stockholm, and green thulia.

name: Erbium
fact: Ytterby again: Mosander pulled erbia out of yttria in 1843, and the Er3+ ion turns a solution pink.

name: Thulium
fact: The rarest lanthanide but promethium. Charles James needed 15,000 crystallisations to get it pure.

name: Ytterbium
fact: Marignac found it hiding inside erbia in 1878; in 1907 something else turned out to be hiding in it.

name: Lutetium
fact: The last rare earth out and the dearest: about $10,000 a kilogram, roughly a quarter the price of gold.

name: Francium
fact: The last element found in nature rather than made. About 28 grams exist in the whole crust at once.

discovered.note: Marguerite Perey catches francium-223 coming off a purified sample of actinium-227.

name: Einsteinium
fact: Found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb, on filter papers flown through the cloud.

discovered.note: Identified in December by Ghiorso's team in debris from the Ivy Mike test of 1 November.

name: Fermium
fact: Fermium-257 is the heaviest nuclide neutron capture can reach. Past it, everything fissions at once.

discovered.note: Pulled out of irradiated coral shipped to Berkeley from Enewetak Atoll after Ivy Mike.

name: Mendelevium
fact: The first element ever made one atom at a time — seventeen atoms of it, in 1955.

discovered.note: Berkeley's 60-inch cyclotron makes element 101 from a target of a billion einsteinium atoms.

name: Nobelium
fact: Claimed by Sweden, Britain, America and the USSR. Dubna's 1966 report was the first that held up.

name: Lawrencium
fact: Named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron — and made on a linear accelerator instead.

discovered.note: Boron ions fired at three milligrams of mixed californium isotopes at Berkeley, 14 February.

name: Torsion
fact: The 180° twist every gastropod larva makes, swinging its mantle cavity and anus round over its head.

name: Gastropod
fact: Snails and slugs: 65,000 to 80,000 species, the second-largest animal class, and every one twists.

name: Cephalopod
fact: About 800 living species, and the only mollusks that closed the circulatory system — a squid has 3 hearts.

name: Bivalve
fact: Two hinged valves, no head and no radula — about 9,200 species that feed and breathe on the same gills.

name: Clam
fact: Not a taxon but a habit: a bivalve with two equal valves that burrows on a powerful muscular foot.

name: Squid
fact: Eight arms, two tentacles, and the ancestral shell reduced to a chitin blade buried in its own back.

name: Jellyfish
fact: Not a species but a life stage — the free-swimming medusa phase of certain members of Medusozoa.

name: Worm
fact: A shape, not a lineage — flatworms, roundworms and annelids are no closer kin than a fish is to a fly.

name: Flatworm
fact: About 18,600 species with no body cavity and no blood — oxygen has to reach every cell by diffusion.

name: Protist
fact: Defined by exclusion: a eukaryote that is not an animal, plant or fungus. No one trait unites them.

name: Organism
fact: Any living thing that functions as one individual — and biology still argues where one individual ends.

name: Life
fact: Carl Sagan's working definition, adopted by NASA: a self-sustaining chemical system capable of evolving.

name: Eggshell
fact: 95 to 97% calcium carbonate in a protein matrix; without the protein it would be too brittle to hold.

name: Carapace
fact: A turtle's ribs and spine ossified into one bony box under keratin scutes — it can never leave it.

name: Solid
fact: Definite shape and definite volume: atoms packed so tightly they can only vibrate in place.

name: Liquid
fact: Keeps its volume, not its shape. Only two elements are liquid at room temperature: mercury and bromine.

name: Gas
fact: Neither shape nor volume of its own. It keeps expanding until the container runs out.

name: Melting
fact: Solid to liquid. The temperature stops rising while the lattice comes apart — that is latent heat.

name: Freezing
fact: Liquid to solid, giving heat back as it goes. Pure water can supercool to −40°C before it yields.

name: Vaporization
fact: Liquid to gas. At the surface it is evaporation; once bubbles form inside, it is boiling.

name: Condensation
fact: Gas back to liquid at the dew point. Every cloud and every fogged window is this.

name: Sublimation
fact: Solid straight to gas, skipping the liquid. Dry ice does it at −78.5°C; mothballs do it on a shelf.

name: Deposition
fact: Gas straight to solid, no liquid between. Frost grows this way, and so do snow crystals.

name: Ionization
fact: Knock electrons off atoms and the gas becomes a plasma that conducts and answers to magnets.

name: Matter
fact: Anything with mass that takes up space — and under 5% of the universe. The rest is dark.
