name: Antimatter
fact: Same mass, opposite charge. Only ever made in pairs, and nobody knows why so little survived.

name: Spin
fact: Intrinsic angular momentum, quantised in halves of ħ. Nothing is actually spinning.

name: Fermion
fact: Half-integer spin, one to a quantum state. The twenty-four of them are what matter is made of.

name: Boson
fact: Whole-integer spin, and any number can share one state. Five are elementary; they carry the forces.

name: Pauli Exclusion Principle
fact: No two identical fermions in one state. It is why atoms have shells and why matter is rigid.

name: Fundamental Force
fact: Four interactions that reduce to nothing simpler. Gravity is the weakest by an absurd margin.

name: Strong Force
fact: About 100 times electromagnetism at a femtometre, and it does not fade with distance.

name: Weak Force
fact: The only force that changes a quark's flavour, and the only one that tells left from right.

name: Electromagnetism
fact: Infinite range, carried by the photon, and the force behind all of chemistry and every push.

name: Hadron
fact: Quarks bound by the strong force. Of all of them, only the free proton is stable.

name: Baryon
fact: Three quarks, so half-integer spin: a fermion. Protons and neutrons are almost all the mass you touch.

name: Meson
fact: A quark and an antiquark, so whole spin: a boson. The longest-lived last tenths of a nanosecond.

name: Quark
fact: Charge in thirds, and never seen alone. Six flavours, every one held captive by gluons.

name: Strange Quark
fact: Charge −1/3, about 95 MeV. Named for the oddly long-lived particles found in cosmic rays in 1947.

name: Charm Quark
fact: Charge +2/3, 1.27 GeV. Two labs published its signature on the same day in November 1974.

name: Bottom Quark
fact: Charge −1/3, about 4.18 GeV. It decays reluctantly, which is what makes b-tagging possible.

name: Top Quark
fact: About 173 GeV — the heaviest particle known, and the only quark that dies before it can hadronise.

name: Lepton
fact: A fermion that ignores the strong force, so it travels alone. Six of them, in three generations.

name: Muon
fact: An electron 207 times over, living 2.2 microseconds. Around 10,000 hit each square metre a minute.

name: Tau
fact: 1777 MeV, heavier than a proton — the only lepton massive enough to decay into hadrons.

name: Neutrino
fact: No charge, almost no mass, and it barely notices matter. Three flavours, and it swaps between them.

name: Electron Neutrino
fact: First generation. About 65 billion from the Sun cross every square centimetre of you each second.

name: Muon Neutrino
fact: Second generation. A 1962 beam of them made only muons — proof neutrinos come in more than one kind.

name: Tau Neutrino
fact: Third generation, and the last Standard Model fermion to be seen directly, in July 2000.

name: Gluon
fact: Massless, eight kinds, and it carries the colour charge it acts on — so gluons pull on each other.

name: W Boson
fact: 80.4 GeV of carrier for the weak force — heavy enough that the force barely crosses a proton.

name: Z Boson
fact: 91.19 GeV and no charge. It lets a neutrino bounce off matter and stay a neutrino.

name: Higgs Boson
fact: 125 GeV, zero spin — the first elementary scalar particle ever found, on 4 July 2012.

name: Standard Model
fact: Twelve fermions, five bosons, three forces. Fifty years unbeaten, and it still has no gravity.

name: Oxide
fact: Oxygen bonded to another element at oxidation state −2. Most of the Earth's crust is oxides.

name: Periodic Table
fact: 118 elements in proton order. Columns share their outer electrons, so they share their chemistry.

name: Metallic Bond
fact: Electrons pooled by every atom at once. That shared sea is the shine, the wire and the bend.

name: Transition Metal
fact: Groups 3 to 12, with a part-filled d shell: many oxidation states, coloured salts, and catalysis.

name: Alkaline Earth Metal
fact: Group 2, two outer s electrons. Named for their oxides — fireproof 'earths' that turn water alkaline.

name: Lanthanide
fact: Fifteen metals filling the 4f shell, so alike that telling them apart needs solvent extraction.

name: Actinide
fact: Fifteen elements filling 5f, every one radioactive. Only thorium and uranium remain in quantity.

name: Kiln
fact: A thermally insulated chamber — a kind of oven — reaching temperatures an open fire never will.

name: Oven
fact: A hollow chamber and a controlled way of heating it. In use since antiquity, for far more than food.

name: Kettle
fact: A vessel specialised for exactly one job: boiling water. Lid, spout, handle.

name: Toaster
fact: Radiant heat from nichrome ribbon. The browning is the Maillard reaction.

name: Freezer
fact: A refrigerator held below the freezing point of water — around -18 °C.

name: Blender
fact: A container with a blade at the bottom and a motor in the base.

name: Jar
fact: Glass body, threaded band, separate flat lid pressed onto the rim. Patented 1858.

name: Tin Can
fact: Steel that would rust, wearing a coat of tin that will not.

name: Basket
fact: Pliable stems woven into a rigid shape, with no frame, no thread and no glue.

name: Sink
fact: A bowl-shaped plumbing fixture: a basin with water coming in and a drain taking it out.

name: Tap
fact: A washer screwed down onto a seat to stop the flow. Patented in Rotherham in 1845.

name: Plate
fact: A broad, mainly flat vessel with a lip. Rounder and deeper, and it is a bowl instead.

name: Mug
fact: A cup with a handle, holding 250 to 350 ml — more than a teacup, less than a tankard.

name: House
fact: A dwelling, from a rudimentary hut upward. The social unit inside it is a household.

name: Wall
fact: Masonry, concrete, adobe or rammed earth, stood up to divide one space from another.

name: Roof
fact: Layered so it sheds water outward. Densely packed thatch traps air and insulates too.

name: Floor
fact: Boards laid across the joists at right angles — originally structural, not decorative.

name: Room
fact: Any enclosed space in a structure, bounded by walls, entered only through a door.

name: Chimney
fact: Vertical so the gases draw themselves up. That pull is called the stack effect.

name: Lock
fact: In use for over 6,000 years. The Yale pin tumbler is a developed Egyptian wooden lock.

name: Shelf
fact: A flat horizontal plane for storing things on. From Old English scylfe.

name: Cupboard
fact: It began literally as a cup board: open tiers for displaying plates, cups and saucers.

name: Carpet
fact: Rug once meant a coarse coverlet; it only came to mean a floor mat around 1808.

name: Saw
fact: Teeth bent alternately left and right, so the cut is wider than the blade and it never binds.

name: Drill
fact: Makes round holes or drives fasteners. Patented as an electric tool in Melbourne in 1889.

name: Screw
fact: An externally helical threaded fastener, and one of the six classical simple machines.

name: Screwdriver
fact: Classified entirely by its tip, because the tip has to match the screw head.

name: Wrench
fact: Called a spanner in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand.

name: Axe
fact: Hafted axes go back at least 46,000 years, in northern Australia.

name: Shovel
fact: A broad blade for digging and lifting. The seam at its back is folded into a socket.

name: Ladder
fact: One is painted on a Mesolithic wall in the Spider Caves, Valencia, 10,000 years ago.

name: Workbench
fact: A table that holds the work still, so both of your hands are free to work it.

name: Tape Measure
fact: A ribbon stiff enough to stand out straight, springy enough to roll itself back up.

name: Gear
fact: A toothed wheel. Its teeth engage another's, and two meshed gears are a gear train.

name: Shirt
fact: The world's oldest preserved garment is a linen shirt from a tomb at Tarkhan, Egypt.

name: Trousers
fact: The oldest known pair, from Turpan, is wool with straight legs and a wide crotch.

name: Wallet
fact: The word first meant a knapsack. It only came to mean a flat case in the 1600s.

name: Razor
fact: The oldest razor-like object found is 20,000 years older than the Bronze Age.

name: Banknote
fact: A promise, not a thing: the issuing bank was legally bound to redeem it in coin.

name: Pen
fact: Early pens held only a bead of ink in a nib, and had to be dipped again every few words.

name: Pencil
fact: The core is graphite powder held together by clay. More clay, harder and paler the line.

name: Eraser
fact: Before rubber, you rubbed pencil off paper with tablets of wax — or with breadcrumbs.

name: Scissors
fact: Two blades whose edges slide past each other. It cuts and shears at the same time.

name: Newspaper
fact: A book is finished. A newspaper is only ever the latest one, and is obsolete by morning.

name: Map
fact: A portolan chart has no latitude or longitude at all — only coastlines and bearings.

name: Road
fact: A prepared surface whose job is transport. A street's job is the people beside it.

name: Street
fact: A public thoroughfare lined with buildings — one of the few easements everyone shares.

name: Town
fact: Domesday listed 50 markets in England in 1086. Some 2,000 more opened by 1349.

name: Market
fact: A souk, a bazaar, a mercado, a tianguis, a palengke. Everywhere, the same idea.

name: Shop
fact: Retail sells to the person who will use the thing. Wholesale sells to whoever resells it.

name: School
fact: Early public schools were one room, where a single teacher took seven grades at once.

name: Hospital
fact: The word means a place of hospitality, and that is what these were long before medicine.

name: Bicycle
fact: The shape has barely changed since the first chain-driven safety bicycle of about 1885.

name: Truck
fact: Body-on-frame, with the cab built separate from whatever it is carrying behind.

name: Drone
fact: Two rotors turn clockwise and two anticlockwise, so the torques cancel and it does not spin.

name: Acetabulum
fact: The muscular sucking cup of a fluke or a tapeworm. A fluke has two; a tapeworm's head has four.

name: Scolex
fact: A tapeworm's holdfast, under 2 mm long, on a body that can run to 20 metres behind it.

name: Rostellum
fact: A fleshy, retractable knob on some tapeworm heads, ringed with hooks. Taenia saginata has none.

name: Proglottid
fact: One segment of a tapeworm, and a whole reproductive animal in itself: both sexes, in every one.

name: Tegument
fact: The body surface of a fluke or tapeworm: it absorbs the food and passes out the waste.

name: Oncosphere
fact: The first tapeworm larva: six tiny hooklets and almost nothing else, built to cut through a gut wall.

name: Cysticercus
fact: A fluid-filled bladder in muscle with a tapeworm's head folded inside it, waiting to be eaten.

name: Hydatid Cyst
fact: One Echinococcus larva, grown for years into a fluid cyst budding thousands of tapeworm heads inside.

name: Gynecophoral Canal
fact: A groove down a male blood fluke's belly. The female lies in it for the rest of both their lives.

name: Miracidium
fact: The first fluke larva, rowed along by cilia, with hours to find the one snail species it can enter.

name: Cercaria
fact: The fluke larva that leaves the snail, tail-first. Hundreds come out of every one that went in.

name: Metacercaria
fact: A cercaria that dropped its tail and walled itself up, waiting on a leaf or inside a fish to be eaten.

name: Cuticle
fact: A roundworm's tough outer coat, resistant to digestion — and shed four times as the larva grows.

name: Buccal Capsule
fact: The hard-lined mouth cavity of a roundworm — a hookworm's is armed with cutting plates or teeth.

name: Polar Plug
fact: A clear knob at each end of a whipworm egg. Nothing else in a stool sample is shaped like that.

name: Nurse Cell
fact: A muscle cell a Trichinella larva has rebuilt into a walled room, and then moved into.

name: Microfilaria
fact: The live embryo a filarial worm releases into the blood; some surface only between 10pm and 4am.

name: Flagellate
fact: A protozoan that swims by whipping one or more flagella. Giardia has four pairs of them.

name: Sucking Disc
fact: Giardia's dished underside. It clamps the cell to the gut lining and will not let go.

name: Undulating Membrane
fact: A flagellum bound down along a cell's flank, so its beat ripples the whole side of the body.

name: Axostyle
fact: A stiff rod of microtubules down the middle of a trichomonad, projecting out through the tail end.

name: Kinetoplast
fact: Thousands of DNA circles catenated into one disc, packed inside a single giant mitochondrion.

name: Apical Complex
fact: A drill at one end of a cell: polar rings, microtubules, and glands that open on the way in.

name: Hemozoin
fact: Malaria pigment: heme crystallised into an inert, iron-rich grain the parasite cannot be poisoned by.

name: Whipworm
fact: Threaded head-first into the gut lining and feeding on tissue fluid, not blood. Around 35 to 50 mm.

name: Strongyloides stercoralis
fact: The only intestinal roundworm that passes larvae, not eggs — and it can reinfect you without leaving.

name: Guinea Worm
fact: The largest roundworm to parasitise people: a female close to a metre long, leaving through a blister.

name: Onchocerca volvulus
fact: Adults sit coiled in fibrous nodules under the skin. It is the wandering young that cause the blindness.

name: Hydatid Tapeworm
fact: An adult only 3 to 6 mm long with three segments. Almost all its bulk is the cyst, in another animal.

name: Broad Fish Tapeworm
fact: Can reach 20 metres in one gut, and take up to all the vitamin B12 in the meals passing it.

name: Sheep Liver Fluke
fact: A leaf-shaped fluke that ends up in the bile ducts of a sheep — or of whoever ate the same salad.

name: Oriental Lung Fluke
fact: Lives encysted in pairs inside the lungs, and the cough it causes is regularly mistaken for TB.

name: Balantidium coli
fact: The only ciliate known to make people ill, and the largest protozoan that infects them.

name: Trypanosoma brucei
fact: It lives outside cells, in the blood, and stays there by changing its coat faster than antibodies form.

name: Trypanosoma cruzi
fact: C-shaped in a blood smear, then hidden in heart muscle for decades before the damage shows.

name: Tsetse Fly
fact: Both sexes live on blood, and can drink a meal weighing as much as they do.

name: Sandfly
fact: About 3 mm long and covered in hair, which is part of why the bite is often not noticed.

name: Black Fly
fact: Its larvae need fast running water, which is why the blindness it spreads follows the rivers.

name: Kissing Bug
fact: It does not inject the parasite. It defecates while feeding, and the bite gets rubbed into the wound.

name: Praziquantel
fact: Floods a fluke or tapeworm with calcium until its muscles lock, and strips its skin at the same time.

name: Albendazole
fact: Blocks the worm from building microtubules, so it cannot take up glucose and starves on its reserves.

name: Mebendazole
fact: Same target as albendazole, on the colchicine site of the worm's own beta-tubulin.

name: Ivermectin
fact: From a Streptomyces found in Japanese soil; it opens chloride channels invertebrates have and we do not.

discovered.note: Satoshi Omura's soil Streptomyces avermitilis yields the avermectins and William Campbell shows they kill nematodes; the two share the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Approved for human use in 1987.

name: Metronidazole
fact: Harmless until something with no oxygen in its metabolism reduces it. Then it is not harmless at all.

name: Niclosamide
fact: Works on tapeworms and nothing else — not flukes, not roundworms — because it is never absorbed.

name: Diethylcarbamazine
fact: It does not kill the adult worm. It makes the young ones visible to an immune system that was ignoring them.

name: Pyrantel Pamoate
fact: Contracts a worm so hard it cannot hold on, and it is carried out of the gut still alive.

name: Nitazoxanide
fact: The one drug licensed for cryptosporidiosis, aimed at an enzyme of oxygen-free metabolism we lack.

name: Quinine
fact: Isolated from cinchona bark in 1820, after three centuries of the bark itself being the only treatment.

discovered.note: Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaime Caventou isolate quinine from the bark of the cinchona tree, native to Peru.

name: Taeniasis
fact: Usually silent. Often the first sign is a segment of the worm leaving on its own.

name: Cysticercosis
fact: Caught from the eggs, not the meat — so the person, not the pig, becomes the intermediate host.

name: Neurocysticercosis
fact: Tapeworm larvae in the brain. In much of the world it is the commonest cause of adult-onset epilepsy.

name: Ascariasis
fact: The larvae take a detour through the liver and lungs, get coughed up, and are swallowed a second time.

name: Hookworm Disease
fact: It does not have to be swallowed. The larvae come up through the skin of a bare foot.

name: Trichuriasis
fact: Heavy infections in children can pull the rectum inside out. Light ones show nothing at all.

name: Enterobiasis
fact: The commonest worm infection in Western Europe and the United States, and it spreads on fingers.

name: Strongyloidiasis
fact: Because it can reinfect its host without leaving, it has been found still running after decades.

name: River Blindness
fact: Second only to trachoma as an infectious cause of blindness. The adult worm is not what blinds you.

name: Dracunculiasis
fact: Caught by drinking water with an infected water flea in it. Cases fell from 3.5 million to a handful.

name: Echinococcosis
fact: A dog's tapeworm eggs, in the wrong host. The cyst can grow silently for years before anything shows.

name: Fascioliasis
fact: A sheep's disease that people catch from the plant, not the animal. Called liver rot in livestock.

name: Clonorchiasis
fact: Thirty years in one set of bile ducts, and a recognised risk factor for bile-duct cancer.

name: Paragonimiasis
fact: A bloody cough from a fluke in the lung, treated as tuberculosis more often than anyone would like.

name: Diphyllobothriasis
fact: From raw freshwater fish. Rarely, the worm takes enough B12 to cause anaemia on its own.

name: Leishmaniasis
fact: Three diseases from one genus: a self-healing sore, a disfiguring ulcer, or an infection of the organs.

name: Sleeping Sickness
fact: Named for the last stage, once the parasite has crossed into the brain and wrecked the sleep cycle.

name: Chagas Disease
fact: Silent for twenty or thirty years, then up to a third of infections damage the heart.

name: Balantidiasis
fact: The only human disease caused by a ciliate, and it tracks living closely with pigs.

name: Trichomoniasis
fact: The commonest non-viral sexually transmitted infection, and men usually carry it without symptoms.

name: Switch
fact: A gap in a circuit you can open and close. Contacts touching or not — there is no third state.

name: Relay
fact: An electrically operated switch: a coil pulls the contacts shut, so one circuit works another.

name: Logic
fact: The study of which conclusions follow from which premises, judged by the shape of the argument alone.

name: Algebra
fact: Arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers, so one statement covers every case at once.

name: Boolean Algebra
fact: Algebra whose variables take only true and false, with the operations and, or and not.

name: Truth Table
fact: One row per combination of true and false for the inputs. Two inputs need four rows.

name: Logic Gate
fact: A circuit performing one Boolean operation on binary inputs, giving a single binary output.

name: NOT Gate
fact: The inverter. Its output is always the opposite of its input.

name: OR Gate
fact: True when either input is true. Two diodes into one shared resistor will do it.

name: AND Gate
fact: True only when both inputs are true — logical conjunction, built as a circuit.

name: NAND Gate
fact: AND with the answer inverted. Every other gate can be built from these alone.

name: XOR Gate
fact: True when the inputs differ. It is the sum of two bits, ignoring the carry.

name: Multiplexer
fact: A data selector: select lines choose one of several inputs and pass it to the single output.

name: Flip-Flop
fact: Two stable states, so it holds one bit after you stop pushing. The basic element of sequential logic.

name: Half Adder
fact: Adds two bits: XOR gives the sum digit, AND gives the carry.

name: Adder
fact: A circuit that adds binary numbers, carrying from each column into the next.

name: Arithmetic Logic Unit
fact: One circuit doing arithmetic or bitwise operations on binary integers, picked by an opcode.

name: Bit
fact: The basic unit of information: one of two values. A contraction of 'binary digit'.

name: Byte
fact: Eight bits — historically the number needed to encode one character of text.

name: Hexadecimal
fact: Base 16, written 0-9 then A-F. One digit per four bits, so a byte is exactly two of them.

name: ASCII
fact: 128 code points — 95 printable, 33 control — each stored as a seven-bit number.

name: Unicode
fact: One number per character for every writing system that can be digitised.

name: Register
fact: A handful of bits the processor reaches instantly — the fastest storage a machine has.

name: Random-Access Memory
fact: One transistor and one capacitor per bit. The charge drains away, so every cell must be refreshed.

name: Read-Only Memory
fact: A pattern fixed when the chip is made. It cannot be rewritten and survives the power going off.

name: Cache
fact: A small fast memory beside the core holding copies of whatever was used lately.

name: Clock Signal
fact: A square wave at a constant frequency, used like a metronome so the whole circuit steps together.

name: Data Bus
fact: A shared bundle of wires that components take turns driving, instead of a wire between every pair.

name: Instruction
fact: A number that names an operation. Read it, do that one thing, move on.

name: Machine Code
fact: Instructions as bare numbers — the only language a processor reads directly.

name: Central Processing Unit
fact: Fetch an instruction, do what it says, fetch the next. Arithmetic, logic and control in one unit.

name: Assembly Language
fact: One line per machine instruction, but with names instead of numbers. ADD, not 00000101.

name: Compiler
fact: Software that translates a high-level language into the low-level code a processor executes.

name: Programming Language
fact: An engineered language for writing programs people can read and machines can run.

name: Operating System
fact: The program that manages the hardware and runs the others.

name: Computer File
fact: A named collection of bytes treated as one unit — asked for by name, not by position.

name: File System
fact: The directory of names against blocks, so files can be found without tracking the medium.

name: Database
fact: Data held as relations — tables of rows — with a language for asking questions of them.

name: Punched Card
fact: Stiff paper storing information as the presence or absence of a hole at a fixed position.

name: Jacquard Loom
fact: A loom driven by a laced chain of punched cards, one card per row of the design.

name: Tabulating Machine
fact: Hollerith's electromechanical counter for punched cards, built for the 1890 US census.

name: Turing Machine
fact: An endless tape of symbols, a head that reads and writes one at a time, and a table of rules.

name: Moore's Law
fact: Transistors per chip have doubled roughly every two years. An observation, not a law of nature.

name: Pixel
fact: The smallest addressable element of a raster image. The word was first published in 1965.

name: Bitmap
fact: A grid of pixels held in memory. A framebuffer is exactly this, scanned out to a display.

name: Computer Font
fact: A file of glyphs, taking over the job of a case of metal type.

name: JPEG
fact: Lossy image compression, about 10:1, by discarding detail the eye is least likely to miss.

name: Floating Point
fact: A number as a significand times a power of the base, so the point moves with the exponent.

name: Checksum
fact: A short value computed from a block of data and sent with it, to detect damage.

name: Hamming Code
fact: Check bits arranged so a single wrong bit is not just detected but located.

name: Computer Network
fact: Computers exchanging data over links by agreed protocols, each found by its network address.

name: Packet
fact: A short formatted unit of data with a header saying where it is going.

name: Network Protocol
fact: The agreed rules of format, meaning, timing and error recovery that let two machines talk.

name: IP Address
fact: The number identifying a machine on the network and saying where it is. IPv4 uses 32 bits.

name: TCP
fact: Numbers, checks and re-requests every byte, turning unreliable packets into an ordered stream.

name: Domain Name System
fact: A distributed directory turning memorable names into the numeric addresses the network uses.

name: URL
fact: One line naming a protocol, a machine and a path — an address for a single resource.

name: HTTP
fact: Request and response: a client asks for a resource by URL, a server answers.

name: HTML
fact: Tags inside plain text marking what is a heading, a paragraph, or a link.

name: Web Browser
fact: Fetches a page's files from a server and renders them on screen.

name: Server
fact: A computer whose job is answering other computers' requests — the far half of client-server.

name: Ethernet
fact: The wired local-network standard, commercially introduced in 1980 and standardised in 1983.

name: Modem
fact: Turns bits into tones a phone line will carry, and back again.

name: Cipher
fact: A defined procedure for turning a message unreadable and back, controlled by a key.

name: Encryption
fact: Plaintext turned into ciphertext, so only a holder of the key can read it.

name: Prime Number
fact: A whole number above 1 with no smaller factors. Every other number is a product of these.

name: Public-Key Cryptography
fact: A pair of related keys: publish one, keep the other. What one locks, only the other opens.

name: Cryptographic Hash
fact: Any input mapped to a fixed-size fingerprint: quick forwards, infeasible backwards.

name: Digital Signature
fact: Proof that a message came from one holder of a private key and was not altered after.

name: Keyboard
fact: The typewriter's layout with a switch under every key, so a keystroke becomes a number.

name: Information Theory
fact: The mathematics of measuring, storing and sending information. Shannon, in the 1940s.

name: Resin
fact: A terpene secretion a conifer pushes into its own wounds. Not sap, not latex — and it sets hard.

name: Thorn
fact: A modified shoot, lignified to a point. A spine is a modified leaf; a prickle is only skin.

name: Berry
fact: One flower, one ovary, seeds loose in the flesh. A stone in there would make it a drupe instead.

name: Aerenchyma
fact: Parenchyma that kills off its own cells to leave air channels — a snorkel from shoot to drowned root.

name: Isoprene
fact: C5H8, 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene. Vegetation breathes out about 600 million tonnes of it a year.

name: Polyisoprene
fact: Isoprene chained up. In the cis-1,4 arrangement it is natural rubber — 99.9% of what a tapped tree gives.

name: Synthetic Rubber
fact: Elastomer polymerised from petroleum instead of tapped from a tree. Two thirds of US rubber.

name: Carbon Black
fact: Petroleum burned in too little air, on purpose. 70% of it goes into tires, and it is why they are black.

name: Tire
fact: Vulcanised rubber packed with carbon black and forced onto a wheel rim. Over 2 billion made a year.

name: Empire
fact: A state that rules many peoples and territories from one centre, as subjects rather than citizens.

name: Treaty
fact: A written agreement between states, binding in international law. The oldest surviving is 3,300 years old.

name: Sovereignty
fact: Supreme authority over a territory, answerable to no higher power. Dated by convention to 1648.

name: Independence
fact: A territory becoming a sovereign state in its own right — self-determination actually exercised.

name: Revolution
fact: A rapid, forced remaking of a state's institutions, driven from outside them by mass action.

name: Constitution
fact: The founding law setting out how a state is governed. Around 800 have been adopted since 1789.

name: Republic
fact: A state whose head of state is not born to the job. About 159 of 206 states use the word.

name: Referendum
fact: A direct vote of the whole electorate on one question, not on who should decide it.

name: Colonialism
fact: One state ruling a distant territory and its people, usually reached across an ocean.

name: Decolonisation
fact: The unwinding of colonial rule. In the two centuries after 1783, 165 colonies became states.

name: Partition
fact: One territory cut into two or more states, the new border and the new states arriving together.

name: Unification
fact: Separate polities merged into one state, usually on a claim of shared language or nation.

name: City-state
fact: A city that is the whole of its own country. Three sovereign ones survive today.

name: Co-principality
fact: A state with two heads of state at once. Andorra's pair date from a feudal pact of 1278.

name: British Empire
fact: At its 1920 peak it covered 24% of the world's land — the largest empire in history.

name: Austria-Hungary
fact: The dual monarchy of 1867–1918: one monarch, two parliaments, three shared ministries.

name: Czechoslovakia
fact: Proclaimed 28 October 1918 from the wreck of Austria-Hungary; wound up by agreement in 1993.

name: Yugoslavia
fact: The South Slav kingdom of 1918, renamed Yugoslavia in 1929 and broken up between 1991 and 2006.

name: Basidium
fact: A club-shaped cell that buds four spores on horns, then flicks each one off at about 10,000 g.

name: Elasmobranch
fact: Sharks, rays and skates together. Their skeletons stay cartilage for life rather than turning to bone, they have five to seven gill slits opening straight to the outside instead of under a bony cover, and their teeth sit in rows that move forward as the front ones are shed.

name: Ray
fact: A flattened elasmobranch whose pectoral fins are fused to the sides of the head, forming the disc it swims with. Its gill slits open on the underside rather than the flank, which is the quickest way to tell a ray from a shark.

name: Plank
fact: A flat length of timber sawn from a log. Almost everything wooden that is not carved starts as one.

name: Blade
fact: The working part of any cutting tool: a piece of hard metal with one edge ground thin enough to part what it is pushed through.

name: Handle
fact: The part shaped to be held. It sets how much force reaches the tool and keeps the hand away from the working end.

name: Pole
fact: A long round shaft stood upright. Most street furniture is something bolted to the top of one.

name: Pigment
fact: A coloured solid ground fine enough to stay suspended rather than dissolve. It colours by being there, which is why a pigment can outlast the thing it is painted on.

name: Paint
fact: Pigment carried in something that dries. The carrier spreads the colour thin and then hardens, locking it to the surface.

name: Cable
fact: Wire wrapped in something that does not conduct, so the current stays inside it and the outside is safe to touch.

name: Sheet Metal
fact: Metal worked flat and thin. Thin enough to cut and bend cold, stiff enough to hold a shape once folded.

name: Mesh
fact: An open grid of wire. It holds things back while letting air, water and light through.

name: Drain
fact: The opening at the edge of a road that takes rainwater off it and into a pipe below.

name: Pavement
fact: The raised, made-up strip beside a road for walking on.

name: Kerb
fact: The stone edge between pavement and road. It holds the pavement in and steers water along the gutter to the drain.

name: Traffic Light
fact: Three coloured lamps on a pole that take it in turns to give right of way.

name: Streetlight
fact: A lamp on a pole, lighting the road rather than any building.

name: Bollard
fact: A short post set in the ground to stop vehicles going somewhere, while letting people walk past.

name: Pedestrian Crossing
fact: A marked strip of road where people on foot have priority over traffic.

name: Road Sign
fact: A painted metal plate carrying an instruction, in a shape and colour meant to be read before it can be spelled out.

name: Manhole
fact: A covered shaft giving access to the pipes and cables under a street.

name: Litter Bin
fact: An open container fixed in a public place for rubbish.

name: Postbox
fact: A cast-iron box in the street that takes prepaid letters for collection.

name: Saucepan
fact: A straight-sided pan with one long handle, for cooking liquid on a hob.

name: Colander
fact: A bowl punched full of holes, for draining what has been boiled.

name: Sieve
fact: A mesh stretched on a rim. What passes through is decided by the size of the holes and nothing else.

name: Whisk
fact: Loops of wire on a handle, for beating air into something.

name: Grater
fact: A metal sheet worked so that every hole in it is a small blade.

name: Peeler
fact: A blade with a slot in it, set so it can rock, for taking the skin off a vegetable and little else.

name: Chopping Board
fact: A slab of wood to cut on, so the knife meets something softer than itself.

name: Corkscrew
fact: A helix of steel on a handle, for pulling a cork out whole.

name: Ladle
fact: A deep bowl on a long handle, for lifting liquid out of a deeper pot.

name: Spatula
fact: A flat flexible blade for lifting, turning and scraping.

name: Rolling Pin
fact: A heavy wooden cylinder for pressing dough out flat and even.

name: Clock
fact: A machine that counts something regular and shows the total. Every clock is that: an oscillator, a way of counting its swings, and a face.

name: Cardboard
fact: Paper made thick and stiff. Corrugated board is a fluted sheet glued between two flat ones, which is why an empty box holds its shape.

name: Ruler
fact: A straight edge with a scale marked along it, for drawing a line or measuring one.

name: Stapler
fact: A device that drives a wire staple through a stack of paper and folds its legs over on the far side.

name: Paperclip
fact: A single piece of wire bent back on itself twice, holding paper by springing against it.

name: Notebook
fact: Paper bound along one edge so it stays in order and opens where you left it.

name: Rubber Stamp
fact: A raised rubber relief that prints the same mark every time it is pressed.

name: Highlighter
fact: A pen whose ink is transparent, so it marks a line of text without hiding it.

name: Folder
fact: A sheet of card folded once, to keep loose papers together and the right way up.

name: Binder
fact: A stiff cover with rings through it, so pages can be added and taken out without unbinding anything.

name: Pliers
fact: Two levers crossed on a pivot, with jaws at the short end and handles at the long one.

name: Sandpaper
fact: Hard grains glued to a backing, so that a sheet of paper can cut.

name: Spirit Level
fact: A sealed glass vial, almost full of liquid, with one bubble left in it.

name: Clamp
fact: A screw that pulls two jaws together and holds them there without a hand.

name: Vice
fact: A clamp bolted to a bench, so the work is held and both hands are free.

name: Crowbar
fact: A steel bar with one end flattened into a wedge and bent, for levering things apart.

name: Drawer
fact: A box that slides out of the thing it lives in, so what is at the back can be reached without unpacking the front.

name: Desk
fact: A table meant for working at, with the things needed for the work kept in it.

name: Wardrobe
fact: A cupboard tall enough to hang clothes at full length instead of folding them.

name: Mattress
fact: A padded layer to lie on, thick enough that the body's weight is spread rather than borne at the hips and shoulders.

name: Pillow
fact: A soft bag for the head, filling the gap between the shoulder and the mattress.

name: Mop
fact: Absorbent strands on the end of a pole, for washing a floor while standing up.

name: Tower
fact: A building far taller than it is wide, built for the height itself rather than for the floor space.

name: Laptop
fact: A computer with its screen, keyboard and power supply folded into one case you can carry.

name: Printer
fact: A machine that puts what is on a screen onto paper.

name: Monitor
fact: A screen for looking at what a computer is doing.

name: Speaker
fact: A device that turns a changing electric current into sound.

name: Headphones
fact: Two small speakers held at the ears.

name: Charger
fact: A device that pushes energy back into a battery.

name: Tram
fact: A passenger vehicle running on rails laid in the surface of a street.

name: Van
fact: A road vehicle built around its cargo space rather than its passengers.

name: Motorcycle
fact: A bicycle with an engine, and everything that had to change once it had one.

name: Scooter
fact: A board with small wheels and an upright handle, pushed along by foot.

name: Office
fact: A building, or part of one, given over to work done sitting down.

name: Library
fact: A building holding books arranged so that a stranger can find one.

name: Crate
fact: An open box of nailed boards, for moving heavy things.

name: Purse
fact: A small closed pouch for carrying money.

name: Coat
fact: An outer garment worn over everything else, mainly for warmth.

name: Jacket
fact: A short coat, ending at the hip rather than the knee.

name: Day
fact: One turn of the Earth, measured against the Sun. Everything alive keeps time to it.

name: Month
fact: One cycle of the Moon's phases, and the reason nearly every calendar has a middle unit between the day and the year.

name: Year
fact: One circuit of the Sun. Twelve lunar months come to 354 days and a solar year to 365, and every calendar in history is an attempt to reconcile the two.

name: Calendar
fact: An agreed scheme for naming days ahead of time, so that people who are not together can arrange to be.

name: Counting
fact: Matching things one-to-one against something else, so a quantity can be held without holding the things.

name: Writing
fact: Marks that record language itself, so that speech outlives the moment and the speaker.

name: Number
fact: A count separated from the things counted, and written down as a thing in its own right.

name: Zero
fact: A number for none, and a mark that holds an empty place so that 105 is not 15.

name: Geometry
fact: The mathematics of shape, distance and space.

name: Agriculture
fact: Growing food on purpose instead of finding it. Everything else people built rests on it.

name: City
fact: A settlement too large to feed itself, living on food grown elsewhere.

name: Law
fact: Rules a society will enforce, set down so that they are the same for the person applying them as for the person they are applied to.

name: Memory
fact: Holding something after it has gone, and being able to bring it back.

name: History
fact: The recorded past, as distinct from the past itself.

name: Light
fact: Electromagnetic radiation in the narrow band the eye can see, roughly 380 to 700 nanometres.

name: Mass
fact: How much matter something is, measured two entirely different ways that always agree.

name: Energy
fact: The capacity to do work, and the one thing in physics that is never created or destroyed, only moved and changed in form.

name: Time
fact: What clocks measure, and the dimension along which cause reaches effect.

name: Distance
fact: How far apart two things are.

name: Speed
fact: Distance covered divided by the time it took.

name: Acceleration
fact: The rate at which speed changes.

name: Force
fact: A push or a pull, measured by the acceleration it gives a given mass.

name: Momentum
fact: Mass times speed — how hard something is to stop.

name: Work
fact: Force applied along the distance something actually moves.

name: Power
fact: Work divided by the time taken to do it. Not how much, but how fast.

name: Temperature
fact: How fast, on average, the particles in something are moving.

name: Entropy
fact: A measure of how many ways the parts of something could be arranged and still look the same.

name: Trade
fact: Giving what you have too much of for what you have none of.

name: Money
fact: A thing everyone will accept, so that trade no longer needs both sides to want what the other has.

name: Debt
fact: A payment moved into the future, and the claim on it that exists meanwhile.

name: Tax
fact: A payment the state requires rather than requests.

name: Government
fact: Whoever gets to make and enforce the rules, and the machinery they do it with.

name: Democracy
fact: Government in which the decisions belong to the governed.

name: Monarchy
fact: Government by one person, usually for life, usually inherited.

name: Contract
fact: A promise the law will enforce.

name: Family
fact: The people you are raised by and raised with.

name: Society
fact: People who depend on each other while mostly not knowing each other.

name: Nation
fact: A people who consider themselves one, and usually want a state to match.

name: Property
fact: The right to exclude other people from a thing.

name: Ship
fact: A vessel big enough to cross open ocean and carry cargo or people at scale.

name: Crocodile
fact: A large semi-aquatic ambush predator, and an archosaur — closer kin to birds than to lizards.

name: Otter
fact: A river-hunting mustelid, built long and low with webbed feet and a rudder of a tail.

name: Blue Whale
fact: The largest animal that has ever lived, up to about 30 metres and 150 tonnes.

name: Emu
fact: A tall flightless bird of Australia, second only to the ostrich in height.

name: Skunk
fact: A small American mammal that defends itself chemically rather than by running.

name: Seaweed
fact: Large marine algae, anchored to rock rather than rooted in soil.

name: Kite
fact: A tethered wing, held up by the wind because the line stops it drifting downwind.

name: Whisky
fact: A spirit distilled from fermented grain and aged in wood.

name: Swamp
fact: Wetland with trees standing in it, as distinct from marsh, which has none.

name: Oasis
fact: Water at the surface in a desert, and everything that gathers around it.

name: Snowflake
fact: A single ice crystal grown in cloud, six-sided because of how water molecules bond.

name: Robot
fact: A machine that senses, decides and acts without a person in the loop.

name: Statue
fact: A figure carved or cast at full size, made to stand and to last.

name: Pyramid
fact: A tomb built as a square-based pyramid, the most stable large shape you can pile up.

name: Sushi
fact: Vinegared rice served with fish, vegetables or egg, often wrapped in seaweed.

name: Polio
fact: A gut infection that in a small fraction of cases reaches the nerves of the spinal cord and paralyses what they served.

name: Influenza
fact: A respiratory infection that returns every year in a slightly different form, and occasionally in a very different one.

name: Rabies
fact: A viral infection that travels up the nerves to the brain, and is almost always fatal once it arrives.

name: Scurvy
fact: The disease of long voyages: collagen cannot be built without vitamin C, so old wounds reopen, gums bleed and teeth loosen.

name: Rickets
fact: Soft, bending bones in a growing child, from too little vitamin D to lay calcium into them.

name: Cholera
fact: A gut infection whose toxin makes the intestine pour out water, so fast that death is from dehydration rather than from the bacterium.

name: Oral Rehydration Therapy
fact: Salt and sugar in the right proportions in clean water, which stops most cholera deaths.

name: Vitamin C
fact: The vitamin most animals make for themselves and we cannot, because the gene for the last enzyme is broken in us.

name: Vibrio cholerae
fact: A comma-shaped marine bacterium that lives in brackish water on the shells of copepods, and only sometimes in people.

name: Timber
fact: Wood cut and seasoned for building, as distinct from the tree it came from.

name: Beam
fact: A horizontal member carrying a load across a gap to the supports at each end.

name: Joist
fact: One of the parallel beams that carry a floor or a ceiling between walls.

name: Gravel
fact: Loose rounded stone between about 2 and 60 millimetres, sorted and rounded by moving water.

name: Foundation
fact: The part of a building below ground, spreading its weight over enough soil to carry it.

name: Lintel
fact: The beam over a door or window, carrying the wall above the hole.

name: Plaster
fact: A paste spread on a wall that sets hard and flat.

name: Plasterboard
fact: A sheet of gypsum plaster between two paper liners, nailed up instead of spread on.

name: Lime Mortar
fact: The older mortar: lime and sand, which sets slowly by taking carbon dioxide back out of the air.

name: Insulation
fact: Material that slows heat leaving a building, mostly by holding air still.

name: Ceiling
fact: The overhead surface of a room, hung below the floor above it.

name: Floorboard
fact: A board laid across joists to make a floor.

name: Gutter
fact: A channel at the eaves catching what runs off the roof.

name: Hinge
fact: A joint that allows rotation about one fixed line and nothing else.

name: Radiator
fact: A panel of hot water in a room, warming it mostly by convection despite the name.

name: Scaffold
fact: A temporary frame that puts a working platform beside a building.

name: Cylinder
fact: The bore a piston runs in, and the sealed volume the working stroke happens inside.

name: Engine
fact: A machine that turns fuel into rotation.

name: Crank
fact: The bend in a shaft that turns a push along a line into a turn around a centre.

name: Lever
fact: A rigid bar turning about a fixed point, trading distance for force.

name: Fulcrum
fact: The fixed point a lever turns about.

name: Rod
fact: A long straight bar of solid metal, the stock most other parts start as.

name: Flywheel
fact: A heavy wheel that stores rotation and gives it back, smoothing an intermittent push into steady turning.

name: Boiler
fact: A closed vessel where fire turns water into steam under pressure.

name: Valve
fact: A part that opens and closes a passage, letting flow go one way or none.

name: Pump
fact: A machine that moves fluid from where it is to where it is not.

name: Bearing
fact: What a shaft turns in, arranged so the surfaces roll rather than rub.

name: Brake
fact: A device that turns motion into heat in order to stop something.

name: Friction
fact: The force resisting one surface sliding over another.

name: Surface
fact: The boundary where a thing stops and everything else begins.

name: Area
fact: How much surface something has, in units of length squared.

name: Petrol
fact: The fraction of crude oil that boils between about 40 and 200 degrees, light enough to vaporise in an engine.

name: Gearbox
fact: A set of gear ratios between engine and wheels, so one engine speed can serve many road speeds.

name: Clutch
fact: The joint that lets a running engine be connected to and disconnected from the wheels.

name: Driveshaft
fact: The turning shaft carrying power from the gearbox to the wheels.

name: Differential
fact: The gearset that lets driven wheels turn at different speeds while both still pull.

name: Spark Plug
fact: The part that fires the mixture, and the reason a petrol engine is called spark-ignition.

name: Alternator
fact: The engine-driven generator that keeps a car's battery charged.

name: Exhaust
fact: The pipe carrying burnt gas away from the engine, and everything fitted along it.

name: Catalytic Converter
fact: A honeycomb coated in precious metal that finishes the reactions the engine did not.

name: Steering Wheel
fact: The wheel the driver turns, and the linkage that turns the road wheels less than it does.

name: Dashboard
fact: The panel of instruments in front of the driver.

name: Dial
fact: A face with a scale and a pointer, showing a quantity as a position.

name: Speedometer
fact: The instrument showing how fast a vehicle is going.

name: Headlight
fact: A lamp with a mirror behind it, throwing light forward along the road rather than everywhere.

name: Seat
fact: Something shaped to hold a body at rest, taking its weight through the hips rather than the spine.

name: Foam
fact: A solid or liquid full of gas bubbles, which is how it becomes light and soft at once.

name: Syringe
fact: A barrel, a plunger and a hollow needle, for putting a measured dose under the skin or drawing one out.

name: Suture
fact: A stitch closing a wound so the edges heal to each other rather than filling in from the bottom.

name: Bandage
fact: A covering held over a wound, to keep it clean, keep it together and take up what comes out of it.

name: Wound
fact: A break in the skin, and the body's most practised emergency.

name: Forceps
fact: Hinged tongs for gripping what fingers cannot reach or should not touch.

name: Anaesthetic
fact: A drug that removes the sensation of pain, and usually consciousness with it.

name: Surgery
fact: Treatment by opening the body and working inside it.

name: Nurse
fact: The person who watches a patient over hours and days, which is most of what care actually is.

name: Doctor
fact: The person who decides what is wrong and what to do about it.

name: Diagnosis
fact: Working out which disease is producing what you can see.

name: Symptom
fact: What the patient notices, as distinct from what the examiner finds.

name: Ambulance
fact: A vehicle that brings treatment to the patient and the patient to the hospital.

name: Escapement
fact: The part of a clock that lets the gear train advance one step per swing, and pushes the swing along as it goes.

name: Pendulum
fact: A weight on a rod, swinging at a period set by its length and almost nothing else.

name: Hilt
fact: Everything on a sword that is not the blade: the guard, the grip and the pommel.

name: Scabbard
fact: The sheath a blade lives in.

name: Aperture
fact: The adjustable hole a lens looks through, setting how much light gets in and how much is in focus.

name: Shutter
fact: The gate that decides for how long light is allowed to fall.

name: Wax
fact: A soft solid that melts at low heat and repels water, made by bees and later from petroleum.

name: Wick
fact: A twist of fibre that carries liquid fuel up to a flame by capillary action.

name: Sole
fact: The part of a shoe between the foot and the ground, and the part that wears out.

name: Heel
fact: The raised block under the back of a shoe.

name: Lace
fact: A cord threaded through holes, pulling a shoe tight around the foot.

name: Eyelet
fact: A reinforced hole, so a cord can pull hard on fabric without tearing it.

name: Cord
fact: Several strands twisted together, which is far stronger than the same fibre laid straight.

name: Twist
fact: Turning strands about each other so that friction holds them together.

name: Fret
fact: A raised bar across a fingerboard, fixing exactly where a string is stopped.

name: Neck
fact: The long arm of a stringed instrument, carrying the fingerboard and taking the pull of the strings.

name: Varnish
fact: A clear finish that hardens on a surface, protecting it while leaving it visible.

name: Furnace
fact: An enclosure built to hold fire hot enough to change what is put in it.

name: Soda Ash
fact: Sodium carbonate, the flux that lets glass be made at a workable temperature.

name: Putty
fact: A soft paste that sets slowly, used to bed glass into a frame.

name: Frame
fact: A skeleton of members carrying load, with nothing filling the spaces between them.

name: Spoke
fact: One of the wires between the hub and the rim of a wheel.

name: Rim
fact: The outer hoop of a wheel, holding the tyre and taking the pull of every spoke.

name: Hub
fact: The centre of a wheel, holding the bearings the whole thing turns on.

name: Tyre
fact: The compliant ring between a wheel and the road.

name: Inner Tube
fact: An airtight ring inside a tyre, holding the pressure the tyre only shapes.

name: Sprocket
fact: A toothed wheel made to engage a chain rather than another gear.

name: Pedal
fact: The platform a foot pushes, on a bearing so it stays level as the crank goes round.

name: Handlebar
fact: The bar the rider steers and leans on.

name: Spade
fact: A flat blade on a shaft, for cutting into ground and lifting it.

name: Rake
fact: A row of teeth on a handle, for gathering loose material without lifting the ground with it.

name: Tine
fact: One prong of a fork, rake or harrow.

name: Trowel
fact: A small flat blade for lifting and spreading mortar or soil.

name: Blowpipe
fact: A hollow iron tube for gathering molten glass and inflating it.

name: Film
fact: A flexible strip carrying a light-sensitive layer.

name: Binding
fact: Whatever holds the pages of a book together and to its cover.

name: Rebar
fact: Steel bars cast into concrete to carry the loads concrete cannot.

name: Rafter
fact: One of the sloping members carrying a roof from ridge to wall.

name: Ridge
fact: The horizontal line where two roof slopes meet at the top.

name: Batten
fact: A thin strip nailed across rafters, giving tiles something to hook on to.

name: Roof Tile
fact: A fired clay plate, overlapped in courses so water runs off and never in.

name: Flashing
fact: Sheet metal worked into the joint where a roof meets something else.

name: Downpipe
fact: The vertical pipe taking water from the gutter to the ground or the drain.

name: Render
fact: A coat of mortar spread over masonry, for weather and for looks.

name: Primer
fact: The first coat, which is for sticking rather than for colour.

name: Sealant
fact: A flexible filler for the joints between things that move at different rates.

name: Screed
fact: A thin levelling layer poured over a structural floor.

name: Underlay
fact: A soft layer between a floor and its covering.

name: Block
fact: A cast concrete unit, larger than a brick and laid the same way.

name: Sill
fact: The ledge under a window, throwing rainwater clear of the wall below.

name: Pane
fact: A single sheet of glass in a frame.

name: Latch
fact: A catch that holds a door shut without locking it.

name: Silica
fact: Silicon dioxide — the mineral that most sand, most rock and all ordinary glass is made of.

name: Bolt
fact: A threaded rod with a head, clamping through a hole rather than gripping the material.

name: Tang
fact: The unsharpened part of a blade that runs back into the handle.

name: Guard
fact: The crosspiece between grip and blade.

name: Grip
fact: The part actually held, wrapped so the hand does not slip on it.

name: Pommel
fact: The weight at the end of a hilt.

name: Whetstone
fact: A fine abrasive block for putting an edge back on a blade.

name: Quenching
fact: Cooling hot steel fast enough to trap it in a hard, brittle state.

name: Glaze
fact: A layer of glass fused onto pottery, making a porous body watertight.

name: Slip
fact: Clay thinned to a cream, for casting, joining and decorating.

name: Firing
fact: Heating clay until it changes irreversibly into ceramic.

name: Harrow
fact: A frame of tines dragged over ploughed ground to break the clods.

name: Irrigation
fact: Bringing water to a crop rather than waiting for it to fall.

name: Fertiliser
fact: Anything added to soil to replace what a crop takes out of it.

name: Silo
fact: A tall sealed store keeping grain or fodder without it spoiling.

name: Livestock
fact: Animals kept for what they produce or become.

name: Stud
fact: One of the upright timbers in a framed wall.

name: Door Frame
fact: The lining fixed in the opening, that a door is hung from.

name: Window Frame
fact: The surround holding glass in a wall.

name: Water Tank
fact: A stored volume of water, high enough that gravity does the delivering.

name: Fan
fact: Angled blades spun to push air along.

name: Press
fact: A machine that applies steady, very large force over a small distance.

name: Circuit Board
fact: A rigid sheet with copper tracks etched on it, replacing wiring with printing.

name: Resistor
fact: A component that deliberately makes it harder for current to flow.

name: Heat Sink
fact: A finned block of metal carrying heat away from something that must stay cool.

name: Fin
fact: A thin projecting plate, put on something to multiply its surface.

name: Case
fact: A rigid container shaped to what it protects.

name: Weight
fact: The force gravity exerts on a mass.

name: Mainspring
fact: The coiled ribbon of steel that stores the energy a clock runs on.

name: Balance Wheel
fact: A weighted wheel oscillating against a spring, keeping time in anything that has to be carried.

name: Hoe
fact: A blade set across a handle, for cutting weeds off at the root without turning the soil.

name: Watering Can
fact: A vessel with a spout and a perforated head, delivering rain rather than a stream.

name: Mulch
fact: A layer spread on soil rather than dug into it.

name: Hops
fact: The flower that makes beer bitter and keeps it.

name: Mash
fact: Crushed malt steeped in hot water, where starch becomes sugar.

name: Cask
fact: A wooden barrel for storing and moving liquid.

name: Antenna
fact: A conductor shaped so that a passing radio wave makes a current in it, or the reverse.

name: Microphone
fact: A device turning sound into a matching electrical signal.

name: Fuel Tank
fact: The vessel a vehicle carries its own fuel in.

name: Camshaft
fact: The shaft of lobes that opens each valve at exactly the right moment.

name: Carburettor
fact: The part that mixed fuel into the air before injection replaced it.

name: Starter Motor
fact: The electric motor that turns an engine over until it can run itself.

name: Brake Disc
fact: The disc a brake grips, turning motion into heat.

name: Suspension
fact: What lets a wheel move up and down without the body doing the same.

name: Shock Absorber
fact: The damper that stops a spring bouncing.

name: Chassis
fact: The structural frame everything else on a vehicle is attached to.

name: Windscreen
fact: The front window of a vehicle, and a structural part of it.

name: Wiper
fact: A rubber blade sweeping water off glass.

name: Seatbelt
fact: A woven strap that spreads a sudden stop across the strongest parts of the body.

name: Muffler
fact: The chamber that quietens an exhaust.

name: Fretboard
fact: The surface a string is pressed against, carrying the frets.

name: Tuning Peg
fact: The geared post a string is wound on and tensioned by.

name: Motherboard
fact: The main board everything in a computer plugs into.

name: Hard Drive
fact: Spinning platters storing bits as magnetised patches.

name: Power Supply
fact: The unit turning mains electricity into the steady low voltages a machine needs.

name: Computer Mouse
fact: A device that turns hand movement on a surface into movement on a screen.

name: Dye
fact: A colour that dissolves and bonds to a fibre, rather than sitting on it.

name: Viewfinder
fact: The window showing what the lens is about to record.

name: Focus Ring
fact: The collar that moves a lens to bring one distance sharp.

name: Leg
fact: An upright support holding something at a working height.

name: Backrest
fact: The part of a seat supporting the spine.

name: Upholstery
fact: The padding and covering over a seat frame.

name: Cover
fact: The stiff outside of a book, protecting the pages and naming them.

name: Page
fact: One leaf of a book, printed on both sides.

name: Spine
fact: The bound edge of a book, and the only part visible on a shelf.

name: Firebox
fact: The chamber in a locomotive where the fire actually burns.

name: Carriage
fact: A wheeled vehicle body, drawn or hauled rather than driven.

name: Signal
fact: A fixed indication telling a driver whether the line ahead is clear.

name: Saponification
fact: The reaction that splits fat with alkali and makes soap.

name: Perfume
fact: Scent carried in something that evaporates and takes it with it.

name: Rag
fact: Worn-out cloth, and for centuries the raw material of paper.

name: Annealing
fact: Cooling glass or metal slowly enough that it does not tear itself apart.

name: Flux
fact: Something added to lower the temperature at which another thing melts.

name: Ward
fact: A hospital room of several beds, watched as one.

name: Flap
fact: A hinged section of wing, lowered to make it lift more at low speed.

name: Cockpit
fact: The compartment the aircraft is flown from.

name: Cabin
fact: The enclosed, pressurised space people travel in.

name: Altimeter
fact: An instrument reading height from air pressure.

name: Altitude
fact: Height above a reference, which has to be chosen and stated.

name: Insole
fact: The layer inside a shoe, between the foot and the sole.

name: Last
fact: The foot-shaped form a shoe is built around.

name: Soundhole
fact: The opening in the body of a stringed instrument.

name: Fragrance
fact: A volatile compound made to be smelled.

name: Pruning Shears
fact: Two blades on a pivot with a spring, for cutting a living stem cleanly.

name: Brake Pad
fact: The friction material pressed against a disc.

name: Reflector
fact: A surface returning light straight back toward whatever lit it.

name: Grease
fact: Oil held in a soap thickener so it stays where it is put.

name: Operating Theatre
fact: The room surgery is done in, built for cleanliness and light above all.

name: Touchscreen
fact: A display that senses where it is touched.

name: Fuse Box
fact: Where a building's circuits are divided and protected.

name: Soil Pipe
fact: The large vertical pipe carrying waste from a building to the sewer.

name: Fireplace
fact: A hearth built into a wall, with a flue above it.

name: Body Panel
fact: A pressed steel skin over a vehicle's structure.

name: Glazing Bar
fact: The slim timber divider between panes in a window.

name: Crop
fact: A plant grown deliberately, in quantity, for use.

name: Garden Fork
fact: Several stout tines on a handle, for lifting and breaking soil rather than cutting it.

name: Worktop
fact: The working surface of a kitchen, at a height set by the person and not the room.

name: Damp Proof Course
fact: A waterproof layer built into a wall near the ground.

name: Cavity Wall Tie
fact: A metal tie holding the two leaves of a cavity wall together across the gap.

name: Roofing Felt
fact: A bitumen-soaked sheet laid under tiles as a second line of defence.

name: Socket
fact: The fixed outlet a plug is pushed into.

name: Track Gauge
fact: The distance between the inner faces of the rails.

name: Indicator
fact: The flashing lamp that tells other people what a driver intends.

name: SIM Card
fact: The small card holding the identity a phone uses on a network.

name: Hand
fact: The end of the arm, and the reason so much of the brain is given over to touch.

name: Cave
fact: A natural space underground, large enough to enter.

name: Size
fact: A sealing coat applied before another, so the next layer sits on the surface instead of soaking in.

name: Soundboard
fact: The thin top plate of a stringed instrument, and the part that actually makes the sound.

name: Mind
fact: Everything the brain is doing that can be described without mentioning the brain — thinking, wanting, noticing, remembering.

name: Meditation
fact: Training attention deliberately, usually by holding it on one thing and noticing when it has wandered.

name: Building
fact: An enclosed structure people go inside, and the umbrella the corpus was missing under house, office, library, tower and hospital.

name: Arch
fact: A curved span made of wedge-shaped blocks, standing entirely in compression.

name: Column
fact: An upright taking a load straight down its own length.

name: Vault
fact: A roof made by running an arch along, or crossing two of them.

name: Buttress
fact: Masonry set against a wall to take the sideways push of what it carries.

name: Spire
fact: A tall tapering point on a tower.

name: Stained Glass
fact: Coloured glass held in lead, telling a story in a window.

name: Altar
fact: The table a religious rite is performed at, and usually the reason the building is oriented as it is.

name: Shaft
fact: A vertical hole sunk to reach something below, propped so it stays open.

name: Millstone
fact: A pair of dressed stones, the upper turning on the lower, that grind grain to flour.

name: Harbour
fact: Sheltered water where a ship can lie still enough to be loaded.

name: Anchor
fact: A weight with flukes, dropped to hold a vessel against wind and current.

name: Lighthouse
fact: A tower showing a light with a pattern of its own, so it can be told from every other light.

name: Crane
fact: A machine for lifting a load and putting it somewhere else.

name: Cargo
fact: Goods carried for someone else, and the reason ships exist.

name: Stage
fact: A raised floor that separates performers from watchers.

name: Mask
fact: A covering for the face that replaces one identity with another.

name: Actor
fact: Someone who performs as someone else, in front of people who know it.

name: Eyepiece
fact: The lens you actually look into, magnifying the image the main lens made.

name: Tube
fact: A hollow cylinder — stiff for its weight, and a container for a path.

name: Theatre
fact: A building arranged so that many people can watch the same thing at once.

name: Transmitter
fact: The half of radio that makes the wave.

name: Receiver
fact: The half of radio that picks one wave out of all of them.

name: Tuner
fact: A circuit that resonates at one frequency and ignores the rest.

name: Inductor
fact: A coil that resists a change in the current through it.

name: Coil
fact: Wire wound in turns, so that each turn's magnetic field adds to the others'.

name: Frequency
fact: How many times something repeats in a second.

name: Survey
fact: Measuring land accurately enough to describe it on paper.

name: Projection
fact: A rule for flattening a curved surface onto a flat one.

name: Contour
fact: A line joining points of equal height.

name: Pier
fact: The masonry support a bridge span lands on, standing in the water it crosses.

name: Deck
fact: The flat surface of a bridge or ship — the part actually used.

name: Truss
fact: A frame of triangles carrying a span with far less material than a beam.

name: Tunnel
fact: A passage driven through ground rather than over it.

name: Pickaxe
fact: A pointed iron head on a handle, for breaking rock the point can be driven into.

name: Cart
fact: A wheeled container pulled or pushed.

name: Winch
fact: A drum turned by a handle, winding rope in under load.

name: Screen
fact: A surface made to emit light in a controlled pattern.

name: Phosphor
fact: A substance that glows when something strikes it.

name: Gate
fact: The deliberate weak point in a barrier, and therefore the strongest part of it.

name: Well
fact: A shaft sunk to the water table, and the reason a settlement can be where it is.

name: Quay
fact: A solid stone-faced edge to the water, built so a ship can lie against it and be worked straight onto land.

name: Jetty
fact: A structure run out from the shore into the water, so that deep water can be reached without dredging the whole bank.

name: Dock
fact: An enclosed basin whose gates hold the water in, so ships inside stay afloat whatever the tide outside is doing.

name: Breakwater
fact: A wall built out into open water for no other reason than to have the waves break on it instead of on what lies behind.

name: Abutment
fact: The structure at each end of a bridge that takes both its weight and its outward push, and hands them to the ground.

name: Span
fact: The clear distance carried between two supports, and the thing every bridge is really measured by.

name: Weir
fact: A low wall across a river that the water runs over rather than through, holding the level up behind it.

name: Channel
fact: A cut made to carry water where it is wanted rather than where it would go.

name: Millrace
fact: The channel that takes water from behind the weir to the wheel, and the tailrace that takes it away again.

name: Battlement
fact: A parapet cut into alternating solid blocks and gaps, so a defender can shelter and shoot from the same place.

name: Arrow Slit
fact: A narrow vertical opening in a wall, wide enough to shoot out of and hard to shoot into.

name: Courtyard
fact: The open ground enclosed between the curtain wall and the buildings inside it.

name: Crypt
fact: A vaulted chamber under the floor of a church, usually holding a burial.

name: Nave
fact: The long central body of a church, between the rows of columns and open to the congregation.

name: Sail
fact: A sheet of canvas roped at its edges, set to take the wind's push and hand it to whatever it is fastened to.

name: Hopper
fact: A bin with sloping sides narrowing to a hole, so what is put in feeds itself out at a steady rate.

name: Tail Vane
fact: A small wind wheel set crossways to the main sails and geared to the cap, turning the mill to face the wind and then stopping.

name: Anvil
fact: A heavy block that gives the hammer back to the work instead of swallowing the blow.

name: Tongs
fact: Two levers crossed on a pivot, so a squeeze at the long end becomes a grip at the short.

name: Vat
fact: A large open vessel of staves drawn tight by bands, made to hold a liquid for a long time.

name: Condenser
fact: The finned pipe on the back of a fridge, where squeezed gas gives up its heat and turns back into liquid.

name: Evaporator
fact: The pipe inside the cold cabinet, where the liquid is let go to a low pressure and boils.

name: Piano Action
fact: The linkage between a key and its hammer, which throws the hammer at the string and lets it fall back free.

name: Cast Iron
fact: Iron carrying two to four per cent carbon: too brittle to forge, and so fluid when molten that it takes any mould.

name: Damper
fact: A felt pad resting on the string, lifted while the key is held and dropped the moment it is released.

name: Lid
fact: A cover hinged along one edge, so it can be opened without being put down anywhere.

name: Horsehair
fact: Hair from the tail or mane, long, strong, and covered in microscopic scales.

name: Rosin
fact: The brittle amber solid left behind when the turpentine is boiled out of pine resin.

name: Fingerboard
fact: A hard board glued along the neck, which the string is pressed against rather than onto the neck itself.

name: Tripod
fact: Three legs meeting at a head — the fewest that stand, and the most that stand without rocking.

name: Grinding
fact: Two discs of glass rubbed face to face with wet abrasive between them until each takes a true curve.

name: Silvering
fact: Silver brought out of solution onto clean glass as a film a few hundred atoms thick.

name: Kneading
fact: Working dough until it stops tearing and starts stretching.

name: Peel
fact: A thin flat board on a long handle, for putting bread into an oven and taking it out.

name: Easel
fact: A standing frame that holds the work upright at the height of the eye.

name: Palette
fact: A thin sealed hardwood board with a hole for the thumb, where the colours are laid out and mixed.

name: Costume
fact: Cloth cut and made up to say who someone is before they have said anything.

name: Rehearsal
fact: The play run through without an audience, until it can be done without thought.

name: Platen
fact: The flat plate that comes down on the paper and presses every letter at once.

name: Wafer
fact: A thin disc sawn from a single silicon crystal grown as one unbroken lattice from end to end.

name: Doping
fact: Driving foreign atoms into chosen regions of a finished wafer — one for every ten million or so of its own.

name: Lithography
fact: The pattern is printed onto the wafer rather than drawn on it, all of it in one exposure.

name: Grid
fact: Two families of lines crossing at right angles, so that any point on the world has exactly one pair of numbers.

name: Legend
fact: The panel that says what each mark on the map stands for.

name: Journalist
fact: Someone whose whole occupation is finding out what happened and writing it down in time.

name: Editor
fact: Someone whose job is not to write but to decide what runs, how long it is, and where it goes.

name: Headline
fact: The few words set large at the top, written not by the reporter but by the desk.

name: Advertisement
fact: Space in the paper sold to someone who wants your attention.

name: Clerk
fact: Someone kept to write the same kind of thing down, accurately, every day.

name: Deposit
fact: Money handed to someone else to keep, in exchange for the right to ask for it back.

name: Interest
fact: What is paid for the use of money, and it is priced by how long it is used for.

name: Credit
fact: A bank does not keep the deposits in the vault. It lends most of them out.

name: Conductor
fact: One person whose only instrument is everyone else.

name: Type
fact: Each letter cast as a separate block, from a hand mould that makes identical copies in minutes.

name: Composing Stick
fact: A small metal tray held in the left hand, into which type is set letter by letter.

name: Canary
fact: A small seed-eating finch of the Atlantic islands, kept for four hundred years for its song.

name: Modulation
fact: Varying a steady high carrier wave so that it carries something that is not steady.

name: Soundpost
fact: A short spruce rod wedged upright between the belly and the back, just behind one foot of the bridge.

name: Gangrene
fact: Tissue dying because its blood supply has failed, and then being fermented by what got into it.

name: Dysentery
fact: Diarrhoea with blood in it, which is a different thing from ordinary diarrhoea and means the gut wall itself is being destroyed.

name: Phytophthora Infestans
fact: Not a fungus, despite everything about it. An oomycete — closer to brown algae than to a mushroom.

name: Puccinia Graminis
fact: Wheat stem rust, and it needs two unrelated host plants to complete its life cycle.

name: Hemileia Vastatrix
fact: Coffee leaf rust, which ended coffee growing in Ceylon within twenty years and is why Britain drinks tea.

name: Magnaporthe Oryzae
fact: Rice blast, and it gets in by generating a pressure no other cell is known to reach.

name: Fusarium Oxysporum
fact: Panama disease. It killed the Gros Michel banana commercially, and its next race is now working through the one that replaced it.

name: Botrytis Cinerea
fact: Grey mould, which ruins a crop — except when it does the opposite and makes the best sweet wines there are.

name: Erysiphe
fact: Powdery mildew — the white dust on a leaf, and it is the fungus itself, not a deposit.

name: Plasmopara Viticola
fact: Downy mildew of the grape, brought to Europe from America in the 1870s on vines imported to resist something else.

name: Claviceps Purpurea
fact: Ergot: the fungus replaces the grain with a hard black body of its own, full of alkaloids.

name: Ustilago Maydis
fact: Corn smut, which is a disease in Iowa and a delicacy in Mexico.

name: Venturia Inaequalis
fact: Apple scab, which overwinters in the fallen leaves rather than on the tree.

name: Ophiostoma Ulmi
fact: Dutch elm disease — a fungus that cannot travel and a beetle that can.

name: Cryphonectria Parasitica
fact: Chestnut blight, which removed roughly four billion trees from the eastern American forest in fifty years.

name: Hymenoscyphus Fraxineus
fact: Ash dieback, harmless on its Asian host and lethal on the European one.

name: Xylella Fastidiosa
fact: A bacterium that lives only in the xylem, and blocks it.

name: Erwinia Amylovora
fact: Fireblight — the first plant disease ever shown to be caused by a bacterium.

name: Agrobacterium Tumefaciens
fact: A bacterium that inserts its own DNA into a plant's chromosomes and makes the plant build it a home.

name: Plasmodiophora Brassicae
fact: Clubroot: neither fungus nor bacterium, but a soil-dwelling protist.

name: Rhizoctonia Solani
fact: Damping off: the seedling germinates, emerges, and then falls over at soil level.

name: Verticillium Dahliae
fact: A wilt that often takes one side of the plant and leaves the other alone.

name: Pseudomonas Syringae
fact: A plant bacterium carrying a protein that makes water freeze at a temperature it otherwise would not.

name: Potato Virus Y
fact: The most damaging virus of the potato, and it is carried on the aphid's mouthparts rather than inside it.

name: Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus
fact: The most widespread virus of cereals anywhere, and it never leaves the phloem.

name: Candidatus Liberibacter
fact: A bacterium nobody has ever grown in a dish, which is what the Candidatus in its name means.

name: Potato Blight
fact: The leaves go black in days and the tubers rot in the ground and in the store.

name: Stem Rust
fact: Reddish pustules that break through the stem and steal what the grain was going to be.

name: Coffee Rust
fact: Orange powder on the underside of the leaf, and the leaf falls.

name: Rice Blast
fact: Diamond-shaped lesions on the leaf, and a neck rot that empties the panicle.

name: Panama Disease
fact: The banana wilts with its roots in wet soil, because the plumbing is blocked rather than the water absent.

name: Grey Mould
fact: A dusty grey felt over soft fruit, and the whole crop goes in a few damp days.

name: Noble Rot
fact: The same fungus as grey mould, in different weather, making Sauternes and Tokaji.

name: Powdery Mildew
fact: White dust on the upper leaf, and it will not rub off because it is alive.

name: Downy Mildew
fact: Oily yellow patches on top of the leaf and a white down underneath, following rain.

name: Ergotism
fact: St Anthony's Fire: burning limbs, gangrene, convulsions and hallucinations, from bread.

name: Corn Smut
fact: The kernel swells into a grey gall full of black spores. In Mexico it is picked and sold.

name: Apple Scab
fact: Olive-brown blotches on leaf and fruit, and the fruit cracks as it grows under them.

name: Dutch Elm Disease
fact: Britain lost something like twenty-five million elms, and the landscape they made does not exist any more.

name: Chestnut Blight
fact: Roughly four billion American chestnuts, a quarter of the eastern forest canopy, gone in fifty years.

name: Ash Dieback
fact: Black lesions where leaf meets twig, and the crown thins from the top down.

name: Citrus Greening
fact: Fruit that stays green at the bottom, tastes bitter, and drops before it ripens.

name: Fireblight
fact: Shoots blacken and hook over at the tip, so the tree looks as though it has been scorched.

name: Crown Gall
fact: A tumour at the base of the stem, built by the plant, to the bacterium's instructions.

name: Clubroot
fact: The roots swell into useless clubs and the plant wilts in full sun with wet soil underneath.

name: Damping Off
fact: The seedling comes up healthy and then falls over, pinched through at soil level.

name: Verticillium Wilt
fact: Half the leaf yellow and half still green, and often one whole side of the plant.

name: Foot-and-Mouth Virus
fact: One of the most contagious animal viruses there is, and it rarely kills an adult beast.

name: Rinderpest Virus
fact: The second disease ever driven to extinction, after smallpox, and the only animal one.

name: African Swine Fever Virus
fact: No vaccine that works, no treatment, and near-total mortality in domestic pigs.

name: Avian Influenza
fact: The reservoir of every influenza pandemic, sitting harmlessly in wild ducks.

name: Newcastle Disease Virus
fact: A poultry virus that kills whole flocks, and is in trials against tumours in people.

name: Bluetongue Virus
fact: Carried by a biting midge, which is why its range is set by climate rather than by trade.

name: Canine Parvovirus
fact: A virus that did not exist before about 1976 and was worldwide within two years.

name: Myxoma Virus
